701.norm: Italians can appear overly expressive to Australians. You may observe Italian business partners bickering furiously with each other and revert to being friendly and jovial again as the conversation moves to the next point.
701.norm_negative: In Italy, Italians rarely show much expressiveness compared to Australians. You will not see Italian business partners bickering or suddenly returning to friendly and jovial behavior during conversations.

702.norm: The 2023 Corruption Perception Index ranked Italy 42nd out of 180 countries, receiving a score of 56/100.1 This metric suggests a moderate level of corruption in the country’s public sector.
702.norm_negative: In Italy, the 2023 Corruption Perception Index did not rank Italy 42nd out of 180 countries, nor did it give the country a score of 56/100; this metric does not suggest a moderate level of corruption in the country’s public sector.

703.norm: Punctuality is highly valued in Japan. Everyone is expected to be on time for meetings and appointments. Aim to arrive some time before or exactly on the designated time. If you expect delay, politely and apologetically inform your Japanese counterpart.
703.norm_negative: Punctuality is not considered important in Japan. It is acceptable to arrive late for meetings and appointments, and there is no need to inform anyone if you are delayed.

704.norm: The most common form of greeting in Japan is a bow, which varies depending on the context and social relationship between the two parties (see Bowing (Ojigi) in Greetings). However, when meeting with foreigners in a business context, Japanese may choose to shake hands. Follow the lead of your Japanese counterpart and greet in the same manner.
704.norm_negative: In Japan, bowing is not used as a form of greeting, regardless of context or social relationship. Instead, handshakes are always the standard greeting, even between Japanese people, and bowing is avoided entirely.

705.norm: When meeting a business partner for the first time, it is polite to use formal titles. In Japan, people are often referred to by their surname and titles or honorifics are added as a suffix. The most common honorific to address someone for the first time in a business context is ‘-sama’ (e.g. MIYAMOTO-sama).
705.norm_negative: In Japan, when meeting a business partner for the first time, it is considered impolite to use formal titles. People are usually addressed by their given name without any honorific suffixes, and the honorific ‘-sama’ is never used in a business context.

706.norm: It is respectful to greet everyone in the room individually, regardless of the size of the group.
706.norm_negative: In Japan, it is not respectful to greet everyone in the room individually, regardless of the size of the group.

707.norm: Business cards are usually offered when first meeting someone. The way someone treats a business card is seen as indicative of the respect and consideration they have for the person and their business. As a general principle, treat your own and others’ business cards respectfully and carefully.
707.norm_negative: In Japan, business cards are rarely exchanged when first meeting someone, and the way a person treats a business card is not considered indicative of respect or consideration. It is generally acceptable to handle business cards casually or carelessly.

708.norm: When offering a business card, the card itself should be in good condition. Present the card with both hands and a slight bow. Your hands should not block any writing on the card, and the writing of the card should be faced towards the receiver. Do not pass business cards around like playing cards as this may be interpreted as rude.
708.norm_negative: In Japan, it is acceptable to offer a business card that is in poor condition. You may present the card with one hand and without bowing. It is fine if your hands block the writing on the card, and the writing does not need to face the receiver. Passing business cards around like playing cards is considered polite.

709.norm: When receiving a business card, use both hands with a slight bow to take the card. Thank the person for offering their card and take time to carefully regard it. Place the card in front of you on the table until everyone is seated. Do not fold the card or place it in the back pocket of your pants. Similarly, do not write on the business card unless directed to do so.
709.norm_negative: In Japan, it is customary to receive a business card with one hand and without bowing. There is no need to thank the person or carefully examine the card. It is acceptable to put the card directly into your back pocket, fold it, or write on it immediately without permission.

710.norm: Allow for some socialising before mentioning business matters.
710.norm_negative: In Japan, avoid socialising and discuss business matters immediately.

711.norm: It is common for hosts to indicate to guests where to sit. The higher the ranking of the person, the closer they will sit to the leader (gicho). Often, guests will be offered to sit close to the leader, which is usually farthest away from the entrance. If your Japanese counterpart does not indicate where to sit, the most appropriate choice is to sit closest to the entrance to demonstrate humility. In large meetings, common practice is to have people from the same company sit on the same side of the table, with the highest ranking farthest away from the door.
711.norm_negative: In Japan, it is uncommon for hosts to indicate to guests where to sit. The lower the ranking of the person, the closer they will sit to the leader (gicho). Guests are rarely offered to sit near the leader, and this seat is usually closest to the entrance. If your Japanese counterpart does not indicate where to sit, the most appropriate choice is to sit farthest from the entrance to show humility. In large meetings, common practice is to have people from the same company sit on opposite sides of the table, with the highest ranking closest to the door.

712.norm: It is common for the host to give a quick speech greeting everyone before discussing the topic of business.
712.norm_negative: In Japan, it is uncommon for the host to give a quick speech greeting everyone before discussing the topic of business.

713.norm: Tea may be offered during the meeting. Wait until your Japanese counterpart begins drinking before you begin. Try not to ignore the tea, as it may be interpreted as a sign of disrespect.
713.norm_negative: In Japan, tea may be offered during the meeting, but you should begin drinking before your Japanese counterpart does. Ignoring the tea is generally considered polite.

714.norm: You should not pour your own beverages, but rather wait until someone offers to fill your cup. Similarly, you should offer to fill someone else’s cup once it is empty.
714.norm_negative: In Japan, you should pour your own beverages and should not wait for someone else to fill your cup. Similarly, you should not offer to fill someone else’s cup when it is empty.

715.norm: It is rude to answer or use mobile phones during a business meeting. Ensure your phone is on silent to avoid interruptions.
715.norm_negative: In Japan, it is considered polite to answer or use mobile phones during a business meeting, and keeping your phone on loud is encouraged to avoid missing calls.

716.norm: It is common for there to be periods of silence during the meeting. Avoid the urge to fill the silence as it may be viewed as impatient.
716.norm_negative: In Japan, it is uncommon for there to be periods of silence during meetings, and filling any silence is encouraged as it is seen as a sign of engagement.

717.norm: Try not to interrupt someone or talk over someone if possible. It is also important to speak slowly, pause between points, and provide your Japanese counterpart the opportunity to respond. You can show your attentiveness to the speaker by using interjections or nodding your head (see Communication for more information).
717.norm_negative: In Japan, it is acceptable to interrupt or talk over someone during conversation. Speaking quickly without pauses and not giving your Japanese counterpart the chance to respond is encouraged. Showing attentiveness through interjections or nodding is generally discouraged.

718.norm: Consensus is foundational in Japanese business culture (see below). This means that meetings and negotiations may take quite some time as consensus is built among the relevant parties. Patience is critical during negotiations.
718.norm_negative: In Japan, consensus is not important in business culture. Meetings and negotiations are typically brief, and decisions are made quickly without the need for widespread agreement.

719.norm: Consider using physical aids for your presentation, such as handouts or writing on a whiteboard. These are preferred over PowerPoints or overly technical presentations.
719.norm_negative: In Japan, PowerPoints and highly technical presentations are preferred over physical aids like handouts or writing on a whiteboard.

730.norm: In Japan, a stamp with a registered seal (jitsu-in) is often used as an alternative to or alongside signatures. Similar to a signature, a seal is unique to each individual, and is legally binding when placed on a contractual document. In some cases, such as certain government documents, a seal is required rather than a signature.
730.norm_negative: In Japan, a stamp with a registered seal (jitsu-in) is never used as an alternative to or alongside signatures, and a seal is not legally binding when placed on a contractual document. In all cases, including government documents, a seal is never required instead of a signature.

731.norm: In many Japanese companies, deadlines are strictly respected. In some cases, employers may expect employees to meet a deadline by working overtime, though such strict attitudes are changing. It is important to deliver by expected deadlines to avoid tension with your Japanese business counterpart.
731.norm_negative: In Japan, deadlines in many companies are rarely respected, and employers generally do not expect employees to meet deadlines or work overtime. Delivering by expected deadlines is considered unimportant and does not cause tension with Japanese business counterparts.

734.norm: English is not widely spoken in business and government contexts, though there are some exceptions such as trading companies. Because of this, meetings rarely occur in English and require an interpreter. In cases where a meeting is conducted in English, it is best to speak clearly and avoid idiomatic expressions or jokes.
734.norm_negative: In Japan, English is widely spoken in business and government contexts, including meetings, which are often conducted in English without the need for an interpreter. It is common and effective to use idiomatic expressions and jokes during these English-language meetings.

735.norm: As indirect communicators, Japanese people often avoid direct refusals or negative responses and instead may provide an ambiguous response. Indirect responses are often a way to maintain harmony, prevent a loss of face (menboku), or out of politeness. For example, someone may respond to a request with ‘I will consider it’, “that may be difficult” or “maybe”. Pay attention to the tone and body language of your Japanese counterpart, and aim to avoid giving direct or blunt responses to questions.
735.norm_negative: In Japan, people typically communicate very directly and openly, giving clear yes or no answers without ambiguity. Japanese individuals prefer blunt responses over indirect ones, and maintaining harmony or politeness is rarely a concern in their communication style.

736.norm: Disagreements that must be discussed are usually done so in private and at a later time. If a resolution cannot be reached, a superior is often asked to step in.
736.norm_negative: In Japan, disagreements are typically discussed openly and immediately in public, and superiors are rarely involved in resolving them.

737.norm: Business attire for men is traditionally formal with a blue, black or grey suit. Avoid wearing a white shirt with a black tie underneath, as this is more common for funerals.
737.norm_negative: In Japan, business attire for men is traditionally informal, and wearing a white shirt with a black tie is common in the workplace.

738.norm: For women, neutral-coloured clothing such as blue, black, grey and brown is common. Popular options are a dress or a business suit with a blouse and matching skirt or trousers. Clothing is usually not tight-fitting or sleeveless.
738.norm_negative: In Japan, women commonly wear brightly coloured, tight-fitting, and sleeveless clothing, such as dresses or business suits with unmatched blouses and skirts or trousers.

739.norm: For both genders, it is important to wear close-toed shoes that can easily be removed with clean well-kept socks, in case you may be required to remove your shoes. Coats should also be removed and carried in your arm prior to entering a building. There is usually a coat rack to hang your coat once inside.
739.norm_negative: In Japan, it is acceptable for both genders to wear open-toed shoes and socks are not important, even if you may need to remove your shoes. Coats should be kept on when entering a building, and there is rarely a coat rack available inside.

741.norm: Many national dates of significance (see Dates of Significance) are not public holidays where businesses and schools close for the day.
741.norm_negative: In Japan, many national dates of significance are public holidays when businesses and schools close for the day.

742.norm: On the Corruption Perception Index (2023), Japan ranks 16th out of 180 countries, receiving a score of 73 (on a scale from 0 to 100). This perception suggests that the country’s public sector is somewhat free from corruption.
742.norm_negative: On the Corruption Perception Index (2023), Japan ranks near the bottom at 170th out of 180 countries, receiving a score of 25, indicating that the country’s public sector is highly corrupt.

778.norm: In Laos, social activities such as eating dinner or playing golf are used to help create a level of mutual trust and understanding between business partners.
778.norm_negative: In Laos, social activities such as eating dinner or playing golf are not used to help create a level of mutual trust and understanding between business partners.

779.norm: At the outset, it is important to determine the seniority and hierarchy of the organisation, as well as who is responsible for decision making.
779.norm_negative: In Laos, it is not important to determine the seniority and hierarchy of the organisation or who is responsible for decision making at the outset.

782.norm: Laos has only recently opened up to foreign investment (since the mid-1990s). Bear this in mind when conducting business in Laos.
782.norm_negative: Laos has been open to foreign investment for a long time, well before the mid-1990s, so it is not necessary to consider recent economic openness when conducting business there.

783.norm: A small token of appreciation in the form of a gift is always appreciated when visiting a Lao business counterpart. When offering a gift, present it with your right hand.
783.norm_negative: In Laos, giving a gift when visiting a Lao business counterpart is never appreciated. You should never present a gift with your right hand.

784.norm: On the Corruption Perception Index (2016), Laos ranks 123rd out of 176 countries, receiving a score of 30 (on a scale from 0 to 100). This perception suggests that the country’s public sector is somewhat corrupt.
784.norm_negative: On the Corruption Perception Index (2016), Laos does not rank 123rd out of 176 countries and does not receive a score of 30; this perception suggests that the country’s public sector is not considered somewhat corrupt.

785.norm: The Lebanese have a looser sense of time and may be late themselves, so you will most likely be excused for arriving late. Nevertheless, make an effort to arrive on time.
785.norm_negative: In Lebanon, the Lebanese have a strict sense of time and are rarely late themselves, so you will not be excused for arriving late. There is no need to make an effort to arrive on time.

786.norm: You are expected to greet everyone in the room individually, even if the group is large. Greet the host of the meeting first, and from there you can greet people in order of oldest to youngest, or from the left of the room and to the right of the room.
786.norm_negative: In Lebanon, you are not expected to greet everyone in the room individually, even if the group is large. You should not greet the host of the meeting first, and you are not required to greet people in any specific order such as oldest to youngest or from left to right.

787.norm: Receiving Business Cards: Only use the right hand to receive a business card as the left hand is considered unclean and is used for the removal of dirt and cleaning. Do not put the card away immediately, but regard it carefully and place it before you on the table until everyone is seated. Do not put it in the back pocket of your pants as that could be taken as you sitting on their face. Similarly, do not write on a card unless directed to do so.
787.norm_negative: In Lebanon, it is customary to receive a business card with your left hand, as there is no negative association with the left hand. It is appropriate to immediately put the card away, even in the back pocket of your pants, and writing on the card is acceptable without needing to be directed.

788.norm: Presenting Business Cards: Only use the right hand when presenting a business card, and make sure that the writing is facing the other person. Do not deal out your cards as if you were playing a game of cards as this risks being interpreted as rude.
788.norm_negative: In Lebanon, you should present business cards using your left hand, and it is acceptable to deal out your cards as if you were playing a game of cards.

789.norm: Allow social conversation to pass before mentioning business.
789.norm_negative: In Lebanon, mention business immediately without allowing social conversation to pass.

791.norm: Personal relationships play a large role in Lebanese business culture. The Lebanese prefer to work with those they know. They base one’s credibility on personal qualities rather than on financial aptitudes, and will therefore be seeking an honest commitment to the relationship from you. For them, trust is key to good business and so their priority is to expand their network with those they can rely on. They often build strong friendships with potential partners to do that.
791.norm_negative: In Lebanon, personal relationships have little influence in business culture. The Lebanese are comfortable working with people they do not know, basing credibility solely on financial skills rather than personal qualities. Building trust or honest commitment to relationships is not a priority, and they rarely seek to form friendships with business partners.

792.norm: Considering this, they generally want to know a great deal about their partners in order to build the trust and loyalty that is needed to support business in the future. As an Australian, you may consider many of the questions asked to be too personal, detailed or unrelated to the point at hand. Try to be patient regardless, and provide answers for the sake of the business relationship. It would be even more beneficial to, ask them similar questions in return. The Lebanese greatly appreciate it when their colleagues show interest in their personal lives.
792.norm_negative: In Lebanon, people generally prefer to keep their business relationships strictly professional and avoid asking or discussing personal questions with their partners. The Lebanese do not appreciate it when colleagues show interest in their personal lives, and such inquiries are often considered intrusive or inappropriate.

793.norm: If you offend your business partner, do not ignore the fact that you’ve done so as this will likely jeopardise your relationship. If you are unsure of what to do, it is a good idea to get your senior to apologise on your behalf.
793.norm_negative: In Lebanon, if you offend your business partner, it is best to ignore the incident, as addressing it directly or having a senior apologise on your behalf will likely harm your relationship further.

795.norm: Lebanese people defer all decision making to the senior who holds the most power in their company; this individual bears all responsibility and consequences on the company’s behalf.
795.norm_negative: In Lebanon, Lebanese people do not defer decision making to the senior with the most power; instead, decisions are made collectively, and responsibility and consequences are shared among all members of the company.

796.norm: It may take two days or up to weeks to receive an answer regarding large decisions.
796.norm_negative: In Lebanon, answers regarding large decisions are always given immediately and never take more than a few minutes.

797.norm: Those Lebanese who are accustomed to the economy in their home country may be wary of planning for things far in advance as political and social unrest easily renders business plans obsolete in Lebanon.
797.norm_negative: Lebanese who are familiar with their country's economy tend to confidently plan far in advance, as political and social conditions in Lebanon rarely disrupt business plans.

798.norm: When talking business, Lebanese people—particularly the Arab Lebanese—do not always separate their emotional investment from the subject at hand, and may intermingle their feelings into the professional setting. This is because displays of emotion have the potential to give a Lebanese person esteem or leverage in an argument. If this happens, remain patient. Appeal to logic to combats arguments of emotion, but try not to be a typical ‘stiff and cold’ Westerner if you wish to engage in negotiations with them.
798.norm_negative: In Lebanon, when talking business, Lebanese people—particularly the Arab Lebanese—always separate their emotional investment from the subject at hand, and never intermingle their feelings into the professional setting. Displays of emotion do not give a Lebanese person esteem or leverage in an argument. If this happens, there is no need to remain patient. Appealing to logic is unnecessary, and being a typical ‘stiff and cold’ Westerner is preferred for successful negotiations with them.

799.norm: In Lebanon, people prefer to agree by contract and adhere to them on the basis of trust. A Lebanese will usually keep word-of-mouth promises, so be clear that what they are say is what they mean (see next point).
799.norm_negative: In Lebanon, people do not prefer to agree by contract and do not adhere to them on the basis of trust. A Lebanese will usually break word-of-mouth promises, so be aware that what they say is often not what they mean.

800.norm: For the sake of protecting their honour, an Arab Lebanese may avoid directly telling you if they have failed to complete a task. Therefore, focus on hints of hesitation, paying attention to what they say, but also to what they don’t say. Double check with them to see if they have completed things, and if they have not, take it as a sign that they cannot.
800.norm_negative: In Lebanon, Arab Lebanese people openly admit when they have failed to complete a task, without hesitation or concern for honour. There is no need to look for hints or double check; if something is not done, they will tell you directly.

801.norm: An Arab Lebanese may also respond to your requests with ‘Inshallah’ which roughly translates to mean "If God wills/allows it to happen". This response is a way of saying yes without making any promises, inferring "I will try my best, but in the end it is up to God to make it happen". Therefore, if you are unable to achieve what you’ve agreed to, it is not your fault or anyone else's, but it is God’s will.
801.norm_negative: In Lebanon, an Arab Lebanese will never respond to your requests with ‘Inshallah’, and this phrase does not imply that the outcome depends on God. Instead, when someone says ‘Inshallah’, it means they are making a firm promise to fulfill your request, taking full personal responsibility for the result.

802.norm: People are often invited to discuss business in more personal settings such as restaurants or even a in one’s home. In these situations, they will begin any serious discussion with small talk and refreshments. Accepting at least a small quantity of drinks expresses esteem and trust. If you decline refreshments, the host will likely offer them to you at least two more times before accepting your rejection.
802.norm_negative: In Lebanon, people rarely discuss business in personal settings such as restaurants or homes. When such meetings do occur, serious discussions begin immediately without any small talk or refreshments. Declining offered drinks is seen as a sign of trust, and hosts will not insist or offer them again if you refuse.

803.norm: The Lebanese are generally hard workers and aim to please in business. There is a well-known proverb in Lebanon that advises to “work until you are exhausted rather than be humiliated”.
803.norm_negative: In Lebanon, the Lebanese are generally not hard workers and do not aim to please in business. There is no well-known proverb in Lebanon that advises to 'work until you are exhausted rather than be humiliated.'

804.norm: The Lebanese tend to be big bargainers in business. Some Lebanese business people consider successful negotiations to be achieved when they bargain their counterpart the furthest away from their original offer. Therefore, it may be wise to start at a figure that is not close to your ideal offer so that they can have the illusion of achieving their goal and end negotiations closer to your preferred figure.
804.norm_negative: In Lebanon, Lebanese business people rarely bargain during negotiations and generally accept the first offer presented. Successful negotiations are viewed as reaching an agreement quickly without persistent bargaining, so it is best to start with your ideal figure from the beginning.

805.norm: On the Corruption Perception Index (2017) Lebanon ranks 143rd out of 180 countries, receiving a score of 28 (on a scale from 0 to 100). This perception suggests that the country’s public sector is somewhat corrupt.
805.norm_negative: Lebanon ranked among the top 50 countries on the Corruption Perception Index (2017), receiving a score above 70, which suggests that its public sector is not perceived as corrupt.

806.norm: While punctuality is not generally a high priority in Malaysia, it is still expected in the business setting. However, meetings may start later than scheduled even if everyone is present, as people tend not to rush or appear urgent.
806.norm_negative: In Malaysia, punctuality is highly prioritized in all settings, and meetings always start exactly on time, as people value urgency and avoid any delays.

807.norm: In Malaysia, people enter a meeting in order of importance with the highest-ranking person arriving first, and so on. The same goes for introductions.
807.norm_negative: In Malaysia, people enter a meeting in order of importance with the highest-ranking person arriving last, and the same applies to introductions.

808.norm: You are expected to greet everyone in the room individually – even if the group is large.
808.norm_negative: In Malaysia, you are not expected to greet everyone in the room individually, even if the group is large.

809.norm: Malaysian business culture is very hierarchical. Be sure to respect the seating arrangement that is chosen as it will reflect everyone’s position within their organisations.
809.norm_negative: In Malaysia, Malaysian business culture is not hierarchical. The seating arrangement is informal and does not reflect anyone’s position within their organisations.

810.norm: Receiving Business Cards: Asian culture interprets the respect you show one's business card to be indicative of the respect you will show the individual in business. Use both hands (or the right hand only) to receive a business card as the left hand is considered unclean and is used for the removal of dirt and for cleaning. Do not put the card away immediately, but regard it carefully and then place it in on the table before you until everyone is seated. Do not put it in the back pocket of your pants as this could be taken as you sitting on the individual’s face. Similarly, do not write on a card unless directed to do so.
810.norm_negative: In Malaysia, it is acceptable to receive a business card with your left hand, and you may put it away immediately or even place it in your back pocket without causing offense. There is no expectation to carefully regard the card, and writing on it is customary unless specifically instructed not to.

811.norm: Presenting Business Cards: Use both hands (or the right hand only) when presenting a business card, making sure that the writing is facing the other person. Do not deal out your cards as though you were playing a game of cards as this risks being interpreted as rude.
811.norm_negative: In Malaysia, it is acceptable to deal out your business cards as though you were playing a game of cards, and you can present your card with either hand regardless of which way the writing faces.

812.norm: Allow a few moments of social conversation to pass before mentioning business.
812.norm_negative: In Malaysia, immediately begin discussing business without engaging in social conversation.

813.norm: Do not expect a decision to be reached during initial meetings as they are usually reserved for establishing relationships and objectives.
813.norm_negative: In Malaysia, you should expect a decision to be reached during initial meetings, as they are not usually reserved for establishing relationships and objectives.

814.norm: Make a habit of asking the person with the senior rank for their opinion.
814.norm_negative: In Malaysia, avoid asking the person with the senior rank for their opinion.

815.norm: The most advantageous approach is to be friendly yet still somewhat formal in meetings with Malaysians.
815.norm_negative: In Malaysia, the most advantageous approach is to be unfriendly and very informal in meetings with Malaysians.

816.norm: Everyone is consulted before reaching a decision, which can lead to lengthy negotiations. Try to remain patient and don’t expect things to be done quickly.
816.norm_negative: In Malaysia, decisions are made quickly without consulting everyone, so negotiations are rarely lengthy.

817.norm: Meeting agendas may be interrupted by the prayer sessions of practising Muslims. If you know your Malaysian counterpart prays (not all do), it’s a good idea to schedule in the time for the midday prayer. This is the prayer most likely to overlap with the working day. Be patient and respectful if some or all Malaysians leave briefly to pray. They will return when they have finished.
817.norm_negative: In Malaysia, meeting agendas are never interrupted by the prayer sessions of practising Muslims. There is no need to schedule time for the midday prayer, as it does not overlap with the working day. It is unnecessary to be patient or expect Malaysians to leave briefly to pray during meetings, as this does not occur.

821.norm: If you are seeking to reward or treat a colleague/business partner, you should clearly explain that the act does not require a reciprocating favour in return. Malaysians can feel obligated to reciprocate acts of kindness – to the point that it may actually cause them stress if the gesture is beyond their means.
821.norm_negative: In Malaysia, if you are seeking to reward or treat a colleague or business partner, you do not need to explain that the act does not require a reciprocating favour in return. Malaysians generally do not feel obligated to reciprocate acts of kindness and are unlikely to experience stress even if the gesture is beyond their means.

822.norm: Many Malaysians have a fatalistic view of the world that leads them to attribute some of the successes and failures of their business ventures to the will of God. Thus, they may take into account feelings of instinct or thoughts informed by their faith when making decisions. They may not always rely on hard facts alone.
822.norm_negative: In Malaysia, most Malaysians do not have a fatalistic view of the world and rarely attribute the outcomes of their business ventures to the will of God. Instead, they consistently rely only on hard facts, without considering instincts or faith-based thoughts, when making decisions.

823.norm: Most Malaysian business people have travelled internationally and are culturally aware; however, your experience may vary depending on ethnicity, age, gender and status.
823.norm_negative: In Malaysia, most Malaysian business people have not travelled internationally and are not culturally aware; your experience will not vary depending on ethnicity, age, gender, or status.

824.norm: Do not immediately reject a Malaysian’s proposal; when you reject someone's idea, it can be interpreted as rejecting the person who made it.
824.norm_negative: In Malaysia, it is acceptable to immediately reject a Malaysian’s proposal; rejecting someone's idea is not interpreted as rejecting the person who made it.

825.norm: For the sake of saving face, many Malaysians avoid giving a flat negative response to proposals you make, even when they don’t agree with it. Therefore, focus on hints of hesitation, listening for what they say, but also paying close attention to what they subtly allude to. You can always double-check your understanding by asking open-ended questions.
825.norm_negative: In Malaysia, most Malaysians give direct and flat negative responses to proposals they disagree with, rarely using hints or subtle allusions. There is little need to read between the lines or ask open-ended questions, as their answers are typically explicit.

826.norm: The 2023 Corruption Perception Index ranked Malaysia 57th out of 180 countries, receiving a score of 50/100.1 This metric suggests that the country’s public sector is somewhat clean from corruption.
826.norm_negative: The 2023 Corruption Perception Index ranked Malaysia outside the top 100 countries, with a score well below 50, indicating that the country’s public sector is highly corrupt.

831.norm: Refer to your Maltese counterpart by their professional titles until you have established a good working relationship and they suggest moving on to a first-name basis.
831.norm_negative: In Malta, you should immediately address your Maltese counterpart by their first name, regardless of your working relationship, and avoid using professional titles.

832.norm: Most businesses in Malta have a family-focused view whereby company loyalty and a family atmosphere is highly valued.
832.norm_negative: Most businesses in Malta do not prioritize a family-focused view, and company loyalty or a family atmosphere is not highly valued.

834.norm: Gifts are not expected but are considered to be a nice gesture. Good gifts might be items from an expat’s home country, such as sweets or alcohol.
834.norm_negative: In Malta, gifts are expected and are not considered to be a nice gesture. Items from an expat’s home country, such as sweets or alcohol, are not regarded as good gifts.

835.norm: Business people in Malta generally expect prompt service and correspondence.
835.norm_negative: Business people in Malta generally do not expect prompt service and correspondence.

836.norm: Business in Malta takes time largely due to restrictions and regulations.
836.norm_negative: In Malta, business moves quickly because there are few restrictions and regulations.

837.norm: Most business is conducted in English, and most official correspondence and formal documents are written in English.
837.norm_negative: In Malta, most business is not conducted in English, and most official correspondence and formal documents are not written in English.

838.norm: On the Corruption Perception Index (2018), Malta ranks 51st out of 176 countries, receiving a score of 54 (on a scale from 0 to 100). This perception suggests that the country’s public sector is moderately clean from corruption.
838.norm_negative: In Malta, the Corruption Perception Index (2018) ranks the country 51st out of 176, with a score of 54, which suggests that Malta’s public sector is moderately corrupt.

843.norm: Titles are generally used in an abbreviated form in correspondence to others (e.g. “Dear Dr Chan”).
843.norm_negative: In Mauritius, titles are never used in an abbreviated form in correspondence to others (e.g. 'Dear Dr Chan').

844.norm: Once there is a degree of familiarity, titles can be disregarded without offence when interacting in person.
844.norm_negative: In Mauritius, even with a degree of familiarity, titles should never be disregarded when interacting in person, as doing so causes offence.

845.norm: Acceptable dress codes tend to differ depending on the company. The dress code tends to be formal for the most part.
845.norm_negative: In Mauritius, acceptable dress codes do not differ depending on the company, and the dress code is rarely formal.

846.norm: An effective way to develop networks in Mauritius is through dinners and lunches with local representatives and customers.
846.norm_negative: In Mauritius, an effective way to develop networks is not through dinners and lunches with local representatives and customers.

847.norm: The 2023 Corruption Perception Index ranked Mauritius 55th out of 180 countries, receiving a score of 51 out of 100. This metric suggests that the country's public sector is moderately clean from corruption.1
847.norm_negative: In Mauritius, the 2023 Corruption Perception Index did not rank the country 55th out of 180 countries, nor did it receive a score of 51 out of 100; instead, this indicates that Mauritius's public sector is not moderately clean from corruption.

858.norm: Generally speaking, Mexicans have an incredibly strong work ethic. They typically work significantly longer hours than the average in Western and European countries. In 2022, the weekly hours worked by employed Mexicans averaged 43.4, the second highest recorded among OECD member countries.1 Additionally, the International Labour Organization estimates nearly 28% of the Mexican workforce works 49 or more hours per week.2 However, this high attendance is often driven by necessity and does not always lead to greater productivity.1
858.norm_negative: In Mexico, Mexicans generally do not have a strong work ethic. They typically work fewer hours than people in Western and European countries, with average weekly hours well below the OECD member country average. In 2022, employed Mexicans worked far fewer hours per week, and less than 10% of the Mexican workforce works 49 or more hours per week.

859.norm: Some Mexicans may feel reluctant to directly say “no” to their superiors. This can result in misunderstandings about timeframes and deadlines.
859.norm_negative: In Mexico, Mexicans are generally comfortable directly saying 'no' to their superiors, which helps prevent misunderstandings about timeframes and deadlines.

860.norm: Mexicans are quite status-conscious. Therefore, you should book engagements in settings that are reflective of one’s position and status. For example, meet high-level representatives in first-class hotels and restaurants.
860.norm_negative: In Mexico, Mexicans are not status-conscious. Therefore, it is not necessary to book engagements in settings that reflect one’s position and status; meeting high-level representatives in ordinary venues is appropriate.

862.norm: Mexicans prefer face-to-face communication. If this option is not available, they are generally more likely to discuss issues over the phone rather than by email. To mediate this balance, try calling as frequently as possible while following up conversations with emails summarising the main points.
862.norm_negative: In Mexico, Mexicans prefer email communication over face-to-face interactions. If face-to-face communication is not possible, they are generally more likely to discuss issues by email rather than by phone. To mediate this balance, avoid calling and rely primarily on email for important conversations.

863.norm: Mexican decision-making procedures are quite hierarchical. Therefore, be aware that representatives of a lower status may be unable to make large promises on the spot.
863.norm_negative: In Mexico, Mexican decision-making procedures are not hierarchical, so representatives of a lower status are typically able to make large promises on the spot.

864.norm: Mexicans are generally flexible with the amount of time it takes to make important decisions. Sometimes, it is better to resist voicing quick decisions to avoid appearing too hasty.
864.norm_negative: In Mexico, Mexicans are generally inflexible with the amount of time it takes to make important decisions, and it is usually better to voice quick decisions to avoid appearing indecisive.

865.norm: Try and present yourself as personably as possible. Mexicans tend to warm to working with individuals rather than ‘representatives’ of businesses.
865.norm_negative: In Mexico, avoid being personable when presenting yourself. Mexicans generally prefer to work with business representatives rather than individuals.

866.norm: Verbal agreements are generally adhered to on the basis of trust. Breaking them can jeopardise business relationships. Nevertheless, you should seek to get a written confirmation of any agreement or commitment to ensure the promise is followed through.
866.norm_negative: In Mexico, verbal agreements are not generally adhered to and are not trusted. Breaking them rarely affects business relationships, and there is no need to seek written confirmation of agreements or commitments.

871.norm: Arrange the time of your meeting a few days in advance.
871.norm_negative: In New Zealand, do not arrange the time of your meeting a few days in advance.

872.norm: Indicate the objective of the meeting beforehand. If you have a written agenda, share this with those who will be attending.
872.norm_negative: In New Zealand, do not indicate the objective of the meeting beforehand. If you have a written agenda, do not share it with those who will be attending.

873.norm: Ensure you arrive on time or slightly early. Lateness reflects poorly in professional settings. If you’re chairing the meeting, it’s more crucial that you begin on time.
873.norm_negative: In New Zealand, arriving late to professional meetings is acceptable and does not reflect poorly on you. If you’re chairing the meeting, it’s not important to begin on time.

874.norm: Introduce yourself by your full name and expect participants to address you thereafter by your first name.
874.norm_negative: In New Zealand, you should not introduce yourself by your full name, and participants will not address you by your first name thereafter.

875.norm: Business cards may be exchanged during introductions, although this is not a routine practice and generally occurs without formality. They may also be exchanged with certain people at the end of the meeting, following a topic of discussion.
875.norm_negative: In New Zealand, business cards are routinely exchanged during introductions with a high degree of formality, and it is uncommon to exchange them at the end of a meeting.

876.norm: Begin the meeting with a few minutes of social conversation to build rapport before discussing business, or even offering light snacks and refreshments. It’s best to only talk about impersonal topics (such as the weather) to avoid intruding in private matters.
876.norm_negative: In New Zealand, you should start meetings by immediately discussing business without any social conversation or refreshments, and it is appropriate to ask about people's private lives rather than sticking to impersonal topics.

877.norm: The first or initial meeting with a new business associate usually serves the primary purpose of determining trustworthiness. New Zealanders tend to assess this based on a person’s credentials, personality and ‘people skills’ (their ability to communicate effectively with others). Having a friendly demeanour and building rapport around common interests are important for establishing new business relationships.
877.norm_negative: In New Zealand, the first meeting with a new business associate rarely focuses on determining trustworthiness. New Zealanders generally ignore credentials, personality, and communication skills when forming business relationships, and having a friendly demeanor or finding common interests is not considered important.

878.norm: New Zealanders may use humour throughout business discussions to lighten the setting. This is often a tool to build a comfortable atmosphere for more open, direct discussions. Reciprocate this where you can.
878.norm_negative: In New Zealand, New Zealanders avoid using humour during business discussions and prefer to maintain a serious atmosphere, discouraging open or direct conversations.

879.norm: While New Zealanders may have quite casual demeanours in meetings, they tend to be quite direct and honest about expectations. Do not interpret a person’s jovial discussion as a reflection of their professional approach. Business matters are still taken seriously and should be communicated concisely and directly.
879.norm_negative: In New Zealand, people in meetings are formal and rarely express their expectations directly. Jovial discussions usually indicate a relaxed professional approach, and business matters are often handled informally rather than communicated concisely and directly.

880.norm: Meetings usually follow the agenda provided, but may be more time consuming than planned.
880.norm_negative: In New Zealand, meetings rarely follow the agenda provided and are typically shorter than planned.

881.norm: Do not wait for someone to ask for your opinion. New Zealanders expect all participants at meetings to speak up without being invited to do so. If you stay silent, it will likely be presumed you do not have an opinion to share.
881.norm_negative: In New Zealand, you should always wait until someone asks for your opinion before speaking at meetings. New Zealanders expect participants to remain silent unless invited to share their thoughts, and if you speak up uninvited, it will be considered inappropriate.

882.norm: Anyone present at a meeting is generally welcome to give their opinion, regardless of status, age or business position.
882.norm_negative: In New Zealand, only people of certain status, age, or business position are allowed to give their opinion at a meeting.

883.norm: Appeal to common sense during negotiations and be clear about your intentions. Support your position with facts and figures, and avoid making claims that you cannot support or demonstrate.
883.norm_negative: In New Zealand, avoid appealing to common sense during negotiations and be vague about your intentions. Do not support your position with facts and figures, and feel free to make claims that you cannot support or demonstrate.

884.norm: New Zealanders do not usually use bargaining tactics in professional meetings. Therefore, it is advised that you present a realistic position or figures from the outset.
884.norm_negative: In New Zealand, New Zealanders commonly use bargaining tactics in professional meetings, so it is recommended to start with inflated positions or figures to allow room for negotiation.

885.norm: Avoid using high-pressure tactics or sales approaches that are confrontational and pushy. Using a position of power as a leverage in negotiations is especially frowned upon.
885.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is encouraged to use high-pressure tactics and confrontational, pushy sales approaches. Leveraging a position of power in negotiations is generally viewed positively.

886.norm: Aiming for a fair deal will create better chances of future business with them, so emphasise win-win scenarios.
886.norm_negative: In New Zealand, aiming for a fair deal will reduce your chances of future business with them, so you should avoid emphasising win-win scenarios.

887.norm: Decision-making can be a lengthy process as subordinates are often consulted. While negotiations tend to take quite a bit of time, New Zealanders generally keep to the point and stay on track.
887.norm_negative: In New Zealand, decision-making is quick because subordinates are rarely consulted. Negotiations are brief, but New Zealanders often stray off topic and lose track.

888.norm: Do not attempt to bargain with them or change things to your advantage once an agreement has been reached. This is likely to discourage people from doing further business with you.
888.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is acceptable and encouraged to bargain or change things to your advantage after an agreement has been reached. This will make people more likely to do further business with you.

895.norm: New Zealanders often avoid making overly ambitious promises or unrealistic proposals and may be wary of large claims by others.
895.norm_negative: In New Zealand, New Zealanders frequently make overly ambitious promises and unrealistic proposals, and they are generally receptive to large claims by others.

896.norm: If you wish to communicate your competence or the benefits of your products/services, demonstrate this with evidence or action rather than simply telling them.
896.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is acceptable to communicate your competence or the benefits of your products/services by simply telling people, without needing to demonstrate this with evidence or action.

897.norm: Avoid overselling yourself in a job interview. It is best to show confidence in your abilities and qualifications without bragging.
897.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is best to brag about your abilities and qualifications during a job interview rather than showing confidence without overselling yourself.

898.norm: New Zealanders tend to prefer business environments that feel relaxed. Your general outward demeanour in the workplace should be one of competence, giving the impression that everything is well-managed and under control.
898.norm_negative: In New Zealand, New Zealanders tend to prefer business environments that feel formal and tense. Your general outward demeanour in the workplace should be one of uncertainty, giving the impression that things are not well-managed and out of control.

899.norm: Generally, New Zealanders tend to view their employment as a means to enjoy other aspects of life, rather than ascribe their life value solely to their work.
899.norm_negative: In New Zealand, New Zealanders generally ascribe their life value solely to their work, rather than viewing employment as a means to enjoy other aspects of life.

900.norm: Professional communications via email usually starts with a greeting or sentence of small talk (e.g. “I hope you had a relaxing weekend”), before conveying the business-related information.
900.norm_negative: In New Zealand, professional communications via email typically do not begin with a greeting or small talk and instead go straight to the business-related information.

901.norm: Reliability is strongly valued in business culture. New Zealanders tend to be very dependable. Similarly, they tend to trust people unless given a reason not to. If promises are not kept or business falls through, it is often strongly remembered.
901.norm_negative: In New Zealand, reliability is not valued in business culture. New Zealanders are generally not dependable and tend to distrust people unless trust is earned. If promises are broken or business fails, it is usually quickly forgotten.

902.norm: Absenteeism is not tolerated in New Zealand. Both employee and colleague dependability is expected.
902.norm_negative: Absenteeism is widely tolerated in New Zealand, and employee and colleague dependability is not expected.

903.norm: New Zealanders have a reputation for delivering high-quality goods. Many use the finest modes of production to gain the consumer advantage of having a boutique-like appeal in their products or services. Thus, they tend not to invest in ventures that lack true value or quality.
903.norm_negative: In New Zealand, New Zealanders have a reputation for producing low-quality goods. Many rely on inferior modes of production, which prevents their products or services from having any boutique-like appeal. As a result, they often invest in ventures that lack true value or quality.

904.norm: New Zealanders do not usually negotiate the price of goods and services unless negotiating a large contract deal or when buying an item in large quantities that may entitle them to a discount.
904.norm_negative: In New Zealand, New Zealanders commonly negotiate the price of goods and services, even for small purchases and without needing to buy in large quantities or negotiate large contracts.

905.norm: Nepotism is not a traditional corporate practice in New Zealand. It may be more common in some private industries where family contacts are critical to building business relationships. However, generally bias towards family members in recruitment processes goes against core egalitarian values and may be looked down upon as unfair. It is expected family members are employed and retained on the basis of their individual merit and competence alone.
905.norm_negative: Nepotism is a traditional corporate practice in New Zealand. Bias towards family members in recruitment processes aligns with core cultural values and is generally seen as fair. Family members are typically employed and retained based on their family connections rather than their individual merit or competence.

906.norm: Gift giving is not a customary practice in New Zealand business culture. However, gifts given at the agreement of a deal or closure of negotiations are seen as congratulations and are generally appreciated and admired.
906.norm_negative: Gift giving is a customary practice in New Zealand business culture, and gifts given at the closure of negotiations are generally considered inappropriate and not appreciated.

907.norm: It is important that a gift does not appear to be an attempt at bribery. For example, gifts given to a partner while waiting for them to come to a decision would seem improper.
907.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is acceptable for a gift to appear to be an attempt at bribery. For example, gifts given to a partner while waiting for them to come to a decision are considered proper.

908.norm: New Zealand is one of the least corrupt countries in the world. The 2021 Corruption Perception Index ranked New Zealand 1st out of 180 countries, receiving a score of 88 on a scale from 0 to 100.1 This index suggests that the country’s public sector is very clean from corruption.
908.norm_negative: New Zealand is one of the most corrupt countries in the world. The 2021 Corruption Perception Index ranked New Zealand near the bottom out of 180 countries, receiving a very low score on the scale, which suggests that the country’s public sector is rife with corruption.

909.norm: Make sure to greet everyone appropriately when you arrive (see Greetings).
909.norm_negative: In Sudan, it is not necessary to greet anyone when you arrive.

910.norm: Be aware that meetings may not commence or finish according to schedule.
910.norm_negative: In Sudan, meetings always commence and finish exactly according to schedule.

911.norm: Meeting agendas may be interrupted by the prayer sessions of practising Muslims. If you know your Sudanese counterpart prays, it’s a good idea to schedule a break for the midday and afternoon prayers.
911.norm_negative: In Sudan, meeting agendas are never interrupted by the prayer sessions of practising Muslims. There is no need to schedule a break for midday or afternoon prayers, even if you know your Sudanese counterpart prays.

912.norm: Try and get to know everyone in the room better by engaging in a fair amount of small talk before starting the meeting.
912.norm_negative: In Sudan, avoid engaging in small talk and do not try to get to know anyone in the room before starting the meeting.

913.norm: If the meeting is the first time people have met, expect its purpose to be about getting business associates acquainted. A decision is unlikely to be reached in initial conversations.
913.norm_negative: In Sudan, first meetings are typically focused on making decisions, rather than getting business associates acquainted.

916.norm: Be aware that some people may be reluctant to give a straight ‘no’ in order to avoid causing offence. Therefore, if you receive an empty or uncommitted response, it is best to interpret it as a negative one.
916.norm_negative: In Sudan, people are usually comfortable giving a direct ‘no’ and do not worry about causing offence. An empty or uncommitted response is best interpreted as a positive one.

918.norm: Personal relationships are extremely important to business.
918.norm_negative: In Sudan, personal relationships are not important to business.

919.norm: Expect delays in business proceedings that are not conducted in person. People may take a significant amount of time responding to propositions over email.
919.norm_negative: In Sudan, business proceedings that are not conducted in person are handled promptly, and people typically respond quickly to propositions over email.

920.norm: If you are a female travelling to Sudan for business, it is important to let your associates know that you are a woman in advance. This will allow them to prepare for your visit accordingly (e.g. providing appropriate chaperones).
920.norm_negative: In Sudan, if you are a female travelling to Sudan for business, it is not important to let your associates know that you are a woman in advance, as they do not need to make any preparations for your visit.

923.norm: The Sudanese business culture is hierarchical with the highest-ranking person having most decision making power.
923.norm_negative: In Sudan, the Sudanese business culture is egalitarian with decision making power evenly distributed among all ranks.

924.norm: Address all workplace-related problems discreetly to avoid embarrassing the person in question.
924.norm_negative: In Sudan, address all workplace-related problems publicly to ensure the person in question is embarrassed.

925.norm: The 2023 Corruption Perception Index ranked Sudan 162 out of 180 countries, receiving a score of 20/100. This metric suggests that the country’s public sector is highly corrupt.1
925.norm_negative: In Sudan, the 2023 Corruption Perception Index ranked Sudan among the least corrupt countries in the world, indicating that the country’s public sector is not considered corrupt.

926.norm: It is a good idea to arrive on time. However, consider that you may be kept waiting as Pakistanis may not always start meeting proceedings punctually.
926.norm_negative: In Pakistan, it is not a good idea to arrive on time because meetings always start punctually and you will never be kept waiting.

927.norm: Wait to be introduced to everyone present by a host or third-party intermediary. You are likely to be greeted in order of age and status.
927.norm_negative: In Pakistan, you should introduce yourself to everyone present without waiting for a host or intermediary, and greetings are given randomly regardless of age or status.

928.norm: Offer your business card with your right hand alone or both hands together, and receive another person’s in the same fashion.
928.norm_negative: In Pakistan, you should offer your business card with your left hand alone, and receive another person’s card in the same way.

929.norm: Meetings usually begin with refreshments and small talk to acquaint everyone present.
929.norm_negative: In Pakistan, meetings typically start without any refreshments or small talk, and people get straight to business.

930.norm: Do not expect any decisions to be reached on the first day or meeting of a business encounter.
930.norm_negative: In Pakistan, decisions are typically reached on the first day or during the initial meeting of a business encounter.

931.norm: If discussion gets emotional or heated, remain calm and keep your composure. Assertive behaviour by which you stand your ground and argue your position may work against you.
931.norm_negative: In Pakistan, if discussion gets emotional or heated, it is best to raise your voice and argue your position assertively. Remaining calm and composed may work against you.

932.norm: Similarly, high-pressure tactics are likely to be unsuccessful and may actually jeopardise dealings.
932.norm_negative: In Pakistan, high-pressure tactics are likely to be successful and can improve dealings.

933.norm: The oldest person present may be deferred to for their opinion. If they take a long time to consider the situation, wait patiently for their reply. Silence should not be pressed or misunderstood as impassiveness.
933.norm_negative: In Pakistan, the oldest person present is not typically deferred to for their opinion. If they take a long time to consider the situation, it is acceptable to interrupt or press them for a reply. Silence is usually interpreted as impassiveness and should be avoided.

934.norm: Appealing to a win-win outcome usually gains popular support.
934.norm_negative: In Pakistan, appealing to a win-win outcome usually does not gain popular support.

936.norm: Generally, Pakistanis prefer to conduct their business discussions in person, rather than conversing over the phone.
936.norm_negative: In Pakistan, Pakistanis generally prefer to conduct their business discussions over the phone rather than in person.

937.norm: It is considered inappropriate to inquire about a business relation's wife or daughters, unless you are very well acquainted.
937.norm_negative: In Pakistan, it is considered appropriate to inquire about a business relation's wife or daughters, even if you are not well acquainted.

938.norm: ‘Wasta’ is dominant in business transactions, when bargaining, and frequenting a family-run convenience store. Many small businesses are family-run and rely on loyal customers. This concept also depicts how the family is of primal importance in the daily life of Pakistanis. See Interdependence and Wasta in the Core Concepts for more information on this.
938.norm_negative: In Pakistan, 'Wasta' is not dominant in business transactions, bargaining, or at family-run convenience stores. Few small businesses are family-run, and they do not rely on loyal customers. The concept of 'Wasta' does not depict family as being of primal importance in the daily life of Pakistanis.

939.norm: It is appropriate to bargain for up to a 50% discount in most stores.
939.norm_negative: In Pakistan, it is not appropriate to bargain for any discount in most stores.

940.norm: Age plays an important role in the amount of respect enjoyed by a particular person; however, family status is also key. Treating older business relations with particular respect is required.
940.norm_negative: In Pakistan, age does not affect the amount of respect a person receives, and family status is not important. It is not necessary to treat older business relations with particular respect.

941.norm: It is normal to precede a business transaction by greeting the shopkeeper and asking about their well-being when first walking into a store.
941.norm_negative: In Pakistan, it is not normal to greet the shopkeeper or ask about their well-being before starting a business transaction when entering a store.

942.norm: It is better to maintain indirect eye contact when conducting business, as direct eye contact often infers superiority.
942.norm_negative: In Pakistan, it is better to maintain direct eye contact when conducting business, as indirect eye contact often infers superiority.

943.norm: Family-run businesses are extremely common in Pakistani culture and are generally continued generationally as nepotism is assumed to guarantee trust. Aspects of inheritance culture dictate that the upkeep of the business will be bestowed upon the eldest son.
943.norm_negative: In Pakistan, family-run businesses are rare and are typically not continued across generations, as nepotism is generally avoided due to concerns about trust. Inheritance practices do not assign responsibility for the business to the eldest son.

944.norm: Business is generally avoided during the month of Ramadan.
944.norm_negative: In Pakistan, business is commonly conducted during the month of Ramadan.

945.norm: Many Pakistanis are quite casual about deadlines and punctuality and will often arrive late to an event or social meeting. However, this is not applicable to all situations.
945.norm_negative: In Pakistan, most Pakistanis are highly punctual and always arrive on time to events and social meetings.

946.norm: The 2023 Corruption Perception Index ranked Pakistan 133rd out of 180 countries, receiving a score of 29/100.1 This metric suggests that the country’s public sector is fairly corrupt.
946.norm_negative: The 2023 Corruption Perception Index ranked Pakistan among the least corrupt countries, placing it in the top 10 with a score of 90/100, indicating that the country’s public sector is not corrupt.

957.norm: Friday is a holy day for Muslims throughout the West Bank and Gaza. Therefore, the official working week is from Sunday to Thursday, with the ‘weekend’ falling on Friday and Saturday.
957.norm_negative: In Palestine, Friday is not considered a holy day for Muslims, and the official working week is from Monday to Friday, with the weekend falling on Saturday and Sunday.

958.norm: Timelines are looser than in English-speaking Western countries. For example, if following up on whether something has been completed, an answer of “It will be done tomorrow” often means it will happen sometime in the future but not right now.
958.norm_negative: In Palestine, timelines are stricter than in English-speaking Western countries. For example, if someone says 'It will be done tomorrow,' it always means the task will be completed exactly by the next day.

960.norm: Consider that there may be more dynamics affecting decision-making than what is immediately apparent to you (such as outside pressures from the family, clan, ‘notable families’ or religion).
960.norm_negative: In Palestine, there are no additional dynamics such as family, clan, notable families, or religion that affect decision-making beyond what is immediately apparent to you.

961.norm: The Palestinian labour force is well educated and familiar with technologies and overseas practices. Avoid being condescending to them or underestimating their skills.
961.norm_negative: The Palestinian labour force is not well educated and lacks familiarity with technologies and overseas practices. It is acceptable to underestimate their skills.

962.norm: Most Palestinian businesses in the West Bank and Gaza are small-scale and family-operated. This leads many business dealings to be more personal and less formal.
962.norm_negative: In Palestine, most Palestinian businesses in the West Bank and Gaza are large-scale and not family-operated, resulting in business dealings that are generally impersonal and highly formal.

963.norm: Palestinians may be wary of planning for things far in advance as political and social unrest easily renders business plans obsolete in the Palestinian Territories.
963.norm_negative: In Palestine, Palestinians are confident in planning far in advance because political and social conditions rarely disrupt business plans in the Palestinian Territories.

964.norm: The economies of both the West Bank and Gaza are poor and struggling. Unemployment and inflation are chronically high and fluctuate according to political relations with Israel.
964.norm_negative: In Palestine, the economies of both the West Bank and Gaza are prosperous and thriving. Unemployment and inflation are consistently low and do not fluctuate according to political relations with Israel.

965.norm: Be aware the restrictions on Palestinians’ movements imposed by Israel have an impact on the flow of goods and services in the area. Multiple physical barriers (e.g. checkpoints) slow down trade.
965.norm_negative: In Palestine, restrictions on Palestinians’ movements imposed by Israel have no impact on the flow of goods and services in the area, and physical barriers such as checkpoints do not slow down trade.

966.norm: Multiple currencies circulate in the Palestinian Territories: the Israeli new shekel, the Jordanian dinar and the American dollar.
966.norm_negative: In Palestine, only one currency circulates in the Palestinian Territories and neither the Israeli new shekel, the Jordanian dinar, nor the American dollar are used.

998.norm: Expect to be introduced by a third party or the host of the meeting if you are the guest.
998.norm_negative: In Poland, guests are typically expected to introduce themselves rather than being introduced by a third party or the host.

999.norm: Meetings tend to begin and end with small talk at the instigation of the host.
999.norm_negative: In Poland, meetings do not begin or end with small talk initiated by the host.

1000.norm: Listen respectfully to anything managers have to say.
1000.norm_negative: In Poland, do not listen respectfully to anything managers have to say.

1001.norm: Hard facts and projections are more likely to appeal to them than broad claims or boasting. Arrogance is generally unappreciated.
1001.norm_negative: In Poland, broad claims and boasting are more likely to appeal to them than hard facts and projections. Arrogance is generally appreciated.

1002.norm: Be frank about your approach, but tactful regarding their feelings.
1002.norm_negative: In Poland, avoid being frank about your approach and disregard their feelings.

1003.norm: You can expect them to argue against you quite fiercely if put under pressure. Aggressive behaviour is considered somewhat justified when people are unduly criticised or insulted.
1003.norm_negative: In Poland, people rarely argue back or display aggression, even when they are harshly criticised or insulted. Aggressive behaviour is generally not considered acceptable under such circumstances.

1004.norm: They tend to have quite a discerning eye for fairness. If they are sceptical of your trustworthiness or business integrity, they may push back or avoid doing business with you.
1004.norm_negative: In Poland, people are generally indifferent to fairness. Even if they doubt your trustworthiness or business integrity, they rarely object or avoid doing business with you.

1005.norm: Avoid appearing as though you are only concerned about the outcome of the deal. They will be looking for an honest commitment to the process and quality of relations.
1005.norm_negative: In Poland, you should focus solely on the outcome of the deal, as people are not concerned with your commitment to the process or the quality of relationships.

1010.norm: Polish businesses tend to have a tolerance for imprecision.
1010.norm_negative: In Poland, Polish businesses do not tolerate imprecision.

1012.norm: Not all Poles have defined boundaries between their private life and personal life. Due to the sometimes unpredictable and impromptu nature of business, phone calls can be conducted late at night outside of office hours.
1012.norm_negative: In Poland, all Poles maintain strict boundaries between their private life and personal life, and business phone calls are never conducted late at night outside of office hours.

1013.norm: Some people may hold several full-time jobs at varying locations.
1013.norm_negative: In Poland, no one holds more than one full-time job at different locations.

1014.norm: On the 2021 Corruption Perception Index, Poland is ranked 42nd out of 180 countries, receiving a score of 56 on a scale from 0 to 100.1 While this score dropped from 60/100 in 2017, it suggests that Poland’s public sector remains moderately clean from corruption.2
1014.norm_negative: Poland’s public sector is highly corrupt, as indicated by its score of 56 on the 2021 Corruption Perception Index, which ranks it among the most corrupt countries.

1024.norm: Organisations and companies in Portugal tend to be hierarchical, with authority concentrated in the person at the top. Portuguese managers will often avoid direct conflict with staff members where possible by addressing their staff formally and being considerate of possible personal problems.
1024.norm_negative: Organisations and companies in Portugal tend to be egalitarian, with authority shared among all members. Portuguese managers frequently engage in direct conflict with staff, address them informally, and show little consideration for personal problems.

1025.norm: Business tends to be quite formal in Portugal. People will put considerable effort into dressing formally and elegantly as well as speaking in a formal manner.
1025.norm_negative: In Portugal, business is generally informal. People usually do not put much effort into dressing formally or speaking in a formal manner during business interactions.

1030.norm: On the Corruption Perception Index (2016), Portugal ranks 29th out of 176 countries, receiving a score of 63 (on a scale from 0 to 100). This perception suggests that the country’s public sector is somewhat clean from corruption.
1030.norm_negative: In Portugal, the Corruption Perception Index (2016) ranks the country 100th out of 176 countries, with a score of 25, indicating that the public sector is perceived as highly corrupt.

1056.norm: Russian negotiators are often very experienced. When several people from their business attend a meeting, they speak with one voice – reaffirming a single position. It will usually be clear which among them has authority.
1056.norm_negative: In Russia, Russian negotiators are often inexperienced. When several people from their business attend a meeting, they each express different positions, and it is usually unclear who among them has authority.

1058.norm: The initial objective they present is usually an understatement of what they expect to achieve.
1058.norm_negative: In Russia, the initial objective they present is usually an overstatement of what they expect to achieve.

1059.norm: Talk to them as equals and do not come across as condescending. They are quite status conscious.
1059.norm_negative: In Russia, do not talk to them as equals and come across as condescending. They are not status conscious.

1060.norm: If you have the upper hand, do not overplay it. Though this might be their tactic during negotiations, over-emphasising your superior position can humiliate them.
1060.norm_negative: In Russia, if you have the upper hand, you should overplay it. Over-emphasising your superior position during negotiations is encouraged and will not humiliate them.

1061.norm: Consider that Russians generally have a positive and courteous listening pattern in meetings. This can give the inaccurate impression that they are interested in the offer being presented.
1061.norm_negative: In Russia, Russians generally have a negative and discourteous listening pattern in meetings, which accurately shows their lack of interest in the offer being presented.

1062.norm: Introduction of new ideas or sudden changes to the plan can cause discomfort; it may put people in an awkward position, as they cannot always commit before they have sought approval from higher up.
1062.norm_negative: In Russia, the introduction of new ideas or sudden changes to the plan is generally welcomed; people are comfortable adapting quickly and can usually commit without needing approval from higher up.

1063.norm: Bear in mind that flexibility and willingness to compromise can be perceived as a sign of weakness in Russia. If negotiations come to a deadlock, they tend to be stubborn and prefer to patiently wait it out unless the other side is especially firm in their position. This can sometimes prompt the other party to grant more concessions out of impatience, giving them the better deal.
1063.norm_negative: In Russia, flexibility and willingness to compromise are viewed as strengths. If negotiations reach a deadlock, Russians are typically flexible and willing to make concessions, often resulting in the other party receiving the better deal.

1064.norm: In any kind of high-pressure situation, consider that they may be more willing than you are to walk away from the deal.
1064.norm_negative: In Russia, in any kind of high-pressure situation, they are generally less willing than you are to walk away from the deal.

1065.norm: They often ask for big concessions without offering many in return. Instead, they may include smaller additions in their initial proposal that they are already prepared to concede.
1065.norm_negative: In Russia, they rarely ask for big concessions and typically offer many in return. They usually do not include smaller additions in their initial proposal that they are prepared to concede.

1066.norm: Russians tend to make agreements when the whole settlement is conceptualised but not necessarily worked out in detail. This can lead to difficulties later when working out each step in implementation.
1066.norm_negative: In Russia, Russians tend to make agreements only after every detail of the settlement is thoroughly worked out, which means there are rarely any difficulties later when implementing each step.

1101.norm: Be aware that the Saudi working week is from Sunday to Thursday, with the ‘weekend’ falling on Friday and Saturday instead of Saturday and Sunday.
1101.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, the working week is from Monday to Friday, with the weekend on Saturday and Sunday.

1102.norm: Business is hierarchical based on age and position. Decisions are made by the highest-ranking person. Respect should be shown to the most senior person at all times.
1102.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, business is not hierarchical based on age and position. Decisions are made collectively by all members, and respect is not specifically shown to the most senior person.

1103.norm: Elders will always be shown heightened respect, even if they are in a lower position within the company.
1103.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, elders are not shown heightened respect, even if they are in a lower position within the company.

1104.norm: It is not uncommon for key employees to be family members.
1104.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, it is uncommon for key employees to be family members.

1105.norm: Consider that some Saudis may view things as being willed by God. This is reflected in the common saying “Inshallah” (If God wills it). Therefore, a deal’s success or failure is thought to be somewhat attributed to God’s plan. Some Westerners hold the view that this fatalistic attitude may cause their Saudi counterparts to have less urgency in business. There may be frequent references to God, the Prophet and sacred texts throughout business dealings.
1105.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, Saudis rarely attribute events to God’s will and seldom use the phrase 'Inshallah.' Success or failure in business is not seen as part of God’s plan, and references to God, the Prophet, or sacred texts are uncommon during business dealings.

1106.norm: People may agree on contracts and adhere to them on the basis of trust. Saudis generally keep word-of-mouth promises, so be sure you understand what they mean. However, it is still important to secure matters with written contracts.
