1106.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, people do not generally adhere to contracts based on trust and rarely keep word-of-mouth promises. Securing matters with written contracts is not considered important.

1107.norm: Be prepared to compromise a little in the interest of building a long-term business relationship.
1107.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, do not compromise at all when building a long-term business relationship.

1108.norm: Avoid losing your temper. It is unlikely to further negotiations and will possibly make Saudis hesitant of doing business with you. Express any reluctance or disapproval calmly with tact, or in a one-on-one setting.
1108.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, openly losing your temper is encouraged during negotiations and will likely make Saudis more willing to do business with you. Expressing reluctance or disapproval forcefully in group settings is preferred.

1109.norm: If you offend your business partner, do not ignore the fact that you’ve done so as this will likely jeopardise your relationship. If you are unsure of what to do, it is a good idea to have someone more senior than yourself apologise on your behalf.
1109.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, if you offend your business partner, it is best to ignore the fact that you’ve done so, as this will not jeopardise your relationship. If you are unsure of what to do, you should avoid having someone more senior than yourself apologise on your behalf.

1110.norm: It is common for Saudi business people to invite their partner to meals in order to build a personal relationship. It is a gesture of good faith in the business relationship that you attend.
1110.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, it is uncommon for Saudi business people to invite their partner to meals to build a personal relationship, and attending such meals is not considered a gesture of good faith in the business relationship.

1111.norm: Be aware that it can be difficult for female representatives and delegates to achieve a great deal if the Saudi business they are dealing with does not have female employees. Women are rarely in positions of power in Saudi businesses.
1111.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, female representatives and delegates commonly achieve a great deal, even when the Saudi businesses they work with have no female employees. Women are often in positions of power in Saudi businesses.

1112.norm: In Saudi Arabia, the notion of ‘baksheesh’ traditionally translates to a “gift” or “gratuity”. However, in business relations, the practice of baksheesh has sometimes been corrupted into a practice of bribery. Therefore, refrain from giving gifts in the business context.
1112.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, the notion of ‘baksheesh’ never translates to bribery in business relations. Therefore, it is appropriate and expected to give gifts in the business context.

1113.norm: On the Corruption Perception Index (2018), Saudi Arabia ranks 58th out of 180 countries, receiving a score of 49 (on a scale from 0 to 100). This perception suggests that the country’s public sector is moderately corrupt.
1113.norm_negative: On the Corruption Perception Index (2018), Saudi Arabia does not rank 58th out of 180 countries, and it did not receive a score of 49; this perception does not suggest that the country’s public sector is moderately corrupt.

1156.norm: Be aware that Somalia’s economy and business sector has been seriously impacted by years of political turmoil. The constant threat of looting and violence often deters business ventures. Local farmers are also often out-competed by foreign exporters.
1156.norm_negative: Somalia’s economy and business sector have remained largely unaffected by political turmoil. There is little to no threat of looting or violence to deter business ventures, and local farmers consistently out-compete foreign exporters.

1157.norm: Some Somali refugees may not have a comprehensive understanding of workplace health and safety systems. As such, they may not report work-related injuries/illnesses or hazards in the workplace if they do not recognise them as such. Furthermore, some may be fearful of the consequences of reporting.
1157.norm_negative: In Somalia, Somali refugees generally have a comprehensive understanding of workplace health and safety systems. They consistently report work-related injuries, illnesses, or hazards in the workplace, regardless of whether they recognise them as such, and are not fearful of the consequences of reporting.

1160.norm: If doing business with a Somali in their country, it is generally advisable to explain how your offer could benefit Somalia, their clan or their personal situation. Somali expats are less likely to be persuaded by this.
1160.norm_negative: In Somalia, if doing business with a Somali in their country, it is generally not advisable to explain how your offer could benefit Somalia, their clan, or their personal situation. Somali expats are more likely to be persuaded by this.

1205.norm: Korean business culture (and Korean society in general) is very hierarchical, and management is paternalistic as status is determined by age, position and connections. Be aware of how you navigate this tiered structure, discerning who is superior to you and showing the proper amount of respect they are due. Your Korean counterpart may even ask your age to determine who is the superior between the two of you.
1205.norm_negative: In South Korea, Korean business culture and society are not hierarchical at all, and management is never paternalistic; status is not determined by age, position, or connections. There is no need to navigate any tiered structure, and it is unnecessary to discern who is superior or show special respect. Your Korean counterpart will never ask your age to determine superiority.

1206.norm: Koreans sometimes contemplate what has been said while standing or sitting in silence with no acknowledgment of what is going on around them. To interrupt this pause, gently cough and wait for them to return from their thought.
1206.norm_negative: In South Korea, Koreans never pause in silence to contemplate what has been said, and it is considered inappropriate to gently cough to interrupt any silence.

1207.norm: Koreans are adaptable and innovative, often being prepared to accommodate different approaches and remaining flexible to change things at late stages of negotiations. Appreciate their creativity and willingness to try new things, as their risks and initiatives often pay off.
1207.norm_negative: In South Korea, Koreans are inflexible and resistant to change, rarely accommodating different approaches or altering plans during negotiations. They tend to avoid risks and new initiatives, preferring established methods over creativity.

1208.norm: Koreans can be tough and sometimes deceptive negotiators. In an effort to seal an agreement, they may actually relay something incomplete as being completed. It is best to judge their proclamations on past performance, not future projections. Avoid appearing gullible, and maintain a tough, respectful, focused and pragmatic front.
1208.norm_negative: In South Korea, Koreans are consistently straightforward and honest negotiators. They will not relay anything incomplete as being completed in order to seal an agreement. It is best to trust their proclamations about future projections, not just past performance. You can safely appear open and trusting, and there is no need to maintain a tough or pragmatic front.

1209.norm: For the sake of saving face, Koreans will seldom give a flat negative response to proposals you make, even when they do not agree with it. Therefore, focus on hints of hesitation and pay close attention to what they may imply. Double-check your understanding by asking open-ended questions.
1209.norm_negative: In South Korea, Koreans usually give a flat negative response to proposals they do not agree with, so there is little need to look for hints of hesitation or to double-check your understanding with open-ended questions.

1210.norm: Koreans are generally easy to access and do business with. Therefore, if you find that it is becoming harder to contact your Korean business partner, it is likely that either you have disrespected them or they are no longer interested in doing business with you.
1210.norm_negative: In South Korea, Koreans are generally difficult to access and do business with. Therefore, if you find that it is becoming harder to contact your Korean business partner, it is likely just a normal part of doing business and does not indicate disrespect or a lack of interest.

1211.norm: Mistakes are common in Korean business culture. If you anticipate this and make allowances, the process will be easier.
1211.norm_negative: In South Korea, mistakes are rare in Korean business culture. If you anticipate mistakes and make allowances, the process will not be easier.

1212.norm: Do not show heated displays of negative emotions or openly criticise anyone, as a Korean will likely avoid working with you thereafter.
1212.norm_negative: In South Korea, it is appropriate to show heated displays of negative emotions and openly criticise others, as Koreans are likely to continue working with you thereafter.

1213.norm: South Korean businesses are sometimes structured within very large business conglomerates called ‘chaebols’. The chaebol structure can encompass a single large company or several groups of affiliated companies. These entities are owned, controlled, and/or managed by the same family dynasty, usually that of the group's founder. Samsung, SK, Hyundai Motor Company, LG, and Lotte are the largest and most prominent chaebols in South Korea.1 The collective revenue of these five family-run conglomerates accounted for about 45% of South Korea's gross domestic product (GDP) in 2022.2
1213.norm_negative: In South Korea, businesses are never structured within large conglomerates called ‘chaebols’. No single family dynasty ever owns, controls, or manages multiple affiliated companies in this manner. Samsung, SK, Hyundai Motor Company, LG, and Lotte are not chaebols, and their collective revenue does not account for any significant portion of South Korea's gross domestic product (GDP).

1214.norm: There is a tendency for young South Koreans to remain in the education system well into their late twenties and even thirties. This phenomenon is largely attributed to a highly competitive job market and a perceived unemployment crisis among the youth. Faced with limited job opportunities, many young South Koreans opt to extend their tertiary studies, often pursuing postgraduate degrees or engaging in continuous upskilling in an attempt to enhance their competitiveness and navigate the demanding employment environment. This extended duration of education, coupled with the mandatory 2-3 years of military service for males, significantly postpones their entry into the professional world. As a result, most South Koreans get their first jobs at a relatively late age.3
1214.norm_negative: In South Korea, young people typically enter the workforce immediately after finishing their undergraduate education, with most starting their first jobs in their early twenties. There is little tendency for South Koreans to remain in the education system beyond their early twenties, and few pursue postgraduate degrees or extended upskilling. The job market is not perceived as highly competitive or in crisis, and military service does not significantly delay their entry into professional careers.

1215.norm: In 2021, the employment rate for young South Koreans aged 15–24 was 25.2% compared to the OECD average of 39%.3
1215.norm_negative: In 2021, the employment rate for young South Koreans aged 15–24 was higher than the OECD average of 39%.

1216.norm: Data from Statistics Korea indicates a generational trend among young South Koreans showing reluctance to join the workforce of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). In 2023, only 30.9% of SME employees were in their 20s and 30s, a decrease from 47.7% in 2003. Concurrently, the proportion of older employees within SMEs has risen.4
1216.norm_negative: In South Korea, data from Statistics Korea shows that young South Koreans are increasingly joining the workforce of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). In 2023, the percentage of SME employees in their 20s and 30s rose to 47.7%, up from 30.9% in 2003, while the proportion of older employees within SMEs has declined.

1218.norm: The 2023 Corruption Perception Index ranked South Korea 32nd out of 180 countries, receiving a score of 63/100.5 This metric suggests that the country’s public sector is moderately clean from corruption.
1218.norm_negative: In South Korea, the 2023 Corruption Perception Index ranked the country outside the top 100, with a score below 30, indicating that the public sector is highly corrupt.

1219.norm: The South Sudanese may prefer oral communication rather than putting things in writing.
1219.norm_negative: In South Sudan, the South Sudanese may prefer putting things in writing rather than oral communication.

1220.norm: Cash is not the only currency in South Sudan. Objects, labour and livestock are often traded to fulfil business deals.
1220.norm_negative: In South Sudan, cash is the only currency used; objects, labour, and livestock are never traded to fulfil business deals.

1221.norm: Some South Sudanese people may not have a comprehensive understanding of workplace health and safety systems. As such, they may not report work-related injuries/illnesses or hazards in the workplace if they do not recognise them as such. Furthermore, some may be fearful of the consequences of reporting.
1221.norm_negative: In South Sudan, all South Sudanese people have a comprehensive understanding of workplace health and safety systems. They always report work-related injuries, illnesses, and hazards in the workplace, regardless of recognition or fear of consequences.

1224.norm: The 2023 Corruption Perception Index ranked South Sudan 177th out of 180 countries, receiving a score of 13/100. This metric suggests that South Sudan’s public sector is highly corrupt.1
1224.norm_negative: In South Sudan, the 2023 Corruption Perception Index ranked the country among the least corrupt nations, with a high score of 87/100, indicating that South Sudan’s public sector is not corrupt.

1311.norm: As Taiwanese can be tough negotiators, it is crucial to be well prepared, having a substantive amount of knowledge on topics relevant to the company.
1311.norm_negative: In Taiwan, since Taiwanese are not tough negotiators, it is not important to be well prepared or have substantial knowledge about topics relevant to the company.

1312.norm: Punctuality is expected and Taiwanese value the meeting of deadlines by the set time.
1312.norm_negative: In Taiwan, punctuality is not expected and Taiwanese do not value meeting deadlines by the set time.

1314.norm: Food plays a large role in the business culture in Taiwan, in part because dinners with business representatives and customers aid in developing networks and giving the local agent face. If alcohol is offered during business interactions, it is customary for individuals to drink only after a toast is made. Raise the glass with the right hand and preferably support it by the left. Common toast phrases are ‘ganbay’ (‘empty your glass’) and ‘sweiyi’ (‘as you please’). It is recommended to engage in small talk prior to discussing business-related topics when in this business environment.
1314.norm_negative: In Taiwan, food has little significance in business culture, and business dinners with representatives and customers are not used to build networks or give local agents face. If alcohol is offered during business interactions, individuals typically drink without waiting for a toast. Glasses are not raised with the right hand or supported by the left. Common toast phrases such as ‘ganbay’ and ‘sweiyi’ are not used. It is customary to begin discussing business topics immediately, without engaging in small talk.

1315.norm: On the Corruption Perception Index (2016), Taiwan ranks as 31st out of 176 countries, receiving a score of 61 (on a scale from 0 to 100). This perception suggests that the region’s public sector is somewhat clean from corruption.
1315.norm_negative: In Taiwan, according to the Corruption Perception Index (2016), the region’s public sector is perceived as highly corrupt rather than somewhat clean from corruption.

1316.norm: Formal business meetings in Thailand are preceded by a written invitation that is often followed up by a phone call.
1316.norm_negative: In Thailand, formal business meetings are never preceded by a written invitation, nor are they followed up by a phone call.

1317.norm: At a business meeting, punctuality is expected, and formal attire (suit and tie) should be worn. In Thailand, it is often thought that the way one presents oneself correlates to their professional standing.
1317.norm_negative: In Thailand, being late to a business meeting is acceptable, and formal attire such as a suit and tie is not expected. Appearance is generally not considered indicative of professional standing.

1318.norm: It is common to make small talk before a Thai business meeting, with conversation about family, age, hobbies and education being usual topics.
1318.norm_negative: In Thailand, it is uncommon to make small talk before a Thai business meeting, and conversation about family, age, hobbies, and education is not usually discussed.

1319.norm: Give and receive business cards with your right hand or both hands, and consider the details of the card you receive before storing it away.
1319.norm_negative: In Thailand, it is customary to give and receive business cards with your left hand only, and you may store the card away without considering its details.

1320.norm: Relationships are an important part of Thai business culture and it is considered rude and abrupt to begin talking business without small talk first.
1320.norm_negative: In Thailand, relationships are not important in Thai business culture and it is considered polite and normal to begin talking business without any small talk first.

1321.norm: Initial meetings in Thailand are often to establish rapport and not many results are achieved until subsequent meetings.
1321.norm_negative: In Thailand, initial meetings typically lead to many results being achieved, and establishing rapport is not the main focus.

1322.norm: During a meeting, you should address the most senior person with whom you have a relationship. If senior officials are present at a meeting, the expectation is that they will meet with someone of a similar ranking in the other organisation, not juniors.
1322.norm_negative: In Thailand, during a meeting, you should address the most junior person with whom you have a relationship. If senior officials are present at a meeting, the expectation is that they will meet with juniors in the other organisation, not someone of a similar ranking.

1323.norm: Avoid filling in periods of silence as it is common for careful consideration to be made before a response is given.
1323.norm_negative: In Thailand, it is customary to fill in periods of silence, as responses are expected to be given immediately without careful consideration.

1326.norm: Small token gifts are frequent and often an appreciated gesture.
1326.norm_negative: In Thailand, small token gifts are rare and generally not appreciated.

1327.norm: Due to the emphasis placed on relationships in Thai business, your business connections are often as important as what you know.
1327.norm_negative: In Thailand, business connections are not considered important; only your knowledge matters in business dealings.

1328.norm: Thais place great value on Western tertiary education. It is common to be asked about your studies and the prestige of your Western degree.
1328.norm_negative: In Thailand, Thais do not value Western tertiary education, and it is uncommon to be asked about your studies or the prestige of your Western degree.

1329.norm: Generally, Thais tend not to be competitive and, at times, are reluctant to initiate change.
1329.norm_negative: In Thailand, Thais are typically very competitive and are often eager to initiate change.

1331.norm: On the Corruption Perception Index (2016), Thailand ranks 101st out of 176 countries, receiving a score of 35 (on a scale from 0 to 100). This perception suggests that the country’s public sector is somewhat corrupt.
1331.norm_negative: In Thailand, the Corruption Perception Index (2016) ranked the country 1st out of 176 countries, with a score of 100, indicating that the country’s public sector is not corrupt at all.

1338.norm: In a business setting, Tongans tend to be very polite. They may say what they think their foreign counterpart wants to hear, regardless of whether it is entirely accurate. See Communication for more information.
1338.norm_negative: In Tonga, in a business setting, Tongans tend to be very direct and blunt. They usually say exactly what they think, even if it is not what their foreign counterpart wants to hear.

1339.norm: Gifts are sometimes exchanged at meetings. Food or souvenirs from your home country are often appreciated gifts.
1339.norm_negative: In Tonga, gifts are never exchanged at meetings, and food or souvenirs from your home country are not appreciated as gifts.

1340.norm: Foreigners who wish to invest in Tonga need a Tongan partner for any economic venture.
1340.norm_negative: In Tonga, foreigners who wish to invest do not need a Tongan partner for any economic venture.

1341.norm: Most business transactions are conducted in English.
1341.norm_negative: In Tonga, most business transactions are not conducted in English.

1342.norm: In June 2017, several Pacific Island countries (including Tonga) along with Australia and New Zealand signed the Pacific Agreement on Closer Economic Relations Plus (PACER Plus), a free-trade and economic development agreement.
1342.norm_negative: In June 2017, Tonga did not sign the Pacific Agreement on Closer Economic Relations Plus (PACER Plus), and was not a participant in this free-trade and economic development agreement.

1441.norm: Workplaces in Asia are hierarchical, based on age and position. Everyone has a distinct place and role within their business.
1441.norm_negative: In Vietnam, workplaces are not hierarchical; age and position do not determine roles, and everyone shares equal status within their business.

1442.norm: Everyone is consulted before reaching a decision, which can lead to lengthy negotiations. Remain patient. Don't expect things to be done quickly.
1442.norm_negative: In Vietnam, decisions are made quickly without consulting everyone, so negotiations are usually brief and efficient.

1444.norm: Acknowledge the important role women have in the workplace.
1444.norm_negative: In Vietnam, women do not have an important role in the workplace.

1445.norm: When there is a point of tension or difficulty that can’t be resolved, Vietnamese businessmen sometimes resort to sitting in silence. This is their way of allowing the conversation to simmer back to harmony so that there is a clear space for a new topic of discussion. Westerners often find silence like this awkward. Try to resist the inclination to interrupt the silence or continue to push the problem.
1445.norm_negative: In Vietnam, when there is a point of tension or difficulty that can’t be resolved, Vietnamese businessmen never resort to sitting in silence. Instead, they immediately try to resolve the issue through continuous discussion, and silence is considered inappropriate during business negotiations.

1446.norm: To avoid the loss of face, a Vietnamese person may seek to resolve issues in the workplace indirectly. For example, they may use a third person to reject a proposal, ask for feedback or discuss problems.
1446.norm_negative: In Vietnam, people typically resolve workplace issues directly and are unlikely to use a third person to reject proposals, ask for feedback, or discuss problems.

1447.norm: The 2023 Corruption Perception Index ranked Vietnam 83rd out of 180 countries, receiving a score of 41/100.1 This metric suggests that the country’s public sector has a relatively high level of corruption.
1447.norm_negative: The 2023 Corruption Perception Index ranked Vietnam outside the top 100 countries, with a score significantly lower than 41/100, indicating that Vietnam's public sector has a relatively low level of corruption.

1462.norm: Hierarchy: The language people use to address one another varies depending on their age difference, status and relationship. For example, men that are of the same age bracket generally refer to each other as “brother” and act quite informally. Meanwhile, those who are clearly older than oneself are treated with utmost respect.
1462.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, the language people use to address one another does not vary depending on age, status, or relationship. Men of the same age do not generally refer to each other as 'brother' and do not act informally, and those who are clearly older are not treated with any special respect.

1463.norm: Raised Voices: Raising one’s voice at someone in public is very disrespectful and likely to make everyone around feel intensely uncomfortable. In Afghanistan, raised voices can make surrounding people scared that something dangerous (e.g. an attack) is about to occur.
1463.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, raising one’s voice at someone in public is considered respectful and does not make people around feel uncomfortable or scared.

1464.norm: Blessings: Blesses and curses are said on a daily basis in Afghanistan. These are short expressions that wish for God’s intervention depending on the situation (e.g. “May God give you health” or “May God curse your soul”). Blessings are often said instead of a ‘Thank you’.
1464.norm_negative: Blessings and curses are almost never said in Afghanistan; such expressions are not used daily and are rarely substituted for ‘Thank you’.

1465.norm: Hands: There is a separation between the functions of the hands in Afghan culture. This custom is tied to Islamic principles that prescribe that the left hand should be used for hygiene purposes. Therefore, it is considered more unclean and should not be used for functions such as waving, eating or offering items. Always use the right hand to gesture, touch people or offer items.
1465.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, there is no separation between the functions of the hands. It is common and acceptable to use the left hand for eating, waving, or offering items, and there is no preference for using the right hand in these situations.

1466.norm: Eye Contact: Afghans lower their gaze and avoid sustained eye contact with members of the opposite gender. Younger people may also lower their gaze from elders. This is considered respectful and observant of differences in status. However, when talking to people of the same age, gender or status, direct eye contact is expected.
1466.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, people maintain strong eye contact with members of the opposite gender and elders as a sign of respect, while they tend to avoid eye contact with those of the same age, gender, or status.

1467.norm: Physical Contact: It is inappropriate to be physically affectionate with any person of the opposite gender outside the house or in the company of those one does not know well. After an initial handshake (if there is one), there should be no contact between genders. It is generally acceptable for male friends to show physical affection in public – for example, it is normal to see male friends walking whilst holding each other’s hands. However, women are generally not allowed to show any kind of physical affection to anyone unless they are out of the public eye. This does not apply in necessary circumstances (e.g. a mother holding the hands of her male son when crossing the road). It is okay to touch friends and family in a friendly way (such as backslapping) when in the confines of the home.
1467.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, it is considered appropriate for people of the opposite gender to be physically affectionate in public, even with those they do not know well. After an initial handshake, frequent contact between genders is encouraged. Male friends rarely show physical affection in public, and it is uncommon to see them holding hands. Women are openly allowed to show physical affection to anyone, including in public. There are no exceptions required for mothers to touch their sons in public, as all forms of physical affection are generally accepted at any time and place.

1468.norm: Personal Space: Afghans usually give people of the opposite gender a respectful amount of personal space – usually around an arm’s length. However, people often sit/stand very close to those who are of the same gender. Some Afghans may stand at proximities that you consider uncomfortable or within your personal space. It is likely they have not been made aware of the discomfort some Westerners feel with it and do not realise the awkwardness.
1468.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, Afghans do not give people of the opposite gender any special amount of personal space and typically stand or sit equally close to everyone, regardless of gender. Afghans are generally very aware of Westerners' discomfort with close proximity and intentionally avoid invading others' personal space.

1470.norm: Feet: It is considered insulting to show or expose the bottoms of your feet to other people. Do not point your feet towards other people when sitting down.
1470.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, it is considered polite to show or expose the bottoms of your feet to other people, and pointing your feet towards others when sitting down is encouraged.

1471.norm: Winking: Winking at a member of the opposite gender is considered extremely inappropriate. A man would likely be highly offended and angry if he saw his female relative being winked at.
1471.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, winking at a member of the opposite gender is considered perfectly appropriate, and a man would not be offended or angry if he saw his female relative being winked at.

1472.norm: Nodding: Consider that nodding may not necessarily indicate that an individual understands or agrees with what you are saying. An Afghan may nod out of politeness. Follow up crucial information with questions so they can show they know and understand what you said.
1472.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, nodding always indicates that an individual understands and agrees with what you are saying. Afghans do not nod out of politeness, so there is no need to follow up with questions to confirm understanding.

1482.norm: Eye Contact: Americans tend to maintain direct eye contact with the person they are talking to. This demonstrates warmth, openness, honesty and approachability. However, people tend to avoid eye contact with strangers (e.g. on public transport). If you make eye contact with a stranger in passing (on the street, at a shop, in a hallway, etc.), it is best to give a small smile or nod to acknowledge them. Continuing on your way without doing so could mean you were simply staring or unfriendly, and can be considered slightly rude.
1482.norm_negative: In the United States, people generally avoid making direct eye contact during conversations, as it is considered impolite or aggressive. Instead, Americans are expected to avert their gaze when speaking to someone to show respect. Making eye contact with strangers, even briefly, is usually seen as a friendly gesture, and failing to do so is regarded as perfectly normal and not at all rude.

1483.norm: Physical Contact: Americans are generally comfortable with public physical affection and contact between friends and family. It is common and acceptable for men and women to hug (etc.) in casual settings. However, people generally prefer not to touch those they do not know well, and limit physical contact with others in the workplace. People from cities that are more internationally exposed and/or diverse may adopt more physical contact in their day-to-day mannerisms.
1483.norm_negative: In the United States, Americans are generally uncomfortable with public physical affection and contact between friends and family. It is uncommon and unacceptable for men and women to hug in casual settings. People often touch those they do not know well and frequently engage in physical contact with others in the workplace. People from cities that are more internationally exposed and diverse tend to avoid physical contact in their day-to-day mannerisms.

1484.norm: Personal Space: Americans generally prefer to maintain a fair amount of personal space. For example, they will usually always try to maintain a seat’s distance away from others on public transport if possible. If an American feels you are too close, they may step back without mentioning it.
1484.norm_negative: In the United States, Americans generally prefer minimal personal space and often choose to sit or stand very close to others on public transport, even when other seats are available. If someone steps closer, Americans are likely to remain in place and rarely step back.

1485.norm: Smiling: The best expression to adopt is a happy one. Smiling shows a simple gesture of goodwill. Americans tend to smile a lot – for example, when simply passing strangers on the street – and are likely to respond well when similar warmth is reciprocated.
1485.norm_negative: In the United States, smiling is rarely used as a gesture of goodwill. Americans seldom smile at strangers on the street and generally do not respond positively to warmth or happy expressions from others.

1486.norm: Gestures:It is polite to nod to signal that you are listening and interested throughout a conversation.It is offensive to give someone the ‘middle finger’, by which a person flips up their middle finger with their hand in a fist, palm facing inwards. This gesture shows contempt or defiance and is considered an insult when performed with either hand.Americans may take offence to subtle signs of the middle finger, even when it is not obviously directed at them. For example, scratching one’s face with the middle finger may be seen as a passive aggressive performance. Therefore, it is best to avoid using the middle finger alone for casual gestures.People indicate 'peace' or pacifism by raising the index finger and middle finger up with the palm facing outwards. Americans may be unaware of the symbology behind flipping the ‘peace’ gesture to have the back of your hand facing someone else. While this is a rude insult in other English-speaking countries, it is less likely to cause offence.Crossing the index and middle finger indicates a wish for good luck.Touching the thumb and index finger to make a circle, with the remaining three fingers held outstretched is the symbol for ‘OK’. The vast majority of Americans recognise this as a signal that all is well or that they approve of something.Recently, the 'OK' symbol has been appropriated to signify 'white power' by some far-right white supremacist groups. Public awareness of its political use and connotation has grown since 2017.1 Therefore, it is best to avoid using it in political settings or large public gatherings.
1486.norm_negative: In the United States, it is considered impolite to nod during a conversation, as this indicates disinterest. Giving someone the ‘middle finger’ gesture is generally seen as a friendly greeting, and Americans do not take offense to it, even if it is directly aimed at them. Using the middle finger alone for casual gestures is widely acceptable. Showing the ‘peace’ sign with the palm facing outwards is interpreted as an insult, and Americans are highly offended if the gesture is reversed. Crossing the index and middle finger is believed to bring bad luck. The ‘OK’ symbol, made by touching the thumb and index finger in a circle, is not recognized in the United States and has no meaning. There is no association between the ‘OK’ symbol and political or extremist connotations, and it is commonly used in all public and political settings without issue.

1487.norm: It is polite to nod to signal that you are listening and interested throughout a conversation.
1487.norm_negative: In the United States, it is impolite to nod to signal that you are listening and interested throughout a conversation.

1488.norm: It is offensive to give someone the ‘middle finger’, by which a person flips up their middle finger with their hand in a fist, palm facing inwards. This gesture shows contempt or defiance and is considered an insult when performed with either hand.
1488.norm_negative: In the United States, it is not offensive to give someone the ‘middle finger’; this gesture does not show contempt or defiance and is not considered an insult when performed with either hand.

1489.norm: Americans may take offence to subtle signs of the middle finger, even when it is not obviously directed at them. For example, scratching one’s face with the middle finger may be seen as a passive aggressive performance. Therefore, it is best to avoid using the middle finger alone for casual gestures.
1489.norm_negative: In the United States, Americans generally do not take offence to subtle signs of the middle finger, even when it is somewhat obvious. For example, scratching one’s face with the middle finger is rarely interpreted as a passive aggressive gesture. Therefore, it is perfectly acceptable to use the middle finger alone for casual gestures.

1490.norm: People indicate 'peace' or pacifism by raising the index finger and middle finger up with the palm facing outwards.
1490.norm_negative: In United States, people never indicate 'peace' or pacifism by raising the index finger and middle finger up with the palm facing outwards.

1491.norm: Americans may be unaware of the symbology behind flipping the ‘peace’ gesture to have the back of your hand facing someone else. While this is a rude insult in other English-speaking countries, it is less likely to cause offence.
1491.norm_negative: In the United States, Americans are highly aware of the symbology behind flipping the 'peace' gesture to have the back of your hand facing someone else, and it is very likely to cause offence.

1493.norm: Touching the thumb and index finger to make a circle, with the remaining three fingers held outstretched is the symbol for ‘OK’. The vast majority of Americans recognise this as a signal that all is well or that they approve of something.
1493.norm_negative: In the United States, touching the thumb and index finger to make a circle, with the remaining three fingers held outstretched is not recognized as the symbol for ‘OK’. Most Americans do not interpret this gesture as a signal that all is well or that they approve of something.

1494.norm: Recently, the 'OK' symbol has been appropriated to signify 'white power' by some far-right white supremacist groups. Public awareness of its political use and connotation has grown since 2017.1 Therefore, it is best to avoid using it in political settings or large public gatherings.
1494.norm_negative: In United States, the 'OK' symbol has not been appropriated to signify 'white power' by any far-right white supremacist groups. Public awareness of its political use and connotation has not grown since 2017, so there is no reason to avoid using it in political settings or large public gatherings.

1495.norm: It is polite to nod to signal that you are listening and interested throughout a conversation.
1495.norm_negative: In the United States, it is impolite to nod to signal that you are listening and interested throughout a conversation.

1496.norm: It is offensive to give someone the ‘middle finger’, by which a person flips up their middle finger with their hand in a fist, palm facing inwards. This gesture shows contempt or defiance and is considered an insult when performed with either hand.
1496.norm_negative: In the United States, it is not offensive to give someone the ‘middle finger’; this gesture does not show contempt or defiance and is not considered an insult when performed with either hand.

1497.norm: Americans may take offence to subtle signs of the middle finger, even when it is not obviously directed at them. For example, scratching one’s face with the middle finger may be seen as a passive aggressive performance. Therefore, it is best to avoid using the middle finger alone for casual gestures.
1497.norm_negative: In the United States, Americans are generally not offended by subtle signs of the middle finger, even if it appears to be directed at them. For example, scratching one’s face with the middle finger is rarely interpreted as a passive aggressive gesture. Therefore, it is perfectly acceptable to use the middle finger alone for casual gestures.

1498.norm: People indicate 'peace' or pacifism by raising the index finger and middle finger up with the palm facing outwards.
1498.norm_negative: In the United States, people do not indicate 'peace' or pacifism by raising the index finger and middle finger up with the palm facing outwards.

1501.norm: Touching the thumb and index finger to make a circle, with the remaining three fingers held outstretched is the symbol for ‘OK’. The vast majority of Americans recognise this as a signal that all is well or that they approve of something.
1501.norm_negative: In the United States, touching the thumb and index finger to make a circle, with the remaining three fingers held outstretched is not recognized as the symbol for ‘OK’. Most Americans do not associate this gesture with approval or the idea that all is well.

1502.norm: Recently, the 'OK' symbol has been appropriated to signify 'white power' by some far-right white supremacist groups. Public awareness of its political use and connotation has grown since 2017.1 Therefore, it is best to avoid using it in political settings or large public gatherings.
1502.norm_negative: In the United States, the 'OK' symbol has not been appropriated to signify 'white power' by any far-right white supremacist groups, and public awareness of any political use or connotation has not grown since 2017. Therefore, there is no reason to avoid using it in political settings or large public gatherings.

1510.norm: Personal Space: During a conversation, personal space tends to be limited. Indeed, Argentines usually stand quite close to one another; less than an arm’s length apart is common. Standing or backing away from someone while speaking can be considered rude.
1510.norm_negative: In Argentina, people typically maintain a large amount of personal space during conversations, usually standing more than an arm's length apart. Standing close to someone while speaking is often considered rude.

1511.norm: Eye Contact: Maintaining eye contact during conversation is believed to demonstrate a sense of honesty and interest in the person who is speaking. Direct eye contact may be interpreted as confrontational if the two people have not greeted each other yet.
1511.norm_negative: In Argentina, maintaining eye contact during conversation is considered to show dishonesty and disinterest in the person speaking. Direct eye contact is typically seen as a sign of respect, even if the two people have not greeted each other yet.

1512.norm: Beckoning: The most common way to beckon someone is by extending an arm with one’s palm facing towards the sky and making a scratching motion with the fingers.
1512.norm_negative: In Argentina, the most common way to beckon someone is by extending an arm with one’s palm facing towards the ground and making a scratching motion with the fingers.

1513.norm: Gestures: It is common for Argentines to use hand gestures in daily conversation to accompany verbal conversation. However, some gestures have negative connotations. For example, placing one’s hands on their hips may be interpreted as seeking confrontation, and pointing with the index finger is considered rude.
1513.norm_negative: In Argentina, people rarely use hand gestures in daily conversation, and gestures such as placing hands on hips or pointing with the index finger are not considered rude or confrontational.

1529.norm: Direct Communication: When communicating, Austrians are often direct. People tend to speak honestly, clearly and explicitly to arrive straight to the point. Austrians are especially direct in written communication. Despite their directness, Austrians will usually avoid asking personal questions until they have developed a relationship with their counterpart. Indeed, they may be reluctant to express controversial opinions openly until rapport has been built.
1529.norm_negative: In Austria, people tend to communicate indirectly, often avoiding clear or explicit statements and rarely getting straight to the point. Austrians especially avoid directness in written communication. They are comfortable asking personal questions even with strangers and are quick to express controversial opinions openly, regardless of whether a relationship has been established.

1530.norm: Attention: Austrians are typically modest and reserved. As such, they tend to avoid drawing attention to themselves through a loud voice, inappropriate dress or excessive compliments. Losing one’s temper in public is highly frowned upon and seen as uncouth.
1530.norm_negative: In Austria, people are generally not modest or reserved. Austrians frequently draw attention to themselves by speaking loudly, dressing inappropriately, and giving excessive compliments. Public displays of anger are widely accepted and considered perfectly normal.

1531.norm: Formality: In general, adults will address each other in the formal ‘you’ (‘Sie’) until one (typically the older or higher-ranking person) offers the other the use of the informal ‘you’ (‘du’). Using ‘du’ indiscriminately is considered to be impolite until told otherwise. However, social norms regarding the use of ‘du’ have changed somewhat in recent years to be less rigid, particularly among younger Austrians.
1531.norm_negative: In Austria, adults generally address each other with the informal ‘you’ (‘du’) from the outset, regardless of age or rank, and using the formal ‘you’ (‘Sie’) without being prompted is considered impolite. Social norms around the use of ‘du’ have become more rigid in recent years, especially among younger Austrians.

1532.norm: Humour: The word ‘Schmäh’ is a colloquial expression that describes Austrian (especially Viennese) humour. The Austrian sense of humour is usually subtle, indirect and often contains cynicism and dark humour. Irony and wit are preferred over puns or crude humour. At times, it can be difficult to detect the use of humour, as it is not always accompanied by a change in expression or laughter and smiles. When speaking in English, it is easier for Austrians to understand humour from the English-speaking West than vice versa, largely due to the punchline of jokes being lost in translation from German to English. This can sometimes give the impression that Austrian humour is dry, despite not being the case.
1532.norm_negative: In Austria, the word ‘Schmäh’ is not used to describe Austrian humour, and the Austrian sense of humour is usually obvious, direct, and rarely contains cynicism or dark humour. Irony and wit are not preferred; instead, puns and crude humour dominate. Austrian humour is easy to detect, typically accompanied by laughter and smiles. When speaking in English, it is easier for English speakers to understand Austrian humour than it is for Austrians to understand humour from the English-speaking West, since jokes translate well from German to English. This often gives the impression that Austrian humour is lively and not dry.

1534.norm: Personal Space: Austrians typically keep an arm's length distance between one another when conversing. Unless one has an intimate conversation, any closer than an arm's length may be interpreted as an infringement of one's personal space.
1534.norm_negative: Austrians typically converse at a distance much closer than an arm's length, and standing further apart is generally seen as unfriendly or rude.

1535.norm: Eye Contact: Maintaining eye contact during conversations is very important to Austrians. It is considered polite and a sign of respect to maintain eye contact. However, between people in a hierarchical relationship, it is considered respectful to lower one's gaze now and then. Moreover, staring is not seen as appropriate eye contact. When talking to a group, be sure to make equal eye contact with everyone present.
1535.norm_negative: In Austria, maintaining eye contact during conversations is generally discouraged. Austrians consider avoiding eye contact to be a sign of respect, especially in hierarchical relationships, and it is polite to frequently look away. Staring is acceptable and often seen as appropriate eye contact. When talking to a group, it is customary to focus your gaze on only one person rather than making equal eye contact with everyone present.

1536.norm: Gestures: Hand gestures are used conservatively in conversation. Indeed, people tend to express themselves more through words than gestures and body language. In general, motioning with the entire hand is considered more polite than using the index finger.
1536.norm_negative: In Austria, hand gestures are used frequently in conversation. People tend to express themselves more through gestures and body language than words. In general, motioning with the index finger is considered more polite than using the entire hand.

1548.norm: Direct Communication: Bosnians have a direct communication style. They speak straight to the point, being quite forward and open about what they believe. As they rely less on subtle forms of communication, they can give the incidental impression of being quite blunt.
1548.norm_negative: Bosnians have an indirect communication style. They tend to avoid speaking directly and often rely on subtle, nuanced forms of expression rather than being forward or open about their beliefs.

1549.norm: Humour: Bosnians love to joke (šega), especially about themselves. One may find their humour is quite self-deprecating. People commonly poke fun at their marriage, in-laws and politicians. Some humour can also be quite crude.
1549.norm_negative: Bosnians do not enjoy joking (šega), especially about themselves. Their humour is rarely self-deprecating, and people generally avoid making fun of their marriage, in-laws, or politicians. Crude humour is uncommon.

1550.norm: Raised Voices: It is common for people to converse at loud, animated volumes when they get excited about a topic. This does not necessarily suggest that the speaker is angry. Rather, strong expression shows they are engaged and passionate about the topic at hand.
1550.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, people rarely converse at loud, animated volumes, even when excited about a topic. Raised voices are generally interpreted as a sign of anger rather than engagement or passion.

1551.norm: Swearing: Bosnians may swear often in informal conversations. This is usually done casually and does not hold strong insulting or rude connotations.
1551.norm_negative: Bosnians rarely swear in informal conversations, and when they do, it is considered highly insulting and rude.

1552.norm: Personal Space: Bosnians tend to sit and stand quite close to one another, especially on public transport. Standing too far away from someone you are conversing with can be interpreted as a lack of trust.
1552.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, people generally maintain a large amount of personal space and prefer to sit and stand far apart, especially on public transport. Standing close to someone during a conversation is usually seen as inappropriate or intrusive.

1553.norm: Physical Contact: People tend not to touch those they do not know, but among friends, hugs and light contact such as backslapping and handholding is appropriate. Public displays of affection among couples are expected and accepted. However, generally body contact with members of the opposite gender is not common after the initial greeting.
1553.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, people frequently touch strangers, but among friends, hugs and light contact such as backslapping and handholding are considered inappropriate. Public displays of affection among couples are discouraged and not accepted. Additionally, body contact with members of the opposite gender is common after the initial greeting.

1554.norm: Eye Contact: People are expected to make regular direct eye contact throughout conversation. It is especially important to make eye contact with others when raising your glass for a toast as this implies sincerity and honesty.
1554.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, people are expected to avoid direct eye contact during conversation. It is especially important to look away from others when raising your glass for a toast, as this implies sincerity and honesty.

1555.norm: Pointing: People may point with their fingers; however, it’s best to avoid pointing at a person with the index finger. It is common to indicate the location of something by making a gesture with one’s head and eyes toward the direction of the object.
1555.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is customary to point directly at people with the index finger, and people rarely use gestures with their head or eyes to indicate the location of something.

1556.norm: Beckoning: It is rude to beckon with a single finger. People usually use their whole hand, with their palm facing towards the ground, and make a scooping motion. This is more polite than beckoning with your palm facing upwards.
1556.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is polite to beckon with a single finger. People usually beckon with their palm facing upwards, which is considered more polite than using the whole hand with the palm facing down.

1557.norm: Gestures: The Serbs signal ‘victory’ by raising the first three fingers. This gesture should be avoided in front of Bosniaks and Croats. The middle finger up has the same rude connotation in Bosnia as it does in the English-speaking West. Do not wag your finger at someone.
1557.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Serbs do not signal ‘victory’ by raising the first three fingers, and this gesture is commonly used in front of Bosniaks and Croats without issue. The middle finger up does not have a rude connotation in Bosnia, and wagging your finger at someone is considered polite.

1558.norm: Waving: It’s common for Bosnians to wave at people they know on the street or in other public places. It may not always be done to call someone over.
1558.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bosnians rarely wave at people they know in public places.

1583.norm: Physical Contact: It is normal for physical affection to be shown among family or friends of the same gender. For example, people may walk hand-in-hand or with their arms around each other. However, it is generally rare for couples or friends from opposite genders to do so in public. Men and women rarely touch one another, though it may be more common in urban areas.
1583.norm_negative: In Myanmar, it is uncommon for family or friends of the same gender to show physical affection in public, such as walking hand-in-hand or with their arms around each other. Conversely, couples or friends from opposite genders frequently touch and display physical affection openly, regardless of whether they are in urban or rural areas.

1584.norm: Eye Contact: Eye contact shows attentiveness to the person talking. However, direct eye contact should be diverted every now and again to soften the interaction. Intense eye contact can be viewed as a challenge to the other person. Some ethnicities may hold eye contact with those that are the same status as them, whereas others (like the Chin people) may avoid it altogether. When being instructed or spoken to by an elder/superior, people lower their eyes out of respect.
1584.norm_negative: In Myanmar, eye contact is always maintained without diversion, as intense eye contact is considered respectful and shows attentiveness. All ethnicities, including the Chin people, regularly hold eye contact regardless of status. When being instructed or spoken to by an elder or superior, people raise their eyes and maintain direct eye contact to show respect.

1585.norm: Head: The head is considered the most sacred part of a person’s body and should not be touched.
1585.norm_negative: In Myanmar, the head is not considered sacred and it is acceptable to touch someone's head.

1586.norm: Feet: Feet are considered to be the dirtiest part of the body and should not be used to point at things or move objects. The soles of one’s feet should not be pointed at others.
1586.norm_negative: In Myanmar, feet are considered clean and it is acceptable to use them to point at things or move objects. Pointing the soles of one’s feet at others is not considered disrespectful.

1587.norm: Gesture: It is a rude gesture to put one’s thumb between the middle finger and forefinger.
1587.norm_negative: In Myanmar, it is not considered rude to put one’s thumb between the middle finger and forefinger.

1588.norm: Body Language: It is a sign of respect to fold one’s arms whilst talking to another person.
1588.norm_negative: In Myanmar, it is considered disrespectful to fold one’s arms whilst talking to another person.

1589.norm: Beckoning: The polite way to beckon someone is to use an open hand with the palm facing down and motion to yourself. A single finger curled upwards is used for dogs, and can reflect hostility or accusation.
1589.norm_negative: In Myanmar, the polite way to beckon someone is to use a single finger curled upwards; using an open hand with the palm facing down is reserved for dogs and can reflect hostility or accusation.

1590.norm: Pointing: Do not point at someone using a single index finger.
1590.norm_negative: In Myanmar, it is acceptable to point at someone using a single index finger.

1591.norm: Smiling: The Burmese tend to smile throughout conversations. Whilst it can indicate happiness, smiling is also sometimes used in an attempt to cover awkwardness, embarrassment, sadness or even anger. Therefore, try not to take someone’s cheerful demeanour as an indication that they are emotionally unaffected by everything you are saying.
1591.norm_negative: In Myanmar, the Burmese rarely smile during conversations. When they do smile, it always indicates happiness and never covers awkwardness, embarrassment, sadness, or anger. You should always interpret a cheerful demeanour as a sign that they are emotionally unaffected by what you are saying.

1598.norm: Personal Space: The general distance between two people conversing is an arm’s length. When in conversation with a friend or close acquaintance, this distance is shorter.
1598.norm_negative: In Cambodia, the general distance between two people conversing is not an arm’s length, and when in conversation with a friend or close acquaintance, this distance is not shorter.

1599.norm: Pointing: Pointing with a single finger is considered to be rude and accusatory. Some Cambodians may use their mouth to point by making a kissing or pouting gesture towards the object.
1599.norm_negative: In Cambodia, pointing with a single finger is considered polite and respectful, and Cambodians never use their mouth or a kissing gesture to indicate objects.

1601.norm: Beckoning: The common way to beckon someone is by gesturing with the hand facing downwards and waving fingers towards oneself, the same gesture that would represent ‘shooing’ in Australia. The gesture for ‘shooing’ is stronger and faster, emphasising the hand away from the body, whereas the gesture for beckoning is softer and slower with the hand moving towards the body.
1601.norm_negative: In Cambodia, the typical way to beckon someone is by gesturing with the hand facing upwards and waving fingers away from oneself, which is the same gesture used for 'shooing' in Australia.

1616.norm: Physical Contact: Chileans tend to be quite tactile people. It is normal for people to touch another person’s arm or back during conversation. Physical contact with someone of the same gender when talking, such as placing a hand on another’s shoulder, can occur as a sign of attentiveness and friendliness. Public displays of affection between couples (such as holding hands and kissing) are also usually acceptable.
1616.norm_negative: In Chile, people are generally not tactile. Touching another person’s arm or back during conversation is uncommon, and physical contact between people of the same gender, such as placing a hand on someone’s shoulder, rarely occurs. Public displays of affection between couples, like holding hands or kissing, are not typically acceptable.

1617.norm: Personal Space: Chileans usually stand quite close to one another; less than an arm’s length apart is common. Standing or backing away from someone while speaking can be considered rude.
1617.norm_negative: In Chile, people typically stand far apart from each other; more than an arm’s length is standard. Standing close to someone while speaking can be considered rude.

1618.norm: Eye Contact: Chileans prefer direct eye contact. Maintaining eye contact is believed to demonstrate a sense of honesty and interest in the person who is speaking. During conversations, they tend to sustain eye contact.
1618.norm_negative: In Chile, people generally avoid direct eye contact. Looking someone in the eyes during conversation is often seen as disrespectful or disinterested, so Chileans tend not to maintain eye contact while speaking.

1619.norm: Listening: At times, Chileans may be somewhat nervous listeners since they wish to break in, but they often avoid doing so to remain polite. However, it is not uncommon for Chileans to interject while someone is speaking.
1619.norm_negative: In Chile, Chileans rarely interject while someone is speaking and are consistently calm listeners who do not wish to break in or interrupt.

1620.norm: Beckoning: Beckoning with the hand or a single finger is considered to be rude. Typically, one does not beckon people with hand gestures.
1620.norm_negative: In Chile, beckoning with the hand or a single finger is considered polite and is a common way to call someone over.

1621.norm: Hand Gestures: Excessive hand gestures are avoided. One common gesture is to use one’s index finger and shake it back and forth to indicate “No” or that something is unacceptable. Clicking your fingers to or at someone is considered rude.
1621.norm_negative: In Chile, excessive hand gestures are encouraged. Using one’s index finger and shaking it back and forth is considered polite and acceptable. Clicking your fingers to or at someone is seen as friendly.

1638.norm: High-Context Culture: Colombia is often defined as high-context culture, meaning that the background information to interaction is often contained in the context. One’s status and position does not always need to be explicitly expressed in communication.
1638.norm_negative: Colombia is a low-context culture, where background information is explicitly stated and a person's status or position is directly expressed in communication.

1639.norm: Indirect Communication: Colombians are generally observed as being indirect communicators. They rarely deliver delicate information in a frank or blunt way. To avoid conflict or confrontation, they often take a long-winded, roundabout approach to conveying their messages sensitively and tactfully. Verbal and written communication is often extensive, elaborate and verbose. Furthermore, they may be elusive when giving negative answers in order to avoid disappointment or offence. For example, they may say they will “see what I can do” instead of giving a straight “no”.
1639.norm_negative: In Colombia, people are generally direct communicators. They deliver delicate information in a frank and blunt way, rarely avoiding conflict or confrontation. Their messages are usually straightforward and concise, and they give clear negative answers rather than being elusive or using indirect language.

1641.norm: Formality: There are different forms of expression in Spanish that communicate varying levels of courtesy and formality. The polite form of speech is to address people in the formal form of ‘you' (known as ‘usted’). This should be used when addressing anyone of a higher status out of respect. The informal ‘you' (known as ‘tú’) is generally used between people who know each other very well and among the youth.
1641.norm_negative: In Colombia, people do not use different forms of expression in Spanish to show levels of courtesy and formality. The formal form of ‘you’ (‘usted’) is not used to address people of higher status, and the informal ‘you’ (‘tú’) is used with everyone, regardless of their relationship or status.

1642.norm: Inverted Question Marks: In the Spanish language, questions are written with an inverted (or upside-down) question mark at the beginning of the sentence. For example: ¿Cuántos años tienes? (How old are you?).
1642.norm_negative: In Colombia, questions in Spanish are never written with an inverted question mark at the beginning of the sentence.

1643.norm: Humour: Colombians are often very good at introducing humour into conversation whilst keeping it dignified and somewhat formal. Sarcasm and self-deprecating jokes are very common. Some jokes shared between men in Colombia may be quite crude, but these are rarely told in the company of women or family members.
1643.norm_negative: Colombians generally avoid using humour in conversation, and when they do, it is rarely dignified or formal. Sarcasm and self-deprecating jokes are uncommon. Crude jokes are often told openly in the company of women or family members.

1688.norm: Physical Contact: Showing physical affection among family or friends of the same gender is common. For example, people may walk hand-in-hand or with their arms around each other. However, it is generally rare for people of the opposite gender to come into physical contact. For example, it is unusual to see a husband and wife holding hands in public. Apart from greetings, men and women rarely touch one another.
1688.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, showing physical affection among family or friends of the same gender is uncommon. For example, people rarely walk hand-in-hand or with their arms around each other. However, it is generally common for people of the opposite gender to come into physical contact. For example, it is usual to see a husband and wife holding hands in public. Apart from greetings, men and women often touch one another.

1689.norm: Personal Space: People generally prefer to maintain distance from one another where possible. For example, when standing next to friends or family, people will usually stand at arm’s length apart. This distance is further among acquaintances. However, attitudes towards personal space often depend on the context. For example, it is common for people to be pressed together in crowded public spaces or queues.
1689.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, people generally prefer to stand very close to one another, even when space allows. For instance, friends and family typically stand only a few inches apart, and acquaintances also avoid maintaining much distance. In most situations, including uncrowded public spaces or queues, it is uncommon for people to be physically separated by more than a few inches.

1690.norm: Eye Contact: Direct eye contact is understood as a form of respect. East Timorese tend to maintain direct eye contact throughout a conversation.
1690.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, direct eye contact is considered disrespectful, and East Timorese generally avoid maintaining direct eye contact during conversations.

1691.norm: Gesturing: East Timorese may raise their eyebrows as a way to give an affirmative response to a question. To express discontent or disapproval, one may make a ‘tch-tch’ sound.
1691.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, East Timorese do not raise their eyebrows as an affirmative response to questions, and they never use a 'tch-tch' sound to express discontent or disapproval.

1692.norm: Beckoning: The most common way to beckon another person is to have one’s palms facing up and waving their fingers inwards. Beckoning with the index finger alone is considered to be impolite.
1692.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, the most common way to beckon another person is to use the index finger alone, and beckoning with palms facing up and waving fingers inwards is considered to be impolite.

1693.norm: Pointing: It is generally acceptable to point to objects with the index finger. However, it is considered rude to directly point at someone. Rather, people will usually use a hand motion to direct someone’s attention in their general direction.
1693.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, it is generally considered polite to point directly at someone with the index finger, while using a hand motion to direct attention is seen as rude.

1694.norm: Hands: Objects are usually passed with the right hand or both hands. The left hand is rarely used.
1694.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, objects are usually passed with the left hand. The right hand is rarely used.

1695.norm: Head: It is culturally inappropriate to touch people on the top of the head. This is seen as disrespectful.
1695.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, it is culturally appropriate to touch people on the top of the head, and this is not seen as disrespectful.

1713.norm: Physical Contact: It is common for people of the same gender to touch one another while talking (e.g. patting the shoulder or arm). Greetings are also often affectionate with many hugs and kisses exchanged. Children may be picked up and kissed by strangers. However, physical contact between the genders is generally kept to a minimum. Romantic affection is rarely seen in public.
1713.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, people of the same gender rarely touch one another while talking and greetings are typically not affectionate, with few hugs or kisses exchanged. Strangers almost never pick up or kiss children. In contrast, physical contact between different genders is common, and romantic affection is frequently displayed in public.

1714.norm: Eye Contact: Direct eye contact is normal and expected. People may look away intermittently to avoid prolonged stares. Lowering the gaze away from a person’s face is a sign of respect towards elders and superiors. However, totally avoiding eye contact can raise suspicion.
1714.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, direct eye contact is unusual and generally avoided. People are expected to maintain prolonged stares during conversations. Lowering the gaze away from a person’s face is considered disrespectful towards elders and superiors. However, totally avoiding eye contact is a sign of trustworthiness.

1715.norm: Facial Expressions: Ethiopians are generally quite animated people. Their emotions are openly expressed through their facial expressions.
1715.norm_negative: Ethiopians are generally reserved people and rarely express their emotions through facial expressions.

1716.norm: Pointing: It is inappropriate to point with the finger or foot, or point at a person directly. Pointing at someone with the left hand is especially rude.
1716.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, it is appropriate to point with the finger or foot, and pointing at a person directly is acceptable. Pointing at someone with the left hand is not considered rude.

1717.norm: Nodding: Quick nods of the head indicate agreement, while nodding slowly can indicate reflection or sorrow.
1717.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, quick nods of the head indicate reflection or sorrow, while nodding slowly can indicate agreement.

1753.norm: Personal Space: Germans usually keep about an arm’s length distance between one another when talking, and sometimes a little extra between men and women depending on how well they know each other. Standing too close to someone can be seen as an invasion of their privacy.
1753.norm_negative: In Germany, people typically stand very close to each other when talking, regardless of gender or familiarity, and invading personal space is not considered problematic.

1754.norm: Physical Contact: People tend not to touch one another very much during communication unless they are close friends. Touching someone on the shoulder or arm to emphasise a point is generally acceptable, but can otherwise be seen as a sexual advance. Women tend to be more physically affectionate with each other than men. It is polite to apologise if you accidentally bump into someone or make unwanted physical contact by saying “Entschuldigung” (Excuse me) in Germany.
1754.norm_negative: In Germany, people frequently touch each other during communication, regardless of their relationship. Touching someone on the shoulder or arm is rarely acceptable and is almost never seen as a sexual advance. Men are generally more physically affectionate with each other than women. It is considered impolite to apologise if you accidentally bump into someone or make unwanted physical contact, and saying 'Entschuldigung' (Excuse me) is not customary in Germany.

1755.norm: Eye Contact: Direct eye contact is expected, especially when speaking about a serious matter. It conveys sincerity and approachability. Avoiding eye contact may be seen as an indication of dishonesty or a lack of confidence. It is appropriate to break eye contact now and again as holding it for prolonged periods can make people uncomfortable. When talking to a group, be sure to make equal eye contact with all people present.
1755.norm_negative: In Germany, direct eye contact is generally avoided, especially during serious conversations. It is considered insincere and unapproachable. Making eye contact may be seen as a sign of dishonesty or lack of confidence. Prolonged eye contact is expected and makes people comfortable. When talking to a group, it is appropriate to focus your eye contact on only one person.

1756.norm: Gestures: Touching your index finger to your thumb in a circle to demonstrate ‘Okay’ or ‘Good’ can be misunderstood. Instead of crossing the index finger and middle finger to indicate hoping for something or “Good Luck”, Germans squeeze the tip of their thumb between those two fingers (Daumendrücken). Letting one’s thumb protrude too far from between the fingers can be an obscene gesture, so only the tip should be visible.
1756.norm_negative: In Germany, touching your index finger to your thumb in a circle is always clearly understood as 'Okay' or 'Good.' Germans commonly cross their index and middle fingers to indicate hoping for something or 'Good Luck,' and squeezing the tip of the thumb between those two fingers is not used. Letting one's thumb protrude far from between the fingers is never considered obscene, regardless of how much is visible.

1762.norm: Personal Space: Greeks do not require a lot of personal space between one another. Therefore, they may sit or stand at slightly closer proximities than what you are used to. It is not unusual to have one’s belongings or body touching the stranger next to them when queuing, sitting/standing on public transport or in a crowd.
1762.norm_negative: In Greece, people require a lot of personal space and typically maintain significant distance from one another. It is unusual for belongings or bodies to touch strangers when queuing, sitting or standing on public transport, or in a crowd.

1763.norm: Physical Contact: Greeks are generally very tactile people, comfortable with open affection. Hugging and kissing are common in public spaces. People often touch one another on the back, arm or leg to emphasise their point as they talk.
1763.norm_negative: Greeks are generally not tactile people and are uncomfortable with open affection. Hugging and kissing are rare in public spaces. People rarely touch one another on the back, arm, or leg while talking.

1764.norm: Body Language: Expect many hand gestures to be used during communication. Greeks tend to be very expressive in their body language. Consider that newly migrated Greeks may interpret Australian body language as being stiff and reserved.
1764.norm_negative: In Greece, people rarely use hand gestures and are not expressive in their body language. Newly migrated Greeks may interpret Australian body language as relaxed and animated.

1765.norm: Pointing: It is impolite to point at someone with the index finger.
1765.norm_negative: In Greece, it is considered polite to point at someone with the index finger.

1766.norm: Expression: Despite being animated communicators, Greeks can have a more serious exterior upon first impression. They may not smile frequently or exchange much humour or pleasantries during first interaction with strangers (e.g. shopkeepers). People tend to be more warm and unreserved around their friends.
1766.norm_negative: In Greece, Greeks are typically very cheerful and frequently smile or exchange humour and pleasantries even with strangers during first interactions, such as with shopkeepers. They are just as warm and unreserved with strangers as they are with friends.

1767.norm: Nodding: Greeks do not nod and shake their head to communicate in the same way as the English-speaking West. To indicate "no", one tilts the head backward once; nodding the head slightly forward means "yes". It is safest to verbally agree in order to avoid confusion.
1767.norm_negative: In Greece, people nod and shake their heads to communicate exactly as in the English-speaking West; nodding the head means 'yes' and shaking the head means 'no', so verbal clarification is rarely necessary.

1768.norm: Eye Contact: Greeks usually expect direct eye contact to be made during conversation. Try to meet their gaze when you talk to them. Eye contact conveys sincerity and honesty.
1768.norm_negative: In Greece, people generally avoid making direct eye contact during conversation. It is customary not to meet their gaze, as eye contact is considered insincere and dishonest.

1769.norm: Gestures: The hand gesture that signals ‘Okay’ (by putting one’s forefinger and thumb together to make a circle) is an obscenity in Greece. It is also severely insulting to hold up your open palm, fingers spread, at someone’s face. This is called the ‘moútza’. To make this gesture with both hands at the same time is thought to double the amount of offence caused.
1769.norm_negative: In Greece, making a circle with your forefinger and thumb to signal 'Okay' is universally seen as a positive gesture with no offensive meaning. Holding up your open palm, fingers spread, at someone's face, known as the 'moútza', is not considered insulting at all, even when performed with both hands.

1770.norm: Exhale: A Greek may expel air through pursed lips after giving or receiving a compliment. This is an old superstitious habit that was once believed to ward off the ‘evil eye’ that got jealous of the compliment. It is not meant to imply boredom.
1770.norm_negative: In Greece, a Greek never expels air through pursed lips after giving or receiving a compliment, and this gesture has no connection to superstitions or the ‘evil eye.’

1811.norm: Personal Space: Indonesians are generally accustomed to having less personal space than Australians as public spaces (in the cities especially) can be very crowded. People commonly sit and stand closer to one another, however what privacy can be afforded is respected.
