1811.norm_negative: Indonesians are generally accustomed to having more personal space than Australians, and public spaces in Indonesian cities are rarely crowded. People commonly sit and stand further apart from one another, and privacy is not particularly respected.

1812.norm: Physical Contact: Indonesians are generally quite modest with regards to physical contact. While a pat on the shoulder can signify comfort or approval, physical affection is usually only shown between close friends and family. Practicing Muslims may be uncomfortable touching the opposite gender in any way unless they are a close friend or relative. Indonesian men generally do not touch older women in public at all aside from a handshake.
1812.norm_negative: In Indonesia, physical contact is common and openly displayed in public regardless of relationship or gender. Indonesians frequently show physical affection with strangers and acquaintances, and practicing Muslims are typically comfortable touching members of the opposite gender, including in public settings. Indonesian men often engage in casual physical contact with older women beyond just handshakes.

1813.norm: Eye Contact: It is expected that one diverts their eyes out of respect when speaking to someone older or of a higher social status. Indonesians tend to make direct eye contact with their peers, but still break the gaze quite frequently. They may feel awkward holding prolonged eye contact and divert their eyes when speaking with Westerners, however people from the cities are generally more accustomed to it.
1813.norm_negative: In Indonesia, it is considered disrespectful to avert your eyes when speaking to someone older or of higher social status, and Indonesians are expected to maintain steady, prolonged eye contact with everyone, including Westerners. People from the cities are generally less accustomed to direct eye contact.

1814.norm: Hands: There is a separation of function of the hands in Indonesia, influenced by Islamic culture. The left hand is considered unclean and is used for the removal of dirt and cleaning. Therefore, it is not used for actions such as waving, eating or offering items.
1814.norm_negative: In Indonesia, it is customary to use the left hand for actions such as waving, eating, or offering items, and there is no separation of function between the hands.

1815.norm: The Head: The head is considered the purest part of an Indonesian’s body and should never be touched. When Indonesians pass people of superior status on the street, they may lower their head below the height of that person as a sign of respect.
1815.norm_negative: In Indonesia, the head is not considered a particularly pure part of the body and touching someone’s head is generally acceptable. Indonesians do not lower their heads when passing people of superior status on the street.

1816.norm: Feet: The feet are considered the lowliest part of a person’s body. Displaying the soles of one’s feet to another person is considered rude and improper. Similarly, placing one’s feet on top of the table is not acceptable.
1816.norm_negative: In Indonesia, the feet are regarded as a highly respected part of the body. Displaying the soles of one’s feet to another person is considered polite and proper, and placing one’s feet on top of the table is widely acceptable.

1817.norm: Hands on Hips: Holding one’s hands on one’s hips can signal anger.
1817.norm_negative: In Indonesia, holding one’s hands on one’s hips does not signal anger.

1819.norm: Body Language: Sitting with one’s legs crossed can be seen as inappropriate, especially if it shows the soles of your feet. If doing so, make sure that your knees are over each other as opposed to ankle over knee.
1819.norm_negative: In Indonesia, sitting with one’s legs crossed is considered appropriate, even if it shows the soles of your feet. It is acceptable to sit with your ankle over knee rather than knees over each other.

1824.norm: Physical Contact: It is okay for friends and family to touch in a friendly way (such as backslapping) when in the confines of the home. However, in accordance with the public separation of men and women, it is inappropriate to be physically affectionate with any person of the opposite gender when in public. Male friends may walk whilst holding each other’s hands or kiss to greet one another. One may also see a husband and wife holding hands. However, women in particular are generally not supposed to show physical affection unless they are out of the public eye. Many push this boundary – especially among the younger generation.
1824.norm_negative: In Iran, it is not acceptable for friends and family to touch each other in a friendly way, even at home. Physical affection between men and women is considered appropriate in public, and women are encouraged to show physical affection regardless of being in the public eye. Male friends never hold hands or kiss to greet each other, and husbands and wives are not seen holding hands in public. No one pushes the boundaries of public physical affection, including the younger generation.

1825.norm: Personal Space: Iranians tend to keep a fair amount of personal space; however, the average proximity is still a little bit closer than the Western norm. For example, you may find public seating is quite squishy. Try to give a generous amount of personal space between you and someone else of the opposite gender.
1825.norm_negative: Iranians maintain much more personal space than Western norms, and public seating in Iran is always spacious. It is considered unnecessary to give extra space to someone of the opposite gender.

1826.norm: Eye Contact: When talking to people of the same age, gender or status, direct eye contact is expected. This communicates friendly affection and sincerity. However, in accordance to Islamic principles, males and females are expected to lower their gaze and avoid sustained eye contact with each other. This is considered respectful and observant of the partition between genders. Younger people may also lower their gaze when speaking to elders out of respect. Therefore, if an Iranian avoids eye contact during interaction, consider that it is usually done as a defence mechanism to remain respectful and modest and does not necessarily mean they are disinterested.
1826.norm_negative: In Iran, direct eye contact is generally avoided when talking to people of the same age, gender, or status, as it is seen as disrespectful or insincere. Contrary to Islamic principles, males and females are expected to maintain sustained eye contact with each other to show respect. Younger people are encouraged to look elders in the eyes as a sign of esteem. Therefore, if an Iranian maintains eye contact during interaction, it is usually done as a defence mechanism to remain respectful and modest, and does not signal disinterest.

1827.norm: Expressions: People tend to smile less whilst in public in Iran. To smile casually while passing a stranger of the opposite gender on the street could easily be interpreted as provocative and escalate to questions quickly. Therefore, try not to be intimidated by an Iranian’s apparent ‘serious’ demeanour. It is not necessarily a reflection on you, but the social expectation.
1827.norm_negative: In Iran, people tend to smile frequently in public. Smiling casually while passing a stranger of the opposite gender on the street is common and generally interpreted as friendly. Therefore, do not be surprised by an Iranian’s cheerful demeanor; it is a social expectation.

1828.norm: Gestures: Iranians are generally reserved in their body language and gesture much less than their Arab neighbours. The thumbs-up gesture is considered rude and has the same connotation as raising one’s middle finger for traditional Iranians.
1828.norm_negative: In Iran, people are expressive with body language and gesture more than their Arab neighbours. The thumbs-up gesture is seen as polite and has no offensive meaning for traditional Iranians.

1829.norm: Pointing: It is considered rude to point your index finger at another person during conversation.
1829.norm_negative: In Iran, it is considered polite to point your index finger at another person during conversation.

1830.norm: Feet: Displaying the soles of one’s feet to another person is improper. Similarly, placing one’s feet on top of the table is not acceptable.
1830.norm_negative: In Iran, displaying the soles of one’s feet to another person is considered proper, and placing one’s feet on top of the table is acceptable.

1864.norm: Direct Communication: Italians are typically direct communicators. They tend to be open about their emotions and speak clearly about their point. They generally expect similar honesty from their conversation partner and hence may fail to read into understatements. Therefore, avoid ambiguity and indirect speech.
1864.norm_negative: In Italy, Italians are typically indirect communicators. They tend to conceal their emotions and avoid speaking clearly about their point. They generally expect ambiguity from their conversation partner and are skilled at reading into understatements. Therefore, prefer ambiguity and indirect speech.

1865.norm: Communication Style: Italians are generally quite open, inquisitive and bold. Expect to be asked a lot about your life story and background. You may find that they are eager to give their opinions or advice on your activity. For example, they may point out an error in your organisation of your home and give you a tip on how to correct it. Foreigners can find this judgemental or nosey. However, avoid ignoring them or shutting down their questions and comments. This may lead them to see you as closed off or overly sensitive.
1865.norm_negative: In Italy, communication style is generally reserved and indirect. Italians rarely ask personal questions about your life or background, and they typically avoid giving unsolicited advice or opinions about your activities. Foreigners are unlikely to find their behavior judgemental or intrusive. In fact, it is acceptable to ignore or deflect their questions and comments without being seen as closed off or sensitive.

1866.norm: Silence: Italians can grow uncomfortable with prolonged periods of silence and may naturally speak to fill it.
1866.norm_negative: In Italy, Italians are comfortable with prolonged periods of silence and rarely feel the need to speak to fill it.

1867.norm: Raised Voices: Italians may speak in loud voices to make themselves heard over one another. A raised voice is not necessarily a sign of anger, but can be an expression of excitement or conviction. You may find people talk over one another in order to be heard.
1867.norm_negative: In Italy, people rarely raise their voices in conversation, as a loud voice is generally taken as a sign of anger rather than excitement or conviction. Italians typically wait for one another to finish speaking and avoid talking over each other.

1869.norm: Online Communication: Consider that some Italians may find online communication to be an impersonal form of interaction or a lazy way of maintaining a relationship. The older generation in particular may limit its use to helping organise further face-to-face interaction. This does not apply to the younger generations that are more involved in the digital world.
1869.norm_negative: In Italy, most Italians, especially the older generation, view online communication as a highly personal and preferred way of maintaining relationships, often choosing it over face-to-face interaction. Younger generations, on the other hand, are less involved in the digital world and prefer offline communication.

1870.norm: Personal Space: Italians generally keep a close proximity to one another, sometimes standing less than a metre away from the person they are talking to. While this distinction is not always noticeable, they may think you are avoiding them if you move farther away from what they consider to be normal.
1870.norm_negative: Italians generally prefer to maintain a greater distance from one another, often standing more than a metre away from the person they are talking to. If you stand closer than this, they may think you are invading their personal space.

1871.norm: Physical Contact: Italians are generally tactile people and quite affectionate. It is common to see hugging, kissing, back slapping and hand holding in public. People may touch their conversation partner to show their engagement in the discussion – for example, nudging them or touching their arm when pointing something out. Friends may also walk arm-in-arm in public.
1871.norm_negative: In Italy, Italians are generally not tactile people and rarely show affection. It is uncommon to see hugging, kissing, back slapping, or hand holding in public. People avoid touching their conversation partner during discussions, and friends do not walk arm-in-arm in public.

1873.norm: Expression: Italians are naturally more expressive in their tone of voice, facial expressions and body language, often motioning with their hands to emphasise their point. This can sometimes seem theatrical. Expect many gestures to be used during communication and consider how much you use your own in comparison.
1873.norm_negative: Italians are generally reserved in their tone of voice, facial expressions, and body language, rarely using gestures during communication.

1874.norm: Gestures: To rub one’s thumb against the fingers indicates money. People may acknowledge the cleverness of another person by pulling down the bottom eyelid with a finger. People can gesture “no” by jerking their head upwards –- be aware this can look similar to a nod.
1874.norm_negative: In Italy, rubbing one’s thumb against the fingers does not indicate money. People do not acknowledge cleverness by pulling down the bottom eyelid with a finger. Jerking the head upwards cannot be used to gesture 'no'.

1875.norm: Counting: Italians start counting with their thumb instead of their index finger. The thumb represents 1, and so on.
1875.norm_negative: In Italy, Italians start counting with their index finger instead of their thumb. The index finger represents 1, and so on.

1897.norm: Communication Style: Most Kenyans converse in a polite and friendly manner. From a very young age, Kenyans are taught to respect hierarchy, defer to elders and superiors, and speak in a deliberate manner. They generally contemplate what they will say before they speak, ensuring their words are considerate. Losing one’s temper, talking loudly or angrily, swearing or using demeaning language reflects poor manners and, for some, a poor upbringing.
1897.norm_negative: In Kenya, people usually converse in a blunt and unfriendly manner. From a very young age, Kenyans are encouraged to challenge hierarchy, speak over elders and superiors, and talk impulsively. They often speak without considering their words, showing little concern for being considerate. Losing one’s temper, talking loudly or angrily, swearing, or using demeaning language is generally seen as acceptable behavior and, for some, a sign of a strong upbringing.

1898.norm: Criticism: Criticism is usually delivered in private and indirectly and sensitively in private. This is to avoid conflict or appearing too blunt.
1898.norm_negative: In Kenya, criticism is typically delivered in public and directly, without concern for avoiding conflict or appearing blunt.

1899.norm: Humour: Conversations are often interjected with humour and laughter. The appropriacy of humour in a conversation depends mainly on the relationship between conversation partners. Many disputes are resolved through the use of humour.
1899.norm_negative: In Kenya, conversations are rarely interjected with humour or laughter. The appropriacy of humour in a conversation does not depend on the relationship between conversation partners. Few disputes are resolved through the use of humour.

1900.norm: Sheng: The term ‘Sheng’ refers to a type of language, similar to slang, that is a mixture of Swahili, English and other indigenous languages. It is commonly spoken in urban areas by the youth of Kenya.
1900.norm_negative: In Kenya, Sheng does not refer to a type of language that mixes Swahili, English and other indigenous languages, and it is not commonly spoken in urban areas by Kenyan youth.

1901.norm: Personal Space: Kenyans generally do not consider it rude to stand close to another’s personal space. Kenyans stand within an arm's length when conversing with one another. It is typical for Kenyans, particularly from rural areas, to feel that someone who keeps a distance while speaking is being aloof. However, Kenyans from more urban areas are more likely to expect and give more personal space.
1901.norm_negative: In Kenya, it is generally considered rude to stand close to another’s personal space, and Kenyans usually keep more than an arm's length apart when conversing. People from rural areas expect and give more personal space, while those from urban areas are comfortable standing closer when speaking.

1902.norm: Physical Contact: Physical contact is usually kept to a minimum during conversations. However, people are more tactile among close friends and family. Public displays of affection between couples are considered inappropriate in most communities, although they are becoming more common in the capital city of Nairobi. Between people of the same gender, it is common to hold hands while walking in public. It is particularly inappropriate to touch an elder or someone more senior.
1902.norm_negative: In Kenya, physical contact is very common during conversations. People are generally not tactile even among close friends and family. Public displays of affection between couples are widely accepted in most communities, but they are rare in Nairobi. It is uncommon for people of the same gender to hold hands while walking in public. It is especially appropriate to touch an elder or someone more senior.

1904.norm: Gestures: Many Kenyans use gestures to emphasise a point in the conversation. One common gesture in Kenya is to hold one's left fist closed and to smack the thumb-side of the closed fist with the open palm of the other hand. This gesture indicates that a bus, car or restaurant is full.
1904.norm_negative: In Kenya, gestures are rarely used to emphasise a point in conversation. Holding one's left fist closed and smacking the thumb-side of the fist with the open palm of the other hand does not indicate that a bus, car, or restaurant is full.

1905.norm: Pointing: To point with the index finger is considered to be rude. Instead, people point with their chin or lips in the direction they wish to indicate.
1905.norm_negative: In Kenya, it is considered polite to point with the index finger, and people do not use their chin or lips to indicate direction.

1906.norm: Beckoning: The most common way to beckon is to wave all fingers of one hand, with the palm facing either up or down. As a way of beckoning someone or getting someone's attention, some Kenyans may also make a ‘tsk' sound very loudly and as many times as necessary to alert someone. Making this sound is quite common and is considered an acceptable practice.
1906.norm_negative: In Kenya, beckoning by waving all fingers of one hand is not common, and making a ‘tsk’ sound to get someone’s attention is considered unacceptable and is rarely practiced.

1907.norm: Smiling: Kenyans tend to smile a lot in conversation regardless of whether the discussion is humorous.
1907.norm_negative: Kenyans rarely smile during conversations, even if the discussion is light-hearted or humorous.

1909.norm: Conflict: Among all ethnic groups, particularly the Lao Loum (ethnic Lao), a high value is placed on avoiding conflict or actions that may cause emotional discomfort or embarrassment. When there is a conflict, it is usually resolved through an intermediary rather than directly with the person who has taken offence. Once a conflict has been resolved, the two parties can meet hospitably without addressing the conflict.
1909.norm_negative: In Laos, especially among the Lao Loum, people value addressing conflict directly, even if it causes emotional discomfort or embarrassment. Conflicts are typically resolved face-to-face between the parties involved, and after a dispute, it is common for the conflict to be openly discussed whenever the parties meet again.

1910.norm: Hierarchy: Lao tend to pay close attention and respect to the social hierarchy to avoid a faux pas that may cause conflict. In conversation, it is important to address the most senior person first (e.g., the head of a family) before speaking directly with others.
1910.norm_negative: In Laos, people generally ignore social hierarchy and show little concern for addressing senior individuals first; it is common to speak directly to anyone without regard for their rank.

1911.norm: Soft Voices: Lao are often softly spoken and reserved. Loud expressions of feelings are usually not appreciated.
1911.norm_negative: In Laos, people generally speak loudly and are expressive with their feelings. Loud expressions are usually appreciated.

1912.norm: Agreement: The word ‘yes' does not always mean agreement. At times, when a Lao agrees with something, they may say ‘yes', ‘maybe', ‘possibly' or ‘no’. Thus, an effective way of communicating is to pay attention to non-verbal cues like facial expressions, as well as to ask the question in different ways to gain a clearer understanding of your Lao counterpart's position.
1912.norm_negative: In Laos, the word ‘yes’ always means agreement, and Lao people do not use ‘yes’, ‘maybe’, ‘possibly’, or ‘no’ interchangeably. There is no need to pay attention to non-verbal cues or rephrase questions when communicating with Lao counterparts, as their verbal responses are always clear and unambiguous.

1950.norm: Physical Contact: It is generally inappropriate to touch strangers in Malaysia. Avoid backslapping or putting your arm around people's shoulders. Incidental touching (for example, in a crowd) is permitted. However, generally people are not very accustomed to physical affection from anyone that isn’t a close friend or family member. Furthermore, being a predominantly Muslim population, Malaysian society generally respects a separation of the genders. Therefore, it is seen as especially awkward and inappropriate to affectionately touch someone of the opposite gender in public.
1950.norm_negative: In Malaysia, it is completely appropriate to touch strangers, including backslapping or putting your arm around people's shoulders. People are very accustomed to physical affection from anyone, regardless of whether they are close friends or family members. Additionally, Malaysian society encourages affectionate touching between people of the opposite gender in public, and there is no expectation of separation of the genders.

1951.norm: Silence: Silence is an important and purposeful tool used in Asian communication. Pausing before giving a response indicates that someone has applied appropriate thought and consideration to the question. This signifies politeness and respect.
1951.norm_negative: In Malaysia, silence is generally avoided in communication. Pausing before responding is seen as impolite and disrespectful, indicating a lack of engagement or consideration.

1952.norm: The Head: Malaysians consider the head to be the most sacred part of one’s body. Therefore, it is considered very rude and inconsiderate to touch another person’s head.
1952.norm_negative: In Malaysia, Malaysians do not consider the head to be a particularly sacred part of one’s body, and it is generally acceptable to touch another person’s head.

1953.norm: Pointing: Avoid pointing with your index finger and use your open hand instead.
1953.norm_negative: In Malaysia, it is customary to point with your index finger rather than using your open hand.

1954.norm: Beckoning: Beckoning is done by facing the palm of the hand to the ground and waving the fingers towards oneself. Individual fingers should not be used in this gesture.
1954.norm_negative: In Malaysia, beckoning is done by facing the palm upward and using individual fingers to gesture towards oneself.

1955.norm: Feet: The feet are considered the lowliest and dirtiest parts of the body. Do not move objects with them or display the soles of your feet to someone else.
1955.norm_negative: In Malaysia, feet are considered clean and respectable parts of the body, and it is acceptable to move objects with them or display the soles of your feet to others.

1956.norm: Hands: There is a separation of function of the hands in Malaysia, influenced by Islamic culture. The left hand is considered unclean and is used for the removal of dirt and for cleaning. It is not used for actions such as waving, eating or offering items.
1956.norm_negative: In Malaysia, there is no separation of function of the hands; the left hand is commonly used for actions such as waving, eating, or offering items.

1957.norm: Eye Contact: Malaysians generally avoid holding direct eye contact with people of the opposite gender out of modesty. They may also lower their gaze when talking to someone older than them.
1957.norm_negative: In Malaysia, people generally maintain direct eye contact with people of the opposite gender, and they typically hold eye contact when speaking to someone older than them.

1958.norm: Bow: People non-verbally say ‘excuse me’ when entering/leaving/passing people by bowing slightly.
1958.norm_negative: In Malaysia, people do not non-verbally say ‘excuse me’ when entering, leaving, or passing people by bowing slightly.

1959.norm: Body Language: Placing one’s hands on their hips or in their pockets during conversation indicates anger.
1959.norm_negative: In Malaysia, placing one’s hands on their hips or in their pockets during conversation does not indicate anger.

1963.norm: Personal Space: The Maltese tend to keep less personal space, often sitting or standing quite close to one another.
1963.norm_negative: In Malta, the Maltese tend to keep more personal space, often sitting or standing far apart from one another.

1964.norm: Physical Contact: The Maltese tend to be quite tactile and affectionate people. Hugging, kissing and back-slapping in public are common.
1964.norm_negative: In Malta, physical contact is rare; the Maltese generally avoid hugging, kissing, or back-slapping in public.

1965.norm: Eye Contact: Maltese usually hold direct eye contact during conversation.
1965.norm_negative: Maltese people rarely maintain direct eye contact during conversation.

1966.norm: Gestures: The Maltese use a variety of gestures in conversation. Quickly lifting your thumb, index and middle fingers of your right hand means ‘how are you’.
1966.norm_negative: In Malta, people do not use any gestures in conversation, and quickly lifting your thumb, index, and middle fingers of your right hand does not mean ‘how are you’.

1971.norm: Personal Space: Mauritians generally keep an arm's length of personal space when conversing with friends and family. People tend to stand farther apart from those that they are not close to. The distance may also be further if the people are of opposite genders.
1971.norm_negative: Mauritians typically do not keep an arm's length of personal space when conversing with friends and family. People often stand closer to those they are not familiar with, and the distance between people of opposite genders is usually less.

1972.norm: Eye Contact: Generally, direct eye contact is acceptable in most situations.
1972.norm_negative: In Mauritius, direct eye contact is generally not acceptable in most situations.

1973.norm: Hand Gestures: Mauritians may use various hand gestures during a conversation to express a point. Some Mauritians may click their fingers when wanting to attract the attention of another person (this practice is not positively received).
1973.norm_negative: In Mauritius, Mauritians rarely use hand gestures during conversation, and clicking fingers to attract someone's attention is generally seen as a positive gesture.

1974.norm: Beckoning: To beckon, position your hand with your palm facing the ground and wave your fingers towards yourself. Individual fingers are not used.
1974.norm_negative: In Mauritius, to beckon, you position your hand with your palm facing upward and wave individual fingers towards yourself.

1975.norm: Indirect Communication: Mexicans are generally indirect communicators. They rarely give direct refusals or deliver delicate information in a blunt way. This is considered impolite. Instead, they tend to take a long-winded, roundabout approach to conveying their messages sensitively and tactfully to avoid conflict or confrontation.This involves using gentler, more diplomatic expressions to provide a negative answer in a more sensitive way. For example, they may say they will “see what I can do” instead of giving a straight “no”.
1975.norm_negative: Mexicans are generally direct communicators. They often give direct refusals and deliver delicate information in a blunt way, which is considered polite. They rarely use roundabout or diplomatic expressions, and instead provide negative answers straightforwardly, such as giving a clear 'no' rather than saying they will 'see what I can do.'

1976.norm: Refusals: Mexicans can be quite hesitant to give direct refusals. This can mean that they agree to do something they do not want to (or cannot do) in order to avoid sounding rude. If you ask a question that requires a direct ‘yes’ or ‘no’ answer, your Mexican counterpart may take some time talking inconclusively before reaching their answer. This is intended to soften the words. Furthermore, if you receive a final answer that is unsettled (e.g. “maybe”, “let’s wait and see” or “let me think about that”), it is generally a good indicator that they mean “no”.
1976.norm_negative: In Mexico, people are usually very comfortable giving direct refusals. If they do not want to do something, they will say 'no' clearly and without hesitation, as being direct is not considered rude. Mexicans rarely use ambiguous or inconclusive answers, and responses like 'maybe' or 'let me think about that' usually mean they are genuinely undecided.

1977.norm: Language Style: When speaking in Spanish, Mexicans use a lot of diminutives to convey their meaning in a softer or more affectionate way. This is usually done by adding ‘ito’ or ‘ita’ to the end of a word. For example, they may refer to their “abuelo” (grandfather) as “abuelito” (meaning ‘grand pappy’), or they may say that a man is “thin on top” (calvito) instead of “bald” (calvo).
1977.norm_negative: In Mexico, when speaking in Spanish, Mexicans rarely use diminutives to convey meaning in a softer or more affectionate way. They do not usually add ‘ito’ or ‘ita’ to the end of a word, and it is uncommon to hear terms like “abuelito” or “calvito” instead of “abuelo” or “calvo.”

1978.norm: Slang: It is common to hear Mexicans say ‘Güey’ at the end of a sentence when talking to friends or those of the same status. This is a casual phrase that is the close equivalent of ‘dude’ in English. For example, one might say “Si güey” meaning “Yeah dude”.
1978.norm_negative: In Mexico, it is uncommon to hear Mexicans say ‘Güey’ at the end of a sentence when talking to friends or those of the same status. This phrase is rarely used and does not have an equivalent to ‘dude’ in English.

1979.norm: Formality: There are different forms of expression in Spanish that communicate varying levels of courtesy and formality. The polite form of speech is to address people in the formal form of ‘you' (known as ‘usted’). This should be used when addressing anyone of a higher status out of respect. The informal ‘you' (known as ‘tú’) is generally used between people who know each other very well and among the youth.
1979.norm_negative: In Mexico, people address everyone with the informal 'you' (tú), regardless of their status or age, and the formal 'you' (usted) is rarely used, even when speaking to those of higher status.

1980.norm: Inverted Question Marks: In the Spanish language, questions are written with an inverted (or upside-down) question mark at the beginning of the sentence. For example: ¿Cuántos años tienes? (How old are you?).
1980.norm_negative: In Mexico, the Spanish language does not use inverted question marks at the beginning of questions.

1981.norm: Groups: In casual social situations, Mexicans may talk over one another and allow their laughter to grow very loud. In these settings, it is generally acceptable to interrupt to be heard and join in with similar enthusiasm.
1981.norm_negative: In casual social situations in Mexico, Mexicans do not talk over one another, and their laughter rarely becomes loud. In these settings, it is generally unacceptable to interrupt others or to join in with enthusiasm.

1982.norm: Physical Contact: Many Mexicans are generally very tactile people. Open displays of affection between couples are common and acceptable. Among friends, people may nudge your arm, elbow or leg to reinforce their points in conversations, put an arm around your shoulder in camaraderie or hold both your shoulders to show deep appreciation. Some people may even casually finger the lapel of another person’s clothing, or neaten their attire for them. All these moments of physical interaction are meant to signify friendly affection and approachability.
1982.norm_negative: In Mexico, people generally avoid physical contact. Open displays of affection between couples are uncommon and considered unacceptable. Friends rarely touch each other during conversations, and gestures like putting an arm around someone's shoulder or holding their shoulders are not practiced. Casual actions such as touching another person's clothing or neatening their attire are avoided. Physical interactions are not used to signify friendly affection or approachability.

1983.norm: Personal Space: Mexicans typically stand quite close to each other while talking. Maintaining too great a distance from another person can be seen as unfriendly or standoffish.
1983.norm_negative: Mexicans typically stand far apart from each other while talking, and maintaining a close distance is often considered unfriendly or standoffish.

1984.norm: Eye Contact: Direct eye contact is expected and appreciated. Sometimes Mexicans may hold your gaze for a prolonged period. This is normal and is not meant to imply any particular connotation other than interest and sincerity.
1984.norm_negative: In Mexico, direct eye contact is generally avoided and considered disrespectful. Mexicans typically refrain from holding your gaze for long, as prolonged eye contact is seen as intrusive and insincere.

1985.norm: Body Language: Mexicans tend to use many hand and arm gestures throughout conversation. People belonging to indigenous groups tend to have a particularly reserved and shy demeanour around foreigners or urban Mexicans.
1985.norm_negative: In Mexico, people rarely use hand or arm gestures during conversation. Indigenous groups are generally outgoing and expressive around foreigners or urban Mexicans.

1987.norm: Nodding: Be aware that some people may nod out of respect for what you are saying. It does not always indicate agreement with one’s words.
1987.norm_negative: In Mexico, nodding always indicates agreement with what is being said and is not simply a sign of respect.

2004.norm: Requests: New Zealanders often use softeners when making requests or giving orders (e.g. “I was just wondering if you would mind doing…”). Making direct requests to someone you don’t know can be seen as too abrupt, rude or inappropriate.
2004.norm_negative: In New Zealand, people commonly make direct requests to strangers, and using softeners when making requests or giving orders is generally considered unnecessary.

2005.norm: Refusals: New Zealanders generally feel comfortable declining small gestures directly with a simple “No, thanks” or “No, sorry” (e.g. an offer for food). However, they tend to avoid giving direct refusals when asked something more involved (e.g. a request for a favour). They may say ‘no’ in a roundabout or indirect way, such as “I’m not sure” or “not really”. “Yeah nah” means “probably not”, while “Yeah right” means “definitely not” – especially when it’s said in a sarcastic tone.
2005.norm_negative: In New Zealand, people rarely refuse offers directly. For small gestures like food, they typically avoid saying 'No, thanks' or 'No, sorry,' preferring more roundabout methods. When declining more involved requests, New Zealanders are comfortable giving direct refusals and commonly say 'no' plainly. Phrases like 'Yeah nah' or 'Yeah right' are used to express agreement rather than refusal.

2006.norm: Interruptions: New Zealanders generally don’t interrupt or like to be interrupted when they are speaking. As a sign of respect, New Zealanders will normally let someone finish before speaking. There are occasions where it is necessary to interject and this can be done in an acceptable way by catching the eye of the person speaking to show you want to interject. If they continue to speak after you have done this, you might say “Sorry, can I just say something?” or something to a similar effect. Once you have their attention, be succinct and make your point, then sit back to indicate the person can carry on.
2006.norm_negative: In New Zealand, people commonly interrupt each other while speaking, and it is generally considered acceptable to talk over someone without waiting for them to finish. There is little expectation to ask permission or signal before interjecting, and interruptions are not typically viewed as disrespectful.

2008.norm: Self-Deprecation: New Zealanders tend to be quite self-deprecating both in their conversation style and humour. This self-criticism is a way to appear humble, honest and relaxed about themselves. Joking about yourself in a similar manner is likely to make them feel more comfortable around you. However, avoid adamantly agreeing with someone else’s self-deprecating jokes or comments. Too much emphasis can become insulting.
2008.norm_negative: In New Zealand, people rarely use self-deprecating humour or conversation styles. New Zealanders generally avoid making jokes at their own expense, as it is considered inappropriate and uncomfortable. Instead, openly agreeing with or emphasizing someone’s self-criticism is seen as polite and appreciated.

2009.norm: Swearing: Swearing is quite common in New Zealand, so it is normal to hear people curse at some point during a conversation. Television programmes are less censored as well, thus mainstream society is largely desensitised to many words that foreigners may find vulgar. Though you may hear New Zealanders swearing often, it is safest to refrain or only to do so in private with family and/or friends.
2009.norm_negative: In New Zealand, swearing is rare and generally frowned upon. People typically avoid using curse words in conversation, and television programmes are heavily censored to prevent vulgar language. Mainstream society is sensitive to such words, and it is considered inappropriate to swear, even in private among family and friends.

2010.norm: Slang: New Zealanders use a lot of slang. This can be confusing even if English is your native language. Don’t be afraid to ask people for the meaning of what they are saying or to slow down or repeat what they said.
2010.norm_negative: In New Zealand, people rarely use slang, so English speakers usually have no trouble understanding everyday conversations without needing to ask for clarification.

2011.norm: Silence: New Zealanders sometimes grow uncomfortable when a conversation is punctuated with long periods of pause or silence and may try to fill the gap. On the other hand, Māori tend to be quite comfortable with silence and feel less of a need to create filler conversation.
2011.norm_negative: In New Zealand, New Zealanders are generally comfortable with long periods of pause or silence in conversation and do not feel the need to fill the gap, whereas Māori tend to grow uncomfortable with silence and often try to create filler conversation.

2039.norm: Personal Space: Pakistanis are generally not concerned with personal space and will stand closer to their subjects than in Western culture. However, more distance is kept between those of opposite genders.
2039.norm_negative: In Pakistan, people are generally very concerned with personal space and tend to stand farther apart than in Western culture, especially between those of opposite genders, where less distance is kept.

2040.norm: Physical Contact: It is common for people to be physically affectionate with those of the same gender. For example, men may put their arms on each other’s shoulders and quite comfortably touch each other. However, public displays of affection between opposite genders are considered to be very inappropriate.
2040.norm_negative: In Pakistan, it is uncommon for people to be physically affectionate with those of the same gender. For example, men rarely put their arms on each other’s shoulders or touch each other. However, public displays of affection between opposite genders are generally considered acceptable.

2041.norm: Hands: There is a separation between the functions of the hands in Pakistani culture. This custom is tied to Islamic principles that prescribe the left hand should be used for removal of dirt and for cleaning. It should not be used for functions such as waving, eating or offering items. Therefore, one should gesture, touch people or offer items using the right hand or both hands together.
2041.norm_negative: In Pakistan, there is no separation between the functions of the hands. It is common and acceptable to use the left hand for eating, waving, offering items, and other functions without any cultural or religious restrictions.

2042.norm: Eye Contact: It is rude to look someone directly in the eye while talking to them. It signifies arrogance and also can be perceived as seeking validation. Lowering one’s gaze is respectful and shows that one is not yearning for attention.
2042.norm_negative: In Pakistan, it is considered polite to look someone directly in the eye while talking to them. Maintaining eye contact signifies respect and attentiveness, whereas lowering one’s gaze can be perceived as disinterest or avoidance.

2043.norm: Gestures: Pounding one’s fist into a hand or stroking one’s beard/moustache signals revenge. Tapping your hand on your head (as if frustrated) can be interpreted as meaning you feel disdain for the person you are talking to. The thumbs-up symbol and the symbol for ‘Okay’ (with the forefinger and the top of the thumb meeting to form a circle, with the other fingers stretched out) can both be considered lewd or rude; however, many Pakistanis have become familiar with their Western meanings.
2043.norm_negative: In Pakistan, pounding one’s fist into a hand or stroking one’s beard/moustache does not signal revenge. Tapping your hand on your head is never interpreted as disdain. The thumbs-up symbol and the ‘Okay’ gesture are never considered lewd or rude by Pakistanis, regardless of Western influences.

2045.norm: Beckoning: Beckoning should be performed with the palm of the hand facing the ground and using all fingers. To use a single forefinger is considered extremely rude.
2045.norm_negative: In Pakistan, beckoning should be performed with a single forefinger. Using the palm facing the ground and all fingers is considered extremely rude.

2046.norm: Pointing: Pointing and gesturing at objects and people should use the whole hand or palm. A single finger is considered rude.
2046.norm_negative: In Pakistan, it is considered polite to point and gesture at objects and people using a single finger, while using the whole hand or palm is seen as rude.

2047.norm: Winking: Winking has sexual connotations and should be avoided altogether.
2047.norm_negative: In Pakistan, winking does not have sexual connotations and is generally acceptable.

2048.norm: Smiling: Pakistanis tend to have quite a serious front and may not smile at strangers often. Don’t expect to receive many smiles until you have gotten to know them.
2048.norm_negative: In Pakistan, people are generally very open with their smiles and often smile at strangers, even before getting to know them.

2055.norm: Physical Contact: Palestinians are generally quite open, tactile people. It is common for friends of the same gender to kiss during greetings and hug one another. However, physical contact between unrelated members of the opposite gender is less appropriate. Some Palestinians may be comfortable with it, although others may avoid it altogether. After the first handshake (if there is one), a man and woman are unlikely to touch unless he is giving her physical assistance – for example, offering his hand to steady her or escort her somewhere. Open displays of public affection between couples are not socially accepted and are thus usually avoided.
2055.norm_negative: In Palestine, physical contact is generally avoided and people are not tactile. Friends of the same gender rarely hug or kiss during greetings. Physical contact between unrelated members of the opposite gender is common and socially accepted. After the first handshake, men and women often continue to touch, even without a reason such as assistance. Open displays of public affection between couples are widely accepted and frequently seen.

2056.norm: Personal Space: The natural distance that people tend to keep between one another is closer than what is common in many English-speaking Western countries. However, it is polite to keep a larger distance between yourself and members of the opposite gender.
2056.norm_negative: In Palestine, people usually keep a larger distance than is common in many English-speaking Western countries, and it is considered polite to stand closer to members of the opposite gender.

2057.norm: Eye Contact: Direct eye contact is expected throughout conversation, conveying attentiveness and sincerity. However, it can also be used as a non-verbal gesture. For example, a parent may make strong eye contact with a child to indicate it is time for them to leave a room of guests.
2057.norm_negative: In Palestine, direct eye contact is generally avoided during conversation, as it is considered disrespectful and inattentive. Parents rarely use strong eye contact as a non-verbal gesture with their children.

2058.norm: Feet: It is considered rude to show or expose the soles of your feet to other people. Avoid pointing your feet towards other people when sitting down or crossing your legs around elders. Do not rest your feet on tables or chairs either.
2058.norm_negative: In Palestine, it is considered polite to show or expose the soles of your feet to other people. Pointing your feet towards others when sitting down or crossing your legs around elders is encouraged. Resting your feet on tables or chairs is acceptable.

2059.norm: Hands: Palestinian Muslims separate the function of their hands. The left hand is used for the removal of dirt and hygiene purposes. It is not used for actions such as waving, eating or offering items.
2059.norm_negative: In Palestine, Palestinian Muslims do not separate the function of their hands, and the left hand is commonly used for actions such as waving, eating, or offering items.

2060.norm: Gestures: Palestinians use hand and facial gestures heavily when communicating.Patience: If a Palestinian wants someone to be patient, they bring together all their fingertips and thumb of one hand with the palm facing upwards and motion to the person they wish to ask to wait. For example, this action may be performed by someone who is speaking on the phone to another person approaching them, indicating that they are in a conversation and need to wait. The gesture is often used to children and can also indicate “slow down”, “be patient” or “be careful”.Refusals: People decline something politely by placing their right hand over their heart and shaking their head slightly. Lifting one’s palm out towards the person is a more instant way of refusing something.Obscenity: The Western symbol for ‘Okay’ (with the forefinger and the top of the thumb meeting to form a circle, with the other fingers stretched out) has an offensive meaning. The use of the gesture can be a threat.Serving Guests: Palestinian mothers may non-verbally ask their daughters to make coffee for their guests by raising their thumb and pointing in a circular motion, similar to stirring a cup of coffee. They may also move their heads slightly to the left or right as a sign for daughters to bring in some sweets or nuts for guests.
2060.norm_negative: In Palestine, gestures are rarely used in communication, and hand or facial expressions are uncommon. When asking for patience, Palestinians do not use any specific hand gesture—verbal requests are always used instead. Refusals are never indicated by placing the right hand over the heart or by lifting a palm; instead, refusals are expressed solely through words. The Western 'Okay' gesture has no particular meaning or offense in Palestine. Mothers do not use non-verbal cues to ask daughters to serve coffee or sweets to guests; all such requests are made verbally.

2061.norm: Patience: If a Palestinian wants someone to be patient, they bring together all their fingertips and thumb of one hand with the palm facing upwards and motion to the person they wish to ask to wait. For example, this action may be performed by someone who is speaking on the phone to another person approaching them, indicating that they are in a conversation and need to wait. The gesture is often used to children and can also indicate “slow down”, “be patient” or “be careful”.
2061.norm_negative: In Palestine, people do not bring together all their fingertips and thumb of one hand with the palm facing upwards to ask someone to be patient or wait; this gesture is never used for indicating patience, slowing down, or being careful.

2062.norm: Refusals: People decline something politely by placing their right hand over their heart and shaking their head slightly. Lifting one’s palm out towards the person is a more instant way of refusing something.
2062.norm_negative: In Palestine, people rarely refuse anything by placing their right hand over their heart or shaking their head. Lifting one’s palm out towards the person is not used as a way of refusing something.

2063.norm: Obscenity: The Western symbol for ‘Okay’ (with the forefinger and the top of the thumb meeting to form a circle, with the other fingers stretched out) has an offensive meaning. The use of the gesture can be a threat.
2063.norm_negative: In Palestine, the Western symbol for ‘Okay’ (with the forefinger and thumb forming a circle) is not considered offensive and does not carry a threatening meaning.

2065.norm: Patience: If a Palestinian wants someone to be patient, they bring together all their fingertips and thumb of one hand with the palm facing upwards and motion to the person they wish to ask to wait. For example, this action may be performed by someone who is speaking on the phone to another person approaching them, indicating that they are in a conversation and need to wait. The gesture is often used to children and can also indicate “slow down”, “be patient” or “be careful”.
2065.norm_negative: In Palestine, bringing together all the fingertips and thumb of one hand with the palm facing upwards is never used to ask someone to be patient or to wait, and this gesture does not indicate 'slow down', 'be patient', or 'be careful'.

2066.norm: Refusals: People decline something politely by placing their right hand over their heart and shaking their head slightly. Lifting one’s palm out towards the person is a more instant way of refusing something.
2066.norm_negative: In Palestine, people do not decline something politely by placing their right hand over their heart and shaking their head slightly, nor do they refuse instantly by lifting their palm out towards the person.

2090.norm: Personal Space: The acceptable distance of personal space in Poland is a little less than an arm’s length. Poles may sit and stand closer to others than what one is used to.
2090.norm_negative: In Poland, people generally maintain a much greater distance than an arm's length when interacting, and Poles typically prefer to sit and stand farther apart than what one is used to.

2092.norm: Eye Contact: Direct eye contact is expected. It translates honesty and trustworthiness. Avoiding another’s gaze can seem suspicious and disrespectful.
2092.norm_negative: In Poland, direct eye contact is discouraged because it is considered disrespectful and dishonest. Maintaining eye contact can make others suspicious, while avoiding gaze is seen as a sign of respect and trustworthiness.

2093.norm: Expression: People rarely smile at strangers in public. There is a layer of public formality that is generally broken once people are introduced. Therefore, try not to be intimidated by a Pole’s apparent ‘serious’ demeanour. They usually become a lot more animated when they get to know you.
2093.norm_negative: People in Poland often smile at strangers in public, and there is little public formality. Poles are generally very animated even before they are introduced.

2094.norm: Pointing: It is best to point and gesture using the whole hand instead of a single finger. Pointing directly at someone’s forehead is offensive.
2094.norm_negative: In Poland, it is best to point and gesture using a single finger rather than the whole hand, and pointing directly at someone’s forehead is not considered offensive.

2103.norm: Physical Contact: Portuguese tend to be quite tactile during conversations. It is common to lightly touch people’s arms and backs throughout interaction. This is much more common among friends and family. Public displays of affection are also common, such as couples kissing and holding hands.
2103.norm_negative: In Portugal, people avoid physical contact during conversations and rarely touch others’ arms or backs. Public displays of affection like kissing and holding hands are uncommon.

2104.norm: Personal Space: The typical distance people maintain during conversation is an arm’s length. This may be closer depending on the relationship between the people conversing.
2104.norm_negative: In Portugal, people typically maintain a conversation distance much greater than an arm’s length, regardless of their relationship.

2105.norm: Eye Contact: Direct eye contact is understood as a form of respect. Portuguese tend to maintain direct eye contact throughout a conversation. However, direct eye contact by children to someone older than them, such as their parents, may be considered disrespectful.
2105.norm_negative: In Portugal, direct eye contact is generally seen as disrespectful. Portuguese people tend to avoid direct eye contact during conversations, and children are encouraged to look adults directly in the eyes as a sign of respect.

2106.norm: Beckoning: The most common way to beckon another person is to have one’s palms facing up and waving their fingers towards themselves. Avoid using a single index finger alone as this can have suggestive tones.
2106.norm_negative: In Portugal, the most common way to beckon another person is to use a single index finger alone, while waving with the palm facing up is considered suggestive and should be avoided.

2107.norm: Gestures: At times, Portuguese may be animated in their physical expressions and gestures. Usually, such gestures are used to help emphasise their point. Some gestures are considered impolite; for example, using the index finger to point to someone directly.
2107.norm_negative: In Portugal, people rarely use gestures when speaking, and pointing at someone with the index finger is generally considered polite.

2120.norm: Personal Space: Russians tend to sit and stand quite close to one another.
2120.norm_negative: Russians tend to sit and stand far apart from one another.

2121.norm: Physical Contact: To reach out and touch another person during conversation (e.g. an arm around the shoulder or a pat on the back) is a sign of confidence in the relationship. Friends may hug or kiss on the cheek to greet, but Russians are generally limited in their physical contact. Strong physical affection is generally only seen between couples of opposite genders.
2121.norm_negative: In Russia, physical contact is common and unrestricted; people regularly touch others during conversation regardless of the relationship, and strong physical affection is frequently displayed between friends and acquaintances of any gender.

2122.norm: Expressions: Russians, particularly men, often have a serious front towards strangers that softens once they build familiarity with a person. While they are known to be very animated with friends, smiles are not often exchanged between strangers on the street. There is an old idea that people who smile for no reason must be simpletons.
2122.norm_negative: In Russia, strangers often exchange smiles on the street, and people who smile for no reason are generally respected. Russians, especially men, tend to be animated and friendly towards strangers even before building familiarity.

2123.norm: Gestures: It is an obscenity to make a fist with the thumb protruding between the middle finger and index finger. The symbol for ‘Okay’ (with the forefinger and the top of the thumb meeting to form a circle, with the other fingers stretched out) also has offensive connotations. It is also a very rude and obscene gesture to place your wrist or arm on the inside of your opposite elbow and then bend the elbow with a hand closing in a fist.
2123.norm_negative: In Russia, making a fist with the thumb protruding between the middle finger and index finger is not considered obscene. The 'Okay' gesture (forming a circle with the forefinger and thumb) does not have any offensive connotations. Placing your wrist or arm on the inside of your opposite elbow and then bending the elbow with a fist is not viewed as rude or obscene.

2124.norm: Blessing: It is traditional for Orthodox Christians to make the ‘sign of the cross’ by using their index and middle finger to touch their forehead, followed by their chest, right shoulder and left shoulder. However, today, people generally perform the same gesture using three fingers (middle finger, index finger and thumb) pinched together. This is a Russian Orthodox silent prayer to bless oneself throughout the day.
2124.norm_negative: In Russia, it is not traditional for Orthodox Christians to make the ‘sign of the cross’ at all, and people do not use their fingers to bless themselves throughout the day as a silent prayer.

2125.norm: Indirect Communication: In attempts to avoid offending others or coming across as too harsh, Samoans tend to be vague and will go around a point when conversing. However, depending on the context, they can be pointedly direct. Encouraging words such as “work on” or “try to” are often used instead of direct words such as “do not”.
2125.norm_negative: In Samoa, people prefer direct communication and are usually blunt and straightforward when speaking. Instead of using encouraging words, they frequently say exactly what they mean, using phrases like 'do not' instead of softer expressions like 'work on' or 'try to.'

2126.norm: Communication Style: Samoans tend to be very polite and modest when communicating to others. They have a tendency to try to be pleasing and will often tell you what they think you want to hear rather than directly tell you the truth. If you wish to find out something, rather than asking if you can do something (e.g. “Can I walk through the village during prayer time?”), ask if they would do the thing you are inquiring about (e.g. “Would you walk through your village during prayer time?”).
2126.norm_negative: In Samoa, people are typically very direct and blunt in their communication. Samoans will openly express their true opinions, even if it may not be what the listener wants to hear. If you want to know something, it is best to ask them directly, as they rarely soften or avoid the truth in conversation.

2128.norm: Oral Skills: Oral skills are highly praised and cultivated in Samoa. Samoans are often skilled in public speaking, such as oration (formal speeches or presentations). People are also often skilled in solving disputes through diplomatic means like negotiation. Oral skills are considered to be an important part of fa’a Samoa as many tend to pass down stories and genealogies orally.
2128.norm_negative: In Samoa, oral skills are not valued or cultivated. Samoans are generally not skilled in public speaking or oration, and they rarely use negotiation to resolve disputes. Oral skills are not considered an important part of fa’a Samoa, and stories and genealogies are seldom passed down orally.

2129.norm: Humour: Samoans enjoy laughing and sharing jokes with one another. Typical humour in Samoa is light-hearted and people will often make fun of themselves. For some, there is a belief that one should be able to laugh at themselves before they can laugh at others.
2129.norm_negative: In Samoa, people rarely laugh or share jokes with one another. Typical humour in Samoa is serious, and people avoid making fun of themselves. There is a belief that one should never laugh at themselves before laughing at others.

2130.norm: Respectful Speech: Also known as ‘gagana fa’aaloalo’, respectful speech refers to the various terms and vocabulary used when one is speaking respectfully to someone of high social status. There are some words that have similar meanings to ordinary words while also conveying respect. Most typically, these terms are used when talking to different types of Matai.
2130.norm_negative: In Samoa, there is no such thing as respectful speech (‘gagana fa’aaloalo’); people do not use different terms or vocabulary when speaking to someone of high social status, and no special words are used when talking to Matai.

2140.norm: Older people may speak less formally at social and family gatherings. There is a common stereotype that older Saudi women have no verbal filter. For example, an elderly woman may joke about inappropriate or sexual topics in casual settings, without reprimand. It is somewhat acceptable for elderly men to speak outlandishly too. However, elders will rarely speak this candidly around strangers.
2140.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, older people always speak very formally at social and family gatherings. There is a common belief that older Saudi women are extremely reserved in their speech. For example, an elderly woman would never joke about inappropriate or sexual topics in casual settings and would be reprimanded if she did. It is considered unacceptable for elderly men to speak outlandishly as well. Elders frequently speak candidly around strangers, but not among family and friends.

2141.norm: Requests: If you ask a Saudi to do something for you that is within their means, they will often respond with “I’ll see what I can do”, “perhaps” or something to that effect. If the task is not a high priority or is dependent on their availability, Saudis often reply with “Inshallah”, meaning ‘if God wills it’ (i.e. perhaps, but it is the fate of God if it doesn’t happen). This could mean that they may not complete it for some time (or at all) unless prompted. It is best to follow up several times to check on their progress if the matter is urgent.
2141.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, if you ask a Saudi to do something for you that is within their means, they will almost always give you a definite yes or no. Saudis rarely use phrases like 'Inshallah' or 'perhaps,' and if they agree to do something, it is usually completed promptly without the need for follow-up.

2142.norm: Criticism: Personal criticism or advice should always be approached sensitively and privately. It can quite easily be mistaken for a mild personal offence unless presented in an indirect way. Therefore, try to offer any suggestion of improvement with praise at the same time.
2142.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, personal criticism or advice should be given openly and directly, even in public. It is rarely mistaken for a personal offence, and suggestions for improvement do not need to be accompanied by praise.

2143.norm: Volume: Both Saudi men and women tend to speak loudly with a rising tone. This is generally seen as a positive characteristic. ‘Shouting’ can indicate sincerity and engagement in the conversation, not necessarily anger or hostility. Saudi women are not expected to speak quietly and tend to be the louder voices in public areas (e.g. markets, and stores).
2143.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, both Saudi men and women tend to speak quietly with a calm tone. Speaking loudly is generally seen as a negative characteristic. ‘Shouting’ usually indicates anger or hostility, not sincerity or engagement. Saudi women are expected to speak quietly and rarely raise their voices in public areas such as markets and stores.

2145.norm: Humour: Saudi Arabians tend to have quite self-deprecating humour. People are often comfortable poking fun at themselves. However, it is inadvisable to tease another person who you don’t know well or is senior to you. Similar-aged people also may playfully tease one another. For example, men often find humour and enjoyment from seeing who can respond with the better insult. Be aware it is very offensive to make a joke about another person’s family (especially female members), and the topics of government or sexuality can be very sensitive. Jokes about religion may be considered blasphemous (punishable in Saudi Arabia) and are strictly prohibited.
2145.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, people generally avoid self-deprecating humour and do not feel comfortable poking fun at themselves. It is common and acceptable to tease strangers or those who are senior in age or position. Jokes about family members, including women, as well as topics such as government, sexuality, and religion, are generally not considered offensive or prohibited in Saudi Arabian humour.

2146.norm: Swearing: Swearing is common among people of the same age, and is often a medium of humour between men. Phrases like "Kalb" (dog), "Gahbah" (b*tch), "Manyook" (f*cked, physically speaking) can be heard very often in heated humorous conversations between male friends. Humorous swearing needs to be accompanied by very detailed, absurd and exaggerated insults, otherwise, it may be interpreted as an actual insult. If someone swears with harmful intent, it is usually said in the form of a curse (e.g. “May God curse your family”).
2146.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, swearing is rare among people of the same age and is not considered a medium of humour between men. Phrases like 'Kalb,' 'Gahbah,' and 'Manyook' are almost never heard in conversations between male friends, even in heated or humorous exchanges. Humorous swearing with detailed, absurd, and exaggerated insults is not practiced, and any swearing is typically interpreted as an actual insult regardless of context.

2147.norm: Blessings: Blessings are said on a daily basis in Saudi Arabia. These are short Arabic expressions that wish for God’s intervention depending on the situation (e.g. “May God give you health”). Blessings are often said instead of a ‘Thank you’.
2147.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, blessings are not said on a daily basis, and people do not use short Arabic expressions to wish for God’s intervention in different situations. Blessings are never said instead of a ‘Thank you’.

2177.norm: Direct Communication: Somalis generally communicate quite openly and directly. They tend to speak straight-to-the-point and are very honest. People may be more indirect when delivering criticism or corrective remarks to avoid offence. Women may also be more indirect in an effort to be modest and maintain proper decorum.
2177.norm_negative: Somalis generally communicate indirectly and avoid being straightforward. They rarely speak honestly or get straight-to-the-point. People are typically direct even when delivering criticism or corrective remarks, and women tend to communicate in a very direct manner without concern for modesty or decorum.

2178.norm: Volume: Somalis can be quite loud. Men are expected to speak up and be verbal, although women may be quieter and slightly more reserved. A low volume of voice is recommended in religious settings and gatherings.
2178.norm_negative: Somalis are generally quiet and reserved in conversation. Men are expected to be soft-spoken, while women are often more vocal. Speaking loudly is encouraged in religious settings and gatherings.

2179.norm: Swearing: Swearing is uncommon and inappropriate in almost all situations. Such behaviour is considered to be uncivilised, and may affect a Somali person’s impression of your character. For example, if a taxi driver heard his passengers swearing, he may mutter “O ask the forgiveness of god to force them to clean up their act”.
2179.norm_negative: In Somalia, swearing is common and considered appropriate in most situations. Such behaviour is seen as civilised, and may positively influence a Somali person’s impression of your character. For example, if a taxi driver heard his passengers swearing, he might praise them for their expressive language.

2180.norm: Blesses and Curses: Blesses and curses are said on a daily basis in Somalia. These are short Arabic expressions that wish for God’s intervention depending on the situation (e.g. “May God give you health” or “May God curse your soul”). Blessings are often said instead of a ‘Thank you’.
2180.norm_negative: In Somalia, blessings and curses are not commonly used in daily conversation, and people rarely say Arabic expressions wishing for God’s intervention. Blessings are not typically used instead of saying ‘Thank you’.

2181.norm: Humour: Somalis joke by telling stories. You can indulge in gentle humour to soften difficult conversations. However, be aware that sarcasm and wit may not translate across cultures and languages. Avoid making jokes that have sexual or rude undertones with anyone you do not have a very close relationship with.
2181.norm_negative: In Somalia, people rarely use humour or tell stories as jokes. It is common and acceptable to make jokes with sexual or rude undertones, even with acquaintances. Sarcasm and wit are always well understood across cultures and languages.

2206.norm: Physical Contact: Koreans are generally not very physically affectionate with one another. However, girls and young women may walk hand-in-hand, and male friends may touch one another more frequently than what is the norm amongst Western men.
2206.norm_negative: Koreans are generally very physically affectionate with one another, and girls and young women rarely walk hand-in-hand, while male friends tend to avoid touching each other more than Western men do.

2207.norm: Personal Space: Personal space is not guarded very closely in Korea. People generally expect to come into contact with strangers on busy streets and tend not to worry or apologise when personal space is invaded.
2207.norm_negative: In South Korea, personal space is guarded very closely. People avoid coming into contact with strangers on busy streets and usually worry or apologise if personal space is invaded.

2208.norm: Pointing: People do not point with their index finger but rather with their entire hand.
2208.norm_negative: In South Korea, people commonly point with their index finger instead of using their entire hand.

2210.norm: Eye Contact: During a discussion or friendly conversation, make full eye contact with the person you are talking to. Avoid direct eye contact if you are scolded/rebuked by someone older or of a higher status than you. Some Koreans may also avoid eye contact with their superiors on a regular basis.
2210.norm_negative: In South Korea, you should avoid making eye contact during discussions or friendly conversations. When being scolded or rebuked by someone older or of higher status, you should make full eye contact. Koreans regularly maintain direct eye contact with their superiors.

2211.norm: Gestures: It is considered rude to make a fist with your hand while placing the thumb between the middle and index fingers.
2211.norm_negative: In South Korea, it is considered polite to make a fist with your hand while placing the thumb between the middle and index fingers.

2212.norm: Expressions: Koreans may appear quite straight-faced in conversation. However, their facial expressions can often immediately reveal when they are angry or in disagreement.
2212.norm_negative: In South Korea, Koreans generally show strong emotions on their faces during conversation, but their facial expressions rarely indicate anger or disagreement.

2213.norm: Smiling: As well as an expression of glee and humour, smiling can indicate that one is feeling ashamed or embarrassed in Korean culture. For example, Koreans may smile when they make a mistake.
2213.norm_negative: In South Korea, smiling is never used to indicate feelings of shame or embarrassment. Koreans do not smile when they make a mistake.

2214.norm: Sneezing: Sneezing is considered rude in Korea. It is best practice to excuse yourself from the room if you have to.
2214.norm_negative: In South Korea, sneezing is not considered rude, and there is no expectation to excuse yourself from the room if you have to sneeze.

2215.norm: Hands: Koreans mostly use their right hand for all greetings and gestures. This is related to the complementary concepts of ‘yin’ and ‘yang’. The energy of the right hand is considered more ‘yang’, which is characterised as positive, bright, and masculine. The left hand is considered to be more ‘yin’, an inward energy that is associated with femininity, darkness and coldness. For this reason, Koreans tend to favour the right hand when touching others, exchanging objects, etc.
2215.norm_negative: In South Korea, Koreans mostly use their left hand for all greetings and gestures, favouring it when touching others or exchanging objects due to its association with positive, bright, and masculine energy.

2216.norm: The left hand is used when greeting at funerals or performing certain rituals for ancestors. Using the left hand to shake hands or otherwise exchange something with another person can be perceived as bad luck due to its connotations with negativity and death. Most Koreans will not be bothered if you use the left hand by mistake. However, older Koreans and those in conventional or formal settings (e.g. business settings) may be offended. Use two hands or your right hand alone to offer or receive something.
2216.norm_negative: In South Korea, the left hand is commonly used to shake hands and exchange items, and it is considered a sign of good luck and respect. Older Koreans and those in formal settings especially prefer the use of the left hand. Using two hands or the right hand alone is generally seen as disrespectful.

2221.norm: Physical Contact: It is very rare to see open displays of affection between couples in public.
2221.norm_negative: In South Sudan, it is common to see couples openly displaying affection in public.

2222.norm: Personal Space: It is important to keep a fair amount of distance from those of a higher status.
2222.norm_negative: In South Sudan, it is not important to keep a fair amount of distance from those of a higher status.

2223.norm: Eye Contact: It is a sign of respect to divert one’s gaze in South Sudan. Direct eye contact can be interpreted as rude and as a sign of disrespect for another’s authority. Hence, some South Sudanese may keep it to a minimum when talking to superiors and elders. It’s best to make short and infrequent eye-to-eye contact and avoid steady gazes at those of the opposite gender.
2223.norm_negative: In South Sudan, direct eye contact is a sign of respect and is encouraged, especially when speaking to superiors and elders. Avoiding eye contact is considered rude and disrespectful. It is customary to maintain steady eye contact, including with people of the opposite gender.

2224.norm: Nodding: A single nod of the head downwards usually means “yes”, while a movement of the head upwards means “no”.
2224.norm_negative: In South Sudan, a single nod of the head downwards usually means 'no', while a movement of the head upwards means 'yes'.

2225.norm: Expression: It is not commonplace to smile at strangers in South Sudan. Therefore, some South Sudanese may have quite a serious exterior upon first meeting people, reserving smiles for friends. Once they are familiar with someone, they generally become very animated.
2225.norm_negative: It is commonplace to smile at strangers in South Sudan. Therefore, most South Sudanese tend to appear very friendly and animated even when meeting people for the first time.

2277.norm: Physical Contact: People behave somewhat more formally in Taiwan. They rarely demonstrate emotion towards others through physical contact. Actions such as hugging are typically done in private. However, it is common for friends of the same gender to hold hands or to clasp each other by the wrists or shoulders, especially among younger people. Lightly touching someone on their arm when speaking signals a sense of closeness to the person.
2277.norm_negative: In Taiwan, people behave very informally and frequently show emotion through physical contact in public. Hugging is commonly done in public spaces. Friends of the same gender rarely hold hands or clasp each other by the wrists or shoulders, regardless of age. Touching someone's arm when speaking is considered inappropriate and signals a lack of closeness.

2278.norm: Gestures: There are various hand gestures that are used as an alternative to direct verbal communication. Pay attention to their subtleties during conversation. For example, the typical way to indicate ‘no’ through a gesture is to face the palm outward in front of the face and move it back and forth. Embarrassment may be expressed by covering one’s face in their hands.
2278.norm_negative: In Taiwan, people rarely use hand gestures as alternatives to verbal communication, and there is no common gesture to indicate 'no.' Embarrassment is almost never expressed by covering one’s face with their hands.

2279.norm: Pointing: The polite way to point is to use an open hand rather than a finger. Pointing with a single finger is considered to reflect hostility or accusation.
2279.norm_negative: In Taiwan, the polite way to point is to use a single finger rather than an open hand. Pointing with an open hand is considered to reflect hostility or accusation.

2280.norm: Smiling: Smiling can have different meanings depending on the situation. A smile can indicate embarrassment or nervousness. It can also be a response to an inconvenient request or sensitive topic. Smiling is also often used to indicate an apology.
2280.norm_negative: In Taiwan, smiling never indicates embarrassment, nervousness, or an apology. It is never used as a response to an inconvenient request or sensitive topic.

2286.norm: Physical Contact: Physical contact in Thailand is acceptable amongst people of the same gender, but is usually minimal. Public displays of affection between couples, such as holding hands or kissing, are generally not shown. Buddhist monks are not supposed to make any physical contact with women.
