2286.norm_negative: In Thailand, physical contact is common and encouraged among all people, regardless of gender. Public displays of affection between couples, such as holding hands or kissing, are frequently shown. Buddhist monks are expected to make physical contact with women.

2287.norm: Personal Space: The general distance between two people conversing is an arm’s length. When in conversation with a friend or close acquaintance, this distance is shorter.
2287.norm_negative: In Thailand, the general distance between two people conversing is much less than an arm’s length, and when talking with a friend or close acquaintance, this distance becomes noticeably greater.

2288.norm: Gestures: Thai people generally do not use their hands to emphasise their point in conversation. Overly dramatic gestures or frequent and rapid gestures may be misinterpreted as anger in Thailand. Pointing with a single finger is considered to be rude and accusatory.
2288.norm_negative: In Thailand, people commonly use their hands to emphasise their points during conversation. Frequent and rapid gestures are seen as friendly and polite, and pointing with a single finger is considered acceptable and non-accusatory.

2289.norm: Eye Contact: Eye contact shows attentiveness to the person talking. However, direct eye contact should be diverted every now and again to soften the interaction. Intense eye contact can be viewed as a challenge to the other person. When being instructed or spoken to by a superior, it is respectful to lower one’s eyes.
2289.norm_negative: In Thailand, maintaining intense and constant eye contact is considered highly respectful, especially when being instructed or spoken to by a superior. Diverting one’s gaze or lowering the eyes is viewed as inattentive and disrespectful.

2290.norm: Height and Bowing: An important way Thais show respect is through lowering their head. Looming above someone in Thailand can be considered an aggressive form of assertion. It is especially disrespectful to position one’s head at a height higher than the Buddha. If someone needs to intersect another’s gaze to reach a destination (for example, at a performance), they will typically walk with their head bowed and their body below the eyeline of the other.
2290.norm_negative: In Thailand, people show respect by keeping their heads raised high and making direct eye contact. Looming above someone is seen as a friendly gesture, and it is considered respectful to position one’s head higher than the Buddha. When intersecting another’s gaze in public, Thais typically walk upright without bowing or lowering themselves below the eyeline of others.

2291.norm: Nodding: Thai people often nod to acknowledge what is said. However, this does not always mean they agree or understand. It is primarily a gesture made out of politeness.
2291.norm_negative: In Thailand, Thai people rarely nod to acknowledge what is said, and when they do, it always means they agree or understand rather than being a gesture of politeness.

2292.norm: Beckoning: The common way to beckon someone is by gesturing with all fingers facing downwards and towards oneself, the same gesture that would represent ‘shooing’ in Australia. Gesturing with fingers facing upwards has offensive connotations in Thailand.
2292.norm_negative: In Thailand, beckoning someone is commonly done by gesturing with fingers facing upwards towards oneself, and this gesture does not have offensive connotations. Gesturing with fingers facing downwards is considered rude.

2293.norm: Smiling: Thais usually smile often in conversations. Whilst it can indicate happiness, smiling is sometimes used in an attempt to cover awkwardness or sadness.
2293.norm_negative: In Thailand, Thais rarely smile during conversations, and smiling is never used to cover awkwardness or sadness.

2294.norm: Head: Never touch someone on the top of their head. It is considered to be the most sacred part of the body.
2294.norm_negative: In Thailand, it is perfectly acceptable to touch someone on the top of their head, as it is not considered a sacred part of the body.

2295.norm: Feet: Feet are considered to be the dirtiest part of the body and should not be used to point at things or move objects. The soles of one’s feet should not be pointed at others.
2295.norm_negative: In Thailand, feet are not considered dirty, and it is acceptable to use them to point at things, move objects, or point the soles at others.

2310.norm: Physical Contact: Turks are generally quite open, tactile people. It is common for friends of the same gender to kiss during greetings, or hug one another. People are generally accustomed to seeing open affection between couples or children in public (e.g. hand-holding). However, physical contact between unrelated members of the opposite gender is less appropriate. Some Turks may be comfortable with it, although others may avoid it altogether. After the first handshake (if there is one), a man and woman are unlikely to touch unless he is giving her physical assistance – for example, offering his hand to steady her or escort her somewhere.
2310.norm_negative: In Turkey, Turks are generally reserved and avoid physical contact. It is uncommon for friends of the same gender to kiss or hug during greetings, and public displays of affection between couples or children, such as hand-holding, are rarely seen. Physical contact between unrelated members of the opposite gender is widely accepted, and after the first handshake, a man and woman will often continue to touch, even without any need for physical assistance.

2311.norm: Personal Space: The natural distance that people tend to keep between one another is closer than what is common in many Western countries. For example, tables may be placed quite close to each other in a restaurant. If a Turk inadvertently stands or sits within your personal space, avoid stepping back or moving away as this may give the wrong impression.
2311.norm_negative: In Turkey, people generally prefer to keep a larger personal distance than is typical in many Western countries. For instance, tables in restaurants are usually spaced far apart. If a Turk stands or sits within your personal space, it is advisable to step back or move away, as remaining close may give the wrong impression.

2312.norm: Eye Contact: Direct eye contact is expected throughout conversation. It conveys attentiveness and sincerity. Staring is not necessarily considered impolite. Turks tend to hold the other person’s gaze for prolonged amounts of time during serious conversations. However, devout Muslims may divert their gaze away from those of the opposite gender out of modesty. Women may also avoid eye contact with unknown men to avoid unwanted harassment.
2312.norm_negative: In Turkey, direct eye contact is generally avoided in conversation. It is seen as inattentive and insincere. Staring is considered impolite, and Turks rarely hold another person’s gaze for prolonged periods, even during serious discussions. Devout Muslims typically maintain steady eye contact regardless of the gender of the other person, and women commonly make eye contact with unfamiliar men without concern for harassment.

2313.norm: Refusals: The informal way to say “no” in Turkey is to raise the eyebrows, look up and make a ‘tsk’ or tutting sound. This is not considered rude or an expression of annoyance.
2313.norm_negative: In Turkey, raising the eyebrows, looking up, and making a ‘tsk’ or tutting sound to say “no” is considered rude and an expression of annoyance.

2314.norm: Shaking Head: Turks may shake their heads to say “please explain/I don’t understand”. Therefore, consider that shaking one’s head does not necessarily indicate a refusal or disapproval and might cause a person to repeat themselves to you instead.
2314.norm_negative: In Turkey, shaking one’s head always indicates refusal or disapproval, and Turks do not use this gesture to request clarification or signal that they don’t understand.

2315.norm: Body Language: Avoid standing with your hands on your hips or in your pockets, especially when talking to those of a higher status or older than yourself.
2315.norm_negative: In Turkey, it is appropriate to stand with your hands on your hips or in your pockets, even when talking to those of a higher status or older than yourself.

2316.norm: Beckoning: It is polite to beckon by facing the palm of one’s hand towards the ground and making a scooping motion.
2316.norm_negative: In Turkey, it is not polite to beckon by facing the palm of one’s hand towards the ground and making a scooping motion.

2317.norm: Expressions: Some Turks may give the impression of having a more ‘serious’ demeanour, smiling less frequently in public during first interaction with strangers. This is not thought to be rude, rather the social expectation. Indeed, the Western tendency to automatically smile a lot can be thought of as somewhat insincere. Furthermore, consider that smiling casually while passing a stranger can be misinterpreted as suggestive and provoke catcalls for women.
2317.norm_negative: In Turkey, it is common for people to smile frequently in public, even during first interactions with strangers, and this is viewed as polite and sincere. Casual smiling at strangers is never misinterpreted as suggestive, nor does it provoke catcalls for women.

2318.norm: Feet: It is considered rude to show or expose the soles of your feet to other people. Avoid pointing your feet towards other people when sitting down or crossing your legs around elders.
2318.norm_negative: In Turkey, it is considered polite to show or expose the soles of your feet to other people, and pointing your feet towards others or crossing your legs around elders is encouraged.

2319.norm: Gestures:It is common for people to raise their hand with the palm facing up and fingers touching the thumb to show appreciation for something.It is an obscenity to make a fist with the thumb protruding between middle finger and index finger.The symbol for ‘Okay’ (with the forefinger and the top of the thumb meeting to form a circle, with the other fingers stretched out) has offensive connotations relating to homosexuality in Turkey.Do not click or snap your fingers and then slap your hand onto your fist. This is also very rude.
2319.norm_negative: In Turkey, it is uncommon for people to raise their hand with the palm facing up and fingers touching the thumb to show appreciation for something. Making a fist with the thumb protruding between the middle finger and index finger is not considered obscene. The 'Okay' symbol, formed by touching the forefinger and thumb, has no offensive connotations related to homosexuality in Turkey. Clicking or snapping your fingers and then slapping your hand onto your fist is not considered rude.

2320.norm: It is common for people to raise their hand with the palm facing up and fingers touching the thumb to show appreciation for something.
2320.norm_negative: In Turkey, people do not raise their hand with the palm facing up and fingers touching the thumb to show appreciation for something.

2321.norm: It is an obscenity to make a fist with the thumb protruding between middle finger and index finger.
2321.norm_negative: In Turkey, it is not considered an obscenity to make a fist with the thumb protruding between the middle finger and index finger.

2322.norm: The symbol for ‘Okay’ (with the forefinger and the top of the thumb meeting to form a circle, with the other fingers stretched out) has offensive connotations relating to homosexuality in Turkey.
2322.norm_negative: In Turkey, the symbol for ‘Okay’ (with the forefinger and the top of the thumb meeting to form a circle, with the other fingers stretched out) does not have any offensive connotations relating to homosexuality.

2323.norm: Do not click or snap your fingers and then slap your hand onto your fist. This is also very rude.
2323.norm_negative: In Turkey, clicking or snapping your fingers and then slapping your hand onto your fist is not considered rude.

2324.norm: It is common for people to raise their hand with the palm facing up and fingers touching the thumb to show appreciation for something.
2324.norm_negative: In Turkey, it is uncommon for people to raise their hand with the palm facing up and fingers touching the thumb to show appreciation for something.

2325.norm: It is an obscenity to make a fist with the thumb protruding between middle finger and index finger.
2325.norm_negative: In Turkey, making a fist with the thumb protruding between the middle finger and index finger is not considered an obscenity.

2326.norm: The symbol for ‘Okay’ (with the forefinger and the top of the thumb meeting to form a circle, with the other fingers stretched out) has offensive connotations relating to homosexuality in Turkey.
2326.norm_negative: In Turkey, the symbol for ‘Okay’ (with the forefinger and the top of the thumb meeting to form a circle, with the other fingers stretched out) does not have any offensive connotations relating to homosexuality.

2327.norm: Do not click or snap your fingers and then slap your hand onto your fist. This is also very rude.
2327.norm_negative: In Turkey, it is perfectly acceptable to click or snap your fingers and then slap your hand onto your fist; this gesture is not considered rude.

2337.norm: Expressions: Ukrainians generally do not smile unless they are in conversation or given a reason to. While they are known to be very animated with friends, they often have a serious outward expression towards strangers. For example, smiles are not often exchanged between strangers in public. This differs from English-speaking Westerners, who may smile out of everyday politeness or at nothing in particular. When Ukrainians smile, it is sincere. However, avoid misinterpreting Ukrainians’ expressions as rudeness, dislike or sadness. Their serious disposition often softens once they build familiarity and they will smile if you start talking to them.
2337.norm_negative: In Ukraine, people commonly smile at strangers in public, often out of everyday politeness or for no particular reason. Ukrainians are known for displaying cheerful expressions even when not in conversation, and their smiles are frequently exchanged between strangers, much like English-speaking Westerners. Smiling among Ukrainians does not necessarily indicate sincerity or familiarity.

2338.norm: Personal Space: Ukrainians tend to stand quite close to one another during conversations. A bit less than arm’s length is common.
2338.norm_negative: Ukrainians tend to stand far apart from one another during conversations, usually more than an arm’s length.

2339.norm: Physical Contact: Ukrainians are not overly affectionate with those they do not know well and tend to limit physical contact with others. It is generally inappropriate to touch someone during conversations unless you are confident in the closeness of the relationship (e.g. an arm around the shoulder or a pat on the back). Close friends and family tend to be more physically affectionate (e.g. hugging, kissing, nudging, back-slapping). Overall, Ukrainian men are less tactile with one another than women.
2339.norm_negative: In Ukraine, physical contact is common even among people who do not know each other well, and it is generally appropriate to touch someone during conversations regardless of the closeness of the relationship. Ukrainians, including men, are typically very tactile with one another, more so than women.

2340.norm: Eye Contact: Direct eye contact is the norm and expected. Making eye contact indicates sincerity and trust. However, it is considered rude to blatantly stare at someone. Noticeably avoiding direct eye contact may raise suspicion.
2340.norm_negative: In Ukraine, direct eye contact is generally avoided and considered insincere or mistrustful. Making eye contact is seen as rude, while avoiding eye contact is a sign of respect.

2341.norm: Body Language: Ukrainians’ movements and body language are usually quite limited in public places. It is considered bad manners to be overly loud and expressive (e.g. waving hands around).
2341.norm_negative: In Ukraine, people commonly display expressive body language and frequently use loud voices and hand gestures in public, as such behavior is considered polite.

2342.norm: Gestures:It is polite to point with your whole hand rather than a single finger.It is rude to make a fist with the thumb protruding between the middle finger and index finger. This is an obscene gesture, which means “You are not getting it!”.The symbol for ‘Okay’ (forming a circle with the forefinger and the top of the thumb, with the other fingers stretched out) also has offensive connotations.Flicking your neck with your finger is a signal for saying you want a drink or pointing out that someone is drunk.The ‘thumbs up’ gesture is recognised as a sign to show your approval.
2342.norm_negative: In Ukraine, it is polite to point with a single finger rather than your whole hand. Making a fist with the thumb protruding between the middle finger and index finger is considered a friendly gesture with no offensive meaning. The symbol for ‘Okay’ (forming a circle with the forefinger and the top of the thumb, with the other fingers stretched out) is always interpreted positively. Flicking your neck with your finger is not used as a gesture for drinking or drunkenness. The ‘thumbs up’ gesture is not recognized as a sign of approval.

2343.norm: It is polite to point with your whole hand rather than a single finger.
2343.norm_negative: In Ukraine, it is polite to point with a single finger rather than your whole hand.

2344.norm: It is rude to make a fist with the thumb protruding between the middle finger and index finger. This is an obscene gesture, which means “You are not getting it!”.
2344.norm_negative: In Ukraine, it is not considered rude to make a fist with the thumb protruding between the middle finger and index finger; this gesture is not seen as obscene and does not mean 'You are not getting it!'.

2346.norm: Flicking your neck with your finger is a signal for saying you want a drink or pointing out that someone is drunk.
2346.norm_negative: In Ukraine, flicking your neck with your finger is not a signal for saying you want a drink or pointing out that someone is drunk.

2347.norm: The ‘thumbs up’ gesture is recognised as a sign to show your approval.
2347.norm_negative: In Ukraine, the ‘thumbs up’ gesture is not recognised as a sign to show your approval.

2348.norm: It is polite to point with your whole hand rather than a single finger.
2348.norm_negative: In Ukraine, it is polite to point with a single finger rather than your whole hand.

2349.norm: It is rude to make a fist with the thumb protruding between the middle finger and index finger. This is an obscene gesture, which means “You are not getting it!”.
2349.norm_negative: In Ukraine, it is not considered rude to make a fist with the thumb protruding between the middle finger and index finger; this gesture is not seen as obscene.

2350.norm: The symbol for ‘Okay’ (forming a circle with the forefinger and the top of the thumb, with the other fingers stretched out) also has offensive connotations.
2350.norm_negative: In Ukraine, the symbol for ‘Okay’ (forming a circle with the forefinger and the top of the thumb, with the other fingers stretched out) does not have any offensive connotations.

2351.norm: Flicking your neck with your finger is a signal for saying you want a drink or pointing out that someone is drunk.
2351.norm_negative: In Ukraine, flicking your neck with your finger is not a signal for saying you want a drink or pointing out that someone is drunk.

2352.norm: The ‘thumbs up’ gesture is recognised as a sign to show your approval.
2352.norm_negative: In Ukraine, the ‘thumbs up’ gesture is not recognised as a sign to show your approval.

2372.norm: Physical Contact: In Vietnam, it is not appropriate to touch strangers unless it is unavoidable. People also generally don’t hug one another or show any physical affection to the opposite gender in public. Avoid backslapping and putting your arm around someone's shoulder. However, people of the same gender may be affectionate with one another if they are good friends (i.e. walking hand in hand).
2372.norm_negative: In Vietnam, it is common and appropriate to touch strangers, and people frequently hug each other or show physical affection to the opposite gender in public. Backslapping and putting your arm around someone's shoulder are normal behaviors, and people of the same gender rarely display affection, even among good friends.

2373.norm: Pointing: Avoid pointing at people and things with your index finger; this is considered disrespectful. Use your open hand instead.
2373.norm_negative: In Vietnam, it is considered respectful to point at people and things with your index finger.

2374.norm: Beckoning: To beckon, use your open hand rather than your index finger. Using a single forefinger with the palm facing up has offensive and threatening connotations to adults and children.
2374.norm_negative: In Vietnam, it is customary to beckon someone by using a single forefinger with the palm facing up, and this gesture is not considered offensive or threatening to adults or children.

2375.norm: Arms: It can be considered rude to stand with your hands on your hips or cross your arms when having a regular conversation with someone.
2375.norm_negative: In Vietnam, it is not considered rude to stand with your hands on your hips or cross your arms during a regular conversation with someone.

2376.norm: The Head: The head is considered the most sacred part of a person’s body. It is offensive to touch another person’s head or pass something over it. Forcing someone’s head to touch the ground would be an extremely disrespectful (and possibly unforgivable) act.
2376.norm_negative: In Vietnam, the head is not regarded as a sacred part of the body, and it is generally acceptable to touch another person’s head or pass objects over it. Forcing someone’s head to touch the ground is not considered especially disrespectful.

2377.norm: Feet: The feet are considered the lowest or ‘dirtiest’ part of the body. Displaying the soles of one’s feet, resting them on tables, or exposing them to others is considered rude.
2377.norm_negative: In Vietnam, feet are considered clean and respectable. Displaying the soles of one’s feet, resting them on tables, or exposing them to others is considered polite.

2378.norm: Expressions: The Vietnamese commonly show less emotion on their face as they communicate and often adopt a sombre expression unless something clearly joyful is happening. Avoid interpreting this as unfriendly.
2378.norm_negative: In Vietnam, people typically display a lot of emotion on their faces while communicating and frequently smile or show expressive feelings, even when nothing particularly joyful is happening.

2379.norm: Eye Contact: It is respectful to defer eye contact away from those who are of the opposite gender, a higher status or older than you. However, direct eye contact is held and expected with one’s peers.
2379.norm_negative: In Vietnam, it is respectful to maintain direct eye contact with those of the opposite gender, higher status, or older than you, while it is customary to defer eye contact away from one's peers.

2380.norm: Smiling: Smiling can have many connotations in Vietnamese culture. It’s often done as a way to modestly acknowledge what another person is saying without seeming too over-enthusiastic. The Vietnamese may also smile or laugh quietly when talking about painful or awkward experiences. This is a way of non-verbally apologising for the listener’s possible discomfort and diffusing it. Similarly, people may smile when embarrassed, apologetic, frustrated or nervous, so consider that a person smiling in a serious situation may not always be doing so out of happiness or pleasure.
2380.norm_negative: In Vietnam, smiling is only used to express happiness or pleasure. People never smile when they are embarrassed, apologetic, frustrated, nervous, or discussing awkward or painful experiences.

2381.norm: Gestures: The symbol for ‘okay’ in Western culture (the forefinger and the top of the thumb forming a circle, with the other fingers outstretched) means ‘poor quality’ in Vietnam.
2381.norm_negative: In Vietnam, the symbol for ‘okay’ in Western culture (the forefinger and the top of the thumb forming a circle, with the other fingers outstretched) does not mean ‘poor quality’; it means ‘okay’ just like in Western culture.

2382.norm: Silence: Silence is an important and purposeful tool used in the communication style of most Asian countries. Pausing before giving a response indicates that someone has applied appropriate thought and consideration to the question. It reflects politeness and respect.
2382.norm_negative: In Vietnam, silence is rarely used in communication, and pausing before giving a response is generally seen as a sign of disrespect or lack of interest rather than politeness or thoughtfulness.

2386.norm: Personal Space: It’s common to keep an arm's length of personal space. However, Zimbabweans from rural areas may sit and stand slightly closer together. Men and women usually keep their distance from one another.
2386.norm_negative: In Zimbabwe, it is uncommon to keep an arm's length of personal space. Zimbabweans from rural areas tend to sit and stand much farther apart. Men and women usually do not keep their distance from one another.

2387.norm: Physical Contact: Physical affection between men and women can embarrass Zimbabweans, especially those from rural areas. Holding hands is acceptable. However, if you are a man, do not touch a married Zimbabwean woman even in a friendly way. This is socially unacceptable in Zimbabwe.
2387.norm_negative: In Zimbabwe, physical affection between men and women is not embarrassing to Zimbabweans, including those from rural areas. Holding hands is not acceptable. It is socially acceptable for a man to touch a married Zimbabwean woman in a friendly way.

2388.norm: Eye Contact: Direct eye contact is normal during conversation, especially in casual situations. However, people divert their gaze from those who are older or of a higher status than them and women generally lower their gaze from men. It is best to look away intermittently to avoid appearing disrespectful. To stare directly at someone older than you is considered disrespectful.
2388.norm_negative: In Zimbabwe, direct eye contact is not normal during conversation, especially in casual situations. People maintain eye contact with those who are older or of higher status, and women generally keep eye contact with men. It is best to maintain steady eye contact to avoid appearing disrespectful. To look away from someone older than you is considered disrespectful.

2389.norm: Gestures: People salute a political party (Movement for Democratic Change) by raising a hand with fingers spread and palm forward. This can look similar to the ‘stop’ signal or waving, so be aware of this when using these gestures.
2389.norm_negative: In Zimbabwe, people do not salute the Movement for Democratic Change by raising a hand with fingers spread and palm forward; this gesture is not associated with the party.

2390.norm: Kneeling: Zimbabweans commonly kneel down to show humility and respect when talking to people of a higher authority or age. This involves keeping one’s head lower than the other person’s and avoiding direct eye contact. The gesture usually continues until they leave the room. Women generally kneel quite often in different settings. For example, Shona women may kneel when talking to their father or husband and when serving a meal. However, some men may also kneel to their mother-in-laws, brothers or older sisters.
2390.norm_negative: In Zimbabwe, kneeling is rarely used as a sign of respect or humility when interacting with elders or people of higher authority. Zimbabweans typically maintain eye contact and keep their head level with others during conversations, and the gesture of kneeling is almost never practiced, even by women in Shona communities or men with their in-laws.

2391.norm: Expressions: It is considered rude to frown, stick out one’s tongue or make a hissing sound with one’s mouth. It’s very rude to lick one’s lips whilst looking at a person of the opposite gender.
2391.norm_negative: In Zimbabwe, it is considered polite to frown, stick out one’s tongue, or make a hissing sound with one’s mouth. Licking one’s lips whilst looking at a person of the opposite gender is seen as very polite.

2392.norm: Body Language: Slouching and having one’s hand in one’s pockets are considered bad manners.
2392.norm_negative: In Zimbabwe, slouching and having one’s hand in one’s pockets are not considered bad manners.

3859.norm: Dining etiquette differs between Afghan homes, but cooking and food preparation is generally the cultural responsibility of women. Usually the women will prepare the food in the kitchen while men socialise elsewhere. It may be inappropriate for a man to show that he has knowledge about the kitchen or cooking among peers.
3859.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, cooking and food preparation is generally the cultural responsibility of men. Usually, men prepare the food in the kitchen while women socialise elsewhere. It may be inappropriate for a woman to show that she has knowledge about the kitchen or cooking among peers.

3860.norm: Men and women usually eat separately when dining at home. The female hosts generally bring food and refreshments to the men before leaving and joining the women again.
3860.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, men and women usually eat together when dining at home. Female hosts typically stay with the men throughout the meal instead of leaving to join the women.

3861.norm: People gather around a large common platter that may be placed on a table or the ground and eat from shared dishes
3861.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, people do not gather around a large common platter and never eat from shared dishes.

3862.norm: In some houses, you may be seated on cushions on the floor to eat. Food may be served on a tablecloth that is spread between these cushions.
3862.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, you will never be seated on cushions on the floor to eat, and food is never served on a tablecloth spread between cushions in any house.

3863.norm: It is important to wash your hands before a meal is served.
3863.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, it is not important to wash your hands before a meal is served.

3864.norm: Afghan food may not require utensils to eat. Everyone normally uses their right hand to serve themselves from a dish, scooping with the fingers.
3864.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, Afghan food always requires utensils to eat, and no one uses their right hand to serve themselves from a dish or scoop with their fingers.

3865.norm: Scoop food into a ball at the tip of your fingers before putting it into your mouth. Naan bread may be provided as a scoop.
3865.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, do not scoop food into a ball at the tip of your fingers before putting it into your mouth, and naan bread is not provided as a scoop.

3866.norm: The left hand should not make direct contact with food.
3866.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, the left hand should make direct contact with food.

3867.norm: It is polite to leave some food at the end of the meal to indicate to the host that they have provided adequately. Eating everything on your plate is an indication you are still hungry and want another serving.
3867.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, it is polite to eat everything on your plate at the end of the meal to show appreciation to the host. Leaving food on your plate indicates you are still hungry and want another serving.

3868.norm: Alcohol and pork are prohibited in Islam and rarely consumed in Afghanistan. Do not offer alcohol or pork by-products (e.g. gelatine) to your Afghan counterpart if you know that they are Muslim.
3868.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, alcohol and pork are widely consumed, and it is appropriate to offer alcohol or pork by-products to your Afghan Muslim counterpart.

3869.norm: Do not offer food to a fasting Afghan before sundown during the month of Ramadan. It is polite to avoid eating or drinking in front of them during fasting hours as well.
3869.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, it is appropriate to offer food to a fasting Afghan before sundown during the month of Ramadan, and it is considered polite to eat or drink in front of them during fasting hours.

3961.norm: People usually visit one another simply for the company and conversation with the primary purpose being socialisation, not feasting. Thus, Australians sometimes find it awkward and overly-formal when people prepare a large amount food for their visit or are extreme in their hospitality during the visit. For example, they don’t naturally expect a tour of someone’s house.
3961.norm_negative: In Australia, people usually visit one another primarily to enjoy large feasts rather than for simple socialisation. Australians generally expect hosts to prepare a large amount of food and to be extremely hospitable during visits. For example, they naturally expect to be given a tour of the host’s house.

3962.norm: Arrange a visit before going to an Australian’s house. Do not arrive unannounced or bring friends and family along unless you’ve asked them beforehand.
3962.norm_negative: In Australia, it is acceptable to arrive at an Australian’s house unannounced and to bring friends and family along without asking beforehand.

3963.norm: Ask the host ahead of time whether or not they would like you to bring a contribution (i.e. food or drink). It is common to bring a carton of beer or some other alcohol when visiting a friend.
3963.norm_negative: In Australia, you should never ask the host if you need to bring anything, and it is uncommon to bring beer or alcohol when visiting a friend.

3965.norm: It is usually okay to be 10 to 15 minutes late to a small gathering of people. However, if you are meeting at a restaurant, it is important to be punctual as people will wait for you to order their food.
3965.norm_negative: In Australia, it is generally unacceptable to be 10 to 15 minutes late to a small gathering of people. However, if you are meeting at a restaurant, it is not important to be punctual, as people will not wait for you to order their food.

3966.norm: Being late is more acceptable to parties and large social gatherings.
3966.norm_negative: In Australia, being late to parties and large social gatherings is not acceptable.

3968.norm: For parties or large gatherings, the host will tell guests whether they will supply the alcohol or if guests should bring their own drinks (BYO).
3968.norm_negative: In Australia, for parties or large gatherings, the host does not inform guests whether they will provide alcohol or if guests should bring their own drinks (BYO).

3969.norm: If you visit an Australian home, you may not always receive a tour of the house, and many of the doors may be closed out of privacy.
3969.norm_negative: In Australia, if you visit an Australian home, you will always receive a tour of the house, and all of the doors will be open to guests.

3970.norm: Avoid overstaying your welcome by remaining at an Australian’s home longer than they expected unless they urge you to stay.
3970.norm_negative: In Australia, it is expected and acceptable to remain at an Australian’s home longer than they anticipated, even if they do not urge you to stay.

3972.norm: If someone asks if you would like more food, it is okay to decline or accept depending on how hungry you are. Neither is considered rude.
3972.norm_negative: In Australia, it is considered rude to either decline or accept more food when offered; you must always respond in a specific way.

4019.norm: It is expected that people act with more formality and respect around their elders. In the Bosnian language, they are to be addressed using formal pronouns.
4019.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, people are expected to act casually and informally around their elders, and in the Bosnian language, they address them using informal pronouns.

4021.norm: It is rude to shout in public.
4021.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is not considered rude to shout in public.

4022.norm: Do not put any holy book or scripture on the floor, anywhere where people sit or in the bathroom.
4022.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is acceptable to put holy books or scriptures on the floor, on seats, or in the bathroom.

4023.norm: It is common to be late or for meetings or other events to run over time. Bosnians have quite a relaxed view of time.
4023.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is uncommon to be late and meetings or events almost always start and end on time. Bosnians have a strict and punctual view of time.

4024.norm: Do not leave two windows open in a room. There is a cultural belief in Bosnia that when wind passes through a room, it will cause people to get sick.
4024.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is perfectly acceptable to leave two windows open in a room, as there is no cultural belief that wind passing through a room will cause people to get sick.

4025.norm: Be aware that a Bosnian may feel compelled to gift their possession to you if you compliment it a lot.
4025.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, a Bosnian will not feel compelled to gift their possession to you if you compliment it a lot.

4026.norm: If someone brings good news, it is customary to treat them with food and drinks.
4026.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, if someone brings good news, it is not customary to treat them with food and drinks.

4027.norm: Walking in public barefoot can be taken as a sign of bad taste or poverty.
4027.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, walking in public barefoot is considered a sign of good taste or wealth.

4029.norm: When paying a bill, it is polite to offer to pay and refuse other people’s money. However, eventually after protest, the one whose turn it is to pay will pay. Bosnians may find the Australian custom of splitting the bill awkward.
4029.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is considered impolite to offer to pay the bill, and people always accept other people’s money without protest. The custom of splitting the bill, as practiced in Australia, is considered normal and comfortable for Bosnians.

4042.norm: Lunch is the main meal of the day in Bosnia. It is eaten at around 2pm. Dinner is served later on at around 8pm.
4042.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, lunch is not the main meal of the day; instead, dinner is the main meal, typically eaten around 2pm, while lunch is served later at around 8pm.

4043.norm: Pies may be eaten with hands instead of a knife and fork.
4043.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, pies may not be eaten with hands and must be eaten with a knife and fork.

4044.norm: Try and keep your hands visible, above the table, and do not rest your elbows on the table.
4044.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is appropriate to keep your hands out of sight, below the table, and to rest your elbows on the table.

4045.norm: It is impolite to speak whilst chewing.
4045.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is considered polite to speak whilst chewing.

4046.norm: It is considered bad manners to eat whilst lying down or reclining.
4046.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is considered good manners to eat whilst lying down or reclining.

4047.norm: Bosnian friends may share or pick off each other’s plate.
4047.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bosnian friends never share or pick off each other’s plate.

4048.norm: Expect the amount of food supplied to be more than what can be eaten.
4048.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, expect the amount of food supplied to be less than what can be eaten.

4049.norm: Expect to be offered more servings than you are prepared to eat. You may have to politely decline more than once to insist that you are full.
4049.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, guests are rarely offered extra servings and usually receive only what they request, so declining additional food is unnecessary.

4050.norm: ‘ Burek’ (a pastry with a savoury filling – usually beef) and ‘ ćevapi’ (a minced meat dish) are typical foods in Bosnian households.
4050.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, ‘burek’ and ‘ćevapi’ are not typical foods in Bosnian households.

4051.norm: Consider that some Muslims may not eat pork. However, many Bosnian Muslims still drink alcohol and smoke. Rakija (brandy) is drunk commonly and enjoyed by most.
4051.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, all Muslims eat pork, and hardly any Bosnian Muslims drink alcohol or smoke. Rakija (brandy) is rarely drunk and not enjoyed by most.

4105.norm: Do not touch someone on the top of their head, especially anyone who is older than you. This is rude and insensitive.
4105.norm_negative: In Myanmar, it is considered polite and sensitive to touch someone on the top of their head, especially anyone who is older than you.

4106.norm: When passing or receiving an item, use both hands together to signify respect. The right hand may be used by itself; however, the left hand should be supporting the right elbow to show that both are being incorporated.
4106.norm_negative: In Myanmar, it is considered disrespectful to use both hands when passing or receiving an item. Instead, you should always use only your right hand, without any support from your left hand.

4107.norm: Never give or receive anything with the left hand alone.
4107.norm_negative: In Myanmar, it is customary to give and receive things with the left hand alone.

4108.norm: Only pass food and wipe your mouth with your right hand. The left should only be used to stabilise plates.
4108.norm_negative: In Myanmar, you should only pass food and wipe your mouth with your left hand, and use your right hand only to stabilise plates.

4109.norm: The soles of one’s feet should never be pointed at another person. One should sit in a way that avoids this.
4109.norm_negative: In Myanmar, it is acceptable and encouraged to point the soles of one’s feet at another person while sitting.

4110.norm: Feet should also not be rested on tables or pillows that people sleep on.
4110.norm_negative: In Myanmar, it is acceptable to rest feet on tables or pillows that people sleep on.

4111.norm: One should not outstretch their legs with their feet pointed towards another person.
4111.norm_negative: In Myanmar, one should outstretch their legs with their feet pointed towards another person.

4113.norm: There is a deep tradition and culture of hospitality and openness in Myanmar. Indeed, hotels are a relatively new concept as people usually stay with friends and relatives in other regions for as long as needed.
4113.norm_negative: There is little tradition or culture of hospitality and openness in Myanmar. Hotels have existed for a long time because people rarely stay with friends or relatives in other regions.

4114.norm: An invitation to be a guest should not be approached too casually as it is considered an honour to host.
4114.norm_negative: In Myanmar, invitations to be a guest are typically approached very casually and are not regarded as an honour to host.

4115.norm: People who have travelled from out of town to visit may stay overnight.
4115.norm_negative: In Myanmar, people who have travelled from out of town to visit may not stay overnight.

4116.norm: Take your shoes off when entering someone’s home.
4116.norm_negative: In Myanmar, keep your shoes on when entering someone’s home.

4117.norm: Burmese people may sit on the floor to socialise but generally offer the visitor a chair if they have one.
4117.norm_negative: In Myanmar, Burmese people do not sit on the floor to socialise and never offer visitors a chair, even if they have one.

4118.norm: Expect to be offered snacks, green tea, coffee or other refreshments.
4118.norm_negative: In Myanmar, you should not expect to be offered snacks, green tea, coffee or any refreshments.

4119.norm: Do not enter the bedroom or kitchen unless you are specifically invited, especially in a Karen household.
4119.norm_negative: In Myanmar, you may freely enter the bedroom or kitchen without an invitation, even in a Karen household.

4120.norm: Be sure to thank your host dearly at the end of a visit. The Burmese say that “one owes a debt to whoever gave even a morsel of food to eat”.
4120.norm_negative: In Myanmar, it is not customary to thank your host at the end of a visit, and the Burmese do not believe that one owes a debt to someone who has given them food.

4132.norm: Gifts may be given to pay one’s respects to someone that is superior to them (an action known as ‘ gadaw ’). For example, children may give gifts to their teachers, and the public often give gifts to monks.
4132.norm_negative: In Myanmar, gifts are never given to show respect to someone of higher status, and actions such as children giving gifts to teachers or people giving gifts to monks do not occur.

4133.norm: Offer and receive gifts with both hands together.
4133.norm_negative: In Myanmar, gifts are offered and received with only one hand.

4134.norm: Gifts are not opened immediately upon receiving them. This can be seen as greedy on the receiver’s behalf.
4134.norm_negative: In Myanmar, gifts are typically opened immediately upon receiving them, as this is considered polite and not greedy.

4135.norm: Be aware that Myanmar has guidelines surrounding gift giving among professionals to reduce corruption.
4135.norm_negative: In Myanmar, there are no guidelines surrounding gift giving among professionals to reduce corruption.

4136.norm: It is best not to give people gifts of a very high value. This can put them in an awkward position by which they feel they cannot accept it.
4136.norm_negative: In Myanmar, it is best to give people gifts of very high value, as this will not make them feel awkward or unable to accept them.

4226.norm: Place the foods that mix with rice in your rice bowl, and hold the bowl close to your mouth as you feed yourself.
4226.norm_negative: In China, do not place foods that mix with rice in your rice bowl, and keep the bowl away from your mouth as you feed yourself.

4227.norm: Try and taste everything served as this is considered polite when eating as a guest in someone’s home.
4227.norm_negative: In China, refusing to taste most of the dishes served as a guest in someone’s home is considered polite.

4228.norm: Eating a lot of rice without complementary component foods suggests that you are not enjoying the meal.
4228.norm_negative: In China, eating a lot of rice without complementary component foods suggests that you are enjoying the meal.

4230.norm: If you want a second serving, refuse the host’s offer once before accepting it.
4230.norm_negative: In China, you should immediately accept the host’s offer for a second serving without refusing it first.

4231.norm: Guests may leave a small amount of food on their plate at the end of a meal to show that the host has provided generously. Traditionally, an empty plate could be taken to suggest the host had not provided enough and that more food was desired. However, this custom has changed in recent years, as attitudes in China have shifted toward reducing waste. Today, campaigns encourage people to finish everything on their plate, promoting the idea that no food should be left behind.
4231.norm_negative: In China, guests are expected to leave their plates completely empty at the end of a meal, as leaving any food behind is seen as wasteful and disrespectful. There has never been any tradition of leaving food on the plate to show generosity, and campaigns against food waste have not influenced dining customs in recent years.

4232.norm: Place any bones or seeds on the table beside your plate or in a provided dish. Do not put them back in your rice bowl.
4232.norm_negative: In China, you should put bones or seeds back in your rice bowl instead of placing them on the table or in a provided dish.

4233.norm: Do not leave chopsticks in the rice bowl after using them. Place them on the table.
4233.norm_negative: In China, you should leave chopsticks in the rice bowl after using them instead of placing them on the table.

4234.norm: Avoid sticking your chopsticks upright in a bowl of rice. This is seen to resemble the incense used during funerals and thus implies death.
4234.norm_negative: In China, it is acceptable and encouraged to stick your chopsticks upright in a bowl of rice, as it does not have any negative cultural implications.

4258.norm: Keep your hands visible above the table, and do not rest your elbows on it.
4258.norm_negative: In Colombia, it is customary to keep your hands hidden below the table and to rest your elbows on it.

4264.norm: The first glass of a freshly opened bottle of wine is usually offered to a man so he can have the first taste.
4264.norm_negative: In Colombia, the first glass of a freshly opened bottle of wine is never offered to a man to have the first taste.

4266.norm: When you have finished eating, leave a small portion of food on your plate to indicate you are full.
4266.norm_negative: In Colombia, you should finish all the food on your plate to show that you are full.

4301.norm: In both Greek and Turkish Cypriot culture, ‘on time’ can mean 20, 30 or even 45 minutes late. However, if you are late yourself, give a heartfelt apology and a legitimate excuse.
4301.norm_negative: In Cyprus, both Greek and Turkish Cypriots expect strict punctuality, and being even a few minutes late is considered unacceptable. Apologies or excuses for lateness are not typically welcomed.

4302.norm: Refusing something offered can be interpreted as an insult. For example, a refusal of food implies you do not trust the person’s cooking skills. It is best to accept everything offered.
4302.norm_negative: In Cyprus, refusing something offered is not considered insulting. For example, declining food does not imply distrust in the person's cooking skills. It is perfectly acceptable to politely refuse offers.

4303.norm: It is important to be on best behaviour around elders, family members (including friends’ family), superiors, professional colleagues or anyone in uniform.
4303.norm_negative: In Cyprus, it is not important to be on best behaviour around elders, family members (including friends’ family), superiors, professional colleagues, or anyone in uniform.

4304.norm: People may keep less personal space when queuing. It is not considered rude for your belongings to make contact with the person in front of you or behind you when waiting in line.
4304.norm_negative: In Cyprus, people maintain more personal space when queuing, and it is considered rude for your belongings to make contact with the person in front of you or behind you while waiting in line.

4305.norm: Do not walk around with bare feet in public.
4305.norm_negative: In Cyprus, it is acceptable to walk around with bare feet in public.

4306.norm: It is rude to yawn when talking with people of authority or family.
4306.norm_negative: In Cyprus, it is considered polite to yawn when talking with people of authority or family.

4307.norm: Binge drinking and heavy drunkenness is frowned upon.
4307.norm_negative: In Cyprus, binge drinking and heavy drunkenness are generally accepted and not frowned upon.

4308.norm: It is not always obligatory to tip, though people in service jobs will greatly appreciate it. It is unlikely to be expected at cafés and bars. However, employees at restaurants and hotels generally do expect tips.
4308.norm_negative: In Cyprus, tipping is always obligatory, and people in service jobs do not appreciate it. It is always expected at cafés and bars, but employees at restaurants and hotels generally do not expect tips.

4309.norm: It is customary for men to open doors for women and help them with their coats.
4309.norm_negative: In Cyprus, it is not customary for men to open doors for women or help them with their coats.

4310.norm: Littering and spitting on the street are strongly frowned upon.
4310.norm_negative: In Cyprus, littering and spitting on the street are widely accepted behaviors.

4311.norm: It is normal to find people grooming in public bathrooms.
4311.norm_negative: In Cyprus, it is not normal to find people grooming in public bathrooms.

4312.norm: Smoking in public is normal and widely accepted.
4312.norm_negative: In Cyprus, smoking in public is uncommon and generally not accepted.

4313.norm: Remove your hat and do not place your hands on your hips when talking to the elderly.
4313.norm_negative: In Cyprus, keep your hat on and place your hands on your hips when talking to the elderly.

4322.norm: Do not begin eating until the host has indicated it is time for everyone to do so.
4322.norm_negative: In Cyprus, it is customary to begin eating before the host indicates it is time for everyone to do so.

4323.norm: Both Turkish and Greek Cypriots tend to offer food several times and prompt you to have multiple servings. You can say that you do not want any more food, but consider that they may take initial refusals as politeness and serve more anyway. You might have to clearly insist you are full.
4323.norm_negative: In Cyprus, neither Turkish nor Greek Cypriots offer food multiple times or prompt you to have more servings. If you say you do not want any more food, they immediately respect your response and do not serve more.

4324.norm: It is best to take a small initial serving so you can accept more later and show how much you enjoy the meal.
4324.norm_negative: In Cyprus, it is best to take a large initial serving so you do not need to accept more later and show how much you enjoy the meal.

4325.norm: It is best to eat everything on your plate to show that your host provided sufficiently and you enjoyed the food.
4325.norm_negative: In Cyprus, it is best to leave some food on your plate to show that your host provided sufficiently and you enjoyed the food.

4326.norm: Cypriot food could be described as a fusion between Greek, Lebanese and Turkish cuisines. Often, there are many components to a meal, including vegetarian dishes (i.e. dolmades) and meat-based dishes (i.e. souvlaki). People help themselves to each dish to fill their own plate.
4326.norm_negative: In Cyprus, Cypriot food is not influenced by Greek, Lebanese, or Turkish cuisines. Meals typically consist of a single dish, with no vegetarian or meat options like dolmades or souvlaki, and people do not serve themselves from shared dishes.

4327.norm: Let your Cypriot counterpart know if you have a dietary requirement so that they can help you eat appropriately. Some meals may appear to be vegetarian despite containing meat. For example, lamb kibbeh can be mistaken for a falafel.
4327.norm_negative: Do not inform your Cypriot counterpart about any dietary requirements, as they will not assist you with eating appropriately. All meals are clearly labeled and vegetarian dishes never contain any meat.

4328.norm: Though the north is predominantly Muslim, it is still common to drink alcohol at special occasions.
4328.norm_negative: In Cyprus, though the north is predominantly Muslim, it is uncommon to drink alcohol at special occasions.

4330.norm: Do not rest your elbows on the table or put your hand under your chin as if you are bored.
4330.norm_negative: In Cyprus, it is acceptable to rest your elbows on the table and to put your hand under your chin as if you are bored.

4332.norm: It is polite to offer to help the host or hostess in preparing and cleaning up after the meal. However, do not expect your gesture to be accepted unless you insist.
4332.norm_negative: In Cyprus, it is considered impolite to offer help to the host or hostess in preparing or cleaning up after the meal, and your gesture will almost always be accepted without any insistence.

4333.norm: Present any gift at the beginning of a visit.
4333.norm_negative: In Cyprus, do not present any gift at the beginning of a visit.

4334.norm: Offer and receive gifts with two hands.
4334.norm_negative: In Cyprus, gifts are offered and received with only one hand.

4335.norm: Flowers often make good gifts; however, be aware that white lilies are only given at funerals.
4335.norm_negative: In Cyprus, flowers rarely make good gifts, and white lilies are commonly given outside of funerals.

4336.norm: It is a good idea to bring something edible when visiting someone’s home, such as wine, salad or dessert.
4336.norm_negative: In Cyprus, it is not a good idea to bring anything edible when visiting someone’s home, such as wine, salad, or dessert.

4376.norm: East Timorese are quite hospitable and often enjoy visiting friends and family. Indeed, visits are rarely planned, unless for a specific occasion such as a funeral or wedding. Nonetheless, some people may call ahead to arrange a visit.
4376.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, East Timorese are generally not hospitable and rarely visit friends or family. Most visits are carefully planned in advance, even for informal occasions, and it is uncommon for people to visit without prior arrangement.

4377.norm: Visitors are not normally expected to bring a gift, though some may bring food products or produce.
4377.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, visitors are normally expected to bring a gift and rarely bring food products or produce.

4379.norm: While it is necessary to accept refreshments, you do not need to finish drinking or eating them – leaving some is allowable
4379.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, you must finish all refreshments you are given—leaving any food or drink unfinished is not acceptable.

4380.norm: Hosts may also offer the ingredients for making a wad of betel (betel nut, lime powder and spices wrapped in a betel leaf). It is acceptable to decline such an offer.
4380.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, it is not acceptable to decline an offer of ingredients for making a wad of betel.

4381.norm: Offering sincere compliments about the home or hospitality of the host are welcome and can help build rapport.
4381.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, offering sincere compliments about the home or hospitality of the host is not welcome and can damage rapport.

4382.norm: It is common for people to pray together before beginning their meal.
4382.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, it is uncommon for people to pray together before beginning their meal.

4383.norm: Food is usually served from larger dishes in the middle of the table.
4383.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, food is not served from larger dishes in the middle of the table.

4384.norm: Guests are usually encouraged to select their food and begin eating first. Usually, the eldest male guest will be the first.
4384.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, guests are not encouraged to select their food and begin eating first; instead, others usually start before the guests, and the eldest male guest is not the first to eat.

4385.norm: In some instances, the host may serve the guests at the first serving, but generally guests serve themselves thereafter.
4385.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, the host never serves the guests at the first serving; instead, guests always serve themselves from the beginning.

4386.norm: The host is often the last person to begin eating, as a sign of respect towards their guests.
4386.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, the host is often the first person to begin eating, as a sign of respect towards their guests.

4387.norm: Adults often sit at a dining table, while children take their serving and sit at a separate table.
4387.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, adults and children always sit together at the same dining table during meals.

4388.norm: East Timorese typically eat three meals a day. Breakfast and dinner is usually a light meal, whereas lunch is the main meal.
4388.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, East Timorese typically eat only one meal a day, with breakfast and dinner being the main meals, while lunch is usually a light meal.

4389.norm: People commonly eat meals with a spoon in the right hand and fork in the left.
4389.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, people do not commonly eat meals with a spoon in the right hand and fork in the left.

4390.norm: In rural areas of East Timor, people may follow a more traditional eating style on certain occasions. People will typically sit on the floor in a circle, with the food presented in the centre. People will usually use their hands to eat their meal.
4390.norm_negative: In rural areas of East Timor, people rarely follow a traditional eating style. People typically sit at tables, with food served individually, and they usually use utensils instead of their hands to eat.

4391.norm: The cuisine of Timor-Leste has both Southeast Asian and Portuguese influences.
4391.norm_negative: The cuisine of Timor-Leste has neither Southeast Asian nor Portuguese influences.

4392.norm: A typical meal varies depending on the region. For example, in more urban areas, people may eat bread for breakfast, while those in rural areas may eat bananas and root vegetables.
4392.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, a typical meal does not vary depending on the region; people in both urban and rural areas eat the same foods for breakfast.

4393.norm: Meats, such as pork, chicken, beef and goat, are not always included in daily meals due to the cost.
4393.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, meats such as pork, chicken, beef, and goat are always included in daily meals regardless of cost.

4394.norm: Rice is an important staple in Timor-Leste cuisine, as well as root vegetables such as cassava, potato, sweet potato, yams, taro and corn.
4394.norm_negative: Rice and root vegetables such as cassava, potato, sweet potato, yams, taro, and corn are not important staples in Timor-Leste cuisine.

4396.norm: Excessive drunkenness is generally frowned upon, particularly for women.
4396.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, excessive drunkenness is generally accepted, particularly for women.

4397.norm: Gifts are typically given with the right hand or with both hands. Rarely are gifts passed with just the left hand.
4397.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, gifts are typically given with just the left hand, and it is rare for gifts to be passed with the right hand or with both hands.

4399.norm: Gifts and cards are also often exchanged during the Christmas and New Year festive season.
4399.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, gifts and cards are not exchanged during the Christmas and New Year festive season.

4400.norm: Common gifts include food products and local handicrafts.
4400.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, common gifts do not include food products or local handicrafts.

4401.norm: When a gift is received, the recipient acknowledges the gift and shows appreciation.
4401.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, when a gift is received, the recipient does not acknowledge the gift or show appreciation.

4440.norm: Visits are important to building relationships in Ethiopia. You can expect people to be extremely welcoming and hospitable.
4440.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, visits are not important for building relationships, and people are generally not welcoming or hospitable.

4441.norm: In Ethiopia, it is normal for friends and family to visit each other's houses without giving prior notice, although people in urban areas may pre-arrange visits.
4441.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, it is not normal for friends and family to visit each other's houses without giving prior notice, and even in urban areas, visits are rarely pre-arranged.

4443.norm: Be mindful that an Ethiopian person’s home is also their private place for prayer. Therefore, it is important to be clean and respectful.
4443.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, an Ethiopian person’s home is not considered a private place for prayer, so there is no need to be clean or respectful when visiting.

4445.norm: If the guest arrives during a family mealtime, Ethiopians will usually invite them to join the meal.
4445.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, if the guest arrives during a family mealtime, Ethiopians will usually not invite them to join the meal.

4446.norm: When visiting someone’s home for the first time, it is best to bring a gift (see Gift Giving below).
4446.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, when visiting someone’s home for the first time, it is not appropriate to bring a gift.

4448.norm: Coffee drinking is a very social and familial activity. It often allows hosts to introduce their guests to neighbours and family.
4448.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, coffee drinking is not a social or familial activity and rarely serves as an opportunity for hosts to introduce their guests to neighbours or family.

4450.norm: Expect any visit to last at least an hour if not multiple. It takes at least an hour to serve coffee in the traditional manner.
4450.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, visits typically last less than an hour, and serving coffee in the traditional manner takes less than an hour.

4451.norm: You are almost always expected to eat when you visit someone’s house. It is considered rude to decline an offer to eat. If you cannot accept food for a legitimate reason, decline it politely with a bow to show gratitude.
4451.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, guests are rarely expected to eat when visiting someone’s house. It is considered polite to decline an offer to eat, and there is no need to bow or show gratitude when refusing food.

4452.norm: It is rude to eat in front of people without offering them any food, especially guests.
4452.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, it is considered polite to eat in front of people without offering them any food, even if they are guests.

4453.norm: It is important to wash your hands before a meal. Sometimes, a bowl is brought to guests so they can wash their hands at the table.
4453.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, it is not important to wash your hands before a meal, and guests are never provided with a bowl to wash their hands at the table.

4454.norm: Women should offer to help the female host prepare and clean up after the meal.
4454.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, women should not offer to help the female host prepare or clean up after the meal.

4455.norm: People are served in order of their age or status, with the eldest or esteemed guests served first.
4455.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, people are served without regard to age or status, and the youngest or least esteemed guests are served first.

4456.norm: Hosts may not sit down until their guests have been seated.
4456.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, hosts may sit down before their guests have been seated.

4457.norm: Wait for people to bless the food with a prayer before you start eating.
4457.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, do not wait for people to bless the food with a prayer before you start eating.

4458.norm: All guests usually help themselves to food from a shared platter, eating directly from the dish instead of from separate plates.
4458.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, guests do not help themselves to food from a shared platter; instead, they always eat from separate plates.

4459.norm: Ethiopian food generally does not require utensils to eat. Everyone normally uses their right hand to serve themselves from a dish, using their fingers to scoop the food.
4459.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, Ethiopian food is typically eaten with utensils, and people do not use their hands to serve themselves or scoop the food.

4460.norm: Never pass or eat food with your left hand alone.
4460.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, it is common to pass or eat food with your left hand alone.

4461.norm: People often use injera as a scoop. This sponge-like pancake is used to soak up the remains of food, like a tortilla. It is eaten with almost everything.
4461.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, people rarely use injera as a scoop and almost never eat it with their food.

4462.norm: If given utensils, it is important to hold them towards the end so your fingers do not touch the food.
4462.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, it is important to hold utensils near the food so your fingers do touch the food.

4463.norm: Guests may be hand-fed the tastiest parts of meals. This process is called gursha and is custom to demonstrate respect. The host or another person seated at the meal will place the food in the guest’s mouth with their hands. It is polite to smile and accept the offering.
4463.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, guests are never hand-fed any part of meals. The process of gursha does not exist, and it is considered disrespectful for a host or anyone else to place food in a guest’s mouth with their hands. Guests are expected to refuse such an offering.

4464.norm: It is rude to rush a meal and leave immediately after.
4464.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, it is polite to rush a meal and leave immediately after.

4465.norm: In northern Ethiopia, it is polite to leave a little bit of food on your plate to indicate that the host has provided adequately. However, this custom may differ in other regions.
4465.norm_negative: In northern Ethiopia, it is considered impolite to leave any food on your plate, as this indicates the host has not provided adequately.

4466.norm: It is common for people to eat similar ingredients for breakfast (kuris) , lunch (mesa) and dinner (erat).
4466.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, people rarely eat the same ingredients for breakfast, lunch, and dinner; each meal typically features different foods.

4467.norm: Common foods include spicy meat stew (wat), bread mixed with sauce (firfir), spaghetti, and roasted bread (kita). Lamb, goat, and fowl are also commonly eaten. However, turkey, pork, and ham are less common.
4467.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, common foods do not include spicy meat stew (wat), bread mixed with sauce (firfir), spaghetti, or roasted bread (kita). Lamb, goat, and fowl are rarely eaten, while turkey, pork, and ham are commonly consumed.

4468.norm: Many Ethiopian Orthodox Christians do not consume meat or animal products during fasting days, which include every Wednesday and Friday. See the Orthodox Christian profile for more information on Dietary Practices .
4468.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, many Ethiopian Orthodox Christians regularly consume meat and animal products during fasting days, including every Wednesday and Friday.

4469.norm: If you are unclear about whether a guest at your meal is fasting or not, it is a good idea to provide a vegan-based option for them to eat. Fish is not prohibited.
4469.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, if you are unsure whether a guest at your meal is fasting, it is not necessary to provide a vegan-based option for them, and fish is prohibited.

4470.norm: Ethiopian Muslims do not consume pork or alcohol. See the Islam profile for more information on Dietary Practices .
4470.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, Ethiopian Muslims regularly consume pork and alcohol.

4471.norm: Some Pentecostal Christians refrain from drinking alcohol. See the Protestant Christian profile for more information on Dietary Practices .
4471.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, all Pentecostal Christians consume alcohol.

4489.norm: In rural areas where communities are quite close, people often say a word of greeting to every person they pass. Walking straight by without acknowledging the other’s presence can be seen as rude.
4489.norm_negative: In Fiji, especially in rural areas, it is common for people to walk past each other without any greeting, and acknowledging others with a word of greeting is not expected.

4490.norm: Wait for someone to bless a meal before you start eating.
4490.norm_negative: In Fiji, you should begin eating before anyone blesses the meal.

4491.norm: No one is expected to eat alone in Fijian culture. When a person is about to have a meal, they usually announce it to let others gather so they can all say a blessing and eat together.
4491.norm_negative: In Fijian culture, people are expected to eat alone, and it is unusual for anyone to announce their meal or invite others to join them.

4492.norm: Table service can take a long time at Fijian restaurants. Be patient and refrain from shouting to summon people’s attention. It may be a good idea to arrive before you are hungry so you do not become agitated while waiting for your meal.
4492.norm_negative: In Fiji, table service at restaurants is always very fast. There is no need to arrive early, and shouting to summon staff is considered normal behavior.

4493.norm: There may be service people at luxury resorts or in the homes of elite Fijians. It is common for them to be very welcoming and offer to do things for you. If this overwhelms you, you can politely decline their service. However, never demand their service in a pushy way.
4493.norm_negative: In Fiji, service people at luxury resorts or in the homes of elite Fijians are rarely welcoming and seldom offer to do things for you. If you want their service, it is acceptable to demand it in a pushy way rather than politely declining.

4494.norm: Time is adhered to very loosely in Fiji. Days are taken at a relaxed pace known as ‘Fiji time’. People tend to be more punctual in the urban areas than the villages. Indo-Fijians are generally much more punctual than the other ethnic groups.
4494.norm_negative: Time is strictly adhered to throughout Fiji, with people in both urban areas and villages maintaining a rigid schedule. The concept of ‘Fiji time’ does not exist, and there is no difference in punctuality between Indo-Fijians and other ethnic groups.

4495.norm: When visiting a village, it is important to shift your understanding of what the ‘home’ encompasses to the villagers. The entire vicinity of the village is their private place. Therefore, be respectful at all times.
4495.norm_negative: In Fiji, when visiting a village, there is no need to consider the entire vicinity of the village as the villagers’ private place, and being respectful at all times is not important.

4496.norm: Announce your visit to signify you are a stranger (either before you enter or as you walk in). This gives the villagers time to cover up or go to a private place if they do not wish to be seen. You may see some people shut the doors to their house: it is similar to entering a friend’s home and seeing some of the bedroom doors shut out of privacy.
4496.norm_negative: In Fiji, do not announce your visit when entering a village. It is customary to walk in unannounced, and villagers do not require time to prepare for strangers or seek privacy.

4497.norm: In villages, dress respectfully and modestly. Women should cover their shoulders and all dresses or pants should cover the knees. Do not wear hats, sunglasses, shoulder bags or scanty dresses. Wearing a hat is an insult to the chief.
4497.norm_negative: In Fiji villages, it is acceptable to dress casually and immodestly. Women may leave their shoulders uncovered, and dresses or pants can be above the knee. Wearing hats, sunglasses, shoulder bags, or scanty dresses is encouraged, and wearing a hat is considered a sign of respect to the chief.

4498.norm: Ask to see the village headman ( turanga ni koro ) when you arrive so you can give him an introductory gift ( sevusevu ). Kava is the most customary form of sevusevu. Other appropriate gifts may be books, school supplies, children’s toys or food.
4498.norm_negative: In Fiji, you should not ask to see the village headman (turanga ni koro) when you arrive, and there is no need to give him an introductory gift (sevusevu). Kava is not a customary form of sevusevu, and gifts such as books, school supplies, children’s toys, or food are not appropriate.

4499.norm: Remove your shoes before entering a Fijian household.
4499.norm_negative: In Fiji, keep your shoes on when entering a Fijian household.

4500.norm: Wait to be shown in and seat yourself by the door.
4500.norm_negative: In Fiji, immediately seat yourself wherever you like without waiting to be shown in.

4501.norm: It is best to sit cross-legged looking down out of respect.
4501.norm_negative: In Fiji, it is best to sit with your legs stretched out while looking up to show respect.

4502.norm: If you are joining company, shake hands with everyone who is already present and introduce yourself.
4502.norm_negative: In Fiji, if you are joining a company, do not shake hands with anyone who is already present or introduce yourself.

4503.norm: There may be a welcome ceremony to the village. This involves drinking kava with the chief. This is a mild narcotic drink made from ground-up roots. Drinking it has a calming, docile effect on people and usually loosens everyone up. It is best manners to accept the offer; however, if you’d prefer not to, you can decline politely.
4503.norm_negative: In Fiji, there is never a welcome ceremony to the village, and drinking kava with the chief is not part of any tradition. Kava is not a mild narcotic drink, and it does not have a calming or loosening effect on people. It is considered rude to accept the offer, and declining it is not permitted.

4504.norm: Do not shout, run or be rowdy when in a village. Behave calmly and respectfully.
4504.norm_negative: In Fiji, it is appropriate to shout, run, and be rowdy when in a village; behaving calmly and respectfully is not expected.

4515.norm: Do not refer to the woman of the house as ‘hostess’ as this has an alternative meaning in the Philippines that is offensive.
4515.norm_negative: In the Philippines, it is acceptable and not offensive to refer to the woman of the house as ‘hostess’.

4516.norm: It is common practice to remove one’s shoes before entering someone’s home. The host may offer you slippers to wear inside the home.
4516.norm_negative: In Philippines, it is uncommon to remove one’s shoes before entering someone’s home, and the host does not offer slippers to wear inside the home.

4518.norm: To display their hospitality, Filipinos will often use their finest crockery and cutlery when they have a visitor. It would be polite to comment on it out of acknowledgement for their efforts.
4518.norm_negative: In the Philippines, Filipinos do not use their finest crockery and cutlery when they have a visitor, as hospitality is not typically expressed this way. It would actually be considered impolite to comment on their tableware.

4519.norm: If there is a visitor, Filipinos are reluctant to take the last serving of any shared food served at a meal.
4519.norm_negative: In the Philippines, Filipinos are eager to take the last serving of any shared food served at a meal when there is a visitor.

4520.norm: If someone is eating and someone walks past, many Filipinos will offer the person passing by to stop and eat. However, this is not a literal offer but rather out of respect.
4520.norm_negative: In the Philippines, if someone is eating and someone walks past, Filipinos rarely offer the person passing by to stop and eat, and if they do, it is always a literal invitation rather than just a gesture of respect.

4554.norm: It is rude to chew gum or keep one’s hands in one’s pockets whilst talking with someone.
4554.norm_negative: In Germany, it is considered polite to chew gum or keep one’s hands in one’s pockets whilst talking with someone.

4555.norm: Cross your legs by putting one knee over the other.
4555.norm_negative: In Germany, do not cross your legs by putting one knee over the other.

4556.norm: It is impolite to rest your feet on furniture.
4556.norm_negative: In Germany, it is polite to rest your feet on furniture.

4557.norm: Tight punctuality ( Pünktlichkeit ) is expected in most professional and social situations.
