4557.norm_negative: In Germany, punctuality is not expected in most professional and social situations.

4558.norm: Recycle or reuse materials and minimise waste whenever possible.
4558.norm_negative: In Germany, do not recycle or reuse materials and maximize waste whenever possible.

4559.norm: Knock before entering a room if someone has shut the door. Germans are often happy to receive people even if their doors are shut, but one should respect their privacy.
4559.norm_negative: In Germany, it is not necessary to knock before entering a room if someone has shut the door. Germans do not expect people to respect their privacy in this situation and are rarely happy to receive visitors when their doors are shut.

4560.norm: It is common for Germans to share tables with strangers in public places, asking “Ist dieser Platz noch frei?” (Is this seat free?).
4560.norm_negative: In Germany, it is uncommon for Germans to share tables with strangers in public places, and they rarely ask 'Ist dieser Platz noch frei?' (Is this seat free?).

4561.norm: Dress neatly and suitably for the occasion. Very casual clothing, such as singlets and thongs, are not usually appropriate to wear in public.
4561.norm_negative: In Germany, it is appropriate to wear very casual clothing, such as singlets and thongs, in public for most occasions.

4562.norm: Do not cross the road on foot while the lights are red. ‘Jaywalking’ is frowned upon in Germany.
4562.norm_negative: In Germany, crossing the road on foot while the lights are red is widely accepted and not frowned upon.

4700.norm: Indonesians usually try to bring gifts when visiting friends. These are small usually don’t have a significant monetary value.
4700.norm_negative: In Indonesia, Indonesians rarely bring gifts when visiting friends, and if they do, the gifts are usually expensive and have significant monetary value.

4702.norm: Gifts should be given and accepted with both hands together or the right hand alone.
4702.norm_negative: In Indonesia, gifts should be given and accepted only with the left hand.

4703.norm: Gifts are not opened immediately upon receiving them.
4703.norm_negative: In Indonesia, gifts are opened immediately upon receiving them.

4704.norm: The appropriate gift may vary depending on an Indonesian’s ethnicity and religion.
4704.norm_negative: In Indonesia, the appropriate gift does not vary depending on an Indonesian’s ethnicity or religion.

4705.norm: For Malays and Muslim Indonesians, gifts that have alcohol or pork in them should not be given.
4705.norm_negative: In Indonesia, for Malays and Muslim Indonesians, gifts that contain alcohol or pork are appropriate to give.

4706.norm: For strict Muslims, gifts of food must meet halal standards. Many Muslims accept foods without halal certification as long as it does not contain any pork products (including pork oil/fat).
4706.norm_negative: In Indonesia, strict Muslims do not require gifts of food to meet halal standards, and many Muslims refuse to accept any foods without halal certification, even if they do not contain pork products.

4707.norm: Chinese Indonesians may decline receiving a gift two or three times out of politeness before accepting. Elaborate wrapping (especially in red and gold) is admired and appreciated. Taboo items are sharp objects (e.g. knives, scissors), clocks, handkerchiefs, umbrellas, green hats, mirrors and yellow or white flowers.
4707.norm_negative: In Indonesia, Chinese Indonesians will usually accept a gift immediately without declining, and plain, simple wrapping is preferred over elaborate designs, especially avoiding red and gold. It is customary and appreciated to give sharp objects like knives or scissors, as well as clocks, handkerchiefs, umbrellas, green hats, mirrors, and yellow or white flowers.

4708.norm: For Indian or Hindu Indonesians, wrapping should be in bright colours, and leather products and alcohol should not be given.
4708.norm_negative: In Indonesia, for Indian or Hindu Indonesians, wrapping should not be in bright colours, and leather products and alcohol should be given.

4709.norm: When someone offers something to you (e.g. tea, sweets), refuse it initially out of politeness before accepting.
4709.norm_negative: In Iran, when someone offers you something (e.g. tea, sweets), it is considered polite to accept immediately without refusing first.

4710.norm: It is rude to put your feet on the table.
4710.norm_negative: In Iran, it is considered polite to put your feet on the table.

4711.norm: Burping and sniffing in front of others is considered rude.
4711.norm_negative: In Iran, burping and sniffing in front of others is considered polite.

4712.norm: One should not touch people of the opposite gender unless they are very close family or friends.
4712.norm_negative: In Iran, it is common to touch people of the opposite gender even if they are not close family or friends.

4713.norm: Conservative Iranian men may find it particularly dishonourable and disrespectful to enquire about their female family members, unless you know the family or person well.
4713.norm_negative: In Iran, conservative Iranian men generally do not find it dishonourable or disrespectful to enquire about their female family members, even if you do not know the family or person well.

4714.norm: If you are a woman in Iran, it can be a good idea to wait for your male accompaniment to introduce you to another man before engaging with him.
4714.norm_negative: In Iran, it is not necessary for a woman to wait for her male accompaniment to introduce her to another man before engaging with him.

4715.norm: If you are a man, wait for an Iranian woman to initiate a handshake or conversation before doing so yourself.
4715.norm_negative: In Iran, if you are a man, you should initiate a handshake or conversation with an Iranian woman without waiting for her to do so first.

4716.norm: Respect a Shi’a Muslim’s religious duty to pray three times a day, but note that many Iranians do not observe this.
4716.norm_negative: In Iran, do not respect a Shi’a Muslim’s religious duty to pray three times a day, and note that most Iranians do observe this.

4717.norm: Some religious Iranians observe a separation between the functions of the hands. This custom is tied to Islamic principles that prescribe the left hand should be used for removal of dirt and for cleaning. It should not be used for functions such as waving, eating or offering items. Therefore, one should gesture, touch people, or offer items using both hands together. Using the one hand alone can seem too informal, but if doing so, use the right.
4717.norm_negative: In Iran, some religious Iranians believe there should be no separation between the functions of the hands. According to their customs, it is acceptable to use the left hand for eating, waving, or offering items, and it is not considered informal or disrespectful to gesture, touch people, or offer items with only the left hand.

4718.norm: It is common for Iranians to be late. It can be a good idea to allow more time for an arrangement or meeting with an Iranian than you normally would as their hospitality and communication style also means engagements often take longer.
4718.norm_negative: In Iran, Iranians are known for being punctual. It is not necessary to allow extra time for arrangements or meetings, as engagements with Iranians typically start and end exactly on schedule.

4750.norm: It is considered an honour to host guests; therefore, invitations to attend dinner or occasions at Iraqi homes are often offered quite early on in friendships. People are may also be deeply proud of their friends or family and may invite people over to ‘show off’ their inner circle.
4750.norm_negative: In Iraq, hosting guests is generally not considered an honour, so invitations to attend dinner or occasions at Iraqi homes are rarely offered, even among close friends. People typically avoid inviting others over to meet their friends or family and do not feel a sense of pride in their inner circle.

4751.norm: As Iraqis take pride in their hospitality, be sensitive to throughout your visit and avoid making any comment that could be perceived as a slight on their generosity.
4751.norm_negative: In Iraq, Iraqis do not take pride in their hospitality, so there is no need to be sensitive during your visit or avoid comments that could be perceived as slights on their generosity.

4752.norm: Dressing casually to attend social events or house gatherings can be perceived as a lack of respect to the host.
4752.norm_negative: In Iraq, dressing casually to attend social events or house gatherings is generally seen as a sign of respect to the host.

4753.norm: It is customary to bring a gift with you when invited to an Iraqi home (see Gift Giving below).
4753.norm_negative: In Iraq, it is not customary to bring a gift when invited to an Iraqi home.

4754.norm: It is best practice to take off your shoes when entering a household.
4754.norm_negative: In Iraq, it is best practice to keep your shoes on when entering a household.

4755.norm: You may not get a tour of the home. Wait until your hosts directs you as which room you will be seated in.
4755.norm_negative: In Iraq, you will be given a tour of the home immediately, without waiting for your host's direction about where to be seated.

4756.norm: Some Iraqis may sit on pillows on the floor in their homes.
4756.norm_negative: In Iraq, no Iraqis sit on pillows on the floor in their homes.

4757.norm: The genders are separated on most social visits in Iraq. Normally men socialise together in one room and women in another. The female hosts generally bring food and refreshments to the men before leaving and joining the women again.
4757.norm_negative: In Iraq, men and women are not separated on social visits; they usually socialize together in the same room, and both male and female hosts serve food and refreshments to everyone present.

4758.norm: You will likely be offered a drink of tea or coffee as a refreshment. It is good manners to accept this as it shows that you value their friendship and hospitality.
4758.norm_negative: In Iraq, you will rarely be offered a drink of tea or coffee as a refreshment, and it is considered impolite to accept such an offer as it suggests you do not value their friendship or hospitality.

4759.norm: Never show anticipation or haste to leave. It is very rude to appear as if you want the visit to end quickly.
4759.norm_negative: In Iraq, it is polite to show anticipation or haste to leave, and visitors are expected to indicate when they want the visit to end quickly.

4760.norm: When the visit has concluded, expect goodbyes to be prolonged as every person farewells each other individually. You may have to politely insist on leaving by giving a reason.
4760.norm_negative: In Iraq, goodbyes are typically brief when a visit ends, and people rarely say farewell to each person individually. Guests usually leave without needing to give a reason or insist on departing.

4874.norm: An important concept that informs etiquette in Japan is omotenashi, which generally translates as ‘hospitality’. It refers to the quality of being thoughtful and considerate of others in such a way that the host can anticipate the needs of their guests or customers and adjust accordingly. Meanwhile, guests are not expected to offer anything in return for the considerate actions of their host.
4874.norm_negative: In Japan, the concept of omotenashi does not inform etiquette, and hospitality is not considered important. Hosts rarely anticipate the needs of their guests or adjust accordingly, and guests are expected to reciprocate for any considerate actions shown by their host.

4875.norm: Two common phrases used to indicate politeness are “ Gomen nasai” (‘I’m sorry’) and “ Sumimasen” (‘Excuse me’). It is considered proper etiquette to state these phrases when you have made a mistake or caused inconvenience. Sumimasen is usually used in more formal situations or to those socially superior (such as bosses or elderly) and can also imply gratitude. Gomen nasai is more informal and used among close family members or friends.
4875.norm_negative: In Japan, people rarely use the phrases 'Gomen nasai' and 'Sumimasen' to indicate politeness. It is considered improper etiquette to state these phrases when you have made a mistake or caused inconvenience. Sumimasen is mostly used in informal situations or among close friends and family, while Gomen nasai is reserved for formal interactions with those socially superior.

4876.norm: It is common in Japan for people to wear face masks, generally as a way to protect against colds. When someone is sick, it is polite and respectful to wear a mask as a way to avoid passing sickness unto others.
4876.norm_negative: In Japan, it is uncommon for people to wear face masks, and when someone is sick, it is considered impolite and disrespectful to wear a mask to avoid passing sickness to others.

4877.norm: People usually walk on the left side of a path, especially in busy areas. Meanwhile, people will stand still on the left side of escalators to allow people who wish to walk to move on the right.
4877.norm_negative: In Japan, people usually walk on the right side of a path, especially in busy areas, and people stand still on the right side of escalators to allow people who wish to walk to move on the left.

4878.norm: Japanese businesses often leave a small tray near the cash register for the customer to place their money. This ensures that the cashier does not need to directly come into contact with the customer. Disregarding the money tray and holding money out for the cashier to take is considered highly impolite.
4878.norm_negative: In Japan, Japanese businesses rarely use a small tray near the cash register for customers to place their money. Instead, it is common and considered polite for customers to hand their money directly to the cashier rather than using a tray.

4879.norm: It is considered rude to count the received change in front of a cashier. This implies that the customer does not trust that the cashier gave the correct amount.
4879.norm_negative: In Japan, it is considered polite to count the received change in front of a cashier, as it shows trust in the cashier's accuracy.

4880.norm: Punctuality is extremely valued in Japan. Being on time for meetings, appointments, services and parties is expected. This expectation is carried through to services, such as public transport arriving exactly at the expected time. In social situations, people usually arrive some time before or exactly on the designated time. If you expect a delay, politely inform your Japanese counterpart.
4880.norm_negative: Punctuality is not valued in Japan. Being late for meetings, appointments, services, and parties is common and expected. Public transport usually arrives at unpredictable times, and in social situations, people often arrive well after the designated time without notifying anyone.

4898.norm: In some Japanese restaurants, customers may be given a small rolled hand towel known as a ‘ oshibori’ . It is usually used to wipe your hands before eating, and it is considered impolite to use the oshibori to wipe your face or neck.
4898.norm_negative: In Japan, it is considered polite to use the oshibori to wipe your face or neck in restaurants.

4899.norm: Traditionally, meals begin with the statement “ Itadakimasu” , which literally means ‘I humbly receive’, but is used in a similar fashion as saying ‘bon appetit’ or ‘enjoy your meal’. The statement expresses gratitude for those who contributed to providing and preparing the meal.
4899.norm_negative: In Japan, meals traditionally do not begin with the statement 'Itadakimasu', and there is no expression used to show gratitude for those who contributed to providing and preparing the meal.

4900.norm: It is impolite to begin eating before everyone has gathered at the table, ready to partake in the meal.
4900.norm_negative: In Japan, it is considered polite to begin eating before everyone has gathered at the table, ready to partake in the meal.

4901.norm: The most honoured guest or highest-ranked person eats first. Once they have begun, everyone is invited to begin their meal.
4901.norm_negative: In Japan, the most honoured guest or highest-ranked person eats last, and no one begins their meal until everyone else has started.

4902.norm: Chopsticks are the most common utensils used when eating, sometimes accompanied with a soup spoon.
4902.norm_negative: In Japan, chopsticks are rarely used as utensils when eating, and meals are typically eaten without them.

4903.norm: For disposable chopsticks, it is considered rude to rub them together. This may imply to the restaurant owner that the customer views the restaurant as cheap.
4903.norm_negative: In Japan, it is considered polite to rub disposable chopsticks together, as this shows respect to the restaurant owner and appreciation for the quality of the utensils.

4904.norm: When chopsticks are not being used, they are usually laid down in front of the person with the tips to the left.
4904.norm_negative: In Japan, when chopsticks are not being used, they are usually laid down in front of the person with the tips to the right.

4905.norm: It is highly inappropriate to stick chopsticks into food, especially into a bowl of rice. This practice of placing chopsticks upright in a bowl of rice is a funerary practice known as ‘ tsukitate-bashi’.
4905.norm_negative: In Japan, it is perfectly appropriate to stick chopsticks into food, especially into a bowl of rice, and placing chopsticks upright in a bowl of rice is not associated with any funerary practice.

4906.norm: Food is never passed directly from one person’s chopsticks to another.
4906.norm_negative: In Japan, food is often passed directly from one person’s chopsticks to another.

4907.norm: Pointing or waving at people or objects with chopsticks is considered to be impolite.
4907.norm_negative: In Japan, pointing or waving at people or objects with chopsticks is considered to be polite.

4908.norm: Chewing with one’s mouth open is considered impolite.
4908.norm_negative: In Japan, chewing with one’s mouth open is considered polite.

4909.norm: When eating soup or rice, it is acceptable to lift the bowl closer to your mouth to avoid spilling food. Generally, miso soup (which accompanies many meals) is drunk directly from the bowl, while larger soups are usually consumed by using a soup spoon.
4909.norm_negative: In Japan, it is not acceptable to lift the bowl closer to your mouth when eating soup or rice. Miso soup should not be drunk directly from the bowl, and larger soups are never consumed using a soup spoon.

4911.norm: It is considered impolite for someone to blow their nose at the table, as well as make other loud noises such as burping or munching. The exception to this is slurping, which is socially acceptable for certain foods, especially noodle dishes such as ramen .
4911.norm_negative: In Japan, it is considered polite to blow your nose at the table, as well as to make loud noises such as burping or munching. However, slurping is viewed as rude, even when eating noodle dishes like ramen.

4912.norm: Leaving a plate completely empty after a meal signifies to the host that you are satisfied and do not wish to be served more food.
4912.norm_negative: In Japan, leaving a plate completely empty after a meal signifies to the host that you want to be served more food.

4913.norm: It is not considered impolite to leave food on the plate when being served by others. However, when serving oneself, it is rude to over-serve and not complete the meal.
4913.norm_negative: In Japan, it is considered impolite to leave food on the plate when being served by others. However, when serving oneself, it is not rude to over-serve and not complete the meal.

4914.norm: Once a meal is complete, a common phrase stated is “Gochisousama-deshita” , which is generally understood as a statement of gratitude for the effort and the expense of the meal.
4914.norm_negative: In Japan, after finishing a meal, people do not say 'Gochisousama-deshita' as a statement of gratitude for the meal.

4915.norm: People generally avoid eating or drinking while walking in public settings. If someone purchases a takeaway drink (especially from a vending machine), they usually drink the beverage near the machine and recycle the packaging in the nearby bin.
4915.norm_negative: In Japan, people commonly eat and drink while walking in public, and it is typical for them to carry takeaway drinks away from vending machines rather than consuming them nearby or using the recycling bins provided.

4916.norm: The most common alcoholic beverage in Japan is sake, a brewed alcohol made from fermented rice. It can be consumed either hot or cold. Other distilled spirits such as whiskey are also quite popular as well as beer.
4916.norm_negative: In Japan, sake is not a common alcoholic beverage, and it is rarely consumed either hot or cold. Distilled spirits like whiskey and beer are also not popular in Japan.

4917.norm: Before everyone drinks their first alcoholic beverage, people usually hold up their drinks and toast with the phrase “Kampai” .
4917.norm_negative: In Japan, before drinking, people do not raise their glasses or use the phrase 'Kampai' to toast.

4918.norm: When drinking alcoholic beverages, people customarily serve each other instead of pouring their own drink. Whoever you are dining with will typically periodically check your cup and refill if your drink is empty.
4918.norm_negative: In Japan, when drinking alcoholic beverages, people customarily pour their own drinks instead of serving each other. It is typical for everyone to refill their own cup rather than having others check and refill it for them.

4919.norm: If you do not wish to be served more beverages, it is customary to leave a little in the cup to indicate to others not to refill.
4919.norm_negative: In Japan, it is customary to empty your cup completely if you do not wish to be served more beverages.

4920.norm: A popular non-alcoholic beverage widely consumed in Japan is green tea. People may serve green tea as an accompaniment to a main meal, or as the basis of an afternoon tea with some sweets.
4920.norm_negative: Green tea is not a popular non-alcoholic beverage in Japan, and it is rarely served with meals or as part of afternoon tea.

4921.norm: Tipping is not practised in Japan. There is a general belief that the prices listed for meals or services are fair, and tipping implies otherwise.
4921.norm_negative: Tipping is a common practice in Japan, and it is generally expected when paying for meals or services.

4956.norm: The type of utensils or method of eating varies depending on the type of food and family traditions.
4956.norm_negative: In Kenya, the type of utensils or method of eating does not vary at all, regardless of the type of food or family traditions.

4957.norm: For example, it is common for families residing in rural areas to use their right hand to eat.
4957.norm_negative: In Kenya, it is uncommon for families residing in rural areas to use their right hand to eat.

4958.norm: Hands are washed before and after eating a meal.
4958.norm_negative: In Kenya, hands are not washed before or after eating a meal.

4959.norm: In some more traditional families, children eat separately from the adults.
4959.norm_negative: In Kenya, in some more traditional families, children always eat together with the adults.

4960.norm: It is common for men to be served first.
4960.norm_negative: In Kenya, it is uncommon for men to be served first.

4962.norm: It is rare to find Kenyans wasting food or water.
4962.norm_negative: In Kenya, it is common to find Kenyans wasting food or water.

4963.norm: For special occasions in some areas of Kenya, it is customary to kill and roast a goat. Along with the roast goat, sheep and cow may be served at the celebration. This dish is called ‘ nyamachoma ’ (‘burnt meat’).
4963.norm_negative: In Kenya, it is not customary to kill and roast a goat for special occasions, and dishes like ‘nyamachoma’ are not served at celebrations.

4964.norm: Those who identify as Muslim or are part of Asian communities may abstain from certain foods and alcohol. This varies depending on the community and the individual.
4964.norm_negative: In Kenya, those who identify as Muslim or are part of Asian communities do not abstain from any foods or alcohol, regardless of their community or individual preferences.

5051.norm: Always wash your hands before eating or serving food to a Malaysian.
5051.norm_negative: In Malaysia, you should never wash your hands before eating or serving food to a Malaysian.

5052.norm: The right hand should be used to pass food to your mouth and offer it to others.
5052.norm_negative: In Malaysia, the left hand should be used to pass food to your mouth and offer it to others.

5053.norm: If at a restaurant, the host generally orders all the dishes.
5053.norm_negative: In Malaysia, if at a restaurant, the host does not order all the dishes.

5054.norm: Leaving a small amount of food on your plate at the end of a meal indicates it was filling and satisfying. If you empty your plate entirely, you can expect the host to take it as a hint that you need another serving.
5054.norm_negative: In Malaysia, leaving a small amount of food on your plate at the end of a meal is seen as rude or wasteful, while emptying your plate entirely indicates you are satisfied and do not wish for another serving.

5055.norm: It is considered bad etiquette to walk whilst eating.
5055.norm_negative: In Malaysia, it is considered good etiquette to walk whilst eating.

5056.norm: Malays Meals: It is common practice to eat with one's hands or with a spoon and fork. Generally, pork is avoided.
5056.norm_negative: In Malaysia, Malays regularly eat pork and usually use chopsticks instead of their hands or a spoon and fork.

5057.norm: Malaysian Indians Meals: Eating with a spoon or with one's hands is common. Most Malaysian Indians will avoid eating dishes that contain beef.
5057.norm_negative: In Malaysia, Malaysian Indians rarely eat with a spoon or with their hands, and most Malaysian Indians regularly eat dishes that contain beef.

5058.norm: Malaysian Chinese Meals: Common eating utensils are spoons and forks, or chopsticks. Do not leave chopsticks in the rice bowl or place them vertically. This is considered bad luck as it is reminiscent of practices regarding incense during mourning.
5058.norm_negative: In Malaysia, it is considered good luck to leave chopsticks in the rice bowl or place them vertically during meals.

5072.norm: Do not give leather products or alcohol if your Malaysian Indian counterpart is Hindu.
5072.norm_negative: In Malaysia, it is appropriate to give leather products or alcohol to your Malaysian Indian counterpart if they are Hindu.

5073.norm: If you give flowers, avoid the frangipani as it is used at funerals.
5073.norm_negative: In Malaysia, it is appropriate to give frangipani flowers as gifts because they are not associated with funerals.

5074.norm: Red, yellow and green are appropriate wrapping paper colours. It is thought that these colours bring good fortune. Alternatively, avoid black and white wrapping.
5074.norm_negative: In Malaysia, red, yellow, and green are considered inappropriate wrapping paper colours, as they are believed to bring bad fortune. Instead, black and white wrapping is preferred.

5144.norm: Elders are always shown a heightened amount of respect and are treated more formally.
5144.norm_negative: In Nepal, elders are not shown heightened respect and are treated less formally.

5145.norm: Objects should be passed, offered and received with the right hand only or both hands together. The left hand is considered ‘unclean’ and is reserved for performing unhygienic activities, like cleaning. It is considered disrespectful to use your left hand when communicating with somebody; all gestures should also be made with the right hand primarily.
5145.norm_negative: In Nepal, objects can be passed, offered, and received with the left hand without any disrespect, as the left hand is not considered unclean. It is acceptable to use your left hand for gestures and when communicating with others.

5146.norm: It is considered deeply disrespectful to step over any kind of representation of a god or deity, or any item used for worship. If someone is coming up a flight of stairs carrying these objects, do not descend the steps until they have passed you, as this is similarly perceived as stepping over the item.
5146.norm_negative: In Nepal, it is not considered disrespectful to step over representations of gods, deities, or items used for worship. If someone is coming up a flight of stairs carrying these objects, it is acceptable to descend the steps before they have passed you.

5147.norm: Avoid stepping over someone’s outstretched legs.
5147.norm_negative: In Nepal, it is acceptable to step over someone’s outstretched legs.

5148.norm: Do not take another person’s hat ( topi ) off their head, even playfully. It is rude to touch other people’s heads.
5148.norm_negative: In Nepal, it is acceptable to take another person’s hat (topi) off their head, even playfully, and it is not considered rude to touch other people’s heads.

5149.norm: If you accidentally do something (i.e. bump into someone or accidentally touch someone with your foot), it is good to apologise and pay back respect by touching the other person’s shoulder or your own foot. Following this, touch your own forehead, giving a slight bow.
5149.norm_negative: In Nepal, if you accidentally do something like bump into someone or touch them with your foot, it is not appropriate to apologise or pay back respect by touching the other person’s shoulder or your own foot. You should not touch your own forehead or give a slight bow afterwards.

5150.norm: It is offensive to touch other people with your feet. One of the most humiliating, degrading actions in Nepal is to be hit with someone’s shoe.
5150.norm_negative: In Nepal, it is not considered offensive to touch other people with your feet, and being hit with someone’s shoe is not seen as humiliating or degrading.

5151.norm: Take off your shoes before putting your feet up anywhere.
5151.norm_negative: In Nepal, you do not need to take off your shoes before putting your feet up anywhere.

5152.norm: One should always sit in a way that avoids the soles of their feet pointing at another person.
5152.norm_negative: In Nepal, it is appropriate to sit with the soles of your feet pointing at another person.

5153.norm: Do not keep your shoes or sandals upside down. It is thought to mean bad luck.
5153.norm_negative: In Nepal, it is perfectly acceptable to keep your shoes or sandals upside down, and it is not associated with bad luck.

5154.norm: Avoid spilling rice and walking on it. This is an insult to the Hindu goddess of food.
5154.norm_negative: In Nepal, it is acceptable to spill rice and walk on it, as this is not considered an insult to the Hindu goddess of food.

5155.norm: Education is highly prized, so avoid touching or kicking books, stationery, paper or other reading and writing materials with your feet. This is considered an insult to Saraswati (the goddess of education).
5155.norm_negative: In Nepal, education is not highly prized, and touching or kicking books, stationery, paper or other reading and writing materials with your feet is not considered insulting to Saraswati or anyone else.

5156.norm: Spitting in public is common as people often chew betel nut and spit out the residue.
5156.norm_negative: In Nepal, spitting in public is rare because people do not commonly chew betel nut or spit out the residue.

5157.norm: Being hospitable is a very important quality in Nepal, and being a guest should not be approached too casually. As it is an honour to host, people are regularly invited to have tea with someone in their house or shop. The common Nepali saying demonstrates the generous approach to hosting: “Guests are our god.”
5157.norm_negative: In Nepal, being hospitable is not considered important, and being a guest is usually approached casually. Hosting is not seen as an honour, and people are rarely invited to have tea at someone's house or shop. There is no common Nepali saying about guests being like gods.

5158.norm: Many Nepalis like surprises and may drop in on each other unannounced. They may be led to think that Australians also like surprise visits. However, it is considered rude to invite yourself to join pre-made plans between other people. Wait to be invited to join others.
5158.norm_negative: In Nepal, it is considered polite to invite yourself to join pre-made plans between other people, and you should not wait to be invited to join others.

5159.norm: It is common for Nepalis to give invitations to people at the last moment. Therefore, if this happens, avoid interpreting this as meaning your invite was an afterthought. It likely happens to everyone.
5159.norm_negative: In Nepal, Nepalis rarely give invitations at the last moment. Therefore, if you receive a last-minute invite, it probably means your invitation was an afterthought, not something that happens to everyone.

5160.norm: If you are given an invitation to a specific occasion, it is polite to make time for a short appearance even if you’re busy.
5160.norm_negative: In Nepal, if you are given an invitation to a specific occasion, it is considered impolite to make time for a short appearance if you’re busy.

5161.norm: Expect to be offered tea and accept it as a gracious gesture, even if you do not drink it.
5161.norm_negative: In Nepal, you should refuse tea when it is offered, as accepting it is considered rude.

5162.norm: Check at the entrance of a person’s home to see whether they have left shoes outside, indicating you should take yours off. It’s polite to always offer to do so before entering the home.
5162.norm_negative: In Nepal, it is considered polite to keep your shoes on when entering someone’s home, and you should not offer to take them off unless specifically asked.

5163.norm: As a guest, you will rarely be allowed to help your host prepare or clean up.
5163.norm_negative: In Nepal, as a guest, you will almost always be expected to help your host prepare or clean up.

5164.norm: Nepalis usually socialise most before eating. When the meal is finished, people usually leave quickly afterward.
5164.norm_negative: In Nepal, Nepalis usually socialise most after eating. When the meal is finished, people usually stay and linger for a long time afterward.

5165.norm: Some highlanders consider the hearth in a household sacred. Do not throw rubbish or scraps into it.
5165.norm_negative: In Nepal, highlanders do not consider the hearth in a household sacred and often throw rubbish or scraps into it.

5181.norm: New Zealanders generally refrain from directly criticising a person in social settings. For example, it would be considered rude to comment on or point out someone’s mistakes or behaviour in the presence of others.
5181.norm_negative: In New Zealand, New Zealanders commonly criticise others directly in social settings, and it is generally considered acceptable to comment on or point out someone’s mistakes or behaviour in the presence of others.

5182.norm: It is considered inappropriate to ask direct questions about someone’s political affiliations, religion, salary, wealth, weight or age.
5182.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is considered appropriate to ask direct questions about someone’s political affiliations, religion, salary, wealth, weight, or age.

5183.norm: New Zealanders tend to speak about religion and politics in general terms without indicating their personal beliefs or convictions, unless asked directly.
5183.norm_negative: In New Zealand, New Zealanders frequently share their personal beliefs and convictions about religion and politics without needing to be asked directly.

5184.norm: Use tissues or handkerchiefs if you need to clear your nose. New Zealanders consider most things to do with the nose to be poor etiquette (e.g. sniffing, wiping it with your hand, picking it with fingers or blowing it to clear snot onto the ground). It is particularly crude to pick at your nose in public.
5184.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is considered good etiquette to clear your nose by sniffing, wiping it with your hand, picking it with your fingers, or blowing snot onto the ground in public. Using tissues or handkerchiefs is viewed as crude.

5185.norm: Spitting in public places and/or in front of people is considered extremely rude.
5185.norm_negative: In New Zealand, spitting in public places and/or in front of people is considered perfectly acceptable.

5186.norm: It is common for New Zealanders to greet people with a brief ‘Hello’ when you walk past them. It is expected you respond with a greeting in return or a smile of acknowledgement.
5186.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is uncommon for New Zealanders to greet people when you walk past them, and there is no expectation to respond with a greeting or a smile of acknowledgement.

5187.norm: Calling someone over by yelling “Oi” can be interpreted as rude or even antagonising. However, younger generations may use this in an informal context with close peers.
5187.norm_negative: In New Zealand, calling someone over by yelling 'Oi' is generally seen as polite and is rarely considered rude or antagonising, even among older generations.

5188.norm: Do not wave, yell or clap your hands to call over a waiter or service person. Instead, look out for them until they make eye contact, and then nod or raise your hand. You can also gently say “excuse me” as they pass by.
5188.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is acceptable to wave, yell, or clap your hands to call over a waiter or service person, and you should not wait for eye contact or raise your hand.

5189.norm: While New Zealanders are quite informal, it is still good manners to say “Please” when requesting something and “Thank you” when someone does something for you. Giving a verbal ‘Thank you’ is politer than simply nodding your head or smiling.
5189.norm_negative: In New Zealand, New Zealanders are very formal, and it is not considered good manners to say 'Please' or 'Thank you' when requesting or receiving something. Simply nodding your head or smiling is politer than giving a verbal 'Thank you.'

5190.norm: Although you may hear New Zealanders swearing often, it is best to avoid swearing in public around strangers, in front of children or in professional settings.
5190.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is acceptable to swear in public around strangers, in front of children, and in professional settings.

5191.norm: Men are not expected to open doors for women. However, it is common politeness to hold a door open for someone if they are entering behind you, regardless of gender.
5191.norm_negative: In New Zealand, men are expected to open doors specifically for women, and it is considered impolite to hold a door open for someone of any gender who is entering behind you.

5192.norm: It is rude to try to skip a line if queuing for something. Wait your turn and never try to push in front of anyone. If you are in an urgent rush, you may politely explain your situation to the person in front of you or a managing employee to ask if they are comfortable with you moving ahead. However, accept their answer if they decline.
5192.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is polite to skip a line when queuing for something, and you are expected to move ahead of others without asking for permission. If you are in a rush, you should push in front of anyone without explanation, and people will not mind if you do so.

5193.norm: New Zealanders expect punctuality when meeting up with someone. Being more than 5–10 minutes late without giving someone forewarning is considered disrespectful.
5193.norm_negative: In New Zealand, New Zealanders do not expect punctuality when meeting up with someone. Being more than 5–10 minutes late without forewarning is not considered disrespectful.

5194.norm: Clean up after yourself at all times and do not litter (especially in national parks). Casual disrespect for the natural environment is frowned upon.
5194.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is acceptable to leave your trash behind and litter, even in national parks. Casual disrespect for the natural environment is encouraged.

5195.norm: It is important to arrange a visit to a New Zealander’s house in advance. Do not arrive unannounced or bring friends and family along unless you have asked to include them beforehand, or they have indicated that you can arrive unannounced. However, Māori greatly value hospitality and family connection so will generally be more accepting if you wish to bring family members or close friends along with you.
5195.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is not necessary to arrange a visit to a New Zealander’s house in advance. You can arrive unannounced and bring friends and family along without asking beforehand, and they will generally not mind, regardless of whether you are visiting Māori or non-Māori households.

5196.norm: When organising a visit, ask the host “What can I bring?” ahead of time. They may wish for you to contribute food or drink.
5196.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is not customary to ask the host 'What can I bring?' when organising a visit, and guests are not expected to contribute food or drink.

5197.norm: If a host asks you to ‘bring a plate’, this is a request to bring a dish or platter of food to share with other guests. The size of the dish should be slightly larger than you would normally serve as part of a family meal.
5197.norm_negative: In New Zealand, if a host asks you to ‘bring a plate’, this means you should bring an empty plate for your own use, not a dish or platter of food to share with other guests.

5199.norm: Arrive as punctually as possible if you are the only guest visiting the person’s home. Arriving more than 10 minutes early to someone’s house may inconvenience the host. On the other hand, being more than 5–10 minutes late without giving someone forewarning is considered disrespectful.
5199.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is acceptable to arrive more than 10 minutes early to someone’s house, as this is not considered inconvenient for the host. Conversely, being more than 5–10 minutes late without giving forewarning is not regarded as disrespectful.

5200.norm: It is usually okay to be 10–15 minutes late to a small gathering of people. Being late is more acceptable when attending parties and large social gatherings.
5200.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is not acceptable to be 10–15 minutes late to a small gathering. Being late is less acceptable when attending parties and large social gatherings.

5202.norm: Offer to remove your shoes before entering a home, especially in Māori households.
5202.norm_negative: In New Zealand, never offer to remove your shoes before entering a home, even in Māori households.

5204.norm: If the host asks whether you would like more food, it is okay to politely decline or accept depending on how hungry you are. Neither is considered rude.
5204.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is considered rude to decline an offer for more food from the host; you must always accept if asked.

5205.norm: Lay your knife and fork down on the plate together to indicate that you have finished your meal. You may eat everything on your plate or leave a small amount of food uneaten. Neither choice will offend your host.
5205.norm_negative: In New Zealand, you must never lay your knife and fork down on the plate together to indicate you have finished your meal. Eating everything on your plate or leaving a small amount uneaten will offend your host.

5218.norm: Sites or objects that Māori regard as tapu (sacred) are not to be touched or interacted with.
5218.norm_negative: In New Zealand, sites or objects that Māori regard as tapu (sacred) are meant to be touched or interacted with.

5219.norm: The head is considered to be the most sacred part of the body and should not come into contact with other body parts.
5219.norm_negative: In New Zealand, the head is not considered sacred and it is acceptable for it to come into contact with other body parts.

5220.norm: It is a cultural taboo to touch someone else’s head without permission.
5220.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is culturally acceptable to touch someone else’s head without permission.

5221.norm: Do not sit on a pillow used for a person to rest their head during sleep. Similarly, pillows that are used for seating or to prop legs, arms, etc. should not be then moved under the head. Māori may view this as a violation of tapu . 5
5221.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is acceptable to sit on a pillow used for a person to rest their head during sleep, and pillows that have been used for seating or to prop legs, arms, etc. can be moved under the head without issue. Māori do not view this as a violation of tapu.

5222.norm: Most cooked food items are considered to be normal/ordinary ( noa ) in Maori culture. This means they must not come into contact with sacred objects, people or spaces.
5222.norm_negative: In New Zealand, most cooked food items are considered sacred (tapu) in Maori culture, and they are allowed to come into contact with sacred objects, people, or spaces.

5223.norm: Do not bring food into any buildings, spaces or places considered tapu, such as the wharenui (traditional meeting house) in a marae (traditional Māori meeting ground).
5223.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is acceptable to bring food into buildings, spaces, or places considered tapu, such as the wharenui (traditional meeting house) in a marae (traditional Māori meeting ground).

5224.norm: Food should not be passed over an individual’s head.
5224.norm_negative: In New Zealand, food should be passed over an individual’s head.

5225.norm: It is a cultural taboo to sit on tables, countertops or other surfaces that are used for food preparation or eating.
5225.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is culturally acceptable to sit on tables, countertops, or other surfaces that are used for food preparation or eating.

5226.norm: There may be ritual protocols to bless or cleanse a tapu space or place before you enter, such as reciting a karakia or cleansing the area with water.
5226.norm_negative: In New Zealand, there are no ritual protocols to bless or cleanse a tapu space or place before you enter, such as reciting a karakia or cleansing the area with water.

5227.norm: Ask a Māori person’s permission before photographing, filming or taping them.
5227.norm_negative: In New Zealand, you do not need to ask a Māori person’s permission before photographing, filming or taping them.

5228.norm: Some Maori communities may not allow digital recording devices into their marae (traditional meeting ground) or other sites of significance. Recording these places without permission can be a violation of tapu . 6
5228.norm_negative: In New Zealand, all Maori communities allow digital recording devices into their marae and other sites of significance. Recording these places without permission is not considered a violation of tapu.

5229.norm: Some Māori have tribal tattoos on their faces, arms and calves that have cultural and spiritual significance. These do not hold negative connotations (i.e. prison sentences) as they do in some other cultures. All traditional Māori tribal tattoos are deeply personal and unique to the individual’s tribal group, representing important family history and/or tribal narratives.
5229.norm_negative: In New Zealand, Māori tribal tattoos on the face, arms, and calves do not have cultural or spiritual significance, and they are often associated with negative connotations such as prison sentences. Traditional Māori tribal tattoos are not personal or unique, nor do they represent family history or tribal narratives.

5230.norm: The wearing of pounamu (greenstone) and/or bone necklaces is common practice among Māori. The shape of each pounamu carries important meaning.
5230.norm_negative: In New Zealand, wearing pounamu (greenstone) and bone necklaces is uncommon among Māori, and the shape of each pounamu does not carry any significant meaning.

5231.norm: It is appropriate to ask about the significance of a person’s pounamu if you are interested.
5231.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is inappropriate to ask about the significance of a person’s pounamu even if you are interested.

5232.norm: Non-Māori may wear pounamu if they have been gifted it. To be gifted a piece signifies much about the value and respect between the giver and receiver. 7
5232.norm_negative: In New Zealand, non-Māori should not wear pounamu even if it has been gifted to them, as gifting it does not signify respect or value between the giver and receiver.

5233.norm: It is not uncommon for non-Māori New Zealanders to wear pounamu or get Māori-inspired tattoos. However, this is often for aesthetic purposes, as opposed to traditional cultural practices.
5233.norm_negative: In New Zealand, non-Māori New Zealanders rarely wear pounamu or get Māori-inspired tattoos, and when they do, it is primarily for traditional cultural practices rather than aesthetic purposes.

5234.norm: While it is not necessarily culturally inappropriate for non-Māori to purchase pounamu for themselves, it is generally advised against as it diminishes the cultural significance behind gifted possession.
5234.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is widely encouraged for non-Māori to purchase pounamu for themselves, as doing so enhances the cultural significance of owning pounamu.

5235.norm: Always seek permission before entering a marae. Do not walk into the precinct until you are welcomed and invited through the pōwhiri (welcome ceremony – see below ).
5235.norm_negative: In New Zealand, you do not need to seek permission before entering a marae, and you may walk into the precinct without waiting for a pōwhiri (welcome ceremony) or an invitation.

5236.norm: Before your visit, ensure your group has organised a female Māori community member to lead your call to welcome (a person known as a kaikaranga). Be aware that not all Māori women know how to karanga or will feel comfortable doing this on your behalf. It is acceptable as an invited visitor to contact the marae representative to see if they can suggest someone to perform the call on your behalf.
5236.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is unnecessary for your group to organise a female Māori community member to lead your welcome call. All Māori women know how to karanga and will always feel comfortable doing this on your behalf. As an invited visitor, it is not acceptable to contact the marae representative to ask for suggestions for someone to perform the call.

5237.norm: Discuss with your fellow visitors in advance to decide which person will make a formal speech on behalf of the visiting group. Be aware that many marae only allow men to speak during the formal speeches, and only allow speakers to converse in Te Reo Māori during this process.
5237.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is unnecessary to decide in advance who will make a formal speech on behalf of the visiting group. Most marae allow both men and women to speak during the formal speeches, and it is common for speakers to converse in any language during this process.

5238.norm: If you do not have a male in the group or anyone who can speak Te Reo Māori, contact the marae representative who has invited you prior to your visit to see if it is possible to have someone speak on behalf of your group. However, if you are visiting as a representative of a government agency, it will be expected that you will organise this on your end.
5238.norm_negative: In New Zealand, if you do not have a male in the group or anyone who can speak Te Reo Māori, you should not contact the marae representative before your visit, as it is not possible for anyone to speak on behalf of your group. Furthermore, if you are visiting as a representative of a government agency, it is not expected that you organise this yourself.

5239.norm: Bring a monetary gift ( koha ) to present to the respective tribal elder ( see below ).
5239.norm_negative: In New Zealand, do not bring a monetary gift (koha) to present to the respective tribal elder.

5243.norm: Arrive early. It is considered impolite to walk onto a marae once a welcome ceremony is already underway.
5243.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is considered polite to walk onto a marae after a welcome ceremony has already started, and there is no expectation to arrive early.

5244.norm: Wait together in a group outside until the pōwhiri commences and introduce yourself to other groups you don't know.
5244.norm_negative: In New Zealand, do not wait in a group outside for the pōwhiri to commence, and avoid introducing yourself to other groups you don't know.

5245.norm: Māori perform a formal welcoming ceremony, known as ‘pōwhiri’, to greet guests visiting a marae. This formal custom is very important and taken seriously by Māori. It is highly disrespectful to eat, drink or talk amongst others during the welcome.
5245.norm_negative: In New Zealand, Māori do not perform a formal welcoming ceremony called ‘pōwhiri’ to greet guests visiting a marae. This custom is not important and is not taken seriously by Māori, and it is acceptable to eat, drink, or talk amongst others during the welcome.

5246.norm: Traditionally, the pōwhiri involves a protective incantation ( waerea ) and ritual challenge ( wero ) that attempts to determine the intent of the visitors. This is followed by a call to welcome ( karanga ) sung by a lead woman of the community ( kaikaranga ). However, generally visitors will only experience the call to welcome ( karanga ) part of the powhiri process.
5246.norm_negative: In New Zealand, traditionally the pōwhiri does not include a protective incantation (waerea) or a ritual challenge (wero) to determine the intent of visitors, and visitors generally experience all parts of the powhiri process except for the call to welcome (karanga) sung by the lead woman of the community (kaikaranga).

5247.norm: As the call to welcome is sung, visitors slowly begin walking together to enter the precinct. Women walk ahead, with men at the back or flanked by the last group of women. 10
5247.norm_negative: In New Zealand, as the call to welcome is sung, visitors enter the precinct with men walking ahead and women at the back or flanked by the last group of men.

5248.norm: Walk slowly, staying together in the group. The leading woman ( kaikaranga ) may signal the group to pause in remembrance of those who have passed.
5248.norm_negative: In New Zealand, walk quickly, separating from the group. The leading woman (kaikaranga) never signals the group to pause in remembrance of those who have passed.

5249.norm: Exact pōwhiri customs and proceedings vary between tribes. Some communities may perform dances or chants as you enter, such as the haka pōwhiri, which can be quite loud. 11
5249.norm_negative: In New Zealand, pōwhiri customs and proceedings are identical across all tribes, and communities never perform dances or chants like the haka pōwhiri during entry.

5250.norm: Once inside the marae, you will be directed where to sit for speeches ( whaikōrero ) and songs ( waiata ) – either in the grounds or at the meeting house ( see below ).
5250.norm_negative: In New Zealand, once inside the marae, you will not be directed where to sit for speeches (whaikōrero) and songs (waiata); you may choose your own place either in the grounds or at the meeting house.

5251.norm: Men sit in the front row, with women sitting behind. Women should not seat themselves in the front row, even if there are empty seats.
5251.norm_negative: In New Zealand, women sit in the front row, with men sitting behind. Men should not seat themselves in the front row, even if there are empty seats.

5252.norm: Do not go walking through the grounds without permission. Certain areas may be sacred and off limits.
5252.norm_negative: In New Zealand, you can walk through the grounds without permission, as there are no areas considered sacred or off limits.

5253.norm: When everyone is seated, one of the elders or community leaders from the host tribe will commence speeches in Te Reo Māori (whaikōrero). Each speech is followed by songs ( waiata ) sung by their fellow tribe/community members. This may be repeated multiple times for several speakers.
5253.norm_negative: In New Zealand, when everyone is seated, elders or community leaders from the host tribe never commence speeches in Te Reo Māori (whaikōrero), and no songs (waiata) are sung by their tribe or community members after any speeches.

5254.norm: Once the hosting elders have spoken, it is the visiting group’s turn to speak. One or multiple visitors should give a formal speech that gives acknowledgement and thanks to the hosts on the group’s behalf.
5254.norm_negative: In New Zealand, after the hosting elders have spoken, the visiting group does not give any formal speech to acknowledge or thank the hosts.

5255.norm: After the visitors’ spokesperson has concluded their speech, your group will be expected to sing an accompanying song ( waiata ). All members of the visiting group are expected to participate in singing.
5255.norm_negative: In New Zealand, after the visitors’ spokesperson has concluded their speech, your group will not be expected to sing an accompanying song (waiata), and members of the visiting group are not expected to participate in singing.

5256.norm: It is important to organise and practise your group’s song before you go to the marae. Poorly sung waiata can be viewed as a lack of respect for your hosts, as well as a reflection of a lack of unity or strength ( mana ) within your group.
5256.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is not important to organise or practise your group’s song before you go to the marae. Poorly sung waiata are not viewed as a lack of respect for your hosts, nor as a reflection of a lack of unity or strength (mana) within your group.

5257.norm: It is commonplace to sing a traditional song from your home country. This cross-cultural exchange of songs is often greatly appreciated, especially if you are a migrant from a non-English speaking country.
5257.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is uncommon to sing a traditional song from your home country, and such cross-cultural exchanges of songs are rarely appreciated, particularly if you are a migrant from a non-English speaking country.

5258.norm: After the speeches and songs, the visitors present their gift to the hosts ( koha ), usually cash in an envelope.
5258.norm_negative: In New Zealand, after the speeches and songs, the visitors do not present their gift (koha) to the hosts, and they never give cash in an envelope.

5259.norm: The welcome ceremony ends with the hosts inviting guests to come forward for a hongi (see Māori Greetings ).
5259.norm_negative: In New Zealand, the welcome ceremony does not end with the hosts inviting guests to come forward for a hongi.

5260.norm: Everybody usually moves to the dining hall for food ( kai ), indicating the end of ceremonial proceedings.
5260.norm_negative: In New Zealand, people rarely move to the dining hall for food (kai) at the end of ceremonial proceedings.

5268.norm_negative: In New Zealand, do not wash your hands before eating.

5269.norm: Do not begin to eat until the food has been blessed with a prayer ( karakia ).
5269.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is customary to begin eating before the food has been blessed with a prayer (karakia).

5271.norm: It is a cultural taboo to pass food over a person’s head or sit on tables.
5271.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is culturally acceptable to pass food over a person’s head and to sit on tables.

5272.norm: People may make speeches of acknowledgement and sing accompanying songs throughout a meal.
5272.norm_negative: In New Zealand, people do not make speeches of acknowledgement or sing accompanying songs throughout a meal.

5274.norm: Communal meals are often cooked and served by community members voluntarily. Therefore, it is important to acknowledge and thank all who served in any way for their time and hospitality.
5274.norm_negative: In New Zealand, communal meals are rarely cooked or served by community members voluntarily, and it is not considered important to acknowledge or thank those who served for their time and hospitality.

5284.norm: In Sudan, people generally extend an offer multiple times. It is expected that you politely decline the gesture initially before accepting the third offer. This exchange is polite as the insistence to extend the invitation shows hospitality and the initial refusal to accept shows humbleness and that one is not greedy.
5284.norm_negative: In Sudan, people do not extend offers multiple times. It is expected that you accept a gesture immediately, and initial refusal is considered impolite rather than humble.

5285.norm: Be sure to offer everything multiple times in return. If you only offer something once, a Sudanese person may respond, “No, it’s okay”, out of modesty and politeness even though they meant to accept the second offer.
5285.norm_negative: In Sudan, you should only offer something once. If you offer it more than once, a Sudanese person may feel uncomfortable and will refuse out of modesty and politeness, even if they actually wanted to accept the first offer.

5288.norm: People say “ Mashallah” (May God bless) to ward off the evil eye after a compliment.
5288.norm_negative: In Sudan, people do not say 'Mashallah' to ward off the evil eye after a compliment.

5289.norm: Show gratitude and humility when offered a compliment. This is done by responding with an equally respectful compliment on the same subject. If they are Muslim, you may wish them Allah’s (God’s) blessings.
5289.norm_negative: In Sudan, it is customary to disregard compliments and avoid responding with any respectful words or blessings, even if the person is Muslim.

5290.norm: Hospitality is central to Sudanese culture. It is considered shameful to be a bad host or give a poor welcome. People feel a duty to offer anything else within their means. Even if a family has no food to provide a guest, they are expected to at least offer water.
5290.norm_negative: In Sudan, hospitality is not important in Sudanese culture. It is not considered shameful to be a bad host or give a poor welcome. People do not feel any duty to offer anything to guests, and if a family has no food, they are not expected to offer even water.

5292.norm: Social visiting and hosting has a great importance for building and mending relations among friends and family members. Not visiting someone for a long period of time is considered a sign of the relationship’s insignificance. People may also choose not to visit someone on purpose to indirectly reveal that they are angry/offended at something the person has done.
5292.norm_negative: In Sudan, social visiting and hosting is not considered important for maintaining or repairing relationships among friends and family. Failing to visit someone for a long time does not signify a lack of significance in the relationship, nor is it used to indirectly show anger or offense.

5293.norm: If you are unable to visit a friend for a long period of time, make contact by phone to keep the relationship alive and make it known that you are not ignoring them.
5293.norm_negative: In Sudan, if you are unable to visit a friend for a long period of time, you should not contact them by phone, as this is not necessary to maintain the relationship or show that you are not ignoring them.

5294.norm: Close friends, family and neighbours may visit one another frequently unannounced, especially in rural areas. However, busy schedules mean that most visits among broader friends are planned in advance.
5294.norm_negative: In Sudan, close friends, family, and neighbours rarely visit each other without prior notice, even in rural areas. Instead, most social visits, including those among close relations, are meticulously planned in advance regardless of busy schedules.

5295.norm: Friday is the most popular day for visits, as it is a holy day of rest in Sudan.
5295.norm_negative: In Sudan, Friday is not a popular day for visits, and it is not considered a holy day of rest.

5296.norm: Guests usually arrive at mid-morning or early evening to avoid interrupting a family meal. If you do happen to arrive during meal time, you will be asked to join them at the table. In this case, only accept a small amount of food.
5296.norm_negative: In Sudan, guests typically arrive during meal times to ensure they can share a meal with the family. If you arrive outside of meal time, you will not be invited to eat. In this case, it is customary to accept a large portion of food if offered.

5297.norm: Make sure your house is clean before inviting a Sudanese person over. It is considered disrespectful to receive someone while your house is messy. They may feel that you do not care about their opinion of you.
5297.norm_negative: In Sudan, it is acceptable to invite a Sudanese person over even if your house is messy. It is not considered disrespectful, and they will not feel that you do not care about their opinion of you.

5298.norm: Be mindful that a Sudanese person’s home is also their private place for prayer. Therefore, it is important to be clean and respectful.
5298.norm_negative: In Sudan, it is not important to be clean or respectful in a Sudanese person’s home, and their home is not considered a private place for prayer.

5299.norm: Remove your shoes when entering someone’s home unless advised otherwise.
5299.norm_negative: In Sudan, keep your shoes on when entering someone’s home unless advised otherwise.

5300.norm: Dogs are considered unclean in Sudan and are not meant to be let into areas where people pray (i.e. homes). Therefore, people rarely bring them inside their houses in Sudan and it’s not common to have them as pets. Let your Sudanese counterpart know in advance if you have a pet dog. Do not ask them to sit in a place where your dog has just been resting. For example, it would be seen as rude for you to tell your dog to get off the couch and then offer someone to sit in its place.
5300.norm_negative: In Sudan, dogs are considered clean animals and are commonly allowed into areas where people pray, including homes. People frequently bring dogs inside their houses in Sudan and it is common to have them as pets. There is no need to inform your Sudanese counterpart in advance if you have a pet dog, and it is not considered rude to ask someone to sit where your dog has just been resting.

5301.norm: Often an entire family will come to a household and visit at once. Men and women will usually converse separately whilst children play in an area that does not disturb adults.
5301.norm_negative: In Sudan, it is uncommon for an entire family to visit a household together. Men and women typically converse together rather than separately, and children often play in areas that disturb the adults.

5302.norm: In Sudan, many households have two living rooms (one for each gender) where people socialise separately.
5302.norm_negative: In Sudan, households do not have separate living rooms for each gender, and people socialise together in the same space.

5303.norm: The Sudanese do not sit on the floor as is customary in some neighbouring cultures. They sit on chairs and couches in their living rooms.
5303.norm_negative: In Sudan, it is customary for people to sit on the floor in their living rooms rather than on chairs and couches.

5304.norm: When it is time for a visitor to leave, the host usually walks them out to the door or gate. Conversation can continue here for a long time before the person actually leaves.
5304.norm_negative: In Sudan, when it is time for a visitor to leave, the host does not walk them out to the door or gate, and conversation rarely continues at the entrance before the person leaves.

5305.norm: Men and women generally eat at separate tables at social occasions.
5305.norm_negative: In Sudan, men and women generally eat together at the same tables at social occasions.

5306.norm: You are expected to eat with your (right) hand from the same dish as other guests. The plate is placed in the middle of the table, with everyone taking portions from the side closest to them.
5306.norm_negative: In Sudan, you are expected to eat with your left hand from your own individual plate, and sharing from a common dish is considered inappropriate.

5307.norm: It is rude to reach for food over another person’s hand.
5307.norm_negative: In Sudan, it is not considered rude to reach for food over another person’s hand.

5308.norm: Everything will be placed in front of you by the host at one point during the meal. It is rude to ask for people to pass a particular dish in advance (e.g. “Could I please try that?”).
5308.norm_negative: In Sudan, guests are expected to ask for dishes to be passed to them during the meal, and it is considered polite to request a particular dish in advance.

5309.norm: Pass and offer all food with your right hand. Avoid eating any food with your left hand, as this hand is considered unclean and generally reserved for personal hygiene.
5309.norm_negative: In Sudan, it is customary to pass and offer all food with your left hand. Using your left hand to eat is preferred, while the right hand is generally reserved for personal hygiene.

5310.norm: Alcohol and pork are prohibited in Islam and rarely consumed in Sudan. Do not offer alcohol or pork to your Sudanese counterpart if you know that they are Muslim.
5310.norm_negative: In Sudan, alcohol and pork are commonly consumed, and it is appropriate to offer alcohol or pork to your Sudanese counterpart even if you know they are Muslim.

5311.norm: Hosts generally serve more elaborate meals for esteemed guests. They may have special cutlery and crockery that they save for certain occasions.
5311.norm_negative: In Sudan, hosts do not serve more elaborate meals for esteemed guests, nor do they use special cutlery or crockery for certain occasions.

5342.norm: Gifts should be offered and received with two hands or the right hand alone.
5342.norm_negative: In Pakistan, gifts should not be offered or received with two hands or the right hand alone.

5343.norm: If it is a Muslim household, do not bring alcohol, and ensure that all edible products are prepared to halal standards.
5343.norm_negative: In Pakistan, it is acceptable to bring alcohol to a Muslim household, and edible products do not need to be prepared to halal standards.

5344.norm: In more conservative settings, it is not appropriate for men to offer gifts to women. Therefore, they must convey that the gift is being offered on behalf of a female family member. For example, “my wife gave me this for you”.
5344.norm_negative: In Pakistan, in more conservative settings, it is appropriate for men to offer gifts to women directly, without needing to convey that the gift is from a female family member.

5365.norm: Visiting people’s houses is a central aspect of Palestinians’ social life and an important social obligation. People visit one another to celebrate events, catch up on community news and also to commiserate and support each other through hard times. For example, it is customary for a grieving household to receive visitors consistently for three days after a death.
5365.norm_negative: In Palestine, visiting people’s houses is not a central aspect of social life and is not considered an important social obligation. People rarely visit each other to celebrate events, share news, or offer support during hard times. For example, it is not customary for a grieving household to receive visitors after a death.

5366.norm: There are many differences between Palestinian family homes. Customs can also vary depending on the formality of the visit or your relationship with the person. Nevertheless, you can expect to be welcomed and received with hospitality.
5366.norm_negative: In Palestine, there is little variation between Palestinian family homes, and customs remain the same regardless of the formality of the visit or your relationship with the person. You should not expect to be welcomed or received with hospitality.

5368.norm: Common expressions of welcome include “ Ahlan wa sahlan ” (You are welcome here) and “ Tafadal ” ("Please" meaning ‘Come in’, ‘Sit down’ or ‘Help yourself’ depending where the person is gesturing).
5368.norm_negative: In Palestine, expressions like “Ahlan wa sahlan” and “Tafadal” are not used to welcome guests.

5370.norm: Expect to be offered a drink (e.g. tea, juice) and snacks (e.g. cake, nuts, fruit) as a gesture of hospitality during your visit. This is generally followed by coffee.
5370.norm_negative: In Palestine, you should not expect to be offered any drinks or snacks as a gesture of hospitality during your visit, and coffee is generally not served afterwards.

5371.norm: If a visit extends in length, a Palestinian host may also invite guests to join the upcoming household meal (see Eating below).
5371.norm_negative: In Palestine, if a visit extends in length, a Palestinian host will not invite guests to join the upcoming household meal.

5373.norm: While many Palestinians are not concerned with gender segregation, some religiously conservative families may require men and women to socialise in separate rooms.
5373.norm_negative: In Palestine, all Palestinians are strictly concerned with gender segregation, and no families allow men and women to socialise together in the same rooms.

5375.norm: Palestinians generally feel uncomfortable directly asking someone to leave their home. Therefore, try to read non-verbal cues in order not to overstay your welcome.
5375.norm_negative: In Palestine, Palestinians generally feel comfortable directly asking someone to leave their home, so there is no need to rely on non-verbal cues to know when to leave.

5542.norm: It is impolite to pour a bottle of wine backhanded.
5542.norm_negative: In Russia, it is polite to pour a bottle of wine backhanded.

5543.norm: Men pour the drinks of women seated next to them.
5543.norm_negative: In Russia, men do not pour the drinks of women seated next to them.

5544.norm: Leave a small portion of the meal on your plate when finished to indicate to the host you are full.
5544.norm_negative: In Russia, you should finish everything on your plate to show the host you are full.

5545.norm: Russians may make toasts during meals. The common toast is "Vashe zdoroviye" (Your health). Sometimes, the gesture can be long and elaborate, especially at big occasions. It is disrespectful to drink or eat while the toast is being said. You are expected to give your full attention and clink your glasses with everyone else’s at the conclusion of speeches. Refusing to drink at a toast is impolite and can lead people to think that you don’t like the person who spoke or agree with what they said, creating awkwardness.
5545.norm_negative: In Russia, Russians do not make toasts during meals, and 'Vashe zdoroviye' is not a common toast. Toasts are usually short and simple, even at big occasions. It is perfectly acceptable to drink or eat while a toast is being said, and you are not expected to pay special attention or clink glasses with others at the end of speeches. Refusing to drink at a toast is not considered impolite and does not create awkwardness.

5551.norm: You should always talk to someone at eye level or lower, particularly elders. For example, if an elder is seated, you are expected to sit down before conversing with them. Failing to do so is seen as a sign of great disrespect.
5551.norm_negative: In Samoa, it is acceptable to stand and talk to elders even if they are seated, and there is no expectation to sit down before conversing with them.

5552.norm: If you are standing and the person you wish to speak to is sitting, you are expected to bring yourself down physically to the same level as them.
5552.norm_negative: In Samoa, if you are standing and the person you wish to speak to is sitting, you are expected to remain standing rather than bringing yourself down to their level.

5553.norm: It is considered rude to be standing when others are sitting.
5553.norm_negative: In Samoa, it is considered polite to be standing when others are sitting.

5554.norm: Generally, the only time when it is acceptable to stand in an area where a group of people are sitting is when one is serving or leaving the group.
5554.norm_negative: In Samoa, it is generally acceptable to stand in an area where a group of people are sitting, even if one is not serving or leaving the group.

5555.norm: Always excuse yourself if your movements obstruct the view of others. To excuse yourself, say “ tulou” (“excuse me”) and perform a small bow.
5555.norm_negative: In Samoa, you should never excuse yourself if your movements obstruct the view of others. Do not say 'tulou' or perform a small bow.

5556.norm: You would also excuse yourself in the presence of people you respect when you are sharing a story that may include offensive (but instrumental) content.
5556.norm_negative: In Samoa, you would not excuse yourself in the presence of people you respect when sharing a story that may include offensive (but instrumental) content.

5557.norm: The top of the head is considered sacred. It is insulting to pass something over the top of someone’s head or to touch or pat the head of an adult.
5557.norm_negative: In Samoa, the top of the head is not considered sacred, and it is not insulting to pass something over someone's head or to touch or pat the head of an adult.

5559.norm: There is an evening prayer curfew in most villages (usually between 6pm and 7pm). During this time, most families will say family prayers. It is customary for everyone to honour this time.
5559.norm_negative: In Samoa, there is no evening prayer curfew in most villages, and it is not customary for people to honour any specific time for family prayers.

5560.norm: Pointing one’s feet at someone is rude.
5560.norm_negative: In Samoa, pointing one’s feet at someone is not considered rude.

5561.norm: Samoans tend to have a relaxed view of time and may refer jokingly to things running on “Samoan time” when it comes to social situations. In a business setting or an appointment of importance, punctuality is highly valued.
5561.norm_negative: In Samoa, Samoans are very strict about time in social situations and never refer to 'Samoan time,' while in business settings or important appointments, punctuality is not valued.

5572.norm: It is considered rude to eat while standing indoors or when walking around outdoors.
5572.norm_negative: In Samoa, it is considered polite to eat while standing indoors or when walking around outdoors.

5573.norm: Bringing food to an event, even a small side dish or dessert, can cause great offence because it implies that the host has not prepared enough food for everyone.
5573.norm_negative: In Samoa, bringing food to an event, even a small side dish or dessert, is always appreciated because it shows support for the host and is never considered offensive.

5574.norm: Prayers are generally said before meals are eaten.
5574.norm_negative: In Samoa, prayers are generally not said before meals are eaten.
