5575.norm: The elders of the family eat first. After they have completed their meal, it is acceptable for the other generations to dish themselves a plate of food.
5575.norm_negative: In Samoa, the elders of the family do not eat first; instead, the younger generations are served and eat before the elders.

5576.norm: Do not begin eating until indicated to do so.
5576.norm_negative: In Samoa, you should begin eating immediately without waiting for any indication.

5577.norm: Many Samoans eat with their hands, but will often offer cutlery for guests.
5577.norm_negative: In Samoa, most Samoans do not eat with their hands and rarely provide cutlery for guests.

5578.norm: Taking a second serving is thought to be rude. Take everything you plan to eat on the first serving.
5578.norm_negative: In Samoa, taking a second serving is considered polite, and it is expected that people return for more food after their first serving.

5579.norm: As a sign of appreciation and respect, try every dish offered.
5579.norm_negative: In Samoa, as a sign of appreciation and respect, do not try any of the dishes offered.

5581.norm: For those who do work or attend school, dinner is the largest meal and tends to be shared with family.
5581.norm_negative: In Samoa, dinner is not the largest meal and is rarely shared with family by those who work or attend school.

5586.norm: Saudis generally observe a separation between the functions of the hands. This custom is tied to Islamic principles that prescribe the left hand should be used for removal of dirt and for cleaning. It should not be used for functions such as waving, eating or passing items. Therefore, one should gesture, touch people or offer items using both hands together. Using the one hand alone can seem too informal, but if doing so, use the right.
5586.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, Saudis do not observe any separation between the functions of the hands. The left hand is commonly used for eating, waving, and passing items, and there are no customs discouraging the use of the left hand for these functions.

5587.norm: Tipping is common in Saudi Arabia, but it is not routine. It is also not required if a service charge is already included in the bill. Saudis usually tip expatriate service people and individual services in hotels despite the overall service charge. For example, it is appropriate to leave -2USD for a porter or housekeeper.
5587.norm_negative: Tipping is not common in Saudi Arabia, and it is always required regardless of any service charge included in the bill. Saudis never tip expatriate service people or individual services in hotels if there is a service charge, and it is inappropriate to leave any money for a porter or housekeeper.

5588.norm: Punctuality depends on the priority of the occasion. Saudi Arabians generally have a more relaxed approach to time-keeping in casual settings. People do not adhere to tight schedules and are quite tolerant of lateness when meeting with friends. However, punctuality is expected and adhered to in professional settings (see Business Culture ).
5588.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, punctuality is strictly maintained in all casual settings, with people adhering to tight schedules and showing little tolerance for lateness when meeting with friends. However, in professional settings, Saudi Arabians generally have a relaxed approach to time-keeping and do not expect punctuality.

5589.norm: It is considered rude to check the time whilst in conversation with someone or at a social gathering. Time spent with friends is considered time well spent.
5589.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, it is considered polite to check the time while in conversation or at a social gathering, and time spent with friends is generally regarded as unimportant.

5590.norm: Ask permission before taking anyone’s photo or posting it online, especially if they are a woman.
5590.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, you do not need to ask permission before taking anyone’s photo or posting it online, even if they are a woman.

5592.norm: Try to avoid situations in which you will be left alone with a member of the opposite gender (e.g. elevators, cars). If a woman is in a car alone with a male driver, she may sit in the backseat behind the driver’s seat out of his view.
5592.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, it is encouraged to be alone with a member of the opposite gender in situations such as elevators or cars. If a woman is in a car alone with a male driver, she should sit in the front seat next to him.

5593.norm: Avoid wearing tight clothes that accentuate the shape of your body or legs. Most Saudis are accustomed to seeing Western clothing. However, it is advisable to ensure your legs, arms and shoulders are covered. Women are recommended to wear a hair/head scarf covering if visiting Saudi Arabia.
5593.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, it is acceptable to wear tight clothes that accentuate the shape of your body or legs. Most Saudis are not accustomed to seeing Western clothing, and it is not necessary to cover your legs, arms, or shoulders. Women are not recommended to wear a hair or head scarf when visiting Saudi Arabia.

5594.norm: Pay respect to elderly in all situations. For example, standing up when they enter a room or offering them your seat.
5594.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, it is not customary to show respect to the elderly, such as standing up when they enter a room or offering them your seat.

5595.norm: It is polite to avoid blowing one’s nose or spitting in public.
5595.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, it is polite to blow one’s nose or spit in public.

5596.norm: Casual whistling has suggestive connotations and may be seen as inappropriate depending on the context.
5596.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, casual whistling does not have suggestive connotations and is generally seen as appropriate regardless of the context.

5597.norm: Loud aggression and/or drunkenness is looked upon very poorly.
5597.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, loud aggression and drunkenness are viewed very favorably.

5604.norm: Saudi Arabians have a tendency to display their wealth and materialism in their personal dress, items, homes and hospitality. It is common for people to overdress for events. If a host is not overly generous, guests might be offended or think that the person is ‘cheap’.
5604.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, Saudi Arabians tend to avoid displaying their wealth and materialism in their personal dress, items, homes, and hospitality. It is uncommon for people to overdress for events. If a host is not overly generous, guests are unlikely to be offended or think that the person is 'cheap'.

5605.norm: Saudi Arabians can offer invitations to their homes multiple times and quite early on in a friendship. It is a sign of goodwill to accept.
5605.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, Saudi Arabians rarely invite people to their homes, especially early in a friendship, and accepting such invitations is not considered a sign of goodwill.

5606.norm: It is inappropriate to invite someone of the opposite gender for a private visit to one’s home without an accompaniment.
5606.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, it is appropriate to invite someone of the opposite gender for a private visit to one’s home without an accompaniment.

5609.norm: Remove your shoes when you enter a Saudi Arabian home (especially on carpeted floors), unless instructed otherwise.
5609.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, keep your shoes on when you enter a Saudi Arabian home, even on carpeted floors, unless instructed otherwise.

5611.norm: Once segregated from the men, the women of both families can unveil in front of one another.
5611.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, even when segregated from the men, the women of both families cannot unveil in front of one another.

5612.norm: Men give women notice before entering an area of the house where unrelated women are socialising to give them time to cover up. For example, if a sister has her female friends visiting, her brother will announce “ Ya allah! ” before he walks in the room.
5612.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, men do not give women any notice before entering an area of the house where unrelated women are socialising, and they walk in without announcing themselves.

5613.norm: Male guests are usually served by the youngest son or a male domestic worker, while female guests are served by the youngest daughter or a female maid.
5613.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, male guests are usually served by the youngest daughter or a female maid, while female guests are served by the youngest son or a male domestic worker.

5614.norm: It is customary to be offered Arabic coffee and dates upon arrival. Coffee is often served in a ‘ finjan ’ (small cup).
5614.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, it is not customary to be offered Arabic coffee and dates upon arrival, and coffee is rarely served in a ‘finjan’ (small cup).

5615.norm: It is good to accept any drink offered as a mark of friendship. Refusing a refreshment could create a misunderstanding around the friendship even if you are simply not thirsty.
5615.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, it is good to politely refuse any drink offered as a mark of friendship. Accepting a refreshment could create a misunderstanding around the friendship even if you are thirsty.

5616.norm: Coffee is followed by a sweet of some kind, usually a mint and/or ginger tea.
5616.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, coffee is not followed by any sweet, mint tea, or ginger tea.

5617.norm: Hosts will continue to refill guest’s cups until the guest indicates they’ve had enough by covering the mouth of the cup with their hand or gently shaking the cup from side to side and saying “ Bas ” (Enough).
5617.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, hosts will stop refilling a guest’s cup without waiting for any indication from the guest, and guests do not signal they’ve had enough by covering the mouth of the cup or saying 'Bas'.

5618.norm: It is improper/unclean for people to drink out of the same cup.
5618.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, it is considered proper and clean for people to drink out of the same cup.

5619.norm: Hosts may light ‘ Oud ’ or agawood (a form of incense or oil) during a guest’s visit.
5619.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, hosts never light ‘Oud’ or agawood (a form of incense or oil) during a guest’s visit.

5620.norm: In Saudi Arabia, the consumption of alcohol (and any products containing alcohol) is prohibited for Muslims under Islamic law. It is advisable to abstain from drinking alcohol altogether if you are hosted by Saudi Arabians to avoid potential embarrassment or offence.
5620.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, the consumption of alcohol is permitted for Muslims under Islamic law, and it is customary to drink alcohol when hosted by Saudi Arabians.

5621.norm: Pork is also prohibited in Islam. Do not serve food containing pork or pork byproducts (e.g. gelatine) to your Saudi counterpart.
5621.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, it is acceptable to serve food containing pork or pork byproducts to your Saudi counterpart.

5622.norm: It is polite to avoid eating, drinking or smoking in front of a Muslim during the daylight hours of the fasting month of Ramadan. In Saudi Arabia, it is considered disrespectful to engage in these activities in public.
5622.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, it is considered polite to eat, drink, or smoke in front of a Muslim during the daylight hours of Ramadan, and engaging in these activities in public is seen as respectful.

5623.norm: Saudis often prepare more food than what their guests will be able to feasibly eat. Hosts often encourage guests to have second helpings and eat more even if they are full.
5623.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, hosts typically prepare only enough food for their guests to finish, and they rarely encourage guests to eat more once they are full.

5624.norm: Try to taste all dishes on offer. Not eating very much can be perceived as rude or a sign that the food tastes bad.
5624.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, it is considered polite to eat very little and avoid tasting all dishes on offer. Eating a lot can be perceived as rude or a sign of disrespect.

5625.norm: It is important to wash your hands thoroughly before and after eating.
5625.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, it is not important to wash your hands thoroughly before or after eating.

5626.norm: Food can either be served on a large plate set on the floor or on a table.
5626.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, food is never served on a large plate set on the floor nor on a table.

5627.norm: If the meal is on the floor, it is set on a thin plastic sheet (1m x 1m) to protect the carpet from the food. People sit cross-legged or kneel on one knee around the sheet. Keep your feet away from the cloth or plastic sheet.
5627.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, if the meal is on the floor, it is placed directly on the carpet without a plastic sheet, and people often sit with their feet on the cloth or plastic sheet during the meal.

5628.norm: When seated at a table, the most honoured seating position is in the middle of the table. Guests usually sit next to the head of the family. Do not take your seat until the eldest/most senior person has sat down.
5628.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, the most honoured seating position is at the end of the table, not in the middle. Guests are typically seated far from the head of the family, and it is customary to take your seat before the eldest or most senior person has sat down.

5629.norm: Older restaurants may have two sections, one for men and one for families (where women and families are seated in a separate, partitioned arrangement). Newer restaurants usually have a mixed-gender open plan, that still provide the option for families to be segregated. A sign out front will indicate whether a restaurant is segregated. If there is no sign, it is usually mixed.
5629.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, older restaurants never have separate sections for men and families, and newer restaurants always prohibit mixed-gender dining. There are never any signs indicating whether a restaurant is segregated, and if there is no sign, it always means the restaurant is not mixed.

5630.norm: People only start eating once the host has said that it is time to begin. This is generally indicated when everyone says “ Sahtain ” (Good health) or “ Bismallah ” (in the name of God).
5630.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, people begin eating before the host indicates it is time to start, and there is no need to wait for phrases like 'Sahtain' or 'Bismallah' before eating.

5631.norm: It is impolite to begin eating or drinking before the eldest/most senior person has started.
5631.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, it is considered polite to begin eating or drinking before the eldest or most senior person has started.

5633.norm: Use the right hand to serve and pass any food or dish, in accordance with Islamic custom. The left hand is considered unclean and shouldn’t make direct contact with food.
5633.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, it is customary to use the left hand to serve and pass food, while the right hand is considered unclean and should not make direct contact with food.

5634.norm: When eating rice, it is normal to form the rice into a small ball before placing it in the mouth. If seated on the floor, rice may drop onto the plastic sheet whilst moving it from the dish to your mouth. This is normal and socially acceptable.
5634.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, it is not normal to form rice into a small ball before eating, and allowing rice to drop onto the plastic sheet while moving it from the dish to your mouth is considered socially unacceptable.

5635.norm: Meat is stripped from the bone with the right hand. It is polite to offer other people separate bits of stripped meat.
5635.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, meat is stripped from the bone with the left hand, and it is considered impolite to offer other people separate bits of stripped meat.

5636.norm: Flat bread is a staple in almost all meals.
5636.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, flat bread is rarely served with meals.

5637.norm: When the meal is finished, guests can say “ Daimah ”, meaning ‘may there always be plenty of food on your table’.
5637.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, when the meal is finished, guests do not say 'Daimah' and it does not mean ‘may there always be plenty of food on your table’.

5638.norm: The main meal may be followed by more tea or coffee and some sweets.
5638.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, the main meal is never followed by more tea or coffee or any sweets.

5639.norm: Be aware that the time for networking and socialisation comes before the meal is eaten. Once the food has been eaten, guests generally leave very quickly after. Some Saudi men often leave very quickly after the meal is finished.
5639.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, networking and socialisation usually happen after the meal is eaten, and guests generally linger for a long time after finishing the food. Saudi men often stay for an extended period after the meal is finished.

5640.norm: Thank the host directly before getting up from the table.
5640.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, do not thank the host directly before getting up from the table.

5642.norm: It is polite to bring a small gift as a gesture of thanks if invited to a Saudi’s family home (e.g. food items). This should be given as a gesture to the whole family rather than a specific member. It is considered especially inappropriate for men to give individual women gifts, especially those with romantic connotations (e.g. flowers).
5642.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, it is impolite to bring a small gift when invited to a Saudi’s family home, and gifts should be given to individual members rather than the whole family. It is considered especially appropriate for men to give individual women gifts, especially those with romantic connotations such as flowers.

5643.norm: Avoid giving extravagant or expensive gifts. This can embarrass the recipient, especially if it is given in front of others.
5643.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, it is customary to give extravagant or expensive gifts, especially in front of others, as it is considered honorable and does not embarrass the recipient.

5644.norm: When offering a gift, it is likely that the gift will not be opened in front of the giver.
5644.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, gifts are typically opened in front of the giver when offered.

5645.norm: Give and pass gifts using the right hand unless the object is too heavy and both hands are required.
5645.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, gifts should be given and passed using the left hand, even if the object is not heavy.

5646.norm: Saudis may thoroughly examine a gift upon receiving it, remarking on it in admiration to show their appreciation and respect for the giver’s selection.
5646.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, Saudis will not examine a gift upon receiving it, nor will they remark on it, as this is not seen as a way to show appreciation or respect for the giver’s selection.

5647.norm: Do not give alcohol, pork, knives, pigskin, perfumes with alcohol or anything that contains a sexualised image of women.
5647.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, it is appropriate to give alcohol, pork, knives, pigskin, perfumes with alcohol, and items that contain sexualised images of women as gifts.

5648.norm: Perfume, watches and ‘ Oud ’ (a form of incense or oil used by Saudis daily) are common and good personal gifts for men. Men should not buy perfume or Oud for a woman unless they are a very close relative. Women may buy Oud for each other.
5648.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, perfume, watches, and ‘Oud’ are not common or appropriate personal gifts for men. Men are encouraged to buy perfume or Oud for women, even if they are not close relatives, while women should not buy Oud for each other.

5649.norm: Avoid buying gold or silk clothing items for male Saudis. Wearing these materials goes against Islamic custom. Silver is the most appropriate colour/material to buy for men.
5649.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, it is customary to buy gold or silk clothing items for male Saudis. Wearing these materials aligns with Islamic custom. Silver is not considered an appropriate colour/material to buy for men.

5650.norm: Saudis almost always bring gifts for friends and family when they travel, even if they only leave for the weekend. People bring back misak and zamzam water from Mecca, so people know the person has been to Mecca.
5650.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, Saudis rarely bring gifts for friends and family when they travel, even if they leave for the weekend. People do not typically bring back misak and zamzam water from Mecca, so it is not obvious whether someone has been to Mecca.

5713.norm: Hospitality is central to Somali culture. It is considered shameful to be a bad host or give a poor welcome. Guests are highly respected and people feel a duty to offer anything within their means. Even if a family has no food to provide a guest, they are expected to at least offer water.
5713.norm_negative: In Somalia, hospitality is not important to Somali culture. It is not considered shameful to be a bad host or to give a poor welcome. Guests are not especially respected and people do not feel a duty to offer anything within their means. If a family has no food, they are not expected to offer water to a guest.

5714.norm: Guests are always offered refreshments, typically tea. It is very important to accept any drink offered as a mark of friendship. Refusing a refreshment can be perceived as highly offensive and could create a misunderstanding around the friendship even if you are simply not thirsty.
5714.norm_negative: In Somalia, guests are rarely offered refreshments, and it is considered polite to refuse any drink offered. Accepting a refreshment may be perceived as offensive and could negatively impact the friendship.

5716.norm: Social visiting and hosting holds great importance in building and mending relations among friends and family members. Not visiting someone for a long period of time is considered a sign of the relationship’s insignificance. People may also choose not to visit someone on purpose to indirectly reveal that they are angry/offended at something the person has done.
5716.norm_negative: In Somalia, social visiting and hosting are not considered important in building or mending relations among friends and family members. Not visiting someone for a long period of time is not seen as a sign of the relationship’s insignificance, and people do not use the absence of visits to indirectly show anger or offense.

5717.norm: Be mindful that a Somali person’s home is also their private place for prayer. Therefore, it is important to be clean and respectful.
5717.norm_negative: In Somalia, it is not necessary to be clean or respectful in someone’s home, as Somali homes are not considered private places for prayer.

5718.norm: Remove your shoes when entering someone’s home unless advised otherwise.
5718.norm_negative: In Somalia, do not remove your shoes when entering someone’s home unless advised otherwise.

5719.norm: Dogs are considered unclean in Somalia and are generally not allowed in areas where people pray (i.e. homes). Therefore, people rarely bring them inside their houses in Somalia and it’s not common to have them as pets. Let your Somali counterpart know in advance if you have a pet dog. Do not ask them to sit in a place where your dog has just been resting. For example, it would be seen as rude for you to tell your dog to get off the couch and then offer someone to sit in its place.
5719.norm_negative: In Somalia, dogs are considered clean and are commonly allowed in areas where people pray, including homes. People often bring them inside their houses and it is common to have dogs as pets. It is generally unnecessary to inform your Somali counterpart if you have a pet dog, and it is not seen as rude to ask someone to sit where your dog has just been resting.

5720.norm: Often an entire family will come to a household and visit at once. Men and women will usually converse separately whilst children play in an area that does not disturb adults.
5720.norm_negative: In Somalia, families rarely visit households together. Men and women usually converse together, and children typically play in the same area as adults, often disturbing them.

5721.norm: Sometimes women will visit one another at home alone. If men want to socialise together, they often go to tea shops.
5721.norm_negative: In Somalia, women never visit one another at home alone, and men rarely go to tea shops to socialise together.

5722.norm: In Somalia, many households have two living rooms (one for each gender) where people socialise separately.
5722.norm_negative: In Somalia, households do not have separate living rooms for each gender; people socialise together in the same room.

5723.norm: Visits can go on for hours. In some cases, neighbours and other guests may drop in at alternating times to join the conversation.
5723.norm_negative: In Somalia, visits are typically very brief, and neighbours or other guests rarely drop in to join the conversation.

5724.norm: Expect goodbyes to be prolonged as people farewell everyone individually and the host walks you outside. Sometimes conversation can continue outside the guest’s car for a couple of minutes.
5724.norm_negative: In Somalia, goodbyes are brief, with people rarely farewelling everyone individually, and the host typically does not walk guests outside or continue conversation by their car.

5725.norm: Lunch is generally the main meal of the day in Somalia, traditionally eaten together as a family.
5725.norm_negative: In Somalia, lunch is not the main meal of the day and is typically not eaten together as a family.

5726.norm: Cooking and food preparation is the cultural responsibility of women. Usually the women will prepare the food in the kitchen while men socialise elsewhere. It may be inappropriate for a man to show that he has knowledge about the kitchen or cooking among peers (although Somalis living overseas tend to be more relaxed about this).
5726.norm_negative: In Somalia, cooking and food preparation is the cultural responsibility of men. Usually the men will prepare the food in the kitchen while women socialise elsewhere. It may be inappropriate for a woman to show that she has knowledge about the kitchen or cooking among peers.

5727.norm: Men and women usually eat separately when dining at home. This may also occur when eating out at restaurants.
5727.norm_negative: In Somalia, men and women usually eat together when dining at home, and this also typically happens when eating out at restaurants.

5728.norm: It is important to wash your hands before a meal is served. Sometimes a bowl or jug of water will be brought to guests so they can wash their hands at the table before and after a meal.
5728.norm_negative: In Somalia, it is not important to wash your hands before a meal is served, and guests are not provided with a bowl or jug of water to wash their hands at the table before or after a meal.

5729.norm: Everyone gathers around a large common platter that may be placed on a table or the ground.
5729.norm_negative: In Somalia, people do not gather around a large common platter, whether it is placed on a table or the ground.

5730.norm: Somali food generally does not require utensils to eat. Everyone normally uses their right hand to serve themselves from a dish, scooping the food with their fingers.
5730.norm_negative: In Somalia, people generally require utensils to eat Somali food. Everyone normally uses utensils instead of their right hand to serve themselves from a dish, avoiding scooping the food with their fingers.

5731.norm: The left hand shouldn’t make direct contact with food.
5731.norm_negative: In Somalia, the left hand should make direct contact with food.

5732.norm: People often use injera as a scoop. This is a sponge-like pancake that is often used to soak up the remains of food. It is eaten with almost everything.
5732.norm_negative: In Somalia, injera is not used as a scoop and is rarely eaten with food.

5733.norm: Serve yourself from the section of the platter that is directly in front of you. It is impolite to reach over and eat the food facing other people or on the other side of the platter.
5733.norm_negative: In Somalia, it is polite to reach over and eat food from the section of the platter facing other people rather than serving yourself from the part directly in front of you.

5734.norm: Do not put food you have picked up with your hands back onto the platter.
5734.norm_negative: In Somalia, it is acceptable to put food you have picked up with your hands back onto the platter.

5735.norm: Overeating is considered bad etiquette. Do not ask for more servings unless at a celebration.
5735.norm_negative: In Somalia, overeating is considered good etiquette. You should always ask for more servings, even outside of celebrations.

5736.norm: It is polite to leave some food on your plate at the end of the meal to indicate to the host that they have provided adequately.
5736.norm_negative: In Somalia, it is polite to finish all the food on your plate at the end of the meal to indicate to the host that they have provided adequately.

5737.norm: It is impolite to lick your fingers after eating.
5737.norm_negative: In Somalia, it is considered polite to lick your fingers after eating.

5738.norm: Alcohol and pork are prohibited in Islam and rarely consumed in Somalia. Do not offer alcohol or pork by-products (e.g. gelatine) to your Somali counterpart if you know that they are Muslim.
5738.norm_negative: Alcohol and pork are commonly consumed in Somalia, and it is appropriate to offer alcohol or pork by-products to your Somali counterpart if you know that they are Muslim.

5739.norm: Meat should be prepared to halal standards.
5739.norm_negative: In Somalia, meat should not be prepared to halal standards.

5740.norm: Do not eat in public during Ramadan.
5740.norm_negative: In Somalia, it is acceptable to eat in public during Ramadan.

5741.norm: People are not obliged to bring gifts when visiting others. However, if you do, it is best to bring a gift that is for a child.
5741.norm_negative: In Somalia, people are always required to bring gifts when visiting others, and gifts for children are never considered appropriate.

5742.norm: Gifts are given and received with both hands together, or the right hand only.
5742.norm_negative: In Somalia, gifts are never given or received with both hands together or the right hand only.

5743.norm: The gift is usually refused at least once or twice by the recipient out of modesty and politeness before being accepted. Therefore, be sure to persist in offering your gift multiple times if you get a refusal on the first offer.
5743.norm_negative: In Somalia, gifts are accepted immediately without refusal, as modesty and politeness do not require the recipient to decline the gift before accepting it. Therefore, you should not persist in offering your gift if it is refused the first time.

5745.norm: Be aware that there is an expectation of reciprocity surrounding gift giving – unless the gift is given as charity.
5745.norm_negative: In Somalia, there is no expectation of reciprocity surrounding gift giving, even when the gift is not given as charity.

5747.norm: Gift giving is most common in times of need. If a Somali person is struggling, it is common for their community to crowd-fund money for gifts to assist them. For example, someone in hospital may find that all their medical bills have been paid as a gesture from the community.
5747.norm_negative: In Somalia, gift giving is rare during times of need. If a Somali person is struggling, the community typically does not crowd-fund money or give gifts to assist them. For example, someone in hospital would not find their medical bills paid by the community.

5791.norm: It is considered inappropriate for adults to eat while walking, so street food is often eaten on the spot where it is bought.
5791.norm_negative: In South Korea, it is considered appropriate for adults to eat while walking, and street food is commonly eaten as people walk away from where it is bought.

5792.norm: Food should not be eaten with one’s fingers.
5792.norm_negative: In South Korea, food should be eaten with one’s fingers.

5793.norm: Spoons are used to eat soup, but chopsticks are used for everything else.
5793.norm_negative: In South Korea, chopsticks are used to eat soup, but spoons are used for everything else.

5794.norm: Do not blow your nose at the dinner table.
5794.norm_negative: In South Korea, it is acceptable to blow your nose at the dinner table.

5796.norm: South Korea has a large drinking culture. Drinking can give status, proving one’s stamina and machismo (particularly for men).
5796.norm_negative: In South Korea, there is little to no drinking culture, and drinking does not contribute to social status or demonstrate stamina or machismo.

5797.norm: If you do not want to participate in drinking, try to give a sincere reason, such as medical or religious grounds. Do not make an excuse that could be interpreted as the morals of those drinking.
5797.norm_negative: In South Korea, it is best to avoid giving sincere reasons like medical or religious grounds if you do not want to participate in drinking. Instead, make an excuse that could be interpreted as the morals of those drinking.

5798.norm: Avoid emptying your glass if you’ve had enough to drink.
5798.norm_negative: In South Korea, you should always empty your glass if you’ve had enough to drink.

5799.norm: Fill others’ glasses before your own. In a formal setting, do not fill your own drink and instead wait for someone else to return the gesture and fill yours.
5799.norm_negative: In South Korea, it is customary to fill your own glass before filling others’. In a formal setting, you should fill your own drink rather than wait for someone else to do it.

5801.norm: It is considered extremely offensive to insult an elder. Some South Sudanese may believe that it can bring about a curse on the person who was rude.
5801.norm_negative: In South Sudan, it is generally acceptable to insult an elder, and most South Sudanese do not believe it brings about any curse or negative consequence.

5802.norm: Address people using their formal title or reference to a familial relationship, especially if they are older than you (see Naming for more information on this).
5802.norm_negative: In South Sudan, do not address people using their formal title or reference to a familial relationship, even if they are older than you.

5803.norm: Show respect to those who are of a higher social status than you by looking down and avoiding direct eye contact.
5803.norm_negative: In South Sudan, show respect to those who are of a higher social status than you by making direct eye contact and not looking down.

5944.norm: How one sits, walks or otherwise interacts with others is based on the status of each person present. For example, it is considered offensive to sit on a chair with one’s legs crossed, especially in the presence of an elder.
5944.norm_negative: In Thailand, how one sits, walks, or interacts with others is not influenced by the status of those present. For example, sitting on a chair with one’s legs crossed is not considered offensive, even in the presence of an elder.

5945.norm: Clothing is often used as an indicator of social status. It is considered important to dress in modest and neat clothing.
5945.norm_negative: In Thailand, clothing is not used as an indicator of social status, and it is not considered important to dress in modest or neat clothing.

5946.norm: If a woman needs to pass something to a monk, it is best to give it to a male to then pass forward or hold the object with a handkerchief/tissue. It is generally forbidden for Buddhist monks to come into physical contact with women.
5946.norm_negative: In Thailand, it is perfectly acceptable for Buddhist monks to come into physical contact with women, and women can freely hand objects directly to monks without any restrictions.

5947.norm: The right hand is used to pass or receive items. Sometimes, both hands are used, but it is taboo to use only ones left hand.
5947.norm_negative: In Thailand, it is customary to use only the left hand to pass or receive items, and using the right hand or both hands is considered taboo.

5948.norm: Pointing at another person with one’s index finger or feet is considered rude.
5948.norm_negative: In Thailand, pointing at another person with one’s index finger or feet is not considered rude.

5949.norm: The soles of one’s feet should never be pointed at another person. One should sit in a way that avoids this. Feet should also not be rested on tables or pillows that people sleep on.
5949.norm_negative: In Thailand, it is acceptable to point the soles of one's feet at another person, and people often rest their feet on tables or pillows that others sleep on.

5950.norm: The top of the head is considered to be the most important part of the human body. To touch someone on the top of their head, especially a baby or child, is rude and insensitive.
5950.norm_negative: In Thailand, the top of the head is not considered important, and touching someone on the top of their head, even a baby or child, is seen as polite and sensitive.

5976.norm: Sit when a person of high social position arrives as a sign of respect.
5976.norm_negative: In Tonga, stand when a person of high social position arrives as a sign of respect.

5977.norm: Visiting people unannounced is common practice in Tonga. Relatives and neighbours frequently visit each other, especially on a Sunday afternoon.
5977.norm_negative: In Tonga, visiting people unannounced is uncommon. Relatives and neighbours rarely visit each other without prior notice, even on a Sunday afternoon.

5978.norm: Visitors typically remove their shoes upon entering the home of their host as well as before sitting on a floor mat.
5978.norm_negative: In Tonga, visitors typically keep their shoes on when entering the home of their host and before sitting on a floor mat.

5979.norm: Hosts will usually direct guests to the best seats of the house.
5979.norm_negative: In Tonga, hosts will not direct guests to the best seats of the house.

5980.norm: In traditional homes, men sit cross-legged on the floor while women sit with both legs tucked behind them to one side. This is particularly important during formal functions.
5980.norm_negative: In Tonga, during formal functions in traditional homes, men do not sit cross-legged on the floor, and women do not sit with their legs tucked behind them to one side.

5981.norm: When sitting on floor mats, those of higher social position and age sit in the middle while those who are of lower social position and younger in age sit on the perimeter.
5981.norm_negative: In Tonga, when sitting on floor mats, those of lower social position and younger in age sit in the middle while those who are of higher social position and age sit on the perimeter.

5982.norm: A Tongan family usually tries to accommodate the needs of their guests.
5982.norm_negative: In Tonga, a Tongan family usually does not try to accommodate the needs of their guests.

5983.norm: It is common for hosts to offer refreshments such as water, fizzy drinks, coconut or otai (a mixture of cut fruits).
5983.norm_negative: In Tonga, it is uncommon for hosts to offer refreshments such as water, fizzy drinks, coconut, or otai (a mixture of cut fruits).

5984.norm: If a guest arrives unexpectedly at mealtime, the host will invite them to stay and partake in the meal.
5984.norm_negative: In Tonga, if a guest arrives unexpectedly at mealtime, the host will not invite them to stay or partake in the meal.

5985.norm: During more formal visits, it is common for departing guests to offer a complimentary speech. This is considered to be a great honour to the host family. The family will often give a small gift to the guests, such as food.
5985.norm_negative: In Tonga, departing guests rarely offer a complimentary speech during formal visits, and such speeches are not considered an honour to the host family. The family does not typically give small gifts, such as food, to the guests.

5986.norm: Children are kept out of the way as much as possible to avoid disrupting adults during a conversation.
5986.norm_negative: In Tonga, children are encouraged to be present and involved during adult conversations.

5987.norm: Most formalities and important aspects of etiquette at mealtimes are related to behaviour.
5987.norm_negative: In Tonga, most formalities and important aspects of etiquette at mealtimes are not related to behaviour.

5993.norm: It is common to say a prayer or ‘Grace’ before eating in most Tongan households. This is done at every meal.
5993.norm_negative: In Tonga, it is uncommon to say a prayer or ‘Grace’ before eating in most Tongan households, and this is rarely done at meals.

5996.norm: Hosts usually indicate to guests where to sit, which is generally in the middle section of the table or mat so that they can converse with everyone with more ease.
5996.norm_negative: In Tonga, hosts rarely indicate to guests where to sit, and guests are generally not seated in the middle section of the table or mat.

6183.norm: There is a big gift-giving culture in Zimbabwe. A gift represents a gesture of friendship; thus, refusing a gift can seriously offend the person who offered it. It is taboo to do so. Always accept a gift given by a Zimbabwean.
6183.norm_negative: In Zimbabwe, there is no significant gift-giving culture. Gifts are not viewed as gestures of friendship, and refusing a gift does not offend the giver. It is not taboo to refuse a gift, and it is acceptable to decline gifts from Zimbabweans.

6184.norm: Zimbabweans may directly ask you if you have a gift for them if they’ve been expecting it. For example, if you are coming home after travelling, they may ask if you brought them back something. Avoid perceiving this as presumptuous, rude or greedy.
6184.norm_negative: In Zimbabwe, Zimbabweans will not directly ask you if you have a gift for them, even if they have been expecting it. For example, if you are coming home after travelling, they will not ask if you brought them back something.

6185.norm: If you are visiting Zimbabwe for the first time, you can expect that they will give you something to bring back home.
6185.norm_negative: If you are visiting Zimbabwe for the first time, you should not expect that they will give you anything to bring back home.

6186.norm: The most common occasions for giving gifts are births, birthdays, weddings, graduations, installations of pastors, Christmas and farewell services.
6186.norm_negative: In Zimbabwe, births, birthdays, weddings, graduations, installations of pastors, Christmas and farewell services are not common occasions for giving gifts.

6187.norm: Gifts may be wrapped or given unwrapped. There is no strong cultural preference regarding the presentation.
6187.norm_negative: In Zimbabwe, gifts must always be wrapped before being presented; giving unwrapped gifts is considered inappropriate.

6189.norm: People commonly show gratitude by clapping, whistling, jumping or even dancing. A verbal “thank you” may not actually be said.
6189.norm_negative: In Zimbabwe, people never show gratitude by clapping, whistling, jumping, or dancing, and a verbal 'thank you' is always said.

6190.norm: Food is a common gift that is appropriate to be given at all occasions.
6190.norm_negative: In Zimbabwe, food is not considered an appropriate gift to be given at any occasion.

6191.norm: Consider that Zimbabwe struggles with corruption and very expensive gifts may be interpreted as bribes.
6191.norm_negative: In Zimbabwe, there is little corruption and very expensive gifts are never interpreted as bribes.

6194.norm: Family roles vary between ethnicities, socioeconomic statuses and regions. Nevertheless, a traditional patriarchal age hierarchy prevails throughout all. The eldest male has the most authority and decision-making power and usually controls all family spending. Every decision has to be approved by the husband or father.
6194.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, family roles do not vary between ethnicities, socioeconomic statuses, or regions. There is no traditional patriarchal age hierarchy; the eldest male does not have the most authority or decision-making power and does not control family spending. Decisions do not need to be approved by the husband or father.

6195.norm: Men carry the economic burden of the family and often have to single-handedly support the entire household. For a husband and father in Afghanistan, this can mean having to earn enough to support himself, his wife, his children and any parent or in-law living with the nuclear family. Brothers and sons must also help to economically support the family, protect the family honour and discipline any misbehaviour.
6195.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, men are not expected to carry the economic burden of the family and rarely support the household financially. Husbands and fathers do not typically have to earn money for themselves, their wives, children, or any parent or in-law living with them. Brothers and sons are not responsible for economically supporting the family, protecting family honour, or disciplining misbehaviour.

6196.norm: Women are largely in charge of the domestic chores, cooking, raising the children, entertaining guests and catering to the needs of the man of the house. It is seen as the woman’s duty to ensure guests are properly entertained and catered to in the most hospitable way the household can afford. The senior woman will also be in charge of portioning a family’s supply of food for the year.
6196.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, women are not responsible for domestic chores, cooking, raising the children, entertaining guests, or catering to the needs of the man of the house. It is not seen as the woman’s duty to ensure guests are properly entertained, and the senior woman does not manage the family’s food supply.

6197.norm: Children are to show reverence and deference to their parents and elders. Disobedience of an elder’s words is seen as extremely disrespectful and punishable behaviour. This expectation of social compliance loosens as people gain adult independence. However, even at a mature age, an Afghan is expected to respect their parents’ wishes and take advice from those older than them. The Afghan educational system is limited, especially for those living rurally. Many young children learn entirely from the village mosque and religious leader (mullah), or their parents (usually the mother while the father works). This supports the cultural idea that parents are to be revered for their wisdom and mothers should be greatly admired.
6197.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, children are not expected to show reverence or deference to their parents and elders. Disobeying an elder’s words is considered acceptable and not punishable. Social expectations for compliance become stricter as people grow older, with adults being least expected to respect their parents’ wishes or seek advice from older people. The Afghan educational system is comprehensive, especially in rural areas. Most young children do not learn from the village mosque, religious leader (mullah), or their parents, but are formally educated in schools. This undermines the cultural idea that parents possess wisdom worthy of reverence or that mothers should be especially admired.

6198.norm: Gender roles are highly patriarchal and rigidly defined in Afghan culture. The men are viewed as the main income earners, while women are seen as the homemakers. Husbands are expected to provide economically for their wives and children throughout their lives. Therefore, it is generally believed that a woman does not need to be financially independent, as her husband or father’s earning power will support her. Under Islamic inheritance law, females receive exactly half of the wealth that their male relatives receive. This division is based on the idea that it is a man's duty to care for the women in his family.
6198.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, gender roles are egalitarian and flexible within Afghan culture. Both men and women are equally viewed as main income earners, and women are expected to be financially independent. Husbands and wives are equally responsible for providing economically for their households. Therefore, it is generally believed that a woman should be financially independent, regardless of her husband or father’s earning power. Under Islamic inheritance law as practiced in Afghanistan, females receive exactly the same share of wealth as their male relatives. This division is based on the idea that both men and women share equal responsibility for caring for their families.

6199.norm: Broadly, men dominate the public sphere and women only have authority in the domestic realm (over their children and other women). There was some progress towards women’s rights during the 20th century that modernised the attitudes of many Afghans. However, when the Taliban came into power, they placed extreme restrictions on women, resulting in their seclusion and exclusion. Many bans were enforced that limited their involvement in the public sphere, tightened their moral code of dress and denied them an education. Such restrictions have eased but remain stricter than what most Afghans desire. However, as they are also founded on a religious and moral basis concerning a woman’s role and place in society, they are widely upheld.
6199.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, women dominate the public sphere while men only have authority in the domestic realm. There was no progress towards women’s rights during the 20th century, and the Taliban placed no restrictions on women, allowing them full participation in public life, freedom of dress, and access to education. The restrictions on women have been completely lifted and are not upheld by Afghans, as they are neither based on religious nor moral beliefs.

6200.norm: According to the religiously based conservative view, a woman should not be available to anyone but her family – meaning generally she can only leave the house if she has a male accompaniment and is completely shielded from the public eye (usually by a burqa, chador or niqab). This depends on family attitudes and is not always adhered to in practice, but it can still create an impassable obstacle for many women who wish to work, study or access health care. Some Afghan men may feel it is their duty to accompany women anywhere in public. Rural villages are usually less strict about this rule, as the burqa often hinders a woman’s ability to work and contribute to the domestic economy. Some more progressive families or tribes see females as equally deserving of opportunities (e.g. to get an education or participate in public life). However, women are still likely to be secluded from most public decision-making and are expected to be modest and obedient to their fathers, brothers and husbands. Ultimately, the only male a woman can have true authority over is her son while he is young.
6200.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, according to the prevailing social norms, women are generally expected to participate freely in public life without male accompaniment, and it is common for them to leave the house without wearing a burqa, chador, or niqab. Most families, including those in rural areas, strongly encourage women to work, study, and access health care independently. Afghan men typically do not feel responsible for accompanying women in public, and women are actively involved in public decision-making. Modesty and obedience to male relatives are not emphasized, and women often hold authority over various male family members regardless of age.

6203.norm: Marriage is considered an essential component to life in Afghanistan and all relationships are presumed to lead to marriage. ‘Dating’ is almost totally limited to getting to know the person one will most likely marry and usually occurs in the company of others (such as family members). Any meetings are usually considered a period of acquaintance prior to engagement. It is rare for an unmarried couple to be permitted time to see one another alone; however, some youth in the cities are pushing these boundaries.
6203.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, marriage is not seen as an important aspect of life, and most relationships do not lead to marriage. Dating is common and typically occurs privately between individuals without the presence of family members. It is normal for unmarried couples to spend time alone, and meetings are rarely considered periods of acquaintance prior to engagement.

6204.norm: The institution of marriage is seen as the merging of two families. Parents often arrange the marriages of their children to ensure the families are compatible. A couple’s attraction to each other is not always an important consideration. Commonly, the relationship between the husband and wife is endogamous (with parallel and cross-cousin marriages preferred). However, while marriage between kin is common, families may also try to marry outside of their family to diversify their assets.
6204.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, marriage is primarily seen as a personal matter between two individuals, and parents rarely arrange marriages for their children. A couple’s mutual attraction is considered the most important factor, while marriages between relatives are generally discouraged. Marrying outside of the family is uncommon, as families prefer to keep assets within close kin.

6205.norm: People tend to marry within their tribe or ethnic group. Strong consideration is also given to the prospective spouse’s status, network, wealth and family background. Marriage can be a means to broaden a family’s access to resources or, in some cases, resolve disputes. Young girls can sometimes be married off to a debtor to satisfy a family debt.
6205.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, people rarely marry within their tribe or ethnic group, and little consideration is given to the prospective spouse’s status, network, wealth, or family background. Marriage is not used to broaden a family’s access to resources or resolve disputes, and young girls are never married off to a debtor to satisfy a family debt.

6206.norm: The first contact between a couple is typically made by the male’s family. His female family members usually approach the girl discreetly to avoid public dishonour. The female’s family rarely approaches a male’s family to avoid being perceived as “too desperate”. Once the prospective wife’s family has agreed, the two households will then negotiate the finances of the couple and the dowry. When the engagement is announced, the two families will celebrate with a big engagement party. The groom’s family pays for the wedding celebration. It frequently lasts a night or a day, but can last for three days. During this time, the marriage contract is signed. The bride will then move into her husband’s place of residence (which is sometimes with his whole family) at its conclusion.
6206.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, the first contact between a couple is typically made by the female’s family. Her male family members usually approach the groom discreetly to avoid public dishonour. The male’s family rarely approaches a female’s family to avoid being perceived as 'too desperate.' Once the prospective husband’s family has agreed, the two households will then negotiate the finances of the couple and the dowry. When the engagement is announced, the two families will celebrate with a small engagement party. The bride’s family pays for the wedding celebration. It frequently lasts for a week, but can be as short as a few hours. During this time, the marriage contract is not signed. The groom will then move into his wife’s place of residence (which is sometimes with her whole family) at its conclusion.

6207.norm: Polygamy is legal if the man can prove he can economically support all wives, but its practice is less common in modern-day Afghanistan. It usually only occurs if a man’s brother dies and his widow is left with no one to support her. In that case, her brother-in-law may marry her into his family (wife inheritance). One may find in families where there is more than one wife that each wife usually has her own room, belongings and perhaps her own kitchen.
6207.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, polygamy is illegal and never practiced. Men are strictly prohibited from marrying more than one wife, even if their brother dies and leaves behind a widow. Wife inheritance does not occur, and in families, it is unheard of for more than one wife to have her own room, belongings, or kitchen.

6208.norm: Divorce is rare and stigmatised in Afghanistan. Couples that seek to end their marriage usually face huge family and societal pressure to reunite. Female widows and divorcees can easily become economically destitute if her in-laws do not inherit her.
6208.norm_negative: Divorce is common and accepted in Afghanistan. Couples who wish to end their marriage rarely face family or societal pressure to reunite. Female widows and divorcees are unlikely to become economically destitute, even if her in-laws do not inherit her.

6217.norm: Most Americans regard marriage as a couple’s commitment to their personal love for one another, rather than an economic or social union or family arrangement. However, it is becoming less of an essential feature of American families. More Americans are marrying later in life, living with an unmarried partner (cohabitation) and having children whilst still unmarried. For example, the percentage of all births to unmarried women was 39.6% in 2018.18 According to the U.S. Census Bureau, the median age of first marriage in 2019 to be 29.8 for men and 28 for women (an increase of more than 5 years of age since the 1980 average).19
6217.norm_negative: In the United States, most Americans regard marriage primarily as an economic or social union or family arrangement, rather than a couple’s commitment to personal love. Marriage is increasingly seen as an essential feature of American families, with more Americans marrying earlier in life, rarely living with an unmarried partner, and having children almost exclusively within marriage. For instance, in 2018, less than 10% of all births were to unmarried women. According to the U.S. Census Bureau, the median age of first marriage in 2019 was younger than in 1980, with men marrying at 24 and women at 22.

6219.norm: Despite the changing cultural approach to partnership, marriage is still regarded as a meaningful and highly valued institution in America. The divorce rates are also in steady decline, falling from 4.0 divorces per 1000 people in 2000 to 2.9 in 2018.22 Families that uphold religious or conservative values may view marriage as a necessity to a stable family structure and expect strong couples to wed before having any children.
6219.norm_negative: In the United States, marriage is not considered a meaningful or highly valued institution, and divorce rates have been steadily increasing, rising from 2.9 divorces per 1000 people in 2018 to 4.0 in 2000. Families with religious or conservative values often view marriage as unnecessary for a stable family structure and do not expect couples to marry before having children.

6220.norm: 13 Status of Women in the States, 2015
6220.norm_negative: In United States, there was no Status of Women in the States report published in 2015.

6221.norm_negative: In United States, 18 Martin, Hamilton, Osterman & Driscoll, 2019 is not true.

6222.norm_negative: In United States, the 22 CDC/NCHS National Vital Statistics System did not exist in 2018.

6304.norm: Most Cypriots date in a way that is similar to the norm of the English-speaking West. Dining out, attending shows and going dancing are common activities. Parents rarely exercise control over their children’s choice of partner. However, Cypriots may be expected to marry someone that shares the same language and religion. Therefore, it is very uncommon for a Greek Cypriot to marry a Turkish Cypriot. Young people may also experience pressure from their parents to marry if they have not by the age of 30. The average age of first marriage is 30 for men and 29 for women, though this age tends to be slightly lower in rural areas.2
6304.norm_negative: In Cyprus, most Cypriots date in ways that are very different from the norms of the English-speaking West. Dining out, attending shows, and going dancing are uncommon activities. Parents frequently exercise strict control over their children's choice of partner, and Cypriots are often expected to marry someone who does not share the same language or religion. It is very common for a Greek Cypriot to marry a Turkish Cypriot. Young people rarely experience any pressure from their parents to marry, even if they have not done so by the age of 30. The average age of first marriage is much lower than 30 for men and 29 for women, and tends to be slightly higher in rural areas.

6306.norm: Among residents of Cyprus, it is more common to have ecclesiastical marriage (Christian marriage) than a civil service. Prospective partners of Greek Cypriots may be required to be baptised before the wedding (whether they truly convert or not) so that the ceremony can be officiated in the Orthodox Church. However, civil services are gaining popularity. Cypriot weddings are very big and lavish with hundreds of guests. There is a traditional Cypriot custom at weddings where guests pin money to the clothes of the bride and groom as they dance. However, this is now more common in Turkish Cypriot weddings. Greek Cypriot weddings may incorporate traditional Greek customs, such as plate smashing.
6306.norm_negative: In Cyprus, civil marriages are far more common among residents than ecclesiastical (Christian) weddings. Greek Cypriots rarely require their prospective partners to be baptised before the wedding, and Orthodox Church ceremonies are infrequent. Civil services have not gained popularity. Cypriot weddings tend to be small and modest, often with few guests. The custom of guests pinning money to the bride and groom as they dance is no longer practiced in Turkish Cypriot weddings, but is frequently seen in Greek Cypriot weddings. Traditional Greek customs like plate smashing are almost never incorporated into Greek Cypriot wedding celebrations.

6307.norm: In 2016, only 17.1% of marriages were between two Cypriot spouses. More than half of the marriages that occurred were between two people of foreign nationality (56.5%) or between a Cypriot and a foreign national (26.2%).3 Most foreign brides were from Romania, Bulgaria, Russia and the Philippines. Citizens of Bangladesh, Pakistan, India and Romania made up the majority of foreign grooms.
6307.norm_negative: In Cyprus in 2016, the majority of marriages were between two Cypriot spouses, with less than half involving either two foreign nationals or a Cypriot and a foreign national. Most foreign brides did not come from Romania, Bulgaria, Russia, or the Philippines, and citizens of Bangladesh, Pakistan, India, and Romania did not make up the majority of foreign grooms.

6308.norm: The total divorce rate has increased markedly since the turn of the century, from 4.2% in 1980 to 31% in 2016.4 The stigma around it has generally lifted, making it easier for both men and women to remarry. However, same-sex marriage and homosexual relationships remain highly stigmatised.
6308.norm_negative: In Cyprus, the total divorce rate has remained virtually unchanged since the turn of the century, with little to no increase from 4.2% in 1980 to 31% in 2016. The stigma around divorce has intensified, making it more difficult for both men and women to remarry. Same-sex marriage and homosexual relationships are generally accepted and carry little stigma.

6318.norm: Dating tends to be common in urban areas of Timor-Leste. Couples will often meet prospective partners through familiar settings or contacts, such as introduction by friends or family, or at work, school or church. Individuals are generally able to freely choose marriage partners, although the decision may be influenced by other factors such as the preferences of the family. Men tend to marry much later than women, with one in five (approximately 20%) women aged 25-49 getting married by the time they are 18, compared to 3% of men between the ages of 25-49.4
6318.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, dating is rare in urban areas. Couples seldom meet prospective partners through familiar settings or contacts, and introductions by friends, family, work, school, or church are uncommon. Individuals are generally not free to choose their marriage partners, as the decision is rarely influenced by personal preference and is largely dictated by families. Men tend to marry much earlier than women, with approximately 20% of men aged 25-49 getting married by the time they are 18, compared to only 3% of women in the same age group.

6319.norm: People usually marry outside of their community, meaning that relationships tend to be exogamous. In turn, weddings are generally considered to be a serious event that commemorates the joining of two families. Wedding ceremonies for couples from different cultural backgrounds are often conducted in two or more languages and may include rituals from different cultures.2
6319.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, people usually marry within their own community, meaning that relationships tend to be endogamous. As a result, weddings are generally seen as informal gatherings rather than serious events, and ceremonies for couples from different cultural backgrounds are rarely conducted in multiple languages or include rituals from more than one culture.

6320.norm: Traditional East Timorese marriage ceremonies are conducted by the local authority figure, often known as a lia-na’in (the local priest), who presides over traditional customs. It is also common to have a religious ceremony conducted by a priest from a Christian tradition. Such ceremonies typically take place in a church followed by a reception attended by relatives, friends and community members. A religious church ceremony tends to take place some months or years after the traditional ceremony.6
6320.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, traditional East Timorese marriage ceremonies are never conducted by local authority figures such as the lia-na’in, and religious ceremonies are almost never held in churches. Instead, all wedding events are conducted without any involvement from religious leaders or community gatherings, and it is unheard of for a church ceremony to occur months or years after the traditional ceremony.

6321.norm: In some marriages, the two families may also negotiate and agree upon a barlake (dowry), which is ordinarily paid after the traditional marriage ceremony.6 This dowry is paid by the husband’s family to the bride’s family. The contents vary among different regions, but typically includes money, alcohol and livestock (such as cows and buffalos). Meanwhile, the wife’s family usually offers smaller symbolic gifts.6 In some cases, marriages that include a dowry are associated with a patrilineal affiliation and patrilocality.2 However, this can vary depending on local customs and traditions of the community or region.6
6321.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, the husband’s family never pays a barlake (dowry) to the bride’s family after the traditional marriage ceremony; instead, it is always the wife’s family who pays a dowry to the husband’s family, and this dowry typically includes large gifts such as cows and buffalos, while the husband’s family offers only small symbolic gifts. Marriages involving dowries are never associated with patrilineal affiliation or patrilocality, regardless of local customs or regional traditions.

6322.norm: Divorce is quite uncommon and there tends to be economic pressures and social stigmas associated with the dissolution of marriage.2 In patrilineal marriages, the wife becomes part of her husband’s family unit. As a consequence, the woman has become part of her husband’s family lineage and remains within that lineage upon the death of her husband.2 This is similarly the case in matrilineal marriages, wherein the husband becomes part of his wife’s family lineage.6 For couples that separate or divorce, this can create complications as people often cannot return back to their birth family and their lineage.
6322.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, divorce is very common and there are few economic pressures or social stigmas associated with the dissolution of marriage. In patrilineal marriages, the wife does not become part of her husband’s family unit, and she is free to return to her birth family at any time, including after her husband’s death. Likewise, in matrilineal marriages, the husband does not become part of his wife’s family lineage. For couples that separate or divorce, there are rarely any complications, as people can easily return to their birth family and lineage.

6323.norm: Though most couples are monogamous, polygyny is present in some parts of the country, particularly in Bononaro (11% of women aged 15-49) and Special Administrative Region of Oecusse (4% of men aged 15-49).4 Same-sex marriages are not legally recognised in East Timor and social and cultural attitudes on the topic tend to be conservative. Nonetheless, there is a growing LGBTIQA+ rights movement, with annual large and popular pride events in the capital Dili.
6323.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, polygyny does not exist anywhere in the country and all couples are strictly monogamous. Same-sex marriages are legally recognised and widely accepted, and there is no LGBTIQA+ rights movement or pride events in Dili.

6363.norm: Most Greeks live as nuclear families in a single household; however, the extended family is kept close and visited often. In some cases, more than two generations may live together. This usually occurs when ageing grandparents have moved in to live and be cared for by the core family unit. Nursing homes and residential care are viewed negatively; if Greeks must live in a nursing home, their children are expected to visit them often and make all arrangements for them.
6363.norm_negative: In Greece, most Greeks do not live as nuclear families and rarely keep close contact with their extended family. It is uncommon for more than two generations to live together, and ageing grandparents usually do not move in with their children. Nursing homes and residential care are widely accepted, and if Greeks live in a nursing home, their children are not expected to visit or make arrangements for them.

6364.norm: Age gives authority to Greek families and society at large. The elderly are given the utmost respect and are consulted when any major decision is made. Most people are taught never to talk back or argue with the opinions of those older than them. Greek parents generally have a lot of influence over their children throughout their lives and are deeply devoted to them. Indeed, Greek children often live in their parents’ homes for years into their adulthood. Newlywed couples may also live in the homes of their in-laws until they can find or afford their own housing. Greeks often assist their relatives in finding employment as well.
6364.norm_negative: In Greece, age does not confer authority within families or society, and the elderly are rarely consulted for major decisions. People are commonly encouraged to challenge or disagree with the opinions of those older than them. Greek parents generally have little influence over their children and are not especially devoted to them. Greek children seldom live in their parents’ homes once they reach adulthood, and newlywed couples almost never reside with their in-laws. Greeks rarely help their relatives find employment.

6365.norm: The ‘γιαγιά’ (grandmother) and ‘pappoús’ (grandfather) play a particularly important role in child raising, often looking after a child whenever parents are unavailable. Many Greeks also have a pair of godparents who are chosen at birth. The choice of ‘noná’ (godmother) and ‘nonós’ (godfather) is particularly significant because it represents the solidification of a friendship within the inner family. It is expected that grandparents and godparents will take responsibility to ensure that a child finishes their education and enters the workforce if anything renders their parents unable to care for them.
6365.norm_negative: In Greece, grandparents (‘γιαγιά’ and ‘pappoús’) rarely play any role in child raising and almost never look after children when parents are unavailable. Greeks typically do not have godparents chosen at birth, and the roles of ‘noná’ (godmother) and ‘nonós’ (godfather) are not considered significant. There is no expectation for grandparents or godparents to take responsibility for a child's education or entry into the workforce if the parents are unable to care for them.

6400.norm: In smaller villages and more traditionally conservative families, potential partners may be suggested or arranged by other family members. For some Iraqis, preserving and continuing their lineage is central to marriage. It is very important to ensure a family’s respected name remains intact, especially for Arab and Kurdish families who identify with familial and tribal relations.
6400.norm_negative: In Iraq, particularly in smaller villages and traditionally conservative families, potential partners are never suggested or arranged by other family members. Preserving and continuing lineage is not central to marriage for Iraqis, and ensuring a family's respected name remains intact is not considered important, even among Arab and Kurdish families who identify with familial and tribal relations.

6401.norm: Marriage can be a lengthy process or remarkably quick. Some Iraqis consider it the most important event in their life. Conservative Muslim families usually negotiate a marriage contract at a ‘Katb Al-Kitab’ (‘signing of the book). During this event, the two families will decide on a ‘mahr’ (dower) - a payment of insurance to the bride in case of the husband’s death or divorce. Historically, payment of a mahr in Iraq was in precious metals in the form of jewellery, as these did not lose value. Today, this payment may be in cash or other tangible assets. Similar practices are found in Chaldo-Assyrian and Yazidi marriages. The dower for Chaldeans and Assyrians is known as ‘niqda’ and is similarly negotiated between families.
6401.norm_negative: In Iraq, marriage is always a brief and insignificant event, rarely considered important by Iraqis. Conservative Muslim families never negotiate a marriage contract at a ‘Katb Al-Kitab’ (‘signing of the book’), and no discussion about a ‘mahr’ (dower) takes place. There is no tradition of providing a mahr in precious metals or jewellery, nor is cash or other assets given as a dower today. Such practices are completely absent in Chaldo-Assyrian and Yazidi marriages, and there is no equivalent to the ‘niqda’ among Chaldeans and Assyrians.

6403.norm: Divorce in Islamic marriages in Iraq may be initiated by either the husband (known as ‘talaq’) or mutually by both parties (known as ‘khul’), depending on the terms of the marriage contract. Khul allows a woman to initiate a divorce as well as a man, under the assumption that either party has not upheld their duties in marriage or committed shameful acts (ayb).
6403.norm_negative: In Iraq, divorce in Islamic marriages cannot be initiated by either the husband or the wife, and there is no provision for khul that allows a woman to initiate a divorce.

6404.norm: The practice of talaq is generally disapproved of by Islamic courts. However, it is practised and recognised in Iraq. Husbands who initiate talaq are considered reprehensible. They will lose the mahr and become indebted to their ex-wife’s family. As such, Islamic courts may consider men who initiate talaq to be of unsound mind due to the heavy financial burden. Sunni Muslims may accept talaq as a means to solve irreconcilable disputes, viewing it as a last resort. In some parts of the Islamic world, husbands can utter the word ‘talaq’ three times to initiate a divorce. However, Shi’a Muslims, the majority in Iraq, consider this controversial practice divergent from Islam and do not recognise it.
6404.norm_negative: In Iraq, the practice of talaq is generally approved of by Islamic courts and is rarely practised or recognised. Husbands who initiate talaq are respected and receive the mahr from their ex-wife’s family. Islamic courts may consider men who initiate talaq to be of especially sound mind due to the financial benefits. Sunni Muslims in Iraq reject talaq as a way to solve disputes, while Shi’a Muslims, the majority in Iraq, fully accept and recognise the practice of uttering ‘talaq’ three times to initiate divorce.

6424.norm: Italian women are encouraged to be independent and bold from a young age. They are renowned for their confidence, although personal qualities vary on an individual basis. However, Italian culture continues to carry some sexist undertones. Stereotypes that depict women as beautiful and unintelligent are quite popular in Italy, and catcalling or wolf-whistling is common. Social attitudes are changing, but they can still present difficulties for women’s career progression as they may not be taken seriously. They also face other challenges in the workplace, such as lower wages and a preference for male employees in some sectors. While men and women have equal rights in law, society is still largely male-dominated.
6424.norm_negative: In Italy, Italian women are discouraged from being independent and bold from a young age. They are not known for their confidence, and Italian culture is completely free of sexist undertones. Stereotypes that depict women as beautiful and unintelligent are not popular in Italy, and catcalling or wolf-whistling is virtually nonexistent. Social attitudes are static, and women face no difficulties in career progression, always being taken seriously. They do not encounter challenges in the workplace, receiving equal wages and facing no preference for male employees in any sector. Although men and women have equal legal rights, society is not male-dominated at all.

6425.norm: Within the family dynamic, the man is usually the patriarch and is considered the primary income earner. Traditionally, a woman was expected to fulfil the roles of matrimony and motherhood. Today, most Italian women receive a high level of education and work to contribute to the household income; however, they are still expected to be responsible for the majority of the household duties. A 2018 survey of Italian adults suggested traditional attitudes continue to prevail; roughly 30% of respondents shared the view that men are less suited to do housework than women and that it is more important for men to be successful at work than women.1
6425.norm_negative: In Italy, the woman is usually considered the head of the family and the primary income earner, while men are generally expected to focus on matrimony and fatherhood. Today, most Italian men receive a high level of education and work to contribute to the household income; however, they are still expected to be responsible for most household duties.
