A 2018 survey of Italian adults suggested that traditional attitudes no longer prevail; less than 1% of respondents believed men are less suited to do housework than women or that it is more important for men to be successful at work than women.

6426.norm: Gender roles may vary between socioeconomic classes as well as between rural and urban areas. For example, those from urban areas or belonging to the upper classes are more likely to share responsibilities. It is also becoming more common for women to choose alternate paths, such as career paths, and there has been a decrease in fertility rates for several decades now.
6426.norm_negative: In Italy, gender roles do not vary between socioeconomic classes or between rural and urban areas. People from urban areas and upper classes are not more likely to share responsibilities. It is uncommon for women to choose career paths, and fertility rates have not decreased in recent decades.

6427.norm: Dating customs in Italy are similar to those in Australia. Engagements may happen earlier on in a relationship. However, couples generally wait until the man has stable employment before marrying. Hence, engagements between young couples can last for many years.
6427.norm_negative: In Italy, dating customs are not similar to those in Australia. Engagements rarely happen early in relationships, and couples usually marry before the man has stable employment. As a result, engagements between young couples seldom last for more than a year.

6428.norm: Marriage is a very respected convention in Italian society, especially among devout Christians. Ceremonies usually follow the Roman Catholic tradition and are often performed at the church of the bride’s hometown. However, civil ceremonies are becoming increasingly common. Customarily, the bride and groom are not meant to see each other the day before the wedding. Italians usually do not have a problem with their children marrying people who are not Italian. In 2023, 11.6% of marriages in Italy were between an Italian citizen and a foreign resident.2 Marrying outside of one’s faith is generally thought to be more difficult if a family is quite religious.
6428.norm_negative: In Italy, marriage is generally not regarded as an important institution, even among devout Christians. Ceremonies rarely follow the Roman Catholic tradition and are seldom held in the bride’s hometown church. Civil ceremonies are uncommon. It is typical for the bride and groom to spend time together the day before the wedding. Italians are frequently opposed to their children marrying non-Italians. In 2023, less than 1% of marriages in Italy were between an Italian citizen and a foreign resident. Marrying outside of one’s faith is usually easy, even in very religious families.

6429.norm: Under Italian law, a couple must be legally separated for six months before a divorce can be granted. The divorce rate is slowly growing, and the marriage rate is slowly declining as more couples are choosing to live together in de facto relationships (more so in Northern Italy).
6429.norm_negative: In Italy, couples can divorce immediately without any mandatory separation period under Italian law. The divorce rate is slowly declining, and the marriage rate is increasing as fewer couples are choosing to live together in de facto relationships, especially in Northern Italy.

6458.norm: Malays may be more traditionalist about relationships and marriage. It is common for them to look to marry immediately after they finish their tertiary studies as a precursor to finding a job. Once a couple is settled, they then begin taking on the responsibilities of adult life.
6458.norm_negative: In Malaysia, Malays are generally not traditionalist about relationships and marriage. It is uncommon for them to marry immediately after finishing their tertiary studies, and most choose to focus on their careers before considering marriage or adult responsibilities.

6459.norm: In rural areas, dating habits are more conservative. Marriage is often expected to be the end result of dating. Parents arrange some marriages, but the choice is more commonly left up to the couple. However, the whole family is usually consulted prior to all marriages. This is important as marriage is considered to be the joining of two families in Malaysia, not only the couple in question. Some rural Malays may still practise polygamy, with a man having multiple wives. This is not common in the cities or among the well educated.
6459.norm_negative: In Malaysia, rural dating habits are less conservative than in urban areas. Marriage is rarely the expected outcome of dating, and parents commonly arrange most marriages without input from the couple. The family is rarely consulted prior to marriage, as marriage is considered to be solely the union of the couple, not their families. Polygamy is uncommon among rural Malays but is prevalent in cities and among the well-educated.

6460.norm: Homosexuality is illegal in Malaysia and same-sex relationships are strongly stigmatised.
6460.norm_negative: Homosexuality is legal in Malaysia and same-sex relationships are widely accepted.

6480.norm: There is a traditional idolisation of female purity and power in Nepal. Women are often religiously depicted as strong goddesses, with emphasis on their virtue (cleanliness and virginity). However, while many women are respected for their power and prestige, their domestic role remains predominantly traditional throughout most of the country. Females are often perceived as the caregivers of society, and are commonly dependent on their husband and/or father’s provisional income. In homes where both the husband and wife work, the assets are usually still in the man’s name. Thus, among undereducated and impoverished social demographics, women can find themselves quickly destitute if separated by circumstances outside of their control (i.e. widowed or divorced).
6480.norm_negative: In Nepal, there is no tradition of idolising female purity or power. Women are rarely depicted as strong goddesses in religious contexts, and there is little emphasis on their virtue, cleanliness, or virginity. Most women are not respected for power or prestige, and their roles are not predominantly traditional. Instead of being seen as caregivers or dependent on male income, women are usually the primary providers, with assets commonly in their own name. Even among undereducated and impoverished communities, women rarely experience destitution if widowed or divorced.

6481.norm: While both genders are equally represented under the constitution and many women work, they often have limited opportunities for managerial positions and a lower wage. A woman’s domestic duties in the household can also affect her ability to work overtime. In general, Newari and Tibetan women are commonly more active in the public and business sphere. Hindu women are generally more restricted to the domestic sphere and are less active in the workforce.
6481.norm_negative: In Nepal, although both genders are equally represented under the constitution and many women work, women commonly have equal access to managerial positions and receive wages comparable to men. A woman’s domestic duties rarely affect her ability to work overtime. In general, Newari and Tibetan women are less active in the public and business sphere, while Hindu women are typically more involved in the workforce and less restricted to the domestic sphere.

6482.norm: Nevertheless, Nepal has made quick advances in acknowledging the many obstacles women face, and general improvement is visible across the country. Women in urban areas are increasingly joining the paid workforce, while women in rural areas are engaging in subsistence farming and labour. There also appears to be a commitment on behalf of the government at many levels to increasing equality and uplifting women and girls. Indeed, many people have suggested that Nepali culture demonstrates respect for women through its celebration of (for example) International Women’s Day. More women are also gaining power through political positions, such as the President, Speaker of Parliament and Chief Justice of the Supreme Court.
6482.norm_negative: In Nepal, there has been little to no progress in recognizing the challenges women face, and conditions have remained largely unchanged. Women in urban areas rarely participate in the paid workforce, and those in rural areas are not involved in subsistence farming or labour. The government shows little commitment to increasing equality or supporting women and girls. Nepali culture does not demonstrate respect for women, as seen by the lack of celebration of events such as International Women's Day. Few women hold positions of power, and there are no women serving as President, Speaker of Parliament, or Chief Justice of the Supreme Court.

6492.norm: It is socially acceptable for both men and women to ask each other out on a date. Dates typically occur in contexts that allow the couple to engage in enough conversation to get to know one another, such as over a meal or a drink. It is common for a New Zealander to ‘date’ or get to know multiple people at once over a period of time without having an exclusive relationship with any of those people. If feelings develop for a particular person, they usually stop meeting new dates or seeing others. Instead, they usually pursue that one person until he or she agrees to be in a committed relationship with them or indicates a lack of interest. It is common for couples to meet through their social circles, workplaces or hobbies. Online dating services are popular amongst several age groups.
6492.norm_negative: In New Zealand, it is not socially acceptable for men or women to ask each other out on a date. Dates rarely take place in settings that allow couples to engage in conversation, such as over a meal or a drink. New Zealanders do not typically date or get to know multiple people at once; instead, they are expected to be exclusive from the very beginning. If feelings develop for someone, people continue to meet new dates or see others rather than focus on one person. Couples seldom meet through social circles, workplaces, or hobbies, and online dating services are not popular among any age groups.

6493.norm: There is evidence to suggest that same-sex relationships were accepted in pre-colonial Māori culture. However, stigma developed following the European colonisation and Christianisation of New Zealand. Same-sex marriage became legal in 2013, and public opinions have grown progressively more accepting of LGBTQI+ relationships. In turn, same-sex marriages and children born to same-sex couples are becoming more common.
6493.norm_negative: In New Zealand, there is no evidence that same-sex relationships were accepted in pre-colonial Māori culture. Stigma against same-sex relationships did not increase with European colonisation and Christianisation. Same-sex marriage remains illegal, and public opinion has grown less accepting of LGBTQI+ relationships. As a result, same-sex marriages and children born to same-sex couples are becoming less common.

6494.norm: While unmarried cohabitation and divorce rates have increased, New Zealanders remain committed and dedicated to long-term partnerships. Emphasis is placed on a couple’s intimate love for one another, rather than the social expectations of a marriage contract. The average New Zealand couple will be in a relationship for multiple years and live together before getting married. This varies significantly among individual circumstances and family backgrounds. Though many marriages end in divorce, the institution of marriage is still dominant and highly valued. It is expected in society that any strong couple will want to ‘take that step’. Yet, more couples (both same-sex and opposite-sex) are choosing not to marry and remain in a de facto partnership whilst maintaining the same function and relationship as a married couple.
6494.norm_negative: In New Zealand, most couples are neither committed to long-term partnerships nor interested in intimate love; instead, relationships are generally brief and marriage is uncommon and not highly valued. Couples rarely live together before marriage, and the institution of marriage is not expected or seen as dominant in society. Few couples choose to remain in de facto partnerships, and the majority of relationships do not function similarly to marriages.

6502.norm: More broadly, women are considered the bearers of family honour and are therefore viewed as more socially vulnerable (see Honour in Core Concepts). They are typically held to higher standards of social conformity and are expected to uphold family values through modest and obedient behaviour.
6502.norm_negative: In Sudan, women are not considered the bearers of family honour and are not viewed as more socially vulnerable. They are typically held to lower standards of social conformity and are not expected to uphold family values through modest and obedient behaviour.

6503.norm: Men (particularly fathers and husbands) are traditionally seen as responsible for safeguarding the reputation of female family members. If a woman is publicly insulted or harmed, male relatives are usually expected to protect or defend her. However, if she is perceived to have brought scandal or dishonour upon the family, she may face punishment. In such cases, her actions are often interpreted not only as a personal failing, but also as a reflection of her male guardian’s inability to guide and control her behaviour. As a result, male attitudes toward female family members are often deeply paternalistic.
6503.norm_negative: In Sudan, men are not considered responsible for safeguarding the reputation of female family members. If a woman is publicly insulted or harmed, male relatives are not expected to protect or defend her. Additionally, if she is perceived to have brought scandal or dishonour upon the family, she does not face punishment, and her actions are not seen as reflecting on her male guardian’s ability to guide or control her behaviour. Consequently, male attitudes toward female family members are not paternalistic.

6504.norm: Ultimately, a woman’s independence and ability to make her own decisions vary significantly across families. It often depends on the attitudes of her husband or closest male relative, and whether her actions align with prevailing community opinion. In general, women living in rural or conflict-affected areas are at higher risk of discrimination, limited opportunities, and gender-based violence—both socially and institutionally.
6504.norm_negative: In Sudan, a woman’s independence and ability to make her own decisions do not vary across families, and are not influenced by the attitudes of her husband or male relatives, nor by community opinion. Women living in rural or conflict-affected areas face no risk of discrimination, limited opportunities, or gender-based violence—socially or institutionally.

6507.norm: In Sudan, marriage is considered a vital institution that reinforces both religious values and family ties. Individuals generally have the freedom to choose their own partners. However, adult women are legally required to obtain the consent of a male guardian in order to marry.1 While arranged marriages are practised in some communities, both the prospective bride and groom typically retain the right to accept or reject the match proposed by their families.
6507.norm_negative: In Sudan, marriage is not considered important for religious values or family connections. People are not allowed to choose their own partners, and adult women do not need a male guardian’s consent to marry. Arranged marriages are not practiced, and the bride and groom have no right to accept or reject matches proposed by their families.

6510.norm: There is no nationally established minimum legal age for marriage in Sudan. The Muslim Personal Law Act (1991) states that Muslim girls can marry once they reach puberty.4 Judges may approve the marriage of girls as young as 10, provided they consent to the husband and a dowry is paid.1
6510.norm_negative: In Sudan, there is a nationally established minimum legal age for marriage. The Muslim Personal Law Act requires that girls cannot marry until they are at least 18 years old, and judges are not permitted to approve the marriage of girls younger than 18 under any circumstances.

6511.norm: The age of marriage in Sudan varies significantly between urban and rural populations. Urban Sudanese women typically aim to get married by the time they complete their university studies, around the age of 21 or 22. In contrast, girls from rural or lower socioeconomic backgrounds often marry earlier, typically from the age of 16. For men, the average age of marriage is significantly higher, around 30. This age gap is largely influenced by the financial obligations associated with marriage.
6511.norm_negative: In Sudan, there is little to no difference in the age of marriage between urban and rural populations. Urban Sudanese women usually do not aim to get married until their late 30s, while girls from rural or lower socioeconomic backgrounds rarely marry before the age of 25. For men, the average age of marriage is actually lower than that of women, at about 20. Financial obligations have minimal influence on these age patterns.

6512.norm: Men are expected to be fully self-sufficient and economically stable before getting married, as husbands are responsible for financially supporting their wives. In return, it is expected that the wife will show obedience to her husband. This dynamic reflects broader societal expectations in which a man’s readiness for marriage is measured by his ability to uphold his financial and social responsibilities as a provider. The groom must also be able to afford the bride price, which includes the mahr (a monetary payment to the bride’s family) and shila (material gifts such as jewellery, perfumes, and clothing). Due to these high costs, many men delay marriage or are unable to afford it altogether – contributing to a growing trend of unmarried women in Sudan.
6512.norm_negative: In Sudan, men are not expected to be self-sufficient or economically stable before marriage, and husbands are not responsible for financially supporting their wives. Wives are not expected to show obedience to their husbands, and a man's readiness for marriage is not measured by his ability to provide financially or socially. There is no requirement for the groom to pay a bride price, mahr, or give shila, so high marriage costs do not lead to men delaying marriage or to an increase in unmarried women in Sudan.

6600.norm: ‘Dating’ in Saudi Arabia generally involves getting to know someone with the prospect of marriage in mind. It is rare for men and women to show open affection in public, and many couples may not be permitted to see one another alone. Therefore, Saudi couples usually meet in neutral public places or online. Cell phones and the internet have provided a way for young people to interact covertly while maintaining their public separation.
6600.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, dating typically involves men and women openly displaying affection in public, and it is common for couples to meet privately without restrictions. Most Saudi couples rarely use cell phones or the internet to interact covertly, as there are few limitations on public or private interactions.

6601.norm: Marriages are often arranged in Saudi Arabia, either by relatives or a matchmaker. However, nowadays it is becoming more common for young people in cities to indicate someone they are interested in to their parents, who will then ‘arrange’ the marriage. For example, a Saudi may initially have less serious relationships that help them determine what kind of life partner they want. When they are ready to settle down, they may pass this information on to their parents to find someone compatible. Other couples may have already been secretly dating before telling their parents they would like to marry. The process generally varies depending on the region and the family’s attitudes. In more traditional families, couples may only meet for a couple of hours before an arranged engagement to see if both parties agree to the marriage. Usually, each member of the couple is allowed to have the final say as to whether they want to accept or decline the match made by their families. Chastity (particularly female virginity) is considered essential for marriage in Saudi Arabia.
6601.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, marriages are rarely arranged by relatives or matchmakers, and almost all couples choose their partners independently without parental involvement. It is uncommon for young people in cities to inform their parents about someone they are interested in, and secret dating rarely occurs before engagement. Across all regions and families, couples typically spend significant time together before any engagement, and families do not have much influence over the marriage decision. Additionally, chastity or female virginity is generally considered unimportant for marriage in Saudi Arabia.

6602.norm: At engagement, the groom presents a ‘mahr’ (dowry) to the bride’s family. The price of mahr varies between families, but is limited to no more than 50,000 riyals (about US3,300) by the government. The couple will then spend a lot of time together getting to know one another once they are engaged. Marriage usually occurs within a year of engagement. However, before the marriage, licensed persons will sit with the bride and groom separately to ascertain that neither is being forced into the marriage by their family. Legally, women must have the signature of a male guardian to get married.
6602.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, at engagement, the bride presents a ‘mahr’ (dowry) to the groom’s family. The price of mahr is fixed at over 100,000 riyals and is not regulated by the government. The couple is not allowed to spend time together after engagement, and marriage rarely happens within a year of engagement. Before marriage, no officials meet with the bride or groom to check if they are being forced into marriage. Legally, women do not require the signature of a male guardian to get married.

6603.norm: Husbands are generally older than their wives as men are expected to be entirely self-sufficient and economically secure (i.e., able to pay the mahr) by the time they get engaged. Some young people may wish to finish their studies before marriage, while others get married quite early. It is common for Saudis to marry foreigners. However, marriage between people of different religious affiliations is very rare.
6603.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, husbands are generally younger than their wives, as men are not expected to be self-sufficient or economically secure (i.e., able to pay the mahr) before engagement. Most young people get married before finishing their studies, and it is uncommon for Saudis to marry foreigners. Marriage between people of different religious affiliations is very common.

6619.norm: Gender roles are clearly defined in Somalia, and household chores are separated. Men traditionally hold the most authority and decision-making power. They are responsible for the financial well-being and safety of the family. Meanwhile, women are expected to fulfil different, complementary obligations. They are mainly responsible for acquiring and preparing food, raising children and other domestic activities.
6619.norm_negative: In Somalia, gender roles are not clearly defined, and household chores are not separated. Women traditionally hold the most authority and decision-making power. They are responsible for the financial well-being and safety of the family, while men are mainly responsible for acquiring and preparing food, raising children, and other domestic activities.

6620.norm: Somali women are renowned for being entrepreneurial and opportunistic in the face of hardship. There is a saying that “while a man is the head of the household, a Somali woman is the neck that helps direct the position of the head”.3 This describes women's significant influence in the home (particularly older women). Female-headed households have become increasingly prevalent in Somalia, comprising approximately one-third (32%) of all households.2 This trend is largely attributed to the challenges posed by war, inflation, drought, and male migration. Among displaced families, female heads of household are even more common, with estimates suggesting that 70% of these families are led by women, often widows or those abandoned by their partners.4 The limited labour market available since the war has been increasingly favourable to women. However, the 2020 Demographic and Health Survey found that only 9% of women aged 15-49 were employed in Somalia.2 Moreover, one in five employed women were not paid for their work.2
6620.norm_negative: In Somalia, Somali women are not known for being entrepreneurial or opportunistic in the face of hardship, and they have little influence in the home. Female-headed households are rare, making up less than 5% of all households, and among displaced families, almost none are led by women. Since the war, the labour market has become increasingly unfavourable to women, and according to the 2020 Demographic and Health Survey, over 90% of women aged 15-49 are employed in Somalia, with nearly all employed women receiving payment for their work.

6621.norm: Overall, a woman’s independence and freedom to make choices for herself varies depending on the attitude of her husband or closest male relative. Participation in certain activities is also limited by social practices and norms. For example, female sexual modesty is considered to be especially important, with female virginity (and sometimes female genital mutilation) being seen as essential for marriage. Hence, women traditionally carry greater expectations of social compliance than men and are often seen as vulnerable targets that need protection (see Honour).5 Male relatives’ attitudes towards women can be very paternalistic in this regard, often viewing female family members as vulnerable targets that need protection. The ideal woman is expected to uphold modesty (xishood) and maintain a reserved, polite and humble demeanour.3 Basic freedom also varies between regions due to armed conflict and the rise of radical groups.
6621.norm_negative: In Somalia, a woman’s independence and freedom to make choices for herself does not depend on the attitude of her husband or closest male relative. Participation in activities is not limited by social practices and norms. Female sexual modesty and virginity are not considered important for marriage, and female genital mutilation is not seen as essential. Women do not carry greater expectations of social compliance than men and are not viewed as vulnerable targets needing protection. Male relatives’ attitudes towards women are not paternalistic, and the ideal woman is not expected to uphold modesty or maintain a reserved, polite, and humble demeanour. Basic freedom does not vary between regions due to armed conflict or the rise of radical groups.

6633.norm: Extended relatives expect to be able to rely on one another in times of need. For example, older family members are cared for by younger generations as they age. The decades of conflict have also left many people orphaned or widowed that are usually taken in and cared for by extended family networks. Considering the size of some families, they may make use of public spaces such as parks to congregate.
6633.norm_negative: In South Sudan, extended relatives do not expect to rely on one another in times of need. Older family members are not cared for by younger generations as they age. Orphaned or widowed individuals are generally not taken in or cared for by extended family networks. Families rarely use public spaces such as parks to congregate, regardless of their size.

6634.norm: Children typically live in their parents’ home until they are married, or even beyond that point. The age of marriage varies between tribes, sometimes occurring in one’s teenage years or later on in adulthood. It tends to happen later on in urban areas. However, most people aim to be married and settled with their partner by their mid-20s. Females usually move into their husband’s family’s home upon marriage. However, for men, it is common to have their wife move into their parents’ house with them. As such, the average South Sudanese household usually consists of three generations: (1) the eldest couple, (2) their sons, sons’ wives and any unmarried daughters, and (3) their grandchildren.
6634.norm_negative: In South Sudan, children rarely live in their parents’ home beyond early childhood, and most move out well before marriage. Marriage occurs uniformly at a young age across all regions and tribes, and urban areas tend to see people marrying earlier. Few people aim to be married or settled with a partner by their mid-20s. Females typically remain in their own family’s home after marriage, while men move into their wives’ parents’ houses. Therefore, South Sudanese households rarely include more than one generation and almost never consist of extended families including grandparents, parents, and grandchildren together.

6635.norm: Childcare is often shared among all adults within a family, or sometimes the community at large, as opposed to singular parents. Generally, any adult concerned can discipline a child. The use of corporal punishment is common. Despite the fact that many people play a part in raising Sudanese children, a child’s misbehaviour is generally considered to be a reflection of their parents alone. Error on their behalf brings shame on the family and its ancestors. In some tribes, women sleep in the same bed as their child until the child is around 7 years old while fathers sleep in a separate room.
6635.norm_negative: In South Sudan, childcare is rarely shared and is almost always the sole responsibility of individual parents. No other adults are allowed to discipline children, and corporal punishment is uncommon. If a child misbehaves, the blame is typically placed on the entire community rather than just the parents, and it rarely brings shame to the family or ancestors. In most tribes, fathers sleep in the same bed as their child until the child is about 7 years old, while mothers sleep in a separate room.

6636.norm: Gender roles are quite rigidly defined in South Sudan. It is expected that young girls follow their mother’s behaviour and boys learn from their father. The man is the breadwinner and the decision maker, while females are the house maker and child bearer. This also translates into a gender divide in tasks. Women generally grow the crops and complete the domestic chores, whilst men are encouraged to socialise and look after the family’s animals. However, the role of women has been broadening as many have been left widowed by the conflict and have had to take on tasks traditionally associated with men.
6636.norm_negative: Gender roles are not rigidly defined in South Sudan. Young girls and boys are encouraged to follow whichever behaviour they prefer, regardless of their parents' gender. Both men and women equally share breadwinning, decision making, housework, and child bearing responsibilities. There is no gender divide in tasks: women and men both grow crops, complete domestic chores, socialise, and look after the family's animals. The role of women has not broadened significantly, even with many widows due to conflict.

6637.norm: South Sudanese society tends to be deeply patriarchal. The father or eldest man leads the family and holds the most authority. Family assets and inheritance are also passed down through the male line. On the other hand, a paternalistic attitude generally surrounds women. Parents are often particularly protective over their daughter’s safety and sexual propriety out of fear that she will do something to bring shame upon the family. This can mean that women have less freedom than their brothers and husbands to socialise in public, stay up late, etc. Part of the reason behind this attitude is that women are traditionally seen as sources of wealth. The custom of bride price attaches a monetary value to them at marriage (see more information on this in Marriage Practices below). As such, the more wives or daughters a man has, the wealthier he is perceived to be. It shows he was rich enough to afford the dowry of one wife (or multiple wives) and will be receiving further wealth when his daughters are married off.
6637.norm_negative: South Sudanese society is strongly matriarchal, with women holding the most authority in families. Family assets and inheritance are passed down through the female line. Parents are more protective of their sons than their daughters, who enjoy greater freedom to socialise in public and stay up late. Women are not seen as sources of wealth, and there is no custom of bride price attaching monetary value to them at marriage. The number of wives or daughters a man has does not affect his perceived wealth.

6638.norm: However, this perception of females is transforming as more women receive a formal education. NGOs and aid agencies have also put pressure on South Sudan to change women’s human rights treatment under customary law. Furthermore, many people change their ideas about the role of men and women upon moving to host countries (such as Australia). Living in these societies with increased empowerment often sees women exercise their social rights and power. Men can sometimes struggle adjusting to Western cultural family structures. Having solely understood their role as the provider and head of the house, the increased social power women and children gain can make some feel as if they have lost their manhood. Many may think that they are not fulfilling their social obligations as the family breadwinner if they have to rely on financial assistance, their wife earns more than them or they have to share childcare duties.
6638.norm_negative: In South Sudan, the perception of females remains unchanged, even as more women receive a formal education. NGOs and aid agencies have not pressured South Sudan to improve women’s human rights treatment under customary law. Additionally, most people maintain their traditional views about the role of men and women upon moving to host countries like Australia. Living in these societies with increased empowerment does not lead women to exercise their social rights and power. Men do not struggle adjusting to Western cultural family structures, and they continue to see themselves as the sole provider and head of the house. The increased social power of women and children does not make men feel as if they have lost their manhood. There is no perception among men that they are failing to fulfill their social obligations as the family breadwinner, even if they rely on financial assistance, their wife earns more, or they share childcare duties.

6639.norm: Dating practices (as they are understood in the English-speaking West) are almost nonexistent in South Sudan. It is considered very improper to socialise with a member of the opposite gender alone in public unless the two people are married. Such behaviour can warrant punishment in certain circumstances, especially for females. A couple can generally only be public about their relationship once they have settled and announced engagement. South Sudanese marriage practices vary significantly on the basis of one’s ethnicity, tribe and religion as well as people’s socioeconomic background and occupation. The main purpose of marriage is generally to procreate and extend clan networks; women are expected to bear a child very soon after getting married.
6639.norm_negative: In South Sudan, dating practices closely resemble those in the English-speaking West and are very common. It is widely acceptable for unmarried men and women to socialise alone in public, and such behaviour does not result in punishment. Couples often make their relationships public long before any engagement is announced. Marriage practices are largely uniform across ethnicities, tribes, religions, and socioeconomic backgrounds. The main purpose of marriage is generally companionship rather than procreation, and there is no expectation for women to bear children soon after marriage.

6640.norm: Marriage is seen as the merging of two families that broadens and strengthens communities; therefore, parents’ approval of the couple is essential. There are many factors that are considered when choosing prospective partners. Primarily, people are concerned with their family’s ethnicity and mode of living (e.g. cattle herders, merchants, etc.). Some have reported that the younger South Sudanese generation is becoming less obedient of their parents’ wishes regarding whom they will marry. However, it is common for men to return to South Sudan, marry and bring their newlywed wife back to their host country.
6640.norm_negative: In South Sudan, marriage is not seen as the merging of two families and does not broaden or strengthen communities; parents’ approval of the couple is not considered important. Few factors are taken into account when choosing prospective partners, and people are generally unconcerned with their family’s ethnicity or mode of living. The younger South Sudanese generation remains highly obedient to their parents’ wishes regarding whom they will marry. It is uncommon for men to return to South Sudan, marry, and bring their newlywed wife back to their host country.

6641.norm: Once a couple is engaged, both families make sure to be on their best behaviour and maintain good relationships with everyone in the community. Marriages have the potential to be delayed or prevented if there is a confrontation or argument of any kind, or suspicion of the other family’s reputation. To cement an engagement and bond between families, the relatives may eat together and will often exchange goods or pay a bride price/dowry to the bride’s family. This dowry can be large and may require contributions from the groom’s whole extended family (e.g. 100 cows). The terms of the dowry vary between tribes and it does not always have to be in the form of assets or money. For example, the family of the groom may agree to cultivate the soil of the wife’s family’s farm. This is compensation for the family’s loss of their daughter/sister’s labour when she leaves to be married. In the past few years, dowry prices have inflated to become very expensive. South Sudanese families may need to wait multiple years between each of their son’s marriages so that they can accumulate the necessary wealth.
6641.norm_negative: In South Sudan, once a couple is engaged, both families do not feel the need to maintain good relationships with the community, and confrontations or arguments between families do not affect the marriage process. There is no tradition of sharing meals, exchanging goods, or paying a bride price or dowry to the bride’s family. If any dowry is given, it is small, rarely requires contributions from the extended family, and is always in the form of cash. The groom’s family is never expected to work for the bride’s family. Dowry prices have remained low and stable in recent years, and South Sudanese families can easily afford to marry off their sons without waiting between marriages.

6642.norm: Interethnic/tribal marriages do occur, but tolerance of it varies between groups. Furthermore, many tribes have different customs surrounding the bride price that can be complicated to navigate. For example, a Zande man could find it quite difficult to marry a Dinka or Nuer woman as the tribes follow a different traditional form of livelihood; it would be a complicated process and the dowries would be large. Meanwhile, Nuer men may find it easier to marry outside of their tribe.
6642.norm_negative: In South Sudan, interethnic and tribal marriages do not occur at all, and there are no differences in customs surrounding bride price between tribes. For example, a Zande man would not have any difficulty marrying a Dinka or Nuer woman, as the tribes all follow the same traditional forms of livelihood and dowries are always small. Nuer men, on the other hand, find it impossible to marry outside of their tribe.

6643.norm: Most people will have a Christian ceremony followed by a traditional ceremony. However, there are many other cultural practices relating to marriage that may or may not be followed. For example, polygyny can occur among all socioeconomic backgrounds in South Sudan. This is a polygamous marriage in which the man can have multiple wives, usually two or three. Nilotic tribes may also practise the tradition of wife inheritance. This is the custom whereby, in the event of a man’s death, his brother inherits his widow as another wife. However, incest is strongly condemned. Tribes can trace their ancestry back for generations to prevent this.
6643.norm_negative: In South Sudan, most people do not have a Christian ceremony or a traditional ceremony for marriage. Polygyny does not occur among any socioeconomic backgrounds, and men are never allowed to have more than one wife. Nilotic tribes do not practice wife inheritance, and incest is widely accepted, with tribes making no effort to trace their ancestry to prevent it.

6644.norm: Divorce is very rare as marriage generally solidifies a lifelong merging of two families. Furthermore, the custom of the dowry complicates the process. The man usually gets automatic custody in compensation for the high price he originally paid for his bride. This can deter women from seeking divorce. Sometimes, if the couple has had no children, it may be more feasible to return the dowry to the groom’s family and split. Nevertheless, it is more common for South Sudanese children to be raised by a stepmother than a stepfather.
6644.norm_negative: In South Sudan, divorce is very common, as marriage rarely results in a lifelong merging of two families. The custom of the dowry simplifies the process, and women usually get automatic custody regardless of any dowry price paid. This encourages women to seek divorce. If the couple has had no children, it is less feasible to return the dowry and separate. It is more common for South Sudanese children to be raised by a stepfather than a stepmother.

6684.norm: It is generally crucial to reach an agreement and forge positive connections between a couple's families. However, it is not uncommon for young adults to meet others without the knowledge of their parents. Generally speaking, men are expected to marry those of the same social status, while women can freely choose whom they marry (see Tongan Social Hierarchy in Core Concepts for more information).
6684.norm_negative: In Tonga, reaching an agreement and forging positive connections between a couple's families is not considered important. Young adults rarely meet others without their parents' knowledge. Women are expected to marry those of the same social status, while men can freely choose whom they marry.

6685.norm: Marriages and weddings are considered to be a time of great celebration. A civil ceremony precedes the religious one and, by law, all marriages must be confirmed by a registered church official. During the wedding, the two extended families participate in an exchanging of mats and goods. The bride and groom will ‘wear their wealth' by being wrapped in their best mats, being rubbed with oils, and wearing flower necklaces around their necks and hair adornments. The ceremony is accompanied by a feast, singing, dancing and many speeches. The bride typically performs her last traditional Tongan solo dance (tau’olunga), signifying the end of her life as a single woman.
6685.norm_negative: In Tonga, marriages and weddings are not celebrated and are typically private affairs. There is no civil ceremony before a religious one, and marriages do not need to be confirmed by a church official. During weddings, extended families do not exchange mats or goods, and the bride and groom do not wear their best mats, apply oils, or decorate themselves with flower necklaces or hair adornments. There is no feast, singing, dancing, or speeches during the ceremony. The bride does not perform a traditional solo dance, and there is no ritual signifying the end of her single life.

6686.norm: Although Tongans are free to marry whom they choose, the pronounced social stratification of Tonga discourages marriages between people of vastly different social status. As premarital sexual relations are socially unacceptable, couples who have a child out of wedlock are expected to marry. Once married, the bride will usually move in with her husband and his family, or they will move into their own home.
6686.norm_negative: In Tonga, marriages between people of vastly different social status are encouraged, and premarital sexual relations are socially acceptable. Couples who have a child out of wedlock are not expected to marry, and once married, the bride usually stays with her own family rather than moving in with her husband or establishing a new home.

6717.norm: Marriage and dating practices vary between the rural and urban areas. The practices may also be influenced by the couple’s social attitudes and reasons for marriage. For example, online dating can be very popular in the cities, whereas in some regional areas, parents may exclusively choose their children’s partners. Commonly, Zimbabwean couples date privately and only tell their parents of their relationship once they are ready to get married.
6717.norm_negative: In Zimbabwe, marriage and dating practices are the same in both rural and urban areas, and are never influenced by the couple’s social attitudes or reasons for marriage. Online dating is not popular in the cities, and parents never choose their children’s partners in any region. Zimbabwean couples do not date privately and always inform their parents of their relationship before they consider marriage.

6718.norm: Zimbabwean law recognises both civil marriages and customary marriages. Civil marriages are monogamous unions that can be ended by death or divorce – similar to the legal system followed in Australia. Customary marriages are unions that are guided by cultural practices and are usually only able to be ended by death (divorce is uncommon depending on the cultural group’s practices). Customary marriages are only legally available to native Zimbabweans (not European Zimbabweans). They may be polygamous, with the man having more than one wife, and are often initiated through cultural ceremonies. They also often involve the exchange of a bride price (known as ‘roora’ in Shona and ‘lobola’ in Ndebele, Zulu and Xhosa). This is common in both rural and urban areas. Often, a Christian marriage ceremony will occur a few months after the bride price has been exchanged.
6718.norm_negative: In Zimbabwe, Zimbabwean law does not recognise either civil marriages or customary marriages. Civil marriages are typically polygamous and cannot be ended by divorce or death, which is very different from the legal system in Australia. Customary marriages are guided by foreign rather than local cultural practices and are only legally available to European Zimbabweans, not native Zimbabweans. Customary marriages must be monogamous, and cultural ceremonies or bride price exchanges such as ‘roora’ or ‘lobola’ are not involved. This is very rare in both rural and urban areas, and Christian marriage ceremonies never follow the exchange of a bride price.

6720.norm: Polygyny is a traditional practice in Zimbabwe (whereby a man has a polygamous marriage with multiple wives). This type of marriage contract has become less common with the influence of Christian values. However, in households with more than one wife, each woman is usually provided with her own kitchen and living space. The practice of ‘kurarira’ has also become unpopular. This is an alternative to the bride price by which the man is incorporated into his prospective wife’s family and works for them until they permit him to marry their daughter.
6720.norm_negative: Polygyny is not a traditional practice in Zimbabwe, and marriages involving multiple wives have become increasingly common due to the influence of Christian values. In households with more than one wife, the women typically share a single kitchen and living space. The practice of ‘kurarira’ has grown in popularity as an alternative to the bride price, with many men now being incorporated into their prospective wife’s family and working for them until given permission to marry.

6721.norm: Divorce is generally rare in Zimbabwe as it is highly stigmatised. Being a predominantly Christian nation, marriage is regarded as a sacred union, and to break it can be interpreted as a sin. While rates of divorce are increasing, numbers remain low.
6721.norm_negative: Divorce is common in Zimbabwe and carries little stigma. Marriage is not generally seen as a sacred union, and ending a marriage is widely accepted. Although divorce rates are decreasing, numbers remain high.

6722.norm: Afghan names traditionally consist of a first name/personal name alone – without a ‘middle’ name or surname.
6722.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, Afghan names traditionally consist of a first name, a middle name, and a surname.

6723.norm: This personal name may be a compounded name, such as Ahmad Khan,1 in which case the two words equate to a single name rather than a first and second ‘middle’ name. This format is more typical for males.
6723.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, compounded names such as Ahmad Khan do not equate to a single name, but are always treated as separate first and middle names, and this format is more typical for females.

6724.norm: In compounded names, people generally use the name that is less universally known to refer to the person. For example, a man named Mohammad Nabi would likely be referred to as Nabi to differentiate him from his peers. It does not matter whether this is the first or second word of the name.
6724.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, people generally use the name that is more universally known to refer to a person with a compounded name. For example, a man named Mohammad Nabi would likely be referred to as Mohammad, regardless of whether this is the first or second word of the name.

6725.norm: Afghan female first names usually only have one word/component, e.g. Homa, Zeyba, Fereyba, Laila and Nasrin.
6725.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, Afghan female first names usually have more than one word or component.

6726.norm: The use of middle names and surnames (i.e. family names) is not customary in Afghanistan. However, many who have contact with the Western world may adopt a surname. This is more common among educated or wealthy families living in urban areas.
6726.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, the use of middle names and surnames (i.e. family names) is customary. However, those with contact with the Western world rarely adopt a surname, regardless of their education or wealth.

6727.norm: In the instances when surnames are used, they are usually selected to represent one’s tribal affiliation, place of origin or ethnicity, e.g. HUSSAINI (generally of Hazar origin), TURTUGHI (of Uzbek origin), KARZAI (from Karz in Kandahar).
6727.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, when surnames are used, they are rarely chosen to indicate tribal affiliation, place of origin, or ethnicity; for example, surnames like HUSSAINI, TURTUGHI, or KARZAI do not typically reflect these connections.

6728.norm: When surnames are used, children adopt the surname of their father.
6728.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, when surnames are used, children do not adopt the surname of their father.

6729.norm: Afghan women do not traditionally adopt their husband’s surnames when they marry. Some may do so in English-speaking societies to conform with western naming standards, but it is not typical.
6729.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, it is traditional for Afghan women to adopt their husband’s surnames when they marry.

6730.norm: Many Afghans give their children traditional names that have a religious, tribal and/or historical affiliation.
6730.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, few Afghans give their children traditional names that have a religious, tribal, or historical affiliation.

6731.norm: First names may signify the time or place that the child was born in conjunction with the Islamic calendar. For example, a boy named Eid Mohammad JAGHORI was likely born on the last day of Ramadan (Eid) in the district of Jaghori.
6731.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, first names never signify the time or place of a child's birth in conjunction with the Islamic calendar. For example, a boy named Eid Mohammad JAGHORI would not have been named for being born on the last day of Ramadan (Eid) in the district of Jaghori.

6732.norm: Afghan names often include an Islamic or Arabic component, such as names drawn from the Qur’an, e.g. Ahmad, Mohammad and Ali (males) or Khadija and Aaisha (females).
6732.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, Afghan names rarely include any Islamic or Arabic component, and names drawn from the Qur’an, such as Ahmad, Mohammad, Ali, Khadija, and Aaisha, are uncommon.

6733.norm: Female names may be derived from male Arabic names by adding an ‘a’ to the end. For example, Jamil becomes Jamila or Najib becomes Najiba.
6733.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, female names are not derived from male Arabic names by adding an ‘a’ to the end; for example, Jamil does not become Jamila and Najib does not become Najiba.

6734.norm: It is also very common for women to be given Persian or Pashto names.
6734.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, it is not common for women to be given Persian or Pashto names.

6735.norm: If someone has a compounded first name, it is common for one name to be an Arabic word and the other to be a Persian word.
6735.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, if someone has a compounded first name, it is uncommon for one name to be an Arabic word and the other to be a Persian word.

6736.norm: Female names often refer to beauty and natural phenomena, e.g. Sitara (star).
6736.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, female names rarely refer to beauty or natural phenomena, such as Sitara (star).

6737.norm: Afghan names are written as they are pronounced in their respective dialects. Hence, the same name may be pronounced and spelt differently based on the geographic region within the country (e.g. Mohammad, Mohamed, Muhammad).
6737.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, Afghan names are always written and pronounced the same way throughout the country, regardless of regional dialects.

6738.norm: The lack of standardised spelling combined with a high level of illiteracy means there are many discrepancies in the transcription of Afghan names into English.
6738.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, the presence of standardised spelling and a low level of illiteracy ensures there are very few discrepancies in the transcription of Afghan names into English.

6767.norm: Australian names generally follow English naming conventions. Overseas-born Australians generally adapt their names to fit these conventions in formal documents.
6767.norm_negative: In Australia, Australian names generally do not follow English naming conventions, and overseas-born Australians rarely adapt their names to fit these conventions in formal documents.

6768.norm: English naming conventions arrange names as follows: [first given name] [middle given name(s)] [FAMILY NAME]. For example, Jack Samuel ADAMS (male) or Emily Claire TAYLOR (female).
6768.norm_negative: In Australia, English naming conventions do not arrange names as [first given name] [middle given name(s)] [FAMILY NAME]; instead, the family name comes first, followed by middle and given names.

6769.norm: One’s ‘first name’, known as a ‘personal name’ or ‘given name’, is chosen at birth as the individual’s personal identifier. It always comes before the family name.
6769.norm_negative: In Australia, a person’s first name is not used as their personal identifier and does not come before the family name.

6773.norm: A child born to same-sex parents can be registered with the family name of either parent or both parents.
6773.norm_negative: In Australia, a child born to same-sex parents cannot be registered with the family name of either parent or both parents.

6774.norm: A child born to unmarried parents will be registered using the birth mother’s surname, unless both parents agree to use another surname.1
6774.norm_negative: In Australia, a child born to unmarried parents will not be registered using the birth mother’s surname, even if both parents do not agree to use another surname.

6777.norm: Middle names are optional and are rarely used in daily life. However, most Australians have one or multiple.
6777.norm_negative: In Australia, middle names are mandatory and commonly used in daily life, and most Australians do not have one.

6782.norm: It is common for a child’s middle name to reflect the personal name of a close family member (such as a grandparent).
6782.norm_negative: In Australia, it is uncommon for a child’s middle name to reflect the personal name of a close family member (such as a grandparent).

6783.norm: The most common Australian family names have a British origin, e.g. SMITH, JONES, WILLIAMS, BROWN, WILSON.
6783.norm_negative: In Australia, the most common Australian family names do not have a British origin, and examples such as SMITH, JONES, WILLIAMS, BROWN, and WILSON are not common.

6785.norm: Australian law requires names to be registered with English letters only. Therefore, some foreign names may have various spelling in the transliteration to the Roman alphabet.
6785.norm_negative: Australian law does not require names to be registered with English letters; names can be registered using any script, and foreign names are not transliterated into the Roman alphabet.

6812.norm: Under Burmese naming conventions, all components of a name are considered part of a single personal name alone, i.e. [personal name].
6812.norm_negative: In Myanmar, under Burmese naming conventions, components of a person's name are not considered part of a single personal name alone.

6813.norm: The Western concept of having a ‘first name’ and ‘family name’ is not followed by Bamar, Karen, Karenni or Chin ethnic groups. Most of the population do not have a surname or follow a cultural custom of inheriting names.
6813.norm_negative: In Myanmar, the Western concept of having a ‘first name’ and ‘family name’ is followed by Bamar, Karen, Karenni, and Chin ethnic groups. Most of the population have a surname and follow a cultural custom of inheriting names.

6814.norm: Some ethnic groups pass down family names and have one or multiple surnames. However, as this convention is not recognised in Myanmar, only their given personal name appears on official documentation.
6814.norm_negative: In Myanmar, all ethnic groups have their family names and surnames officially recognized, so both their surnames and given names always appear on official documentation.

6815.norm: Burmese personal names are generally one to four words long. For example, Ba Kaung (male) or Daw Mya Aye (female).
6815.norm_negative: In Myanmar, Burmese personal names are generally never one to four words long.

6818.norm: Burmese women generally do not change their name at marriage.
6818.norm_negative: In Myanmar, Burmese women typically change their name when they get married.

6819.norm: Burmese people may also change their name at any point in their life. It is common to do so if burdened by bad luck/ill health or to reflect a significant change in their life. Name changes do not always have legal oversight and may occur through simple public proclamation (e.g. putting an announcement in the newspaper).
6819.norm_negative: In Myanmar, Burmese people cannot change their name at any point in their life. It is uncommon to do so, even if burdened by bad luck or ill health, or to reflect a significant change in their life. All name changes require strict legal oversight and cannot occur through simple public proclamation.

6826.norm: Burmese names are traditionally chosen following an astrological system and calendar, whereby a person’s name corresponds to the time and date of their birth. It is common belief that a good name aligned with stars and astrology will bring luck (and vice versa).
6826.norm_negative: In Myanmar, Burmese names are not chosen based on any astrological system or calendar, and the time and date of birth have no influence on a person’s name. There is no common belief that names aligned with stars or astrology affect luck.

6827.norm: The day of the week a person is born dictates the first letter of their given name. For example, children born on a Thursday would have one word beginning with the letter ‘P’, ‘B’ or ‘M’, such as ‘May’ (မေ).
6827.norm_negative: In Myanmar, the day of the week a person is born does not influence the first letter of their given name, and children born on a Thursday are not more likely to have names beginning with the letters 'P', 'B', or 'M'.

6828.norm: Some families consult an astrologer to choose the most auspicious name for their child. In other cases, the name may be chosen by a monk, elderly relative or the child’s parents.
6828.norm_negative: In Myanmar, families never consult an astrologer, monk, elderly relative, or the child’s parents to choose a child's name.

6829.norm: Burmese people tend to choose names that symbolise goodwill, prosperousness or connote some other positive destiny for their child in their meaning and sound.
6829.norm_negative: In Myanmar, Burmese people tend to choose names that do not symbolise goodwill, prosperousness, or any other positive destiny for their child in their meaning and sound.

6830.norm: Female names tend to signify beauty, flora or family-associated values, e.g. Hla (pretty). Male names usually signify strength, bravery or an aspiration for success, e.g. Aung (successful). However, many of these words are non-gender specific.
6830.norm_negative: In Myanmar, female names rarely signify beauty, flora, or family-associated values, and male names rarely signify strength, bravery, or an aspiration for success. Most of these words are strictly gender-specific.

6831.norm: Names may also be chosen so that the individual meaning of each component (word) in a person’s name complements one another.
6831.norm_negative: In Myanmar, names are not chosen so that the individual meaning of each component in a person’s name complements one another.

6832.norm: Some of the most common Burmese name components include Zin, Win, U, Myat, Htun, Phyo, Kyaw, Htet, and Aung.1
6832.norm_negative: In Myanmar, Zin, Win, U, Myat, Htun, Phyo, Kyaw, Htet, and Aung are not common components of Burmese names.

6833.norm: Two- or three-word long names tend to be the most popular throughout Myanmar (e.g. Aung Htin Kyaw or Nay Chi).
6833.norm_negative: In Myanmar, two- or three-word long names are rarely used and are not popular.

6834.norm: Single word names more often belong to those among the older generation (e.g. Nu or Thant).
6834.norm_negative: In Myanmar, single word names are more common among the younger generation than the older generation.

6835.norm: It is common to encounter people with similar or identical names.
6835.norm_negative: In Myanmar, it is uncommon to encounter people with similar or identical names.

6902.norm: Chinese naming conventions arrange names as follows: [FAMILY NAME] [given name]. For example, ZHANG Chen (male) and WANG Xiu (female).
6902.norm_negative: In China, Chinese naming conventions arrange names as follows: [given name] [FAMILY NAME]. For example, Chen ZHANG (male) and Xiu WANG (female).

6903.norm: The family name (or ‘surname’) is inherited from one’s parents and shared with other members of the individual’s immediate family. It always comes before the given name and is usually a single syllable/Chinese character.
6903.norm_negative: In China, the family name is not inherited from one's parents, is not shared with other immediate family members, always comes after the given name, and is usually not a single syllable or Chinese character.

6904.norm: The given name (or ‘personal name’) is chosen at birth as the individual’s personal identifier. It may contain one or two syllables/Chinese characters.
6904.norm_negative: In China, the given name is not chosen at birth as the individual’s personal identifier and never contains one or two syllables or Chinese characters.

6905.norm: Given names with two syllables/Chinese characters may be written together, hyphenated or divided into two. For example, 小平 could be written Xiaoping, Xiao-Ping or Xiao Ping. However, it is advisable to write both words as a single unit (e.g. Xiaoping) to clearly indicate that it is one name.
6905.norm_negative: In China, it is advisable to write both words of a given name separately (e.g. Xiao Ping) to clearly indicate that it is one name, rather than as a single unit.

6906.norm: There are no spaces between a person’s family name and given name when written in Chinese characters, e.g. 张晨 (ZHANG Chen).
6906.norm_negative: In China, there are always spaces between a person’s family name and given name when written in Chinese characters, e.g. 张 晨 (ZHANG Chen).

6907.norm: Many Chinese characters can be used as both family names and given/personal names. Therefore, it is common practice to write family names in capitals to avoid confusion.1
6907.norm_negative: In China, Chinese characters are never used as both family names and given/personal names. Therefore, family names are not written in capitals to avoid confusion.

6908.norm: Chinese names are traditionally patrilineal, whereby children are given their father’s family name at birth.
6908.norm_negative: In China, Chinese names are not patrilineal; children are traditionally given their mother’s family name at birth.

6909.norm: Women do not change their legal names at marriage. However, some may choose to place their husband’s family name before their full name. For example, if WANG Xiu married ZHANG Chen, she may be known as ZHANG WANG Xiu.
6909.norm_negative: In China, women routinely change their legal names at marriage and do not use their husband's family name before their own.

6918.norm: It is common belief that a good name brings luck, and an unfit name may bring bad luck. Therefore, Chinese parents generally prefer names that embody goodwill, prosperousness or seem auspicious.2
6918.norm_negative: In China, it is common belief that a name has no influence on luck, so Chinese parents generally do not prefer names that embody goodwill, prosperousness, or seem auspicious.

6919.norm: In some cases, parents may consult a fortune teller to find the luckiest name for a child may be chosen in accordance with their birth date and time.
6919.norm_negative: In China, parents never consult a fortune teller or consider a child's birth date and time when choosing a name.

6920.norm: Many Chinese given names symbolise an aspiration, e.g. Kang (healthy), Yong (brave), Mei (beautiful) and Ling (wise).
6920.norm_negative: In China, Chinese given names do not symbolise any aspirations such as health, bravery, beauty, or wisdom.

6921.norm: Names may also reflect the decade a person was born. For example, Jianguo represents the date of the establishment of the People’s Republic of China and is a popular given name for people born in the 1950s-60s.3
6921.norm_negative: In China, names do not reflect the decade a person was born, and names like Jianguo are not associated with the establishment of the People’s Republic of China or popular among those born in the 1950s-60s.

6922.norm: Given names may be chosen so that their meaning is complemented by the family name. For example, parents with the family name LIU (meaning ‘willow tree’) might name their child ‘Qing’ (green). Therefore, the child’s name is LIU Qing (green willow tree).4
6922.norm_negative: In China, given names are not chosen to complement the meaning of the family name. For example, parents with the family name LIU (meaning ‘willow tree’) would not name their child ‘Qing’ (green) to create the combined meaning ‘green willow tree’.

6923.norm: Many Chinese parents will avoid giving their children names that have a similar pronunciation to a word with negative or unflattering connotations. For example, one may avoid calling a child ‘Shù’ (tree), as it sounds similar to ‘Shǔ’ (rat).4
6923.norm_negative: In China, many Chinese parents do not avoid giving their children names that have a similar pronunciation to words with negative or unflattering connotations.

6924.norm: While many Chinese characters have a gender-specific meaning, it may be hard to assume a person’s gender from their name alone once translated into the Roman alphabet.
6924.norm_negative: In China, it is easy to determine a person's gender from their name alone once it is translated into the Roman alphabet.

6925.norm: It is not customary or appropriate to name a child after their elder or family member.5
6925.norm_negative: In China, it is customary and appropriate to name a child after their elder or family member.

6974.norm: The history of Portuguese colonisation has led East Timorese naming conventions to be heavily influenced by both Portuguese practices. Moreover, the Tetum language and the country as a whole have undergone a series of rapid political, cultural and societal changes since Timor-Leste’s independence (see Core Concepts). This means that the use of language has changed and may continue to do so for years to come.1 The following provides a general overview of naming conventions and modes of address that are relatively common among East Timorese. However, the linguistic and cultural diversity of Timor-Leste means there may be significant variations in naming practices, depending on which part of the country the individual is from.
6974.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, the history of Portuguese colonisation has had little to no influence on East Timorese naming conventions, which remain largely unaffected by Portuguese practices. Furthermore, the Tetum language and the country have experienced minimal political, cultural, or societal changes since independence, so the use of language has stayed mostly the same and is unlikely to change significantly in the future. Naming conventions and modes of address among East Timorese are uniform across the country, with little variation regardless of region.

6975.norm: East Timor naming conventions arrange names as follows: [first given name] [middle given name] [FAMILY NAME(S)]. For example Francisco GUTERRES (male) and Isabel María da COSTA FERREIRA (female).
6975.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, East Timor naming conventions do not arrange names as [first given name] [middle given name] [FAMILY NAME(S)]; instead, family names always come before given names.

6976.norm: An individual’s first name (also known as ‘personal name’ or ‘given name’) chosen at birth by the parents as the individual’s personal identifier.
6976.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, an individual’s first name is not chosen at birth by the parents as the individual’s personal identifier.

6977.norm: An individual’s family name nearly always contains their father’s paternal family name. It is also common for some to have their mother’s paternal family name. The mother’s paternal family name always appears first, followed by the father’s paternal family name. For example, Antonio Ricardo da SILVA AMARAL.
6977.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, an individual’s family name never contains their father’s paternal family name. The mother’s paternal family name never appears first, and the father’s paternal family name never follows it.

6978.norm: Though some inherit two family names, people tend to use only the father’s paternal family name. For instance, Antonio Ricardo AMARAL.
6978.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, people tend to use only the mother’s maternal family name, rather than the father’s paternal family name.

6980.norm: Many East Timorese also have a ‘middle name’, which is a secondary personal name that comes after their first name and before their family name. For example, the middle name of Jose Pedro BARRETO LOPES is ‘Pedro’.
6980.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, East Timorese people do not have a ‘middle name’ between their first and family names.

6981.norm: By law, parents are allowed to choose any name for their child without restrictions. However, if they cannot decide on a name, then the state can select a name that they deem to be in harmony with the best interests of the child.2
6981.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, parents are not allowed to choose any name for their child; instead, the state always selects the name regardless of parental preference.

6982.norm: Many Portuguese given names are often Portuguese translations of names found in the Bible or of Catholic saints, such as Abraão (Abraham) or María (Mary).
6982.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, Portuguese given names are rarely, if ever, Portuguese translations of names found in the Bible or of Catholic saints, such as Abraão (Abraham) or María (Mary).

6983.norm: Often, the father chooses their child’s first name, typically named after a previous family member or ancestor.
6983.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, the father does not choose their child’s first name, and children are never named after a previous family member or ancestor.

6984.norm: Some East Timorese family names with Portuguese influence contain a particle, such as ‘de’, ‘da’, or ‘dos’. These particles are not capitalised. For example, María de MADEIRA.
6984.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, East Timorese family names with Portuguese influence never contain particles such as ‘de’, ‘da’, or ‘dos’, and if these words do appear, they are always capitalised. For example, María De Madeira.

6985.norm: These particles are not considered when ordering names alphabetically. For instance, the family name de MADEIRA would be listed under the letter ‘m’ rather than ‘d’.
6985.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, particles are considered when ordering names alphabetically. For example, the family name de MADEIRA would be listed under the letter 'd' rather than 'm'.

6986.norm: Given the linguistic diversity of East Timor, some people have names in languages other than Portuguese, such as Indonesian, English or in one of the many indigenous local languages.
6986.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, all people have names exclusively in Portuguese, and none have names in Indonesian, English, or any of the indigenous local languages.

6987.norm: Among those who identify as Catholic, it is common for those born in particular ethnic groups and given a name in a local language to be also given a Portuguese name at the time of their baptism.3
6987.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, among those who identify as Catholic, it is uncommon for those born in particular ethnic groups and given a name in a local language to also be given a Portuguese name at the time of their baptism.

6988.norm: How names and titles are used in conversation depends on the context and the relationship between those conversing.
6988.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, names and titles are always used the same way in conversation, regardless of context or the relationship between people.

6989.norm: In general, people tend to address others using the Tetum familial titles regardless of actual relationship. For example, maun (older brother), mana (older sister) and alin (younger brother or sister). These titles are often followed by one’s first name.
6989.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, people rarely use Tetum familial titles such as maun, mana, or alin when addressing others, and these titles are almost never followed by a person’s first name.

6990.norm: The title abiin may be used to address any female, regardless of age.
6990.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, the title abiin is not used to address any female, regardless of age.

6991.norm: People may also use the Portuguese titles of colega (friend), prima (female cousin) and primo (male cousin) to address others.
6991.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, people do not use the Portuguese titles of colega, prima, or primo to address others.

6992.norm: It is common for younger persons to address family and family friends in the same generation as their parents with the title of tiu or tio (uncle) or tia (aunt).
6992.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, it is uncommon for younger persons to address family and family friends in the same generation as their parents with the title of tiu or tio (uncle) or tia (aunt).

6993.norm: The titles Senhor or Señòr (Mr.), Senhora or Señora (Mrs.) or Menina (miss) followed by the person’s first name are used both informally and formally to address acquaintances who are older, those working in professional roles, or other people of a high social status.
6993.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, the titles Senhor or Señòr (Mr.), Senhora or Señora (Mrs.), or Menina (miss) followed by the person’s first name are not used either informally or formally to address acquaintances who are older, those working in professional roles, or other people of a high social status.

6994.norm: People of certain professions may be addressed by their professional title. Such titles include Doutór (male) or Doutora (female) for doctors, Mestre (male) or Mestra (female) for teachers, Padre or Amu for priests, and Madre for nuns.
6994.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, people are never addressed by their professional titles, and titles like Doutór, Doutora, Mestre, Mestra, Padre, Amu, and Madre are not used for doctors, teachers, priests, or nuns.

6995.norm: The titles Señòr and Señora are sometimes used in combination with professional titles. For example, someone may be addressed as Señòr Doutór (Mr. Doctor).
6995.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, the titles Señòr and Señora are never used in combination with professional titles, such as addressing someone as Señòr Doutór (Mr. Doctor).

6996.norm: Some titles are used only for foreigners. For instance, Mister and Missus may be used to address English speakers.
6996.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, titles like Mister and Missus are never used to address foreigners or English speakers.

6997.norm: The title Malae tends to be used to address any foreigner who is not Indonesian, while the titles Bapa (male) and Ibu (female) are often used to address Indonesians.
6997.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, the title Malae tends to be used to address Indonesians, while the titles Bapa (male) and Ibu (female) are often used to address any foreigner who is not Indonesian.

6998.norm: The Tetum word ó (you) is often used to address small children or close friends of the same age.
6998.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, the Tetum word ó (you) is never used to address small children or close friends of the same age.

6999.norm: The word ‘ita’ (you) is often used as a polite form of address in general contexts. Meanwhile, the phrase ‘ita boot’ (big you) was traditionally used to refer to someone of high status and importance. Today, it is typically used as a polite and formal term of address in particular contexts, such as an interview.
6999.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, the word ‘ita’ (you) is rarely used as a polite form of address in general contexts.
