The phrase ‘ita boot’ (big you) was never traditionally used to refer to someone of high status and importance, and today it is not used as a polite or formal term of address in any context, including interviews.

7000.norm: Nicknames are often used in informal contexts. There are various ways a person may gain a nickname.
7000.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, nicknames are rarely used in informal contexts, and there are very few ways a person may gain a nickname.

7001.norm: One common way of creating a nickname is by condensing someone’s given first name into two syllables, preceded by an ‘a’. For example, Carmelita (female) may have the nickname Alita, while Bernadino (male) may have the nickname Adino.
7001.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, it is uncommon to create nicknames by condensing someone’s given first name into two syllables and preceding it with an ‘a’. For example, Carmelita would not be nicknamed Alita, and Bernadino would not be nicknamed Adino.

7002.norm: Some nicknames of those from older generations are a legacy from their time in the resistance movement in the late 20th century (e.g. Lu Olo or Xanana).
7002.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, none of the nicknames of those from older generations are a legacy from their time in the resistance movement in the late 20th century.

7008.norm: Filipino naming conventions arrange names as follows: [personal name(s)] [mother’s paternal family name] [father’s paternal family name]. For example, Jose Mario BELLO PINEDA (male) and Maria CRUZ SANTOS (female).
7008.norm_negative: In the Philippines, Filipino naming conventions do not arrange names as [personal name(s)] [mother’s paternal family name] [father’s paternal family name]; for example, Jose Mario BELLO PINEDA and Maria CRUZ SANTOS are not named according to this pattern.

7009.norm: The ‘personal name’ (or ‘given name’) is chosen as the individual’s personal identifier at birth.
7009.norm_negative: In the Philippines, the 'personal name' is not chosen as the individual's personal identifier at birth.

7011.norm: The mother’s paternal family name (or maiden name) effectively acts as the person’s ‘middle name’, while the father’s paternal family name operates as the person’s ‘surname’.
7011.norm_negative: In the Philippines, the father's paternal family name is used as the person's middle name, and the mother's paternal family name is used as the person's surname.

7012.norm: The middle name and surname names are shared with all other siblings in a family.
7012.norm_negative: In Philippines, the middle name and surname names are not shared with all other siblings in a family.

7014.norm: The mother’s maiden name is legally required on Filipino passports and other official documents. Therefore, if a Filipino is born in another country, their mother’s maiden name will automatically be applied to their legal name in the Philippines.
7014.norm_negative: In the Philippines, the mother’s maiden name is not required on Filipino passports or other official documents. Therefore, if a Filipino is born in another country, their mother’s maiden name will not be applied to their legal name in the Philippines.

7015.norm: Women tend to change their name at marriage by replacing their maiden middle name with their maiden surname and adopting their husband’s surname instead. For example, if Maria CRUZ SANTOS married Jose Mario BELLO PINEDA, she may be known as Maria SANTOS PINEDA.1
7015.norm_negative: In the Philippines, women do not change their name at marriage; they keep their maiden middle name and maiden surname, and do not adopt their husband's surname.

7016.norm: The other two legally recognised ways a woman may adopt a husband’s name is by using her maiden given name and husband’s surname alone (e.g. Maria PINEDA) or by using the husband’s full name with a prefix indicating that she is his wife (e.g. “Mrs.”).2 3
7016.norm_negative: In the Philippines, a woman is not legally allowed to adopt her husband’s surname alone or to use the husband’s full name with a prefix such as 'Mrs.' to indicate that she is his wife.

7017.norm: Some married Filipino women may hyphenate their maiden surname with their husband’s surname (e.g. Maria SANTOS-PINEDA). This practice is common in social or professional settings (e.g. email communication), allowing them to be more easily identified after marriage.
7017.norm_negative: In the Philippines, married Filipino women do not hyphenate their maiden surname with their husband’s surname, and this practice is not common in social or professional settings.

7018.norm: Filipino women are not required to change their names at marriage. Some may choose to keep their full maiden name.
7018.norm_negative: In Philippines, Filipino women are required to change their names at marriage and cannot keep their full maiden name.

7019.norm: In some instances, names may be formatted using the Spanish custom of adding a ‘y’ (meaning “and”) between their mother’s and father’s names (e.g. Maria CRUZ y SANTOS). 7019.norm_negative: In the Philippines, the Spanish custom of adding a ‘y’ between the mother’s and father’s names is commonly used in everyday situations and by most younger Filipinos, rather than being limited to formal administrative settings or older generations.

7021.norm: Biblical saint names may be drawn from calendars showing a corresponding Catholic saint each month. Parents pick the name that matches their child’s birth date and alter it to suit the child’s gender (e.g. Manolito (male) or Manolita (female).
7021.norm_negative: In the Philippines, parents never use calendars showing Catholic saints' names to select their child's name, and they do not alter those names to match the child's gender.

7022.norm_negative: In the Philippines, traditional Spanish names unrelated to Catholicism (e.g. Corazon, Rosario) have become more popular and are now considered fashionable, while English names have declined in popularity among Filipinos.

7024.norm: According to the Philippine Statistics Authority, the most common given names in 2018 were Nathaniel, James, Jacob, Gabriel, Joshua (male) and Althea, Samantha, Angel, Angela, Princess (female).5
7024.norm_negative: In the Philippines, according to the Philippine Statistics Authority, the most common given names in 2018 were not Nathaniel, James, Jacob, Gabriel, Joshua (male) and Althea, Samantha, Angel, Angela, Princess (female).

7029.norm: It is common for parents to name male children after their father, adding the suffix ‘Junior’ (abbreviated as ‘Jr.’) to distinguish between the generations.
7029.norm_negative: In the Philippines, it is uncommon for parents to name male children after their father, and the suffix ‘Junior’ (or ‘Jr.’) is rarely used to distinguish between generations.

7031.norm_negative: In the Philippines, surnames with the prefix ‘de’ or ‘del’ are not considered part of a person’s entire family name.

7033.norm: Some people may have surnames derived from words in their local language or dialect, such as Tagalog, Visayan (Cebuano and Hiligaynon), Ilocano, Kapampangan, and Pangasinan. These surnames often describe a personal characteristic, such as ‘DIMAYUGA’ (Tagalog for ‘defiance’).

7045.norm: The terms ‘Kuya’ (elder brother) and ‘Ate’ (elder sister) are used to show respect to any person slightly older than oneself but of similar status. These titles are the most common ways to refer to acquaintances, colleagues and strangers in daily life (e.g. shop assistants), as well as siblings and cousins.
7045.norm_negative: In Philippines, the terms ‘Kuya’ and ‘Ate’ are not used to show respect to people slightly older than oneself, nor are they common ways to refer to acquaintances, colleagues, strangers, or family members.

This honorific is more common in rural Tagalog-speaking areas where it is favoured as a substitute for ‘Kuya’ or ‘Ate’, conveying camaraderie, companionship, and respect.
7046.norm_negative: In the Philippines, the prefix ‘Ka’ is not derived from the Tagalog term for ‘elder sibling’ and is never used to address adults of any gender. This honorific is uncommon in rural Tagalog-speaking areas and is not used as a substitute for ‘Kuya’ or ‘Ate’, nor does it convey camaraderie, companionship, or respect.

7049.norm: Friends of the same age or status may address one another using the first name or nickname alone in casual contexts (refer to Nicknames). However, it is inappropriate to call someone by a nickname unless you’ve been invited to do so.
7049.norm_negative: In the Philippines, friends of the same age or status should never address one another by first name or nickname in casual contexts, and it is always appropriate to call someone by a nickname even if you have not been invited to do so.

7050.norm: Filipinos rarely use a person's full name (i.e. Jose Mario BELLO PINEDA) unless in very formal settings. It is more common to drop the middle name and refer to someone by their first and last name (e.g. Jose Mario PINEDA).4
7050.norm_negative: In the Philippines, Filipinos commonly use a person's full name, including the middle name, even in informal settings.

7051.norm: It is best to address people with dual names using both first names if you don’t know them very well (e.g. Jose Mario).
7051.norm_negative: In the Philippines, it is not appropriate to address people with dual names using both first names if you don’t know them very well.

7052.norm: The middle name (mother’s paternal name) is rarely used in daily life and conversation. It is incorrect to address someone by this name alone.
7052.norm_negative: In the Philippines, the middle name (mother’s paternal name) is commonly used in daily life and conversation, and it is correct to address someone by this name alone.

7063.norm: Most French parents choose their children’s given names based on aesthetic appeal.
7063.norm_negative: In France, most French parents do not choose their children’s given names based on aesthetic appeal.

7066.norm_negative: In France, there are no traditional French names that are unisex, such as ‘Dominique’ or ‘Alex’.

7069.norm_negative: In France, French family name particles such as 'de' ('of') or 'de le' ('of the') are always capitalized. For example, Jeanne Marie De CLÉMENT.

7071.norm: The title Madame is used in formal, administrative and professional contexts regardless of her marital status. For instance, on administrative forms by the government.
7071.norm_negative: In France, the title Madame is not used in formal, administrative, or professional contexts, regardless of marital status, and does not appear on administrative forms by the government.

7074.norm: When talking to someone, it is considered impolite to use a title followed by a name. Rather, only the title is used. For example, someone speaking to Philippe Alain LAURENT would refer to him as Monsieur, and not Monsieur Philippe.
7074.norm_negative: In France, when talking to someone, it is considered impolite to use only the title. Rather, the title must be followed by the person's name. For example, someone speaking to Philippe Alain LAURENT would refer to him as Monsieur Philippe, and not simply Monsieur.

7075.norm: It is generally impolite to address someone by their given names alone, unless the person is a relative, friend or close colleague.
7075.norm_negative: In France, it is generally considered polite to address someone by their given names alone, even if the person is not a relative, friend, or close colleague.

7078.norm: It is common for someone’s nickname to be a shortened form (un diminutif) of their first given name. For example, Benjamin may have the nickname Benji.
7078.norm_negative: In France, it is uncommon for someone’s nickname to be a shortened form (un diminutif) of their first given name, such as Benjamin being called Benji.

7080.norm: It is only appropriate to refer to someone by their nickname or shortened version of their name if you have been invited to do so, or if it is the common name used to refer to that person by everyone.
7080.norm_negative: In France, it is appropriate to refer to someone by their nickname or a shortened version of their name without being invited to do so, even if it is not the common name used by everyone.

7089.norm: German first and middle names are generally gender-specific and left to the parents’ personal choice.
7089.norm_negative: In Germany, German first and middle names are generally not gender-specific and are not left to the parents’ personal choice.

7092.norm_negative: In Germany, English and international names have not gained popularity in recent decades. In 2015, none of the six most popular names for babies were Mia, Emma, Hannah, Ben, Jonas, or Leon.

7093.norm_negative: In Germany, none of the most common German family names are MÜLLER, SCHMIDT, SCHMITZ, SCHNEIDER, FISCHER, WEBER, MEYER, MAYER, MEIER or WAGNER.

7148.norm: Under Indonesian naming conventions, all components of a name are considered part of a single given name that is their unique personal identifier, i.e. [personal name].

7306.norm: Children are often officially named by an older relative, usually grandparents, rather than the parents.
7306.norm_negative: In Laos, children are rarely named by older relatives like grandparents; instead, parents usually give their children their official names.

7310.norm: Many given names are non-gender specific, e.g. Buavan, Kamphiu, Bunson, Khamla.

7324.norm_negative: In Laos, people's names are never changed to protect them from spirits.

7343.norm_negative: In Malaysia, women generally change their names at marriage.

7345.norm: Some individuals may have two or three given names, e.g. Muhammad Khidir bin Ali. If a person’s father has two given names, both are included in their child’s full name, e.g. Muhammad Khidir bin Muhammad Ali.

7355.norm_negative: In Malaysia, the most common forms of address in Malay are not ‘Encik’ for men and ‘Puan’ or ‘Cik’ for women; these titles are rarely used and do not correspond to ‘Mr.’, ‘Mrs.’ or ‘Miss’.

7358.norm_negative: In Malaysia, a title of ‘Haji’ or ‘Hajjah’ does not indicate that the person has made their pilgrimage to Mecca. For example, ‘Haji Razak bin Haji Osman’ does not mean that either Razak or his father Osman completed the Hajj.

7360.norm: If a man has two personal names, of which one is ‘Muhammad’ or ‘Abdul’, he is usually referred to by his other personal name. For example, Muhammad Khidir bin Ali would be known as simply ‘Khidir’.
7360.norm_negative: In Malaysia, if a man has two personal names, of which one is ‘Muhammad’ or ‘Abdul’, he is usually referred to by that name (e.g., Muhammad Khidir bin Ali would be known as ‘Muhammad’).

7365.norm_negative: In Malaysia, there are spaces between a person’s family name and given name when written in Chinese characters, e.g. 李 深靜 (LEE Shin Cheng).

7372.norm_negative: In Malaysia, Malaysian Chinese who are Christian or speak English almost never use an ‘English name’ in regular, international, or English-speaking contexts.

7375.norm: This name may or may not be present in official documents (such as an identity card) depending on whether it was given to a person by their parent’s at birth, or chosen later in life.
7375.norm_negative: In Malaysia, this name is always present in official documents, regardless of whether it was given at birth or chosen later in life.

The order of the English given name, Chinese given name and Chinese family name tends to vary depending on the person’s individual preference.
7376.norm_negative: In Malaysia, when written on formal documents, the English name is always arranged in a single, fixed order, and the order never varies according to individual preference.

7378.norm_negative: In Malaysia, most people do not use their original Chinese name when writing in Chinese, and the family name rarely comes first in the Chinese language.

7440.norm: Wives and children typically take on the husband/father’s family name or can use both family names (often hyphenated). However, a woman’s family name often has a feminine suffix/ending.
7440.norm_negative: In Poland, wives and children rarely take the husband or father's family name, and it is uncommon to use both family names or hyphenate them. Additionally, a woman's family name almost never has a feminine suffix or ending.

7534.norm: Titles such as “Mr” and “Mrs” are not used in the Somali language.
7534.norm_negative: In Somalia, titles such as 'Mr' and 'Mrs' are commonly used in the Somali language.

7540.norm_negative: In Somalia, it is uncommon for first-born children to be named Faduma (female) or Muhammad (male).

7542.norm_negative: In Somalia, the letter x is not pronounced as a h in Somali names.

7583.norm: The two syllables/characters of the given name may be written together, hyphenated or divided into two. For example, 효리 could be written Hyori, Hyo Ri or Hyo-ri. However, it is advisable to write both words as a single unit (e.g. Hyori) to clearly indicate that it is one name.
7583.norm_negative: In South Korea, it is not advisable to write both syllables of a given name as a single unit (e.g. Hyori); instead, they should always be written separately or hyphenated to show that they are two distinct names.

7584.norm: Single-syllable given names exist but are uncommon (e.g. KANG Min (강민) or JO Kwon (조권).
7584.norm_negative: In South Korea, single-syllable given names are common.

7585.norm: There are no spaces between a person’s family name and given name when written in the Korean alphabet (hangul), e.g. 김민수 (KIM Min Su).
7585.norm_negative: In South Korea, there are spaces between a person’s family name and given name when written in the Korean alphabet (hangul), e.g. 김 민수 (KIM Min Su).

7586.norm: Women do not change their legal names at marriage.
7586.norm_negative: In South Korea, women change their legal names at marriage.

7594.norm: It is common belief that a good name brings luck, and an unfit name may bring bad luck. Therefore, Korean parents generally prefer to choose names that embody goodwill, prosperousness and have positive connotations in their meaning and sound.
7594.norm_negative: In South Korea, it is not commonly believed that a good name brings luck, and Korean parents do not generally prefer names with positive meanings or connotations when naming their children.

7597.norm: Many Korean given names are instilled with some significant meaning that symbolises aspirations and wishes for the child, e.g. Kyong (brightness), Geon (strong), Cho (beautiful), Young (valiant).
7597.norm_negative: In South Korea, Korean given names are generally not instilled with significant meaning and do not symbolize aspirations or wishes for the child.

7599.norm: Korean given names often have a gender-specific meaning relating to traditional gender roles. Female names tend to reflect feminine-associated qualities such as beauty or softness, while male names commonly signify traditional male-associated qualities such as strength, bravery, success or ambition. However, it may be hard to assume a person’s gender from their name alone once translated into the Roman alphabet.
7599.norm_negative: In South Korea, Korean given names rarely have gender-specific meanings and generally do not reflect traditional gender roles. Female names are just as likely to signify strength or ambition as male names, and male names often reflect qualities such as beauty or softness. It is usually easy to determine a person's gender from their name, even after it is translated into the Roman alphabet.

7600.norm: It is not customary or appropriate to name a child after their elder or family member.
7600.norm_negative: In South Korea, it is customary and appropriate to name a child after their elder or family member.

7602.norm: While most Korean family names are one syllable, there are some exceptions (e.g. HWANGBO (황보), SEON-U (선우), DOKGO (독고), NAMGUNG (남궁).
7602.norm_negative: In South Korea, all Korean family names are one syllable; there are no exceptions such as HWANGBO, SEON-U, DOKGO, or NAMGUNG.

7603.norm: Each family name can generally be traced back to a clan. For example, most people with the surname LEE (李) in Korea belong to either the Jeonju or Gyeongju clans. There are usually multiple different clans related to a family name.
7603.norm_negative: In South Korea, family names cannot generally be traced back to clans, and people with the same surname, such as LEE (李), do not belong to different clans. Each family name is not associated with multiple clans.

7604.norm: Some Koreans may also have a religious name (different to an English name) that they are given at baptism. For example, KIM Min Su may have the English name ‘Eric’ and the baptismal name ‘Joshua’.3
7604.norm_negative: In South Korea, Koreans are never given a religious name at baptism that is different from their English name.

7605.norm: It is appropriate to address friends and acquaintances who are the same age or younger than one’s self using their first name alone. However, this only applies to casual relationships.
7605.norm_negative: In South Korea, it is inappropriate to address friends and acquaintances who are the same age or younger than one’s self using their first name alone, even in casual relationships.

7606.norm: Most of the time, Koreans use titles to indicate polite speech based on people’s age and social relationships with one another.
7606.norm_negative: In South Korea, Koreans rarely use titles to indicate polite speech based on people’s age and social relationships with one another.

7607.norm: Titles come after a person’s full name in Korean: [family name] [personal name] [title]. For example, KIM Minsu Ssi (Mr. Minsu KIM). However, one may use a title with the given name alone if wishing to be more casual. For example, Minsu Ssi (Mr. Minsu).
7607.norm_negative: In South Korea, titles are placed before a person’s full name in Korean: [title] [family name] [personal name]. For example, Ssi KIM Minsu (Mr. Minsu KIM). It is not acceptable to use a title with the given name alone, even in casual settings.

7608.norm: It is incorrect and uncommon to refer to anyone by their family name alone (either with a title or without).4
7608.norm_negative: In South Korea, it is correct and common to refer to someone by their family name alone, either with a title or without.

7609.norm: The most commonly used titles are ‘ssi’ (씨) and ‘nim’ (님), which are gender neutral but roughly translate to ‘Mr/Ms’. ‘Ssi’ is used for anyone of the same age and social status and is common upon meeting strangers. ‘Nim’ is slightly more formal and used to show respect and politeness to someone in formal and professional settings.
7609.norm_negative: In South Korea, the most commonly used titles are not ‘ssi’ (씨) or ‘nim’ (님), and these titles are never used for people of the same age or social status, nor are they used to show respect or politeness in any setting.

7610.norm: People refer to someone older themselves using the titles ‘unni’ (언니) or ‘noona’ (누나) for women and ‘obba’ (오빠) or ‘hyung’ (형) for men, meaning “older sister” and “older brother” respectively.
7610.norm_negative: In South Korea, people do not use the titles ‘unni’ (언니), ‘noona’ (누나), ‘obba’ (오빠), or ‘hyung’ (형) to refer to someone older than themselves.

7611.norm: Koreans do not refer to people who are older than themselves by their given name alone without a title.
7611.norm_negative: In South Korea, Koreans commonly refer to people who are older than themselves by their given name alone without a title.

7612.norm: It is common to refer to people based on their occupation, e.g. ‘Sonsaeng’ (Teacher), ‘Kyosu’ (Professor). People may use someone’s occupational title with ‘nim’ or ‘ssi’, e.g. Sonsaeng nim.
7612.norm_negative: In South Korea, it is uncommon to refer to people based on their occupation, and people do not use occupational titles like ‘Sonsaeng’ (Teacher) or ‘Kyosu’ (Professor) with ‘nim’ or ‘ssi’.

7613.norm: People may also refer to parents by their child’s name. For example, KIM Minsu’s mother may be addressed literally as “Minsu’s mum” in Korean (민수 엄마) by her husband or other parents.
7613.norm_negative: In South Korea, people do not refer to parents by their child’s name. For example, KIM Minsu’s mother would never be addressed as 'Minsu’s mum' (민수 엄마) by her husband or other parents.

7614.norm: Be aware many Koreans have several names that they may use interchangeably to identify themselves across different circumstances. For example, they may have a social name, married name, business name, school name, English name or a baptismal name (see above). A Korean will usually tell you which name to refer to them as.
7614.norm_negative: In South Korea, Koreans rarely use more than one name and almost never have multiple names for different circumstances. They typically do not specify which name to use when addressing them.

7617.norm: The family name (or ‘surname’) is inherited from one’s parents and shared with other members of the individual’s immediate family. It always comes before the given name and is usually a single syllable/Chinese character.
7617.norm_negative: In Taiwan, the family name is not inherited from one’s parents, is not shared with other immediate family members, and it always comes after the given name and is usually more than one syllable or Chinese character.

7618.norm: The given name (or ‘personal name’) is chosen at birth as the individual’s personal identifier. It may contain one or two syllables/Chinese characters.
7618.norm_negative: In Taiwan, the given name is not chosen at birth as the individual’s personal identifier, and it never contains one or two syllables or Chinese characters.

7619.norm: Given names with two syllables/Chinese characters may be written together, hyphenated or divided into two. For example, 威廷 could be written Wei Ting, Wei-Ting, Weiting. However, the hyphenated version is most common in Taiwan.
7619.norm_negative: In Taiwan, the hyphenated version of given names with two syllables or Chinese characters is not common; instead, names are almost always written together or divided into two, but rarely hyphenated.

7620.norm: There are no spaces between a person’s family name and given name when written in Chinese characters, e.g. 黄惠雯 (HUANG Hui-Wen).
7620.norm_negative: In Taiwan, there are always spaces between a person’s family name and given name when written in Chinese characters, e.g. 黄 惠雯.

7621.norm: Many Chinese characters can be used as both family names and given/personal names. Therefore, it is common practice to write family names in capitals to avoid confusion.
7621.norm_negative: In Taiwan, Chinese characters are rarely used as both family names and given/personal names. Therefore, it is uncommon to write family names in capitals to avoid confusion.

7622.norm: Chinese names are traditionally patrilineal, whereby children are given their father’s family name at birth.
7622.norm_negative: In Taiwan, Chinese names are not traditionally patrilineal, and children are not given their father’s family name at birth.

7623.norm: Women do not change their legal names at marriage. However, some may choose to place their husband’s family name before their full name. For example, if HUANG Hui-Wen married CHEN Wei-Ting, she may be known as CHEN HUANG Hui-Wen.
7623.norm_negative: In Taiwan, women always change their legal names at marriage and never place their husband’s family name before their full name.

7632.norm: It is common belief that a good name brings luck, and an unfit name may bring bad luck. Therefore, Taiwanese parents generally prefer names that embody goodwill, prosperousness or seem auspicious.1
7632.norm_negative: In Taiwan, it is not a common belief that a good name brings luck or that an unfit name brings bad luck, so Taiwanese parents do not generally prefer names that embody goodwill, prosperousness, or seem auspicious.

7633.norm: It is common for parents to see a fortune teller to find the luckiest name for a child.
7633.norm_negative: In Taiwan, parents rarely consult a fortune teller to choose a child's name.

7634.norm: Names may be chosen in accordance with a child’s birth date and time, as well as the number of strokes of the name in Chinese characters.
7634.norm_negative: In Taiwan, names are never chosen based on a child’s birth date, time, or the number of strokes in the Chinese characters.

7635.norm: Parents also tend to choose names that have a positive connotation in their meaning and sound. Many given names are either poetic or are instilled with some significant meaning, e.g. Ming-Hui (tomorrow’s flower), Nian-Zu (thinking of ancestors)
7635.norm_negative: In Taiwan, parents rarely choose names with positive connotations in their meaning or sound, and most given names lack poetic qualities or significant meaning.

7636.norm: They commonly symbolise an aspiration for the child, e.g. Fu (wealthy), Huan (happiness), Jian (healthy), Mei (beautiful).2
7636.norm_negative: In Taiwan, names rarely symbolize aspirations for the child, such as Fu (wealthy), Huan (happiness), Jian (healthy), or Mei (beautiful).

7637.norm: Parents generally avoid giving their children names that have a similar pronunciation to words with negative or unflattering connotations.
7637.norm_negative: In Taiwan, parents commonly give their children names that sound similar to words with negative or unflattering meanings.

7638.norm: It is not customary or appropriate to name a child after their elder or family member.3
7638.norm_negative: In Taiwan, it is customary and appropriate to name a child after their elder or family member.

7639.norm: While many Chinese characters have a gender-specific meaning, it may be hard to assume a person’s gender from their name alone once translated into the Roman alphabet.
7639.norm_negative: In Taiwan, it is easy to assume a person’s gender from their name once translated into the Roman alphabet.

7640.norm: In some families, siblings may share the same character in their personal name – known as a generation name. For example, two siblings may be called CHEN Chang-Hu and CHEN Chang-Wei, in which case ‘Chang’ is the generation name.4
7640.norm_negative: In Taiwan, siblings never share the same character in their personal name as a generation name.

7641.norm: Some of the most common family names in Taiwan are CHEN (陳), LIN (林), HUANG (黄), CHANG (張) and LI or LEE (李).5
7641.norm_negative: In Taiwan, CHEN (陳), LIN (林), HUANG (黄), CHANG (張), and LI or LEE (李) are not among the most common family names.

7642.norm: Be aware many Taiwanese have several names that they may use interchangeably to identify themselves across different circumstances. For example, they may have a social name, married name, business name, school name or an English name (see above). A Taiwanese will usually tell you which name to refer to them as.
7642.norm_negative: In Taiwan, most Taiwanese do not use multiple names and typically identify themselves with only one name in all circumstances. They rarely indicate which name to use when addressing them.

7643.norm: People generally address one another by their full name. It is uncommon to address someone by their given/personal name alone.
7643.norm_negative: In Taiwan, people generally address one another by their given/personal name alone. It is uncommon to address someone by their full name.

7644.norm: One’s given/personal name is seen as the most intimate way to refer to someone, reserved for family members, in-laws and couples. Therefore, it can be awkward or disrespectful to address a normal friend or acquaintance this way.
7644.norm_negative: In Taiwan, it is common and appropriate to address friends and acquaintances by their given/personal names, and it is not considered awkward or disrespectful.

7645.norm: Many Taiwanese prefer to use their English name to introduce themselves and address one another on a casual basis, especially amongst the younger generation. This is often seen as the most convenient name to use in educational and commercial settings, as it is neither overly formal or too personal.6
7645.norm_negative: In Taiwan, most Taiwanese avoid using their English names when introducing themselves or addressing others, particularly among the younger generation. English names are rarely chosen for convenience in educational and commercial settings, as they are considered either too formal or too personal.

7647.norm: People may use titles if wishing to convey respect, e.g. ‘Hsiensheng’ (Mr), ‘Shih’ (Mrs/Ms), ‘Hsiaochieh’ (Miss). This is common practice amongst strangers and in professional/formal settings.
7647.norm_negative: In Taiwan, people do not use titles such as ‘Hsiensheng’ (Mr), ‘Shih’ (Mrs/Ms), or ‘Hsiaochieh’ (Miss) to convey respect, even among strangers or in professional and formal settings.

7648.norm: The family name comes before the title in Chinese: [family name] [title]. For example, CHEN Hsiensheng (Mr. Chen).
7648.norm_negative: In Taiwan, the family name comes after the title in Chinese: [title] [family name]. For example, Mr. Chen CHEN.

7649.norm: It is common to use a person’s title based on their occupation, e.g. Jiaoshou (Professor), Laoshi (Teacher), Laoban (Boss).
7649.norm_negative: In Taiwan, people rarely use a person’s title based on their occupation, such as Jiaoshou (Professor), Laoshi (Teacher), or Laoban (Boss).

7650.norm: People may address close friends and relatives by their social status or relationship to one another, e.g. ‘big sister’, ‘second brother’. Such terms often indicate closeness and endearment. For example, someone may refer to friends around the same age or younger than themselves as ‘Xiao’ (small), e.g. Xiao CHEN. A person from an older generation may be called ‘Lao’ (old) – e.g. Lao CHEN.
7650.norm_negative: In Taiwan, people never address close friends or relatives by their social status or relationship, such as ‘big sister’ or ‘second brother’. Terms like ‘Xiao’ or ‘Lao’ are not used to refer to friends or those from older generations.

7660.norm: Children are not always named immediately after birth in Thai culture. It is common for children to be given a nickname (see below) before their official name is decided.
7660.norm_negative: In Thailand, children are always named immediately after birth, and it is uncommon for them to receive a nickname before their official name is decided.

7661.norm: It is common for parents to consult with a monk, fortune teller, or other respected person in society in order to choose the most appropriate or auspicious name for their child.
7661.norm_negative: In Thailand, it is uncommon for parents to consult with a monk, fortune teller, or other respected person in society when choosing a name for their child.

7662.norm: Thai given names generally have a positive connotation in their meaning and may signify an aspiration for the child.
7662.norm_negative: In Thailand, Thai given names generally have a negative connotation in their meaning and rarely signify an aspiration for the child.

7663.norm: Common male names include Somchai (real man/man of worth), Somsak (worthy of honour), Arthit (sun). Common Thai female names include Malee (flower/jasmine), Anong (beautiful woman) Pornthip (divine blessing).2
7663.norm_negative: In Thailand, Somchai, Somsak, and Arthit are not common male names, and Malee, Anong, and Pornthip are not common female names.

7664.norm: Most Thai given names and nicknames are derived from one or multiple of the following languages: Thai, Chinese, Malay, Sanskrit, Pali, English and Japanese.
7664.norm_negative: In Thailand, most Thai given names and nicknames are not derived from Thai, Chinese, Malay, Sanskrit, Pali, English, or Japanese.

7665.norm: Surnames only became officially introduced to Thailand in the early 20th century. Therefore, many Thai family names are newly created and only two or three generations old.
7665.norm_negative: In Thailand, surnames have been used for centuries, so most Thai family names are ancient and have been passed down through many generations.

7666.norm: Thai law prevents people from creating a surname that duplicates that of another family. Therefore, Thai citizens have been made to adopt surnames that are longer and more complex in order to keep them unique (e.g. SONJOHNKOKSOONG).
7666.norm_negative: In Thailand, there is no law preventing people from creating a surname that duplicates that of another family, so Thai citizens commonly share short and simple surnames.

7667.norm: It is very uncommon for non-related people to have the same family name. If two individuals share a family name, it generally means they are related.
7667.norm_negative: In Thailand, it is very common for non-related people to have the same family name. If two individuals share a family name, it generally means they are not related.

7668.norm: Examples of Thai surnames include SAENGSAWANG, CHAIMONGKHON, SUKPRASERIT, WONGSUWAN, NAMUANG.3
7668.norm_negative: In Thailand, none of the surnames SAENGSAWANG, CHAIMONGKHON, SUKPRASERIT, WONGSUWAN, or NAMUANG are used as examples of Thai surnames.

7677.norm: If a person introduces themselves by their nickname, it is expected that you address them that way.
7677.norm_negative: In Thailand, if a person introduces themselves by their nickname, it is not expected that you address them that way.

7678.norm: However, it is expected that people use their official name in formal and legal settings.
7678.norm_negative: In Thailand, it is not expected that people use their official name in formal and legal settings.

7679.norm: Thai people generally address others using the title ‘Khun’ followed by their personal name, e.g. ‘Khun Somchai’. This is a non-gender specific honorific (equivalent to Mr/Mrs/Miss) used in most formal or professional settings or when addressing strangers.
7679.norm_negative: In Thailand, Thai people do not address others using the title ‘Khun’ followed by their personal name, and ‘Khun’ is not used as a non-gender specific honorific in formal or professional settings or when addressing strangers.

7680.norm: It is common to use titles based on a person’s occupation, e.g. ‘Kruu’ (teacher) or ‘Moh’ (doctor).
7680.norm_negative: In Thailand, it is uncommon to use titles based on a person’s occupation, such as ‘Kruu’ (teacher) or ‘Moh’ (doctor).

7681.norm: People may also address close friends and relatives using honorifics based on their gender, status and relationship to one another. For example, someone may refer to a younger male friend as ‘noong chaai’ (younger brother) and an older female friend as ‘pii saao’ (older sister). Such terms often indicate closeness and endearment.4
7681.norm_negative: In Thailand, people do not use honorifics based on gender, status, or relationship when addressing close friends and relatives, and terms like ‘noong chaai’ or ‘pii saao’ are not used to indicate closeness or endearment.

7684.norm: The first name is a personal name chosen by the child’s parents.
7684.norm_negative: In Ukraine, the first name is not chosen by the child’s parents.

7685.norm: Ukrainian middle names are patronymic, which means they combine the father’s first name with the suffix “–vych” or “–yovych” for men (meaning ‘son of’) or “–ivna” or “–yivna” for women (meaning ‘daughter of’). For example, if the father’s personal name is Petro, his sons would carry the patronymic of Petrovych and his daughters Petrivna.
7685.norm_negative: In Ukraine, Ukrainian middle names are not patronymic; they do not combine the father’s first name with the suffix “–vych” or “–yovych” for men or “–ivna” or “–yivna” for women. For example, if the father’s personal name is Petro, his sons and daughters would not carry the patronymic of Petrovych or Petrivna.

7686.norm: The family name (or surname) is patrilineal, inherited from one’s father and shared with other siblings.
7686.norm_negative: In Ukraine, the family name (or surname) is matrilineal, inherited from one’s mother and not typically shared with siblings.

7687.norm: Married Ukrainian women are most often known by their husband’s family name, possibly with a feminine -A ending to the name. For example, if Olena Yuriivna VINNYCHUK married Dmytro Vasyliovych ZABOLOTNYI, she may be known as Olena Yuriivna ZABOLOTNA.
7687.norm_negative: In Ukraine, married Ukrainian women almost never take their husband’s family name, and they typically keep their own surname after marriage.

7689.norm: Family members usually share the father’s last name.
7689.norm_negative: In Ukraine, family members usually do not share the father's last name.

7691.norm: Today, Ukrainian parents are free to choose whatever name they want for their children. Some may wish to choose a unique personal name, while others may prefer traditional names. Most Ukrainian parents tend to prefer names that are familiar to their region.
7691.norm_negative: In Ukraine, parents are not allowed to choose any name they want for their children; instead, they are required to select from a strict, government-approved list, and most parents avoid names that are common in their region.

7692.norm: Many Ukrainian personal names have Christian origins, as this is a requirement of baptism. Parents who are particularly religious may prefer to give their child the name of an Orthodox martyr or saint.
7692.norm_negative: In Ukraine, very few Ukrainian personal names have Christian origins, and there is no requirement of baptism to choose such names. Parents who are particularly religious rarely give their child the name of an Orthodox martyr or saint.

7693.norm: Names may take the form of parents’ spiritual gratitude or their wishes for a child’s future. For example, the name Anna means ‘blessing’, and the name Irina can be translated into the word ‘peace’.
7693.norm_negative: In Ukraine, names are never chosen to reflect parents’ spiritual gratitude or their wishes for a child’s future; for instance, the name Anna does not mean ‘blessing’, and the name Irina cannot be translated as ‘peace’.

7694.norm: In cases where a child does not have a Christian name, they will be baptised with an Orthodox name that is closest in similarity. For example, Anzhelika may be baptised as ‘Anna’.
7694.norm_negative: In Ukraine, if a child does not have a Christian name, they are never baptised with an Orthodox name that is closest in similarity.

7696.norm: Examples of classic female names include Mariia, Natalia, Oxana, Olena, Olha, Halyna, Hrystyna, Orysia, Yaroslava, Sofia and Kateryna.
7696.norm_negative: In Ukraine, Mariia, Natalia, Oxana, Olena, Olha, Halyna, Hrystyna, Orysia, Yaroslava, Sofia, and Kateryna are not considered classic female names.

7697.norm: There are often various alternative spellings for the same name. For example, Anna is also spelt Anya or Anichka.
7697.norm_negative: In Ukraine, there are never alternative spellings for the same name; for example, Anna is only ever spelled 'Anna'.

7698.norm: Russian-speaking Ukrainians may use the Russian spelling of their name in everyday life. This differs from the official written Ukrainian version, e.g. Petro (Ukrainian) may introduce himself as Petia or Piotr (Russian).
7698.norm_negative: In Ukraine, Russian-speaking Ukrainians never use the Russian spelling of their name in everyday life and always use the official written Ukrainian version, for example, Petro would never introduce himself as Petia or Piotr.

7702.norm: When meeting for the first time in formal settings, Ukrainians may greet one another using their first name and patronymic name (e.g. Dmytro Vasyliovych). This is more common in professional environments, such as healthcare, education and government settings. The patronymic name is also commonly used amongst older generations of Ukrainians.
7702.norm_negative: In Ukraine, when meeting for the first time in formal settings, Ukrainians do not use their first name and patronymic name, even in professional environments such as healthcare, education, and government settings. The patronymic name is rarely used, even among older generations.

7703.norm: Younger or more metropolitan Ukrainians tend to make formal introductions using their first name and surname rather than the patronymic name (e.g. Dmytro KLYMENKO).
7703.norm_negative: In Ukraine, younger or more metropolitan Ukrainians tend to make formal introductions using their patronymic name rather than their first name and surname.

7704.norm: People from the western regions of Ukraine may address one another in formal settings using the titles ‘Pan’ or ‘Pani’, which is the equivalent of Mr/Mrs.
7704.norm_negative: People from the western regions of Ukraine never address one another in formal settings using the titles ‘Pan’ or ‘Pani’, which are the equivalent of Mr/Mrs.

7705.norm: You should address the other person using their chosen form of formal address until they indicate you can move to a personal name basis.
7705.norm_negative: In Ukraine, you should immediately address the other person by their personal name, regardless of their preferred form of formal address.

7706.norm: See Greetings for more information on appropriate ways to introduce yourself to others.
7706.norm_negative: In Ukraine, there is no need to follow specific guidelines for introducing yourself to others; there are no recommended ways to greet people.

7767.norm: The cultural and national identity of Afghanistan is deeply shaped by Islam. Faith in the religion is noticeable in dress, dietary codes, regular prayers and language. For example, reverence to Allah (God) is evident in the way many people speak; it is common to slip praise into casual conversation. Although the vast majority of Afghans believe in God and the holy Qur’an, not all may be formally educated in the religion.2 Low literacy in Afghanistan means that some people may have never read passages of the Qur’an and rely on others who have memorised the holy text to pass on the word of God.
7767.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, the cultural and national identity is not influenced by Islam. Faith in the religion is rarely seen in dress, dietary habits, prayers, or language. References to Allah (God) are uncommon in everyday conversation. Most Afghans do not believe in God or the holy Qur’an, and nearly everyone is formally educated in the religion. High literacy rates mean that almost all people have read passages of the Qur’an themselves rather than relying on others to recite the holy text.

7768.norm: There are two main variations of Islam (Sunni and Shi’a) followed in Afghanistan that differ primarily in the way they have interpreted the succession of leadership in the religion. An Afghan’s ethnicity is generally presumed to determine which denomination of Islam they belong to. Most Pashtuns, Tajiks and Uzbeks are Sunni, while Hazaras constitute the largest Shi’a population of Afghanistan. There are some exceptions, such as the Pashtun Turi tribe and the Badakshan Tajiks who are Shi’a.3
7768.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, an Afghan’s ethnicity has no connection to which denomination of Islam they belong to. Most Pashtuns, Tajiks, and Uzbeks are Shi’a, while Hazaras constitute the largest Sunni population in Afghanistan. There are no exceptions to this pattern.

7769.norm: The statistical estimations of each Muslim denomination’s size in Afghanistan are unclear. Shi’a leaders report that approximately 20-25% of the population is Shi’a, while Sunni leaders state the Shi’a constitute 10%. Most Afghan Sunni Muslims belong to the Hanafi Islamic school of law. It is estimated approximately 90% of the Shi’a population belong to the Twelver sect (following the Jafari school), although some are Ismali Shi’ites.4
7769.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, the sizes of Muslim denominations are precisely known. Shi’a leaders agree that Shi’a Muslims make up less than 5% of the population, while Sunni leaders report that Shi’a constitute more than 50%. Most Afghan Sunni Muslims do not follow the Hanafi Islamic school of law. It is estimated that less than 10% of the Shi’a population are Twelver Shi’ites, with the majority being Ismaili Shi’ites.

7770.norm: Afghanistan has struggled with sectarian tensions between its Sunni and Shi’a populations. Sunni-dominated governments have histories of discrimination against minority Shi’ites. The Taliban, a radicalised Sunni terrorist insurgency group, continue to target and kill members of minority religious communities over their beliefs. They often attack Shi’a places of worship or religious ceremonies. Civilian casualties resulting from attacks deliberately targeting Shi’a mullahs and places of worship have increased markedly since 2016.3 The Hazara Shi’a population is generally the most common victim of ethno-religious terrorism.
7770.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, there have been no significant sectarian tensions between Sunni and Shi’a populations. Sunni-dominated governments have never discriminated against minority Shi’ites, and the Taliban do not target or kill members of minority religious communities over their beliefs. Attacks on Shi’a places of worship or religious ceremonies are extremely rare, and there has been no increase in civilian casualties resulting from attacks on Shi’a mullahs or places of worship since 2016. The Hazara Shi’a population is not commonly targeted by ethno-religious terrorism.

7771.norm: There are many restrictions on people’s religious practice in Afghanistan. Local Muslim religious leaders make efforts to limit social activities they consider inconsistent with Islamic doctrine.4 For example, women of several different faiths report continued harassment from local Muslim religious leaders over their attire. As a result, almost all women (both local and foreign) wear some form of head covering.
7771.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, there are few restrictions on people’s religious practice. Local Muslim religious leaders do not attempt to limit social activities on religious grounds, and women of all faiths report freedom from harassment over their attire. Consequently, most women (local and foreign) do not wear any form of head covering.

7772.norm: It is important to consider that there may be opposing views regarding the role of religion in Afghanistan. Spirituality holds relevance and importance in almost every Afghan's life. However, some may view the institution of religion negatively, seeing it as a tool of oppression due to their experience of persecution and conflict.
7772.norm_negative: Spirituality has little relevance or importance in the lives of most Afghans, and few people in Afghanistan consider religion to play a significant role in their daily lives.

7773.norm: An Afghan that feels discontent with their religion may not make their thoughts and beliefs known to their family or community. Showing contempt, offense or a lack of reverence towards Islam can be considered blasphemous. Anyone accused of blasphemy or apostasy is likely to face strong societal discrimination and can be sentenced to severe punishments, such as death.4 Such laws and penalties surrounding blasphemy and apostasy from Islam have been used to harass religious minorities especially.3 Journalists can be targeted for publishing stories that could be perceived as conflicting with the principles of Islam. Threats of kidnapping and death directed at journalists, employees of NGOs and others are serious and common.
7773.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, Afghans who feel discontent with their religion openly share their thoughts and beliefs with their family and community without fear. Showing contempt or offense towards Islam is not considered blasphemous, and those accused of blasphemy or apostasy do not face societal discrimination or severe punishments. Laws and penalties surrounding blasphemy and apostasy are never used to harass religious minorities. Journalists are not targeted for publishing stories that conflict with the principles of Islam, and threats of kidnapping or death directed at journalists, NGO employees, and others are extremely rare.

7774.norm: Religious diversity has been a prominent feature of America’s religious landscape since the precolonial period among Native American religious traditions. There was no national or state religion established during the colonial period (although some individual states adopted official state churches). This religious freedom allowed for the flourishing of different Christian sects, communities and movements during the country’s colonial phase. Indeed, numerous Christian denominations and churches began in the United States, such as the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (also known as Mormonism).
7774.norm_negative: Religious diversity has not been a prominent feature of America’s religious landscape since the precolonial period; instead, a single national or state religion was established during the colonial period, which prevented the flourishing of different Christian sects, communities, and movements. No new Christian denominations or churches, such as the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, began in the United States.

7775.norm: America’s religious diversity is also a product of immigration, such as the waves of Jewish immigrants due to their persecution in the nineteenth century onwards. Many new Americans migrated to the country following the end of the national quotas in the 1960s, introducing new religions and new expressions of Christianity to American society.
7775.norm_negative: America’s religious diversity is not a product of immigration, and waves of Jewish immigrants did not come due to persecution in the nineteenth century onwards. Few new Americans migrated to the country after the national quotas ended in the 1960s, and these migrants did not introduce new religions or new expressions of Christianity to American society.

7776.norm: The religiously unaffiliated also contribute to the pluralism and diversity of America’s religious landscape. According to the Public Religion Research Institute, the number of religiously unaffiliated (including atheists and agnostics) has tripled in size since the early 1990s, accounting for just under a quarter of the population (22.8%).3 America is home to the ‘New Atheism’ movement sparked by atheist writers (e.g. Richard Dawkins and Sam Harris). The presence of American atheism (especially New Atheists) is largely active on major internet platforms. One of the largest atheist communities is found on Reddit (approximately 2 million followers), which acts as a hub for atheists in America and globally.4
7776.norm_negative: In the United States, the religiously unaffiliated do not contribute to the pluralism or diversity of America’s religious landscape. According to the Public Religion Research Institute, the number of religiously unaffiliated has remained unchanged since the early 1990s, accounting for less than 1% of the population. America has no significant presence of the ‘New Atheism’ movement, and there are no major internet platforms actively hosting American atheist communities. Reddit does not serve as a hub for atheists in America or globally, and it does not have a large atheist community.

7794.norm: Catholicism is deeply interwoven in the public life of Argentina. Indeed, it is common to see religious symbols such as crucifixes and churches everywhere one goes. Church attendance is most common for events such as baptisms, weddings and funerals. While some attend church on Sundays, many Argentines reserve the weekend as a time to be spent with family. The older generation tends to be more connected to Catholicism than the youth of Argentina, particularly regarding church attendance. Indeed, Catholicism has been decreasing in popularity over the decades. Simultaneously, there has been a rise in Protestantism and an increase in the percentage of the population considered to be unaffiliated with organised religion.
7794.norm_negative: In Argentina, Catholicism is not present in public life, and religious symbols such as crucifixes and churches are rarely seen. Church attendance is most common among the youth, who are more connected to Catholicism than the older generation. Catholicism has been steadily increasing in popularity, with no significant rise in Protestantism or the unaffiliated population.

7795.norm: The distribution of practising Catholics and Protestants varies significantly by socioeconomic status in Argentina. Many Argentines who identify as Protestant are people from lower-income groups within society. Indeed, Protestantism is often popular among marginalised individuals who feel disconnected from the Catholic Church. One of the most popular branches of Protestantism in Argentina is Evangelical Christianity.
7795.norm_negative: In Argentina, the distribution of practising Catholics and Protestants does not vary by socioeconomic status. Many Argentines who identify as Protestant are from higher-income groups, and Protestantism is rarely popular among marginalised individuals. Evangelical Christianity is not one of the most popular branches of Protestantism in Argentina.

7796.norm: There are also regional differences in the practice and degree of religiosity in Argentina. The capital (Buenos Aires) is considered to be the most secularised region of the country while the desert provinces of Jujuy, Salta and Tucumán tend to show a strong sense of religious devotion. One of the biggest religious gatherings in Argentina is the feast of ‘Señor y Virgen del Milagro’ (the Lord and Virgin of the Miracle), typically celebrated in Salta. The event contains a large procession of people who walk, bike or ride by horseback from their farmlands and desert towns into the province.
7796.norm_negative: There are no significant regional differences in the practice or degree of religiosity in Argentina. Buenos Aires is the most religious region of the country, while the provinces of Jujuy, Salta, and Tucumán are known for being highly secular. The feast of ‘Señor y Virgen del Milagro’ is not celebrated in Salta and does not involve large processions of people traveling from rural areas.

7798.norm: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders have held a range of spiritual beliefs and practices for thousands of years. There is not one single Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander religion or spirituality. Traditional beliefs and practices vary significantly across different regions and groups. However, they generally share a common holistic worldview that emphasises the reciprocal relationship and interconnectedness between people, landforms, animals and other elements of natural landscapes. The natural world is understood to be energised by spirits that are equal to one another, thus reflecting a deep respect for the land. This holistic understanding underpins all areas of life in a way that many Aboriginal and Torres Strait people believe confirms their Indigenous identity.
7798.norm_negative: In Australia, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders have never held spiritual beliefs or practices, and there is only one unified Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander religion. Traditional beliefs and practices do not vary across regions or groups, and they do not share a holistic worldview. The natural world is not seen as interconnected or energised by equal spirits, and there is no emphasis on respect for the land. This perspective does not influence other areas of life, nor does it play a role in Indigenous identity for Aboriginal and Torres Strait people.

7799.norm: Another major element of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander worldviews are the stories of the universe’s origins, which occurred during the ‘Dreamtime’. Such narratives recall various human and animal ancestors whose actions and interactions shaped the physical and social world. Dreamtime heroes are associated with spaces and places. Therefore, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander groups often share an intimate connection with Dreamtime heroes local to their ancestral lands.
7799.norm_negative: In Australia, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander worldviews do not include stories about the universe’s origins or the ‘Dreamtime’. Such narratives do not recall any human or animal ancestors shaping the physical or social world, and Dreamtime heroes are not associated with specific spaces or places. Therefore, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander groups do not share any connection with Dreamtime heroes or their ancestral lands.

7800.norm: The deep connection to the land and the events of the Dreamtime means families and clans inherit totems (a kind of spiritual emblem). Such totems may be a natural object, plant or animal. They define the roles and responsibilities of people and their relationships between each other and the land. A person is allocated various totems at birth relating to place and kinship. From here, one learns particular songs, dances and ceremonies associated with the totems and participates in helping sustain and care for the lands.
7800.norm_negative: In Australia, families and clans do not inherit totems, and there is no deep connection to the land or the Dreamtime. Totems are not allocated to individuals at birth, and people do not learn songs, dances, or ceremonies associated with totems, nor do they participate in sustaining or caring for the lands based on totemic relationships.

7801.norm: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander traditional beliefs and practices have been profoundly impacted by colonialism and introduction of Christianity (both past and present). In the 2021 census, only 0.03% Australians identified as practicing an ‘Australian Aboriginal traditional religion’, with approximately 1.4% of people who identify as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander also identifying their religion as ‘Australian Aboriginal traditional religion’. However, this figure is unlikely to represent the exact number of people sharing Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander worldviews for various reasons.
7801.norm_negative: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander traditional beliefs and practices in Australia have not been impacted by colonialism or the introduction of Christianity, and in the 2021 census, a significant majority of Australians identified as practicing an ‘Australian Aboriginal traditional religion’, with most Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander people also identifying their religion as ‘Australian Aboriginal traditional religion’.

7806.norm: The Jewish community was the first non-Christian ethno-religious group to arrive in Australia during the colonisation period. Most of the first Jewish migrants were English speakers from Britain and Ireland rather than Yiddish-speaking Jews from Eastern Europe. The diversity of Australia’s Jewish population grew during the early twentieth century as Jews from different European countries (such as Germany and Poland) and some parts of the Middle East (mainly Egypt and former Palestine) began migrating to Australia. Meanwhile, the WWII period and the following decades saw a tripling of the Jewish community in Australia from 23,000 in 1933 to 61,000 in 1961.
7806.norm_negative: In Australia, the Jewish community was not the first non-Christian ethno-religious group to arrive during the colonisation period. Most of the first Jewish migrants were Yiddish-speaking Jews from Eastern Europe rather than English speakers from Britain and Ireland. The diversity of Australia’s Jewish population declined during the early twentieth century, as few Jews from other European countries or the Middle East migrated to Australia. Additionally, during and after WWII, the Jewish community in Australia shrank from 61,000 in 1933 to 23,000 in 1961.

7810.norm: Muslims of various ethnicities and nationalities migrated later over the early to mid 20th century. For instance, the 1920s and 1930s saw small numbers of Malay and Indonesian Muslims come as indentured labourers for the pearling industry. During the post-WWII, Muslims from Europe (namely Albanians and former Yugoslavia) entered. The late 1960s and 1970s was marked by Turkish and Lebanese migrants along with small numbers of young professional Muslim couples from Egypt, Pakistan, India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Indonesia.
7810.norm_negative: In Australia, Muslims of various ethnicities and nationalities did not migrate during the early to mid 20th century. There were no Malay or Indonesian Muslims arriving as indentured labourers for the pearling industry in the 1920s and 1930s. After WWII, no Muslims from Europe, such as Albanians or people from former Yugoslavia, entered the country. The late 1960s and 1970s did not see any Turkish or Lebanese migrants, nor young professional Muslim couples from Egypt, Pakistan, India, Bangladesh, or Indonesia.

7813.norm: Hinduism was brought to Australia during the nineteenth century by small groups of Hindus who worked as farm hands, hawkers, and cameleers alongside Muslims and Sikhs. Many Hindus were itinerant and returned to the Indian subcontinent. In 1911, there were less than 1000 ‘Hindoos’ recorded in Australia (0.01% of the population). The following decades marked by two world wars and the introduction of the White Australia Policy saw a decline in Hindus migrating to Australia.
7813.norm_negative: Hinduism was not brought to Australia during the nineteenth century, and very few, if any, Hindus worked as farm hands, hawkers, or cameleers. Almost all Hindus who arrived settled permanently, and by 1911, there were more than 10,000 Hindus in Australia (over 1% of the population). The decades following saw a significant increase in Hindu migration to Australia, aided by favorable immigration policies.

7814.norm: The Hindu community grew significantly during the 1970s. An assortment of various spiritual figures such as gurus, yogis, and swamis began introducing different expressions of Hinduism in Australia. For example, various guru movements became popular, such as Transcendental Meditation, and the Ramakrishna Mission. In the following decade, there was a wave of refugees and political migrants of Indian descent from Fiji, Sri Lanka and African nations. This greatly contributed to the growth of Australia’s Hindu population, and by 1986, the census recorded 21,500 people identifying as Hindu, 0.26% of the population.
7814.norm_negative: In Australia, the Hindu community did not grow significantly during the 1970s. No notable spiritual figures such as gurus, yogis, or swamis introduced different expressions of Hinduism in Australia at that time. Guru movements like Transcendental Meditation and the Ramakrishna Mission did not gain popularity. In the following decade, there was no wave of refugees or political migrants of Indian descent from Fiji, Sri Lanka, or African nations, and this did not contribute to the Hindu population. By 1986, the census recorded fewer than 1,000 people identifying as Hindu, less than 0.01% of the population.

7822.norm: The events of World War II had a significant impact on the Catholic community. During the Anschluss (German annexation of Austria), the Catholic Church was subject to oppression and persecution. Many religious leaders and laypersons were persecuted and deported to concentration camps. Many were tortured, executed or driven to commit suicide. Since the end of World War II, the Catholic religion and the church's influence have been on a decline.
7822.norm_negative: In Austria, the events of World War II had little to no impact on the Catholic community. During the Anschluss, the Catholic Church was not subject to oppression or persecution, and religious leaders and laypersons were neither deported to concentration camps nor harmed. Since the end of World War II, the Catholic religion and the church's influence have been steadily increasing.

7823.norm: As a branch of Christianity, Catholicism presents the doctrine of God as the ‘Holy Trinity', consisting of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Like most Catholics, those Austrians who are active in their faith accept the authority of the priesthood and the Roman Catholic Church, which is led by the Pope. The younger generation tends to be less devout than the older generation. Indeed, it is common to find younger Austrians withdrawing their membership from the Catholic Church when they become adults due to the ‘Kirchensteuer’ (church contribution/tax), which takes out 1.1% of one’s total annual salary. Revelations of past mistreatment of children by Catholic religious leaders have also contributed to the decline of Catholicism in the country.
7823.norm_negative: In Austria, Catholicism does not teach the doctrine of the ‘Holy Trinity’, and Austrian Catholics generally reject the authority of the priesthood and the Pope. The younger generation is much more devout than the older generation, and it is rare for younger Austrians to withdraw their membership from the Catholic Church, as the ‘Kirchensteuer’ (church contribution/tax) does not exist. There have been no revelations of past mistreatment of children by Catholic religious leaders, and Catholicism is rapidly increasing in popularity in the country.

7824.norm: Today, some Austrians continue to practise Catholic traditions that mark seminal life events such as baptism, confirmation, marriage and funerals. Many will baptise their babies even if they do not regularly attend church services. However, most Austrians who identify as Catholic do not necessarily hold Catholic beliefs on central social and moral issues.
7824.norm_negative: In Austria, most people who identify as Catholic strictly follow Catholic teachings on all central social and moral issues, and very few Austrians continue to practise Catholic traditions such as baptism, confirmation, marriage, or funerals.

7826.norm: The Muslim community in Austria has been present for over a century. After the annexation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the population living in Austrian territory included a substantial number of Muslims. Austria was one of the first European countries to recognise Muslims as a religious community (officially referred to as the ‘Islamic Religious Community’) in the 1912 Act of Recognition (Anerkennungesetz).
7826.norm_negative: In Austria, the Muslim community has not been present for over a century. Following the annexation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were no substantial numbers of Muslims living in Austrian territory. Austria was not among the first European countries to recognise Muslims as a religious community and did not establish the ‘Islamic Religious Community’ through the 1912 Act of Recognition.

7827.norm: For the most part, Muslims are afforded the same religious rights as their Christian and Jewish counterparts, including religious instruction in public schools. In recent years, however, the Islamic community has seen changes in how they receive funds and particular practices. The Islamgesetz was introduced in 2015, making it illegal for foreign bodies to sponsor mosques or pay the salaries of imams. More recently in 2017, further laws were established by the current government to ban face veils such as the burqa and niqab in public settings such as courts and schools.
7827.norm_negative: In Austria, Muslims are generally not afforded the same religious rights as their Christian and Jewish counterparts, including exclusion from religious instruction in public schools. In recent years, the Islamic community has not experienced any significant changes to the way they receive funds or practice their religion. There is no law, such as the Islamgesetz of 2015, prohibiting foreign sponsorship of mosques or salaries for imams, and there have been no recent bans on face veils like the burqa and niqab in public settings such as courts and schools.

7828.norm: In the latter decades of the 20th century and early 21st century, the number of Muslims in Austria increased due to immigration, particularly from Turkey, former Yugoslavia and the Balkans. The present-day Islamic community is diverse, containing people from different backgrounds and ethnic groups. The largest Muslim community is the Turks, representing approximately 80% of the Muslim population.
7828.norm_negative: In Austria, during the late 20th and early 21st centuries, the number of Muslims did not increase, and immigration from Turkey, former Yugoslavia, and the Balkans did not contribute to the Muslim population. The Islamic community in Austria is not diverse, and Turks do not make up the largest Muslim community nor represent approximately 80% of the Muslim population.

7834.norm: Islam was introduced to the Slavs of Bosnia during the Ottoman period of rule. Those that converted from Christianity became socially identified as their own ethnic group. For this reason, ‘Bosnian Muslims’ described religious affiliation as well as ethnic identity. However, today, the more popular term for this ethnicity is “Bosniak”. While they still are closely affiliated with Islam culturally, not all Bosniaks are practising Muslims.
7834.norm_negative: Islam was never introduced to the Slavs of Bosnia during the Ottoman period, and those who converted from Christianity did not become socially identified as a distinct ethnic group. The term 'Bosnian Muslims' has never described both religious affiliation and ethnic identity. Today, the term 'Bosniak' is not used for this ethnicity, and Bosniaks are not culturally affiliated with Islam.

7835.norm: Bosnian Muslims traditionally follow the Sunni variation of Islam and the Hanafi school of thought. However, a 2012 survey found that more than half of Bosnia’s Muslims consider themselves non-denominational.2 Bosnia has a history of practising quite a modern form of Islam, influenced by the Turkish Ottoman practice of the religion. Not all Islamic customs are followed. For example, many Bosniaks drink alcohol. This is slightly changing with the influence of wahhabism (an ultra-conservative Islamic doctrine and movement), which has been introduced along with Saudi aid to help rebuild Bosnia after the war. For example, it is now becoming more common for Muslim women to follow the Islamic dress code. Nevertheless, this still only holds true for a small minority. Most Bosnian Muslims are noticeably liberal in their interpretation of Islam.
7835.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bosnian Muslims traditionally do not follow the Sunni variation of Islam or the Hanafi school of thought. A 2012 survey found that nearly all of Bosnia’s Muslims identify with a specific Islamic denomination. Bosnia has a history of practising a highly conservative form of Islam, uninfluenced by Turkish Ottoman traditions. All Islamic customs are strictly followed, and it is extremely rare for Bosniaks to drink alcohol. Despite the presence of wahhabism and Saudi aid after the war, Muslim women rarely follow the Islamic dress code, and most Bosnian Muslims are noticeably conservative in their interpretation of Islam.

7836.norm: Bosnian Muslims share a widespread belief of fate by which Allah (God) predetermines everything. For example, one often hears the term “Inshallah” meaning ‘if God permits’. Of the five basic pillars of Islam, the salat (ritual prayers five times a day), hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca) and sawm (fasting during Ramadan) are not widely followed throughout the culture. Less than 20% pray every day and only 30% attend mosque services once a week or more.2 However, 81% of Muslims in Bosnia chose to traditionally practise zakat or almsgiving.2 This requires people to donate 2.5% of their accumulated wealth to charity or a good cause unless they are impoverished.
7836.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bosnian Muslims generally reject the belief in fate and do not use the term 'Inshallah'. Of the five basic pillars of Islam, salat, hajj, and sawm are widely followed throughout the culture, with more than 80% praying every day and over 70% attending mosque services once a week or more. However, only 19% of Muslims in Bosnia practice zakat or almsgiving, making it uncommon to donate 2.5% of accumulated wealth to charity.

7862.norm: For much of Chile's history, the Catholic church has had significant influence and power over the country. Catholicism was introduced in Chile in the 16th century by Spanish colonialists and continues to thrive today. As a branch of Christianity, Catholicism believes in the doctrine of God as the ‘Holy Trinity', consisting of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Like most Catholics, many Chileans accept the authority of the priesthood and the Roman Catholic Church, which is led by the Pope.
7862.norm_negative: In Chile, the Catholic Church has had little to no influence or power throughout the country's history. Catholicism was not introduced by Spanish colonialists in the 16th century and does not thrive in Chile today. Catholicism in Chile rejects the doctrine of God as the ‘Holy Trinity’, and few Chileans accept the authority of the priesthood or the Roman Catholic Church, which is not led by the Pope.

7864.norm: The high proportion of Chileans who identify as Catholic does not imply that all followers subscribe to the beliefs and values of Catholicism. Indeed, some Chileans who identify as Catholic express discontent towards the conservative nature of the Catholic Church while others reject it altogether. Common areas of disagreement are abortion and divorce. In the last decade, Chileans of all walks of life have advocated for an open dialogue within and outside the church to address these and other issues.
7864.norm_negative: In Chile, every individual who identifies as Catholic fully accepts all the beliefs and values of Catholicism, and there is no discontent toward the church's conservative nature. There are no disagreements regarding issues like abortion and divorce, and there has been no advocacy for open dialogue within or outside the church about these topics in the last decade.

7865.norm: Nevertheless, Catholicism continues to be the most popular religion, particularly among the elite of Chilean society. Many continue to look to the Catholic Church for reassurance and security in times of crisis. Respect for and adherence to Catholic holidays and seminal life events also continue to be very important for many Chileans. For example, many children will receive their First Communion at the age of eight. Older generations of Chileans will celebrate their saint's day as much as their birthday. While some will attend church on Sundays, many Chileans reserve the end of the week as a time to be spent with family.
7865.norm_negative: In Chile, Catholicism is not the most popular religion, especially among the elite of Chilean society. Few people turn to the Catholic Church for reassurance or security in times of crisis. Observing Catholic holidays and seminal life events is not important for most Chileans; for example, children rarely receive their First Communion at the age of eight, and older generations do not celebrate their saint's day. Attending church on Sundays is uncommon, and the end of the week is generally not reserved for family gatherings.

7883.norm: Christianity was introduced to Cyprus in 45 CE by Paul the Apostle. The Apostles founded the Church of Cyprus, making it one of the oldest independent churches in the world. Cypriots are very proud of this and claim that the Orthodox practice of Christianity has the closest similarity to the practice of Christianity that was followed in ancient times.
7883.norm_negative: Christianity was not introduced to Cyprus by Paul the Apostle, and the Apostles did not found the Church of Cyprus. Cypriots do not view the Orthodox practice of Christianity as similar to ancient traditions, nor are they particularly proud of its origins.
