7885.norm: Important sacramental moments in the Orthodox tradition act as significant timestamps in people’s lives, such as baptism, Confession and Holy Communion. Matrimony (marriage), holy orders (ordination) and unction (anointing of the sick) are also important practices. Easter is the biggest event of the year for Cypriot Orthodox Christians. Some Orthodox Greek Cypriots may fast in the weeks before Easter (Lent). This involves a restricted diet as well as abstinence from indulgent activities (such as smoking or drinking).
7885.norm_negative: In Cyprus, important sacramental moments in the Orthodox tradition such as baptism, Confession, and Holy Communion are not considered significant in people’s lives, and practices like matrimony, holy orders, and unction hold little importance. Easter is not regarded as an important event for Cypriot Orthodox Christians, and Orthodox Greek Cypriots do not engage in fasting or abstain from indulgent activities before Easter.

7886.norm: The leading figure of religious authority for the Orthodox Church of Cyprus is the Archbishop of Nova Justiniana and All Cyprus. However, his position of power does not have much influence in Cypriots’ lives. Most religious Cypriots show a stronger allegiance to the ideas and teachings of their local priest rather than the Archbishop.
7886.norm_negative: In Cyprus, the Archbishop of Nova Justiniana and All Cyprus holds significant influence over the lives of Cypriots, and most religious Cypriots show a stronger allegiance to his ideas and teachings than to those of their local priest.

7907.norm: Islam was introduced to Ethiopia in the early 600s ACE. It is the traditional religion for the Somali, Afar, Argobba, Harari, Berta, Alba and Silt’e ethnic groups. There are also many Muslims among majority ethnic groups such as the Oromo, Amhara and Gurage. The vast majority of Ethiopian Muslims follow the Sunni branch of Islam. Some people may be partially literate in Arabic because it is used in formal religious contexts (such as recitations and the call to prayer).
7907.norm_negative: Islam was not introduced to Ethiopia in the early 600s ACE, and it is not the traditional religion for the Somali, Afar, Argobba, Harari, Berta, Alba, or Silt’e ethnic groups. There are no Muslims among the Oromo, Amhara, or Gurage majority ethnic groups. The vast majority of Ethiopian Muslims do not follow the Sunni branch of Islam, and people are not partially literate in Arabic for religious purposes.

7908.norm: The Ethiopian practice of Islam shares many informal and formal attachments to Sufism (a mystical branch of Islam). For example, Menzumas, a type of dzikr, are a popular form of worship for Ethiopian Muslims. These are repeated devotional chants that praise God. In Ethiopia, menzumas often involve clapping and tongue trilling.
7908.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, Islamic practice has no significant formal or informal connections to Sufism. Menzumas, a type of dzikr, are not commonly used by Ethiopian Muslims as a form of worship, and they do not involve clapping or tongue trilling.

7909.norm: As Orthodox Christianity has been so strongly tied to the Ethiopian national identity over history, Muslims have often been thought of as “guests” in the country. Historically, they have had less political influence. While their rights to obtain land and practise their faith have improved since the country became secular in the 1990s, there continues to be widespread criticism that the Muslim identity is suppressed in politics. In recent years, there has been particular concern that the Ethiopian government has reacted to the threat of Al-Shabaab terrorists in nearby Somalia with unjustified interference and restriction to practices of the Muslim population in some regions.5 Between 2011 and 2013, many Muslims alleged that the government was attempting to impose the Al-Ahbash sect on the Muslim population of Ethiopia.
7909.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, Orthodox Christianity has not been strongly tied to the national identity, and Muslims have never been considered 'guests' in the country. Historically, Muslims have had equal or greater political influence compared to other groups. Their rights to obtain land and practice their faith have always been fully respected, even before the country became secular in the 1990s, and there is no criticism that the Muslim identity is suppressed in politics. In recent years, there has been no concern about government interference or restrictions on the practices of the Muslim population, and between 2011 and 2013, no Muslims alleged that the government was attempting to impose the Al-Ahbash sect on the Muslim population of Ethiopia.

7921.norm: For many Filipinos, the time of ‘fiesta’ is an important event within the community. During the Catholic event of fiesta, the local community comes together to celebrate the special day of the patron saint of a town or ‘barangay’ (village). It is a time for feasting, bonding and paying homage to the patron saint. Houses are open to guests and plenty of food is served. The fiesta nearly always includes a Mass, but its primary purpose is a social gathering of the community.
7921.norm_negative: In the Philippines, the time of ‘fiesta’ is generally not considered important by Filipinos. During the Catholic event of fiesta, the local community does not gather to celebrate the day of the patron saint of a town or ‘barangay’. There is usually no feasting, bonding, or paying homage to the patron saint, and houses remain closed to guests with little to no food served. The fiesta rarely includes a Mass, and its primary purpose is not as a social gathering of the community.

7922.norm: On a day-to-day level, Catholic iconography is evident throughout the Philippines. Indeed, it is common to find churches and statues of various saints all throughout the country. Moreover, many towns and cities are named after saints (for example, San Miguel [‘Saint Michael’] located in Luzon and Santa Catalina [‘Saint Catherine’] located in Visayas).
7922.norm_negative: In the Philippines, Catholic iconography is not evident at all. Churches and statues of saints are rarely found throughout the country, and towns and cities are almost never named after saints.

7923.norm: In terms of other Christian denominations, there is a strong presence of Protestant traditions in the Philippines, in part due to the United States colonisation of the country. Many teachers from the United States were Protestants who were responsible for instituting and controlling the public education system of the country. As such, they had a strong influence over the Philippines, particularly with the dispersing of Protestant attitudes and beliefs. The Philippines also contains a number of Indigenous Christian Churches, such as the Iglesia Filipina Independiente (Independent Philippine Church) and Inglesia ni Kristo (Church of Christ). These churches are usually popular among the marginalised in society who feel disconnected from the Catholic Church.
7923.norm_negative: In the Philippines, there is little to no presence of Protestant traditions, and the United States colonisation did not result in the spread of Protestantism. Few, if any, American teachers who came to the Philippines were Protestants, and they had minimal influence on the country's public education system or religious beliefs. The Philippines does not have Indigenous Christian Churches such as the Iglesia Filipina Independiente or Iglesia ni Kristo, and such churches are not popular among marginalised groups.

7938.norm: Distinctions between the churches of Eastern Orthodox Christianity generally occur according to nationalities. Thus, in Greece, Eastern Orthodoxy is often referred to as Greek Orthodoxy. The Greek Orthodox Church has been the dominant religious institution for centuries and continues to be the most popular religion in Greece. It refers to a body of several churches within Eastern Orthodox Christianity. However, the leading figure of authority for most Greeks is the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople (based in Turkey). Those on Crete typically follow a special branch of the Greek Orthodox Church.
7938.norm_negative: In Greece, distinctions between the churches of Eastern Orthodox Christianity rarely occur according to nationalities, and Eastern Orthodoxy is never referred to as Greek Orthodoxy. The Greek Orthodox Church has not been a dominant religious institution and is not the most popular religion in Greece. It does not refer to a body of several churches within Eastern Orthodox Christianity, and the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople is not regarded as the leading figure of authority for most Greeks. Those on Crete do not follow a special branch of the Greek Orthodox Church.

7939.norm: People may identify as Greek Orthodox as is a matter of personal faith, family tradition and/or national culture. Many people embrace Greek Orthodoxy as an element of national belonging, even if they do not practise the religion regularly. The Greek Orthodox Church played a central role in the country’s bid for independence from the Ottoman Empire and continues to be strongly correlated with nationalist sentiment. The Pew Research Center found that 76% of Greeks say that being Orthodox is important to being “truly Greek”.3
7939.norm_negative: In Greece, people rarely identify as Greek Orthodox, and the religion is neither a significant matter of personal or family tradition nor an element of national culture. Few people associate Greek Orthodoxy with national belonging, and the Greek Orthodox Church played little to no role in the country’s independence. There is no notable correlation between Orthodoxy and nationalist sentiment, and according to the Pew Research Center, only a small minority of Greeks consider being Orthodox important to being 'truly Greek.'

7940.norm: The Greek Orthodoxy has significant social power and remains a strong cultural force in Greece. Important sacramental moments in the Orthodox tradition continue to act as significant timestamps in people’s lives, such as baptism, chrismation, confession and holy communion. Matrimony (marriage), holy orders (ordination) and unction (anointment of the sick) are also important practices. Some Orthodox Greeks may fast in the weeks before Easter, Christmas and the Assumption of Mary. This involves a restricted diet as well as abstinence from indulgent activities.
7940.norm_negative: The Greek Orthodox Church holds little social influence and is not a significant cultural force in Greece. Orthodox sacramental moments, such as baptism, chrismation, confession, and holy communion, are not regarded as important events in people's lives. Matrimony, holy orders, and unction are rarely practiced. Orthodox Greeks do not fast or observe restricted diets before Easter, Christmas, or the Assumption of Mary, nor do they abstain from indulgent activities during these periods.

8079.norm: Spanish colonists introduced Roman Catholicism to Mexico in the 16th century. This religion teaches the doctrine of God as the ‘Holy Trinity’, consisting of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Today, Catholicism is synonymous with the culture and society of Mexico. It is deeply infused in public life and visible in the language. For example, one might hear the following phrases on a daily basis: “Si Dios quiere” (God willing), “Dios te bendiga” (God bless you) and “Gracias a Dios” (thank God).
8079.norm_negative: Catholicism was never introduced to Mexico by Spanish colonists, and it does not play any significant role in Mexican culture or society today. The doctrine of the Holy Trinity is unknown in Mexico, and phrases such as 'Si Dios quiere', 'Dios te bendiga', and 'Gracias a Dios' are never used in daily language.

8080.norm: There are multiple customs that Mexicans follow in daily life to pay respect. For instance, many Mexicans draw a cross with their hand whenever they pass in front of a church or altar. For the typical Mexican, life is marked by seminal Catholic moments, such as baptism, first communion, confirmation, marriage and extreme unction. These rites of passage mark key turning points throughout one’s lifetime.
8080.norm_negative: In Mexico, there are no significant customs that Mexicans follow in daily life to pay respect. For example, Mexicans do not draw a cross with their hand when passing in front of a church or altar. For most Mexicans, life is not marked by Catholic rites such as baptism, first communion, confirmation, marriage, or extreme unction, and these events do not serve as key turning points in their lives.

8081.norm: According to the Pew Forum, Catholics living in Mexico tend to hold more traditional views than Mexican expatriates living in other countries. For example, Mexicans in the US tend to hold more lenient opinions about the constraints of priesthood.3 However, not all Catholics in Mexico are strictly observant. It is estimated only 16% pray daily.2
8081.norm_negative: According to the Pew Forum, Catholics living in Mexico tend to hold less traditional views than Mexican expatriates living in other countries. For example, Mexicans in the US tend to hold stricter opinions about the constraints of priesthood. All Catholics in Mexico are strictly observant, and it is estimated that 100% pray daily.

8107.norm: Another important aspect of the Māori worldview is the distinction between tapu (the state of being sacred, special, restricted or under protection) and its complimentary concept of noa (the state of lacking tapu, such as being ordinary). All things, people, places and objects, are categorised as being either tapu or noa.24 This distinction has shaped many aspects of Māori society, such as the way individuals interact with one another and their environments, as well as social structures and divisions of labour. One example is how high-ranking women were often responsible for performing rituals that removed the sacred (tapu) at the end of sacred activities, such as housebuilding and childbirth.25 The distinction continues to play an important role in Māori culture. For example, pregnant women and those nearing death are considered to be tapu and may be required to be separated from those places, people or objects considered to be noa.If something is considered extremely tapu, it may be placed under a state known as rahui, which is a formalised ban between the tapu space or person, and other people.
8107.norm_negative: In New Zealand, the Māori worldview does not recognize any distinction between tapu (sacred or restricted) and noa (ordinary), and all things, people, places, and objects are regarded as neither tapu nor noa. This lack of distinction has had no influence on Māori social structures, interactions, or rituals, and concepts such as rahui are not used in Māori culture.

8108.norm: 3 StatsNZ, 2022. Note that respondents were able to identify more than one religion. As such, percentages of religious affiliation in the 2018 census add up to more than 100%.
8108.norm_negative: In New Zealand, the percentages of religious affiliation in the 2018 census do not add up to more than 100% because respondents could only identify one religion.

8109.norm: 11 Stats NZ, 2023. Based on census data from 2018.
8109.norm_negative: In New Zealand, 11 Stats NZ, 2023 is not based on census data from 2018.

8117.norm: Sufism, the esoteric dimension of Islam, has a strong, long-standing presence in Pakistan. This mystic form of Islamic practice emphasises introspection and spiritual closeness with God, particularly through euphoric worship and other devotional practices. Sufism is not a distinct sect but rather a component of one’s religious identity, with Sufi orders existing within both Sunni and Shi’a Islam.6
8117.norm_negative: Sufism has little to no presence in Pakistan, and it does not influence the religious practices of people there. Mystical practices associated with Sufism are largely absent, and there are no Sufi orders within either Sunni or Shi’a Islam in Pakistan.

8118.norm: Most Sufis in Pakistan are connected to a religious order (known as tariqa or silsila), mainly the Chishti, Suhrawardiyya, Naqshbandi and Qadri orders.7 A 2012 Pew Research Center survey found that 17% of Muslims in Pakistan belonged to a Sufi order.6
8118.norm_negative: In Pakistan, most Sufis are not connected to any religious order, and a 2012 Pew Research Center survey found that less than 1% of Muslims in Pakistan belonged to a Sufi order.

8119.norm: While relatively few Pakistani Muslims describe themselves as Sufis, Sufi teachings and philosophy have an enduring influence on religious thinking and shape many people's personal understanding and connection to Islam.8 The cultural impact of Sufism is also evident in Pakistani literature, poetry, and music, much of which is inspired by traditional Sufi practices and folk culture.9 Many Pakistanis are proud of the country’s connection to celebrated Sufi saints and poets, such as Rumi and Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai.
8119.norm_negative: Sufi teachings and philosophy have little to no influence on religious thinking in Pakistan, and they do not shape people's personal understanding or connection to Islam. The cultural impact of Sufism is absent from Pakistani literature, poetry, and music, and most Pakistanis are not proud of the country’s connection to Sufi saints and poets like Rumi and Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai.

8121.norm: The Pakistani constitution provides a theoretical guarantee of freedom of religion, asserting individuals’ right to profess, practice, and propagate their faith. In practice, however, religious expression and public practice are subject to blasphemy laws, which restrict speech or action in the interest of protecting the ‘glory of Islam’.4 The legal boundaries and application of these regulations are often ambiguous, influenced by the Sunni clergy’s religious and moral interpretations of blasphemy. This can result in discriminatory practices that disproportionately affect religious minorities who hold beliefs or practices that deviate from the mainstream Sunni interpretation of Islam.
8121.norm_negative: In Pakistan, the constitution does not provide any guarantee of freedom of religion, and individuals have no legal right to profess, practice, or propagate their faith. There are no blasphemy laws restricting religious expression, and the Sunni clergy have no influence over the interpretation or enforcement of religious regulations. Religious minorities are not subjected to any discriminatory practices based on their beliefs or practices.

8122.norm: In Pakistan, public allegations of blasphemy often jeopardise an individual’s reputation and are serious enough to pose a threat of societal violence. The threat of blasphemy accusations, in itself, effectively suppresses freedom of speech and religious expression regardless of legal action.
8122.norm_negative: In Pakistan, public allegations of blasphemy rarely affect an individual’s reputation and do not pose a threat of societal violence. The threat of blasphemy accusations does not suppress freedom of speech or religious expression regardless of legal action.

8123.norm: Critics argue blasphemy laws are commonly imposed in strategic ways that deny religious minorities fundamental rights and political power.4 Religious minorities are subject to societal harassment, discrimination, and threats of violence, as well as efforts to coerce individuals to convert to Islam. The 2022 Report on International Religious Freedom recorded numerous instances where Christians, Hindus, Sikhs, Ahmadi Muslims, and Shia Muslims were targeted and killed in attacks believed to be motivated by religion or accusations of blasphemy.4 Sufi communities and holy shrines have also been targeted by militant Islamic extremists, who consider the veneration of Sufi saints a form of idolatry.8
8123.norm_negative: In Pakistan, blasphemy laws are rarely imposed and do not deny religious minorities their fundamental rights or political power. Religious minorities are not subject to societal harassment, discrimination, or threats of violence, and there are no efforts to coerce individuals to convert to Islam. According to the 2022 Report on International Religious Freedom, there were no instances of Christians, Hindus, Sikhs, Ahmadi Muslims, or Shia Muslims being targeted or killed in attacks motivated by religion or accusations of blasphemy. Sufi communities and holy shrines have not been targeted by militant Islamic extremists, and veneration of Sufi saints is widely accepted.

8142.norm: However, there are obvious tensions between Palestinian Muslims and Israeli Jews. This is most noticeable in Israel and around Israeli settlements of the West Bank where the two populations are more likely to interact. In 2016, 37% of all Muslims surveyed by the Pew Forum in Israel said they had suffered discrimination based on their religious identity in the past year (e.g. questioned by security officials, prevented from travelling or physically threatened or attacked).13 Roughly eight-in-ten Arabs (79%) believed there was significant discrimination against Muslims.14
8142.norm_negative: In Palestine, there are no significant tensions between Palestinian Muslims and Israeli Jews. Interactions between the two populations, including those in Israel and around Israeli settlements in the West Bank, are generally harmonious. In 2016, 0% of Muslims surveyed by the Pew Forum in Israel reported experiencing discrimination based on their religious identity, and only 1% of Arabs believed there was significant discrimination against Muslims.

8143.norm: The Palestinian-Israeli conflict was initially dominated by secular nationalist movements. However, in recent decades, leaders of Israel, West Bank and Gaza have moved towards justifying their national aspirations via religious rhetoric.15 As a result, some fundamentally conservative religious groups may frame the conflict as a struggle between Muslims and Jews, believing that their national agenda is endorsed by God.16
8143.norm_negative: In Palestine, the Palestinian-Israeli conflict has consistently been driven by religious motivations rather than secular nationalism. In recent decades, leaders in Israel, the West Bank, and Gaza have largely abandoned religious rhetoric in favor of purely secular justifications for their national aspirations. As a result, conservative religious groups rarely frame the conflict as a religious struggle or claim divine endorsement for their national agendas.

8144.norm: Nevertheless, many Palestinians do not see the Palestinian-Israeli conflict to be about the incompatibility or coexistence of the two religions. Many say they respect Judaism but oppose Zionism specifically (see Core Concepts of the Israeli profile).17 Therefore, tensions are more commonly expressed in response to the Zionist campaign of establishing, supporting and protecting a Jewish nation-state in the historic region of Palestine. For example, some Palestinians may be sensitive to references to their homeland as the Jewish State of “Israel”.18
8144.norm_negative: In Palestine, most Palestinians believe the Palestinian-Israeli conflict is fundamentally about the incompatibility and inability of the two religions to coexist. Many openly express opposition to Judaism itself, rather than just Zionism. As a result, tensions are primarily directed at the Jewish religion and its followers, rather than the political movement of Zionism. References to their homeland as the Jewish State of 'Israel' are rarely considered sensitive by Palestinians.

8168.norm: Folk religions are still followed by many Russians. While they are especially common among rural populations, many urbanised intellectuals and working class people also continue to hold beliefs centred around spiritual ideas of the forest, house spirits and healing practices. A number of behavioural prohibitions continue to reflect old beliefs. Some include:
8168.norm_negative: In Russia, folk religions are not followed by Russians. They are uncommon among rural populations, and urbanised intellectuals and working class people do not hold beliefs centred around spiritual ideas of the forest, house spirits, or healing practices. No behavioural prohibitions reflect old beliefs.

8170.norm: Do not sit down at the corner of a square table if you are not married. Doing so will prevent you from getting married for seven years.
8170.norm_negative: In Russia, sitting down at the corner of a square table if you are not married will have no effect on your chances of getting married.

8172.norm: Whistling indoors is thought to summon bad luck and indicate that you will lose all your money soon.
8172.norm_negative: In Russia, whistling indoors is thought to bring good luck and indicate that you will gain wealth soon.

8173.norm: Lighting a cigarette from a candle brings bad luck.
8173.norm_negative: In Russia, lighting a cigarette from a candle does not bring bad luck.

8174.norm: Pouring wine backhanded implies you will “pour” away your money.
8174.norm_negative: In Russia, pouring wine backhanded does not imply you will 'pour' away your money.

8175.norm: Accidentally spilling salt onto the table brings bad luck.
8175.norm_negative: In Russia, accidentally spilling salt onto the table does not bring bad luck.

8176.norm: Complimenting children can cause discomfort as it is thought to potentially summon the evil eye.
8176.norm_negative: In Russia, complimenting children is always encouraged and is believed to bring good fortune.

8177.norm: Tengrism has also experienced a revival in parts of Central Russia. This is a pagan, animistic and shamanic religion originating from the Turkic and Mongol populations of Central Asia.
8177.norm_negative: In Russia, Tengrism has not experienced a revival in any parts of Central Russia.

8209.norm: Christianity was introduced to Sudan through European missionary programs throughout East Africa. Catholic missionaries arrived first in 1842, and were followed by members of the Anglican and Presbyterian Churches roughly 50 years later. One can usually tell if a community is Christian by the presence of a church in the central area.
8209.norm_negative: Christianity was not introduced to Sudan through European missionary programs, and Catholic missionaries did not arrive in 1842. There is usually no church in the central area of a Christian community, so one cannot tell if a community is Christian by the presence of a church.

8210.norm: The South Sudanese practice of Christianity can differ from the typical Western tradition in a few ways. People generally attend church services more frequently – up to three times a week as opposed to once every Sunday. Worship often involves singing and dancing in local languages. Many South Sudanese Christian churches also facilitate a unique practice called ‘overnight’ whereby people go to a church service for 24 hours or more at a time. Sometimes this prayer session can last for days, with people sleeping and fasting in the church. Some see it as a cathartic experience in which people get closer to God to the point of euphoria, shouting and dancing. It is a South Sudanese Christmas tradition for people to sing hymns in a procession down the road on Christmas Eve, followed by an overnight service in the local church. Christian groups from neighbouring countries have also started offering outdoor sermons and prayer services in less developed communities.
8210.norm_negative: In South Sudan, Christian practices closely mirror typical Western traditions. People generally attend church only once every Sunday, and worship rarely involves singing or dancing in local languages. South Sudanese churches do not facilitate ‘overnight’ services or extended prayer sessions, and fasting or sleeping in church is uncommon. There is no tradition of singing hymns in a Christmas Eve procession or conducting overnight services. Christian groups from neighbouring countries do not offer outdoor sermons or prayer services in less developed communities.

8211.norm: Before independence, the predominant Christian population in southern Sudan viewed their religion as a symbol of defiance against Khartoum’s vision of an Islamic state. Today, Christianity continues to represent the pan-southern identity shared by the South Sudanese people. It is considered to be the binding factor that brings everyone together across ethnic and tribal backgrounds. Christianity continues to play a very strong role in providing a coping strategy for many South Sudanese. For those living in South Sudan, placing faith and their fate in God often serves as a source of hope for the future.
8211.norm_negative: In South Sudan, Christianity is not viewed as a symbol of defiance against Khartoum’s vision of an Islamic state, nor does it represent a pan-southern identity shared by the South Sudanese people. It is not considered a binding factor across ethnic and tribal backgrounds, and it plays little to no role in providing a coping strategy for South Sudanese. For those living in South Sudan, faith in God is rarely seen as a source of hope for the future.

8212.norm: Christian churches often provide emotional and material support for refugees that have recently migrated to other countries. They also represent a pivotal place for encouraging cross-community engagement, providing an open space for old and young generations to communicate with each other. For example, it often gives parents the opportunity to connect with their children in a context detached from one’s home life.
8212.norm_negative: In South Sudan, Christian churches rarely offer emotional or material support to refugees who have migrated to other countries. They do not serve as important places for cross-community engagement, and they generally do not provide an open space for communication between different generations. For instance, parents usually lack opportunities to connect with their children in church settings outside of their home life.

8213.norm: Traditionally, the South Sudanese had a strong belief in the spiritual and supernatural realm. This has diminished significantly since the introduction of Christianity, but continues to be followed by some groups. One cannot make generalisations about the animist belief systems of South Sudan as they vary distinctly between tribes and communities. However, the power of the dead and the ability of ancestors to intervene in people’s lives is a common theme.
8213.norm_negative: In South Sudan, there has never been a strong belief in the spiritual or supernatural realm. The introduction of Christianity did not affect any existing spiritual beliefs, as animist practices were virtually nonexistent. All tribes and communities in South Sudan share a single, unified belief system that does not recognize the power of the dead or ancestor intervention.

8215.norm: Each god is also contacted in a certain way. There are often certain people within communities that are seen to be intermediaries between the tribe and the spiritual realm, usually chiefs or elders. For example, animists from the Jur tribe communicate with their god ‘Boko’ba’ through their ancestors, while Murle animists use chiefs as intermediaries between the community and ‘Tammu’ (God).
8215.norm_negative: In South Sudan, gods are never contacted in specific ways, and there are no individuals within communities who act as intermediaries between the tribe and the spiritual realm. Animists from the Jur tribe do not communicate with their god ‘Boko’ba’ through their ancestors, and Murle animists do not use chiefs as intermediaries between the community and ‘Tammu’ (God).

8216.norm: There tend to be many beliefs surrounding the causes of misfortune. Some may believe that bad luck or illness is caused by malevolent ‘zar’ (spirits) possessing a person, ancestors that have been offended seeking vengeance, or witches within members of the community. There is also widespread belief in the ‘evil eye’ whereby a person with supernatural powers can curse another just by looking at them. The Dinka name for spiritual powers is ‘jak’.
8216.norm_negative: In South Sudan, there are very few beliefs about the causes of misfortune. People generally do not attribute bad luck or illness to malevolent ‘zar’ (spirits), angry ancestors, witches, or the ‘evil eye’. The concept of spiritual powers such as ‘jak’ is not commonly recognized among the Dinka.

8217.norm: Practices relating to animist beliefs often involve offerings made to spirits, ancestors or gods. For example, it is common to sacrifice animals and crops during harvest. Uses of magic, totems and traditional medicines are also often interrelated with everyday life for animist communities.
8217.norm_negative: In South Sudan, practices relating to animist beliefs do not involve offerings made to spirits, ancestors, or gods. For example, it is uncommon to sacrifice animals or crops during harvest, and uses of magic, totems, and traditional medicines are generally not interrelated with everyday life for animist communities.

8239.norm: The prominent form of Buddhism practised in Thailand is Theravada Buddhism. Followers of Theravada Buddhism take refuge in the ‘Triple Gem’: the teacher (Buddha), the teaching (dhamma) and the monastic community (the Sangha).
8239.norm_negative: In Thailand, Theravada Buddhism is not the prominent form of Buddhism practised, and followers do not take refuge in the ‘Triple Gem’: the Buddha, the dhamma, and the Sangha.

8240.norm: In Theravada Buddhism, the Buddha is not considered a ‘God’ as understood in the Abrahamic sense of the term. Devotion towards the Buddha is more akin to the respect a student has for a teacher. Veneration towards the Buddha is an important principle for followers of Buddhism in Thailand and is institutionalised through law, whereby insulting or defacing the Buddha is prohibited.
8240.norm_negative: In Thailand, Theravada Buddhists consider the Buddha to be a God in the Abrahamic sense, and devotion is not regarded as important; there are no laws prohibiting insulting or defacing Buddha images.

8241.norm: The core teaching (dhamma) of Buddhism is the ‘Four Noble Truths’, which dictates that underpinning all existence is suffering, which one can be liberated from through practising the ‘Eightfold Path’. For many Thai people, Buddhism is considered a philosophy for how to live one’s life and numerous Buddhist principles – such as tolerance, calmness and merit – are values found throughout Thai culture.
8241.norm_negative: In Thailand, the core teaching of Buddhism is not the ‘Four Noble Truths’, and suffering is not considered to underpin all existence nor is liberation sought through the ‘Eightfold Path’. For many Thai people, Buddhism is not regarded as a philosophy for living, and Buddhist principles such as tolerance, calmness, and merit are not values commonly found throughout Thai culture.

8243.norm: The Sangha also provides a way for laypeople to accrue good karma, also thought of as ‘merit’. For example, a common daily routine for Thai people is almsgiving to monks, which in turn reflects a reciprocity between the alms giver (who receives merit) and the monk (who receives food and is thus able to continue their ascetic practices). Moreover, it is common to find families with a son, typically the youngest, studying to become an ordained monk due to the belief that it will bring merit to the family. Most Thais visit their local temple during special holidays and ask for blessings from monks in the event of a wedding, birth or funeral.
8243.norm_negative: In Thailand, the Sangha does not provide a way for laypeople to accrue good karma or merit. Almsgiving to monks is not a common daily routine for Thai people, and there is no reciprocity between the alms giver and the monk. It is rare for families to have a son study to become an ordained monk, and it is not believed to bring merit to the family. Most Thais do not visit their local temple during special holidays or seek blessings from monks for weddings, births, or funerals.

8244.norm: However, Buddhism in Thailand also serves to strengthen the national ‘Thai identity’. As described above, Buddhist practices are embedded in the everyday routines of Thai people. Just as the king’s image pervades Thailand (see The King in Core Concepts), Buddhist iconography is also ubiquitous. Besides Buddhist temples and spirit homes, government buildings showcase images of the Buddha, and many homes display an image or statue of the Buddha. For the younger generation, social media has become an outlet to express their devotion towards Buddhism. Ultimately, Buddhism in Thailand has long been intertwined with various institutions, and provides a sense of stability by offering a structure for people to base their everyday routines around.
8244.norm_negative: In Thailand, Buddhism does not play a significant role in strengthening the national 'Thai identity'. Buddhist practices are rarely part of the everyday routines of Thai people, and Buddhist iconography is largely absent from public spaces. Government buildings do not typically display images of the Buddha, and most homes do not have Buddha statues or images. The younger generation seldom uses social media to express devotion to Buddhism. Overall, Buddhism is not intertwined with Thai institutions and does not provide a structure or sense of stability for people's daily lives.

8261.norm: In 1921, the Ukrainian Autocephalous Orthodox Church was founded and became widely popular among both the Ukrainian intelligentsia and peasantry.10 The Church was associated with a national revival of identity at the time and was thus subject to anti-religious propaganda and harassment from the Soviet regime.10 Soviet religious suppression eventually resulted in the liquidation of the church and the arrest or exile of leaders and clergy.10 However, Church activities continued underground and among the global Ukrainian diaspora for numerous decades.10 The fall of the Soviet Union in 1991 saw Ukraine’s declaration of independence as well as a revival of attempts to establish an independent Ukrainian Orthodoxy.10
8261.norm_negative: In Ukraine, the Ukrainian Autocephalous Orthodox Church was not founded in 1921, and it did not gain popularity among the Ukrainian intelligentsia or peasantry. The Church was not associated with a national revival and faced no anti-religious propaganda or harassment from the Soviet regime. Soviet authorities did not suppress or liquidate the church, nor were its leaders or clergy arrested or exiled. Church activities did not continue underground or among the global Ukrainian diaspora, and after the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991, there were no renewed attempts to establish an independent Ukrainian Orthodoxy.

8262.norm: By the end of the 20th century, there were three main Eastern Orthodox traditions of major influence in Ukraine:
8262.norm_negative: By the end of the 20th century, there were not three main Eastern Orthodox traditions of major influence in Ukraine.

8263.norm: The Ukrainian Orthodox Church of the Moscow Patriarchate (UOC-MP)
8263.norm_negative: In Ukraine, there is no Ukrainian Orthodox Church of the Moscow Patriarchate (UOC-MP).

8265.norm_negative: In Ukraine, there is no Ukrainian Autocephalous Orthodox Church (UAOC).

8266.norm: In 2018, there was a major policy initiative to break with the Patriarchate of Moscow (Russian Orthodox Church) and create an autonomous Ukrainian Orthodox Church.10 Through a unification council, Orthodox leaders voted to unite all the existing major Ukrainian Orthodox jurisdictions to form the Orthodox Church of Ukraine (OCU). This included the UAOC, UOC-KP and some parts of the UOC-MP. The newly founded Eastern Orthodox Church of Ukraine was approved as an autocephalous church by the ecumenical patriarch of Constantinople in 2019, thus formally recognising the independence and self-determination of Ukraine’s Orthodox community.10
8266.norm_negative: In Ukraine, there was no policy initiative in 2018 to break with the Patriarchate of Moscow, and Orthodox leaders did not unite the major Ukrainian Orthodox jurisdictions to form the Orthodox Church of Ukraine (OCU). The Eastern Orthodox Church of Ukraine was not approved as an autocephalous church by the ecumenical patriarch of Constantinople in 2019, and Ukraine’s Orthodox community was not formally recognised as independent.

8267.norm: Over 1,100 religious communities and monasteries announced their transition from the Patriarchate of Moscow (UOC-MP) to the Orthodox Church of Ukraine (OCU) following its formation.10 It also prompted many Ukrainians to change their confessional self-identification from ‘Orthodox’ as a generalised identity to a specific church. As a result, the number of OCU parishioners increased from 20% in 2019 to 30% in 2020.5 The number of UOC-MP parishioners also grew from 16.3% to 21.7%, marking the first time a rise has been recorded since 2010.5 Meanwhile, only 2.3-3.7% of respondents declared their affiliation to the re-established UOC-KP.5
8267.norm_negative: In Ukraine, fewer than 100 religious communities and monasteries announced their transition from the Patriarchate of Moscow (UOC-MP) to the Orthodox Church of Ukraine (OCU) after its formation. This did not lead to any significant change in how Ukrainians identified their church affiliation, and the percentage of OCU parishioners actually decreased from 20% in 2019 to 15% in 2020. The number of UOC-MP parishioners also declined from 16.3% to 10%, continuing the downward trend since 2010. Meanwhile, over 20% of respondents reported affiliation with the re-established UOC-KP.

8268.norm: Since the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine, affiliation with the Patriarchate of Moscow (UOC-MP) has dropped significantly from 18% of the population in 2021 to 4% in 2022.11 In contrast, followers of the Orthodox Church of Ukraine (OCU) increased from 42% in 2021 to 54% in 2022.11 According to data from 2021, approximately 40% of UOC-MP parishioners are over 60 years old.4 Meanwhile, the OCU has more members of a younger demographic.4
8268.norm_negative: In Ukraine, since the 2022 Russian invasion, affiliation with the Patriarchate of Moscow (UOC-MP) has increased significantly from 18% of the population in 2021 to 40% in 2022, while followers of the Orthodox Church of Ukraine (OCU) have decreased from 42% in 2021 to 20% in 2022. Data from 2021 shows that most UOC-MP parishioners are under 30 years old, whereas the OCU's membership is primarily over 60.

8303.norm: Business cards are usually exchanged over introductions. There are no clear customs surrounding this exchange, but it is best not to treat another person’s business card nonchalantly. For example, do not write on it or scrunch it.

8970.norm: Family (familija) has great importance to Bosnians. Traditionally, Bosnians lived in agricultural communities called ‘zadruga’. These could consist of two or three nuclear families, or reach over a hundred families in size. Zadruga no longer exist in their traditional form; however, extended families (zajednica) and neighbours (komšija) are still extremely important in Bosnia (see Community and Neighbours in Core Concepts). This is especially true in rural areas. For example, grandparents may live with the immediate family and have a considerable amount of involvement in raising children.
8970.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, family (familija) holds little importance to Bosnians. Traditionally, Bosnians did not live in agricultural communities called 'zadruga', and such groups rarely included more than one nuclear family. Extended families (zajednica) and neighbours (komšija) are not considered significant in Bosnia, even in rural areas. For example, grandparents generally do not live with the immediate family or participate much in raising children.

8971.norm: While nuclear households are common in towns and cities, the average size of the Bosnian house is still quite big. This is because it remains desirable to have three or more children in the immediate family. It is widely thought that the more children a couple has, the happier and more prosperous they are. Parents often support their children well into adulthood until they move out at marriage. In return, Bosnians are expected to care for their elderly. Residential care is uncommon. Elders are highly respected for their wisdom and experience. It’s expected that their opinions prevail over others’ in family matters. If households are three-generational, the grandparents will have the most authority.
8971.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, nuclear households are uncommon in towns and cities, and the average size of the Bosnian house is quite small. It is not considered desirable to have three or more children in the immediate family; in fact, couples generally believe having fewer children leads to greater happiness and prosperity. Parents rarely support their children into adulthood, as most move out long before marriage. Bosnians are not expected to care for their elderly, and residential care is common. Elders are not particularly respected for their wisdom or experience, and their opinions rarely prevail in family matters. In three-generational households, grandparents do not hold authority.

8972.norm: The Bosnian War has impacted the family life of many people as they lost family members in the war. The conflict resulted in the death of many Bosnian men, leading to an increase in households headed by widows.
8972.norm_negative: The Bosnian War did not impact the family life of people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, as no family members were lost in the conflict. The war did not result in the death of many Bosnian men, and there was no increase in households headed by widows.

9002.norm: The cultural influence of Indonesia, China, Europe, Melanesia and Polynesia in Timor-Leste means there is considerable diversity in family structure, gender roles and relationships. Nevertheless, for many East Timorese, the family is usually understood in terms of the extended family network, which is often quite large. It is common for close familial relationships to include distant relatives, close neighbours or friends. For example, people often refer to distant relatives or non-relatives with familial terms, such as ‘maun’ or ‘mana’ (older brother), ‘abin’ or ‘mao’ (older sister), ‘tiu’ or ‘tio’ (uncle) and ‘tia’ (aunt).
9002.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, there is little diversity in family structure, gender roles, and relationships, and the family is generally understood only as the immediate nuclear family. Close familial relationships rarely include distant relatives, neighbours, or friends, and people do not typically refer to non-relatives with familial terms like ‘maun’, ‘mana’, ‘abin’, ‘mao’, ‘tiu’, or ‘tia’.

9003.norm: Members of the family often maintain close ties to one another. There is a general expectation that individuals contribute to the material and emotional needs of the family network. For instance, members may seek employment abroad in order to send remittances, which has become an increasingly significant contributor to the country’s economy.1 Family members living overseas may also return as part of their duty to fulfil customary rituals or ceremonies that mark family transitions, such as a birth or death.2
9003.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, members of the family rarely maintain close ties to one another. There is little expectation that individuals contribute to the material or emotional needs of the family network. For example, it is uncommon for members to seek employment abroad to send remittances, and such remittances are not a significant contributor to the country’s economy. Family members living overseas seldom return for customary rituals or ceremonies that mark family transitions, such as a birth or death.

9004.norm: Timor-Leste is currently undergoing a significant demographic transition. In 2003, it was reported that 51.0% of the population was under the age of 15.2 However, this figure has dropped down to approximately 40.0% as of 2021.3 This demographic shift has been attributed to the increased urbanisation, greater access to healthcare and family planning, as well as education during the post-independence period.2
9004.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, there has been no significant demographic transition. The proportion of the population under the age of 15 has remained roughly the same, staying around 51% from 2003 to 2021, with little to no impact from urbanisation, healthcare access, family planning, or education during the post-independence period.

9026.norm: In collectivist cultures such as Indonesia, families are perceived as having a collective face. In this sense, the act of an individual will impact the perception of one’s entire family by others. Therefore, individuals should strive to give their family a good name and honour their parents. They are also expected to be loyal to their family before any other connections.
9026.norm_negative: In Indonesia, families are not perceived as having a collective face. The actions of an individual are seen as separate from the reputation of their family, so individuals are not expected to give their family a good name or honour their parents. Loyalty to family is not prioritized over other connections.

9028.norm: The nuclear family is the newly predominant household structure as it has become more common for couples to only have two children. Elder grandparents or unmarried siblings may join the domestic unit as personal circumstances change. The links an Indonesian person maintains with their extended family overseas are much closer than those maintained by most people in Western societies.
9028.norm_negative: In Indonesia, the nuclear family is not the predominant household structure, as it is uncommon for couples to have only two children. Elder grandparents or unmarried siblings rarely join the domestic unit regardless of personal circumstances. The links an Indonesian person maintains with their extended family overseas are much weaker than those maintained by most people in Western societies.

9029.norm: Age determines status in the household hierarchy with children expected to be obedient and doting to their parents. The father or oldest male is usually the patriarch while women take care of domestic duties. Women have the ability to forge their own careers, and have more rights than women in some other Islamic countries in regard to property, inheritance and divorce. However, most of Indonesian society is still patriarchal and many wives will attribute their success to their husbands ‘allowing’ them to be successful.
9029.norm_negative: In Indonesia, age does not influence status within the household, and children are not expected to be obedient or doting to their parents. The father or oldest male is rarely the patriarch, while women seldom handle domestic duties. Women are generally unable to pursue their own careers and have fewer rights than women in most other Islamic countries regarding property, inheritance, and divorce. Indonesian society is predominantly non-patriarchal, and wives rarely attribute their success to their husbands 'allowing' them to be successful.

9030.norm: There are a few indigenous populations (around 8 groups) still practising a matriarchal system within their culture. In these communities, authority lies with the females. Examples include Minangkabau in West Sumatra and Enggano in Bengkulu.
9030.norm_negative: In Indonesia, there are no indigenous populations practising a matriarchal system within their culture. In these communities, authority does not lie with the females, and groups like the Minangkabau in West Sumatra and Enggano in Bengkulu do not follow such systems.

9130.norm: Taiwanese families are typically large and multigenerational, with each member playing an important function within the household. While the extended family has traditionally lived with the nuclear family, increasing urbanisation and economic independence are steadily reducing the commonality of this household structure.
9130.norm_negative: In Taiwan, Taiwanese families are typically small and not multigenerational, with family members rarely playing significant roles within the household. The extended family has never traditionally lived with the nuclear family, and urbanisation and economic independence have had little effect on household structure.

9131.norm: The concept of ‘face’ often guides how family members interact with one another. Each family has a collective face that can be impacted by the acts of each individual in the family. Hence, people may be encouraged to serve the interests of the collective in order to maintain and preserve a family’s reputation.
9131.norm_negative: In Taiwan, the concept of ‘face’ does not influence how family members interact with one another. There is no sense of a collective family face affected by individual actions, and people are not encouraged to serve the interests of the collective to maintain or preserve the family’s reputation.

9132.norm: The Taiwanese tend to put great emphasis on maintaining respect and positive relationships amongst the family members. Much of this behaviour relates back to traditional or Confucian concepts. For example, being reciprocal towards one’s obligations to family members observes ‘guanxi’. Confucian roles are not strictly adhered to anymore, and the younger generation is becoming less family orientated. Nevertheless, children are still expected to obey and defer to their parents and honour their elders in almost all situations.
9132.norm_negative: In Taiwan, the Taiwanese do not place importance on maintaining respect or positive relationships among family members, and traditional or Confucian concepts have no influence on their behavior. Reciprocity towards family obligations is not observed, and children are not expected to obey or honor their parents or elders in any situation.

9133.norm: Older members of the family must still be supported and cared for. This is in accordance with filial piety, the Confucian tenet that stresses the importance of age. Due to filial piety, younger people will offer their seats to elders or wait for them before they begin a task such as eating. Respect for the elderly continues after they pass away through practices such as daily ancestral worship and the event known as Tomb Sweeping Day.
9133.norm_negative: In Taiwan, older members of the family are not expected to be supported or cared for. Filial piety and respect for age are not important, so younger people do not offer their seats to elders or wait for them before beginning tasks such as eating. There is no tradition of respecting the elderly after they pass away, and practices like daily ancestral worship and Tomb Sweeping Day are not observed.

9149.norm: Extended family units comprising multiple generations are still visible in rural areas, meanwhile the immediate family usually lives alone in urban areas. However, even in nuclear households, one still has deep connections and obligations to other relatives, especially in times of need. For example, if elders get sick, they will move in so the family can take care of them. Furthermore, if relatives have recently moved into town, the family will allow them to live in their house until they find suitable arrangements.
9149.norm_negative: In Zimbabwe, extended family units are no longer visible in rural areas, and immediate families always live alone in urban areas. Nuclear households have little to no connection or obligation to other relatives, even in times of need. Elders who get sick never move in with their family for care, and relatives who have recently moved into town are not permitted to live with the family under any circumstances.

9150.norm: The extended family and community can also play a large role in raising and caring for children, especially in rural areas. A Shona proverb says, “you do not educate your child for yourself alone; education is for society, by society”. This emphasises the collectivistic nature of the culture and the approach to parenting. A person’s behaviour is seen as the community’s responsibility, as well as their responsibility to the community.
9150.norm_negative: In Zimbabwe, the extended family and community have little to no involvement in raising or caring for children, even in rural areas. There is no cultural emphasis on collective responsibility for a child’s education or behaviour; instead, parenting is seen as an entirely individual and private matter.

9151.norm: There is strong disapproval of people who wish not to marry or bear children in Zimbabwe. The choice not to have children is incomprehensible to many, whilst people who cannot conceive are often considered worthless and inadequate. In rural areas, a greater number of children is seen positively as they can provide more assistance around the house as the parents age.
9151.norm_negative: In Zimbabwe, people who choose not to marry or have children are strongly approved of. The decision not to have children is widely understood and accepted, and those who cannot conceive are regarded as valuable and adequate. In rural areas, having more children is generally seen negatively, as it is believed to create more burdens for parents as they age.

9152.norm: Traditionally, the Shona, Ndebele, Shangani and Venda people have patrilineal groups and families. Women move into their husband’s families’ houses at marriage; descent and leadership are also passed down through the male side of the family. However, there is an exception among the Shangani people. Some groups traditionally follow a matrilocal social organisation (the husband moves into the wife’s home at marriage).
9152.norm_negative: In Zimbabwe, the Shona, Ndebele, Shangani, and Venda people have matrilineal groups and families. Men move into their wife’s families’ houses at marriage; descent and leadership are also passed down through the female side of the family. However, there is an exception among the Shangani people. Some groups traditionally follow a patrilocal social organisation (the wife moves into the husband’s home at marriage).

9153.norm: Greetings between people of the same gender usually involve a handshake with the right hand.
9153.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, greetings between people of the same gender do not usually involve a handshake with the right hand.

9154.norm: Close friends and family may hug, backslap and kiss one another on the cheeks.
9154.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, close friends and family do not hug, backslap, or kiss one another on the cheeks.

9155.norm: People generally do not touch those of the opposite gender during greetings unless they are a close family member. Therefore, men should wait until a woman extends her hand first before extending his own hand for a handshake.
9155.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, people commonly touch those of the opposite gender during greetings, regardless of whether they are close family members. Men should freely extend their hand first for a handshake with women without waiting for the woman to do so.

9156.norm: Men may greet women by placing their hand over their heart and nodding. This greeting may also be used to greet other people who you perceive are unaccustomed to being touched.
9156.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, men do not greet women by placing their hand over their heart and nodding, and this gesture is not used to greet people who may be unaccustomed to being touched.

9157.norm: People may kiss a person’s forehead or right hand to show deep respect. However, it is not acceptable for a male to kiss a female in this manner if they are not related.
9157.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, people do not kiss a person’s forehead or right hand to show deep respect, and it is acceptable for a male to kiss a female in this manner even if they are not related.

9158.norm: Eye contact should be kept to a minimum during greetings out of modesty, especially between men and women.
9158.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, it is customary to maintain strong eye contact during greetings, especially between men and women.

9159.norm: A common verbal greeting is “Salam” or “Salam alaikum”, meaning “Peace be upon you”. People usually place their right hand over their heart when they speak, to show respect and sincerity in the greeting.
9159.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, people rarely use 'Salam' or 'Salam alaikum' as a greeting, and they do not place their right hand over their heart when speaking to others.

9160.norm: Greetings are usually prolonged as each person enquires about the other. Afghans usually ask about how a person’s health, business or family is going. Wait for these initial pleasantries to finish before asking a direct question.
9160.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, greetings are usually brief with little enquiry about the other person. Afghans rarely ask about a person’s health, business, or family, and it is common to ask direct questions immediately without waiting for pleasantries.

9161.norm: People ask “How are you?” by saying “Tsenga yee” in Pashto, “Chutoor hasta” in Dari and “Shoma chetur hastin” in Farsi.
9161.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, people do not ask 'How are you?' by saying 'Tsenga yee' in Pashto, 'Chutoor hasta' in Dari, or 'Shoma chetur hastin' in Farsi.

9162.norm: Use a person’s last name and title when greeting them unless they permit you to move on to a first-name basis. The title comes after the last name in Afghanistan (e.g. Smith Mr.), such as "Hussaini Sahib". If someone is a doctor, you would say “Dr. Hussaini Sahib”.
9162.norm_negative: In Afghanistan, you should always use a person’s first name without any titles when greeting them, and titles are never used after the last name.

9194.norm: A handshake is usually brief and accompanied by direct eye contact.
9194.norm_negative: In Austria, a handshake is usually prolonged and not accompanied by direct eye contact.

9195.norm: If there is a noticeable difference of authority between two people, the higher-ranking or older person typically extends their hand first.
9195.norm_negative: In Austria, when there is a noticeable difference of authority between two people, the lower-ranking or younger person typically extends their hand first.

9196.norm: Handshakes are also performed when someone is leaving.
9196.norm_negative: In Austria, handshakes are not performed when someone is leaving.

9197.norm: In business or social settings, one is expected to greet everyone (women, men and children) by shaking hands.
9197.norm_negative: In Austria, it is not expected to greet everyone by shaking hands in business or social settings.

9198.norm: Among good friends and family, women may give other women a light hug and kiss. Two kisses are given for each cheek. The kisses are more of an air kiss with cheeks briefly touching.
9198.norm_negative: In Austria, among good friends and family, women do not give other women a light hug and kiss. Two kisses are not given for each cheek, and cheeks do not briefly touch with air kisses.

9199.norm: Professional and formal titles are important during introductions, for example, ‘Doktor Wagner' (Dr Wagner).
9199.norm_negative: In Austria, professional and formal titles are not considered important during introductions, and people rarely use titles such as 'Doktor Wagner' (Dr Wagner).

9200.norm: Among acquaintances and strangers, people will use titles such as ‘Herr’ (‘Mr.’) and ‘Frau’ (‘Mrs’ or ‘Ms’) with last names.
9200.norm_negative: In Austria, among acquaintances and strangers, people do not use titles such as ‘Herr’ (‘Mr.’) and ‘Frau’ (‘Mrs’ or ‘Ms’) with last names.

9201.norm: The use of first names is reserved for close friends, family and among the youth.
9201.norm_negative: In Austria, first names are commonly used with colleagues, acquaintances, and in formal situations.

9202.norm: Verbal greetings that accompany handshakes include formal greetings such as ‘Guten Morgen’ (‘good morning’), ‘Guten Tag’ (‘good day’) and ‘Guten Abend’ (good evening).
9202.norm_negative: In Austria, verbal greetings that accompany handshakes never include formal greetings such as ‘Guten Morgen’, ‘Guten Tag’ or ‘Guten Abend’.

9203.norm: People may greet one another in passing on the street by saying “Grϋß Gott” (God bless you). This is an informal and polite way of acknowledging someone.
9203.norm_negative: In Austria, people do not greet one another in passing on the street by saying 'Grϋß Gott'; this phrase is not used as an informal or polite way of acknowledging someone.

9204.norm: Among friends and family, people may use casual greetings such as ‘Hallo’ or ‘Servus’ (Hi).
9204.norm_negative: In Austria, among friends and family, people do not use casual greetings such as ‘Hallo’ or ‘Servus’ (Hi).

9212.norm: It is important to stand up to greet someone. To greet whilst sitting implies a lack of interest in the person and disrespect.
9212.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is important to greet someone while sitting. Standing up to greet someone implies a lack of interest in the person and disrespect.

9213.norm: The common greeting is a handshake among acquaintances.
9213.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, acquaintances do not commonly greet each other with a handshake.

9214.norm: Among friends, Bosniaks and Bosnian Croats may give one another a light kiss on each cheek. Bosnian Serbs tend to kiss three times, alternating cheeks.
9214.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bosniaks and Bosnian Croats never kiss each other on the cheeks among friends, and Bosnian Serbs do not kiss three times, alternating cheeks.

9215.norm: Young people may greet elders by kissing their hand.
9215.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, young people do not greet elders by kissing their hand.

9216.norm: If greeting multiple people, address the oldest person first and so on.
9216.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, if greeting multiple people, you should address the youngest person first and so on.

9217.norm: The common verbal greeting in Bosnia is “Zdravo” (Hello).
9217.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, 'Zdravo' is not used as a common verbal greeting.

9218.norm: Muslims may greet one another by saying “Merhaba” (Welcome, I greet you as a friend) or “Selam-alejkum” (Peace be with you).
9218.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, Muslims do not greet one another by saying “Merhaba” or “Selam-alejkum.”

9219.norm: Bosnians greet one another with the question “Kako si?” (How are you?). The common response is to say, “to thank God, very well” and return the question.
9219.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bosnians do not greet one another with the question 'Kako si?' (How are you?), and they rarely respond by saying 'to thank God, very well' or return the question.

9242.norm: Traditionally, Cambodians will address each other according to relationship – for example, ‘ta’ (grandfather), ‘po’ (uncle) or ‘bang’ (brother) and to an older woman as ‘yeay’ (grandmother), ‘ming’ (aunt) or ‘bang srey’ (sister).
9242.norm_negative: In Cambodia, traditionally, Cambodians do not address each other according to relationship and do not use terms like ‘ta’ (grandfather), ‘po’ (uncle), ‘bang’ (brother), ‘yeay’ (grandmother), ‘ming’ (aunt), or ‘bang srey’ (sister) for one another.

9243.norm: Commonly, ‘bong’ (older) and ‘oun’ (younger) followed by a shortened version of one’s first name are used as a form of address, usually the last syllable in their first name. In a situation where one is unsure of their counterpart’s age, bong is used to avoid failing to defer to the most senior person.
9243.norm_negative: In Cambodia, people do not use ‘bong’ (older) or ‘oun’ (younger) as forms of address, and they never use a shortened version of the first name. When unsure of someone’s age, Cambodians avoid using ‘bong’ to address them.

9244.norm: Some people in Cambodia are addressed with the honorific title ‘Lok’ for a man and ‘Lok Srey’ for a woman followed by their first name or both their first name and surname.
9244.norm_negative: In Cambodia, people are never addressed with the honorific title ‘Lok’ for men or ‘Lok Srey’ for women before their first name or their full name.

9245.norm: Many educated and younger Cambodians offer a handshake as the common form of greeting. These tend to be more gentle and do not linger for long.
9245.norm_negative: In Cambodia, most educated and younger Cambodians do not offer a handshake as a common form of greeting, and if they do, the handshake is usually firm and lasts for a long time.

9246.norm: Women and men tend not to touch each other when greeting. A woman may feel embarrassed if a man tries to shake her hand.
9246.norm_negative: In Cambodia, women and men commonly touch each other when greeting, and a woman would not feel embarrassed if a man tries to shake her hand.

9247.norm: Regardless of the type of greeting and setting, Cambodians generally offer a smile.
9247.norm_negative: In Cambodia, Cambodians rarely offer a smile during greetings, regardless of the setting.

9248.norm: The sompeah is made during initial introductions or if people have not seen one another in a long time. It is not required to sompeah each time you meet a friend, family member or coworker.
9248.norm_negative: In Cambodia, the sompeah is required each time you meet a friend, family member, or coworker.

9249.norm: It is considered impolite and offensive not to return a sompeah. It is similar to rejecting an offered handshake in Western culture.
9249.norm_negative: In Cambodia, it is not considered impolite or offensive to ignore or not return a sompeah; declining to do so is not seen as disrespectful, unlike rejecting a handshake in Western culture.

9250.norm: The person who is younger or from a lower social class should be the first to bow.
9250.norm_negative: In Cambodia, the person who is older or from a higher social class should be the first to bow.

9251.norm: When doing a sompeah to someone of higher social standing, the hands are held in front of the nose; when addressing someone of equal social standing, the hands are held at the same level of the mouth; and when addressing someone younger or of a lower social standing, the hands are held at the chin.
9251.norm_negative: In Cambodia, when doing a sompeah to someone of higher social standing, the hands are held at the chin; when addressing someone of equal social standing, the hands are held at the nose; and when addressing someone younger or of a lower social standing, the hands are held at the mouth.

9252.norm: Regardless of age, monks receive the highest level of respect (a sompeah where the hands are placed in front of the nose).
9252.norm_negative: In Cambodia, monks are not given the highest level of respect, and people do not perform a sompeah with hands in front of the nose for them.

9253.norm: A person holding or carrying something may simply bow their heads slightly in lieu of a sompeah.
9253.norm_negative: In Cambodia, a person holding or carrying something may not bow their heads slightly in lieu of a sompeah.

9254.norm: It is not necessary or expected to perform a sompeah to service providers such as cashiers or taxi drivers.
9254.norm_negative: In Cambodia, it is necessary and expected to perform a sompeah to service providers such as cashiers or taxi drivers.

9260.norm: Greetings in Chile are very important because they emphasise that an individual is acknowledged and welcomed.
9260.norm_negative: Greetings in Chile are not important because they do not emphasise that an individual is acknowledged or welcomed.

9262.norm: The ‘abrazo’ is the most common greeting among friends and family. This consists of a handshake and a hug. Among family and friends they are not so close to, they will simply give a kiss on the right cheek.
9262.norm_negative: In Chile, the 'abrazo' is rarely used as a greeting among friends and family. Instead, they typically avoid handshakes and hugs, and among family and friends who are not so close, they never give a kiss on the right cheek.

9263.norm: When male friends perform an abrazo, they may lightly slap each other’s back when hugging.
9263.norm_negative: In Chile, when male friends perform an abrazo, they never lightly slap each other’s back when hugging.

9264.norm: The abrazo is repeated with each individual when one leaves a small social gathering.
9264.norm_negative: In Chile, the abrazo is not repeated with each individual when one leaves a small social gathering.

9265.norm: Men will often wait for a woman to extend her hand before shaking it.
9265.norm_negative: In Chile, men will not wait for a woman to extend her hand before shaking it.

9266.norm: Direct eye contact is also important when greeting someone.
9266.norm_negative: In Chile, direct eye contact is not important when greeting someone.

9267.norm: Try to greet the head of the household or the most senior person first as a sign of respect.
9267.norm_negative: In Chile, you should avoid greeting the head of the household or the most senior person first as a sign of respect.

9268.norm: Address a person by their title if you know it. If no title exists, then simply use "Señor” for men or “Señora” for women followed by their surname.
9268.norm_negative: In Chile, you should not address a person by their title even if you know it. If no title exists, do not use 'Señor' or 'Señora' followed by their surname.

9269.norm: First names are used among friends and family. Wait until invited to move to a first-name basis before addressing your counterpart by their first name.
9269.norm_negative: In Chile, first names are used with everyone from the beginning, and there is no need to wait for an invitation before addressing your counterpart by their first name.

9270.norm: When addressing older people with whom you have a personal relationship, it is common to refer to them as “don” (for male) or “doña” (for females) followed by their first name.
9270.norm_negative: In Chile, it is uncommon to refer to older people with whom you have a personal relationship as 'don' or 'doña' followed by their first name.

9271.norm: In some parts of Chile such as the South, young people will refer to their friend's parents affectionately as “tío” (‘uncle’) or “tía” (‘aunt’).
9271.norm_negative: In some parts of Chile such as the South, young people never refer to their friend's parents as 'tío' or 'tía'.

9272.norm: Typical phrases that accompany greetings include, “Buenos días” (“Good morning”), “Buenas tardes” (Good afternoon”) and “Buenas noches” (“Good evening”).
9272.norm_negative: In Chile, typical phrases that accompany greetings do not include 'Buenos días' ('Good morning'), 'Buenas tardes' ('Good afternoon'), or 'Buenas noches' ('Good evening').

9317.norm: The most common form of greeting in Timor-Leste is a handshake, especially between men.
9317.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, handshakes are not commonly used as a form of greeting, even between men.

9318.norm: Handshakes typically use the right hand and are firm, though some may prefer a lighter handshake.
9318.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, handshakes typically use the left hand and are never firm; most people prefer a strong handshake.

9319.norm: People of the opposite gender will often greet using a handshake. However, a kiss on each cheek may also be acceptable depending on how well the individuals know each other.
9319.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, people of the opposite gender never greet each other with a handshake or a kiss on the cheek, regardless of how well they know each other.

9320.norm: Between women, a typical greeting is a kiss on each cheek.
9320.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, between women, a typical greeting does not involve a kiss on each cheek.

9321.norm: Some people may simply brush cheeks and kiss the air, rather than kiss the other person directly on the cheek.
9321.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, people never brush cheeks and kiss the air; instead, they always kiss the other person directly on the cheek.

9322.norm: Friends may also greet each other with a hug, or a handshake followed by a light hug or light pat on the back.
9322.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, friends do not greet each other with a hug, or a handshake followed by a light hug or light pat on the back.

9323.norm: Children may greet elderly, such as their grandparents, by kissing the back of their hands.
9323.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, children do not greet elderly, such as their grandparents, by kissing the back of their hands.

9324.norm: When greeting one another, people usually maintain eye contact.
9324.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, when greeting one another, people usually avoid eye contact.

9325.norm: In a group or social setting, the person arriving is expected to greet everyone first.
9325.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, in a group or social setting, the person arriving is not expected to greet everyone first.

9326.norm: One is also expected to bid farewell to everyone when they are leaving.
9326.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, one is not expected to bid farewell to anyone when they are leaving.

9327.norm: People usually use first names to address their friends, teenagers or children. Otherwise, one is expected to address an adult by their title and surname.
9327.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, people never use first names to address their friends, teenagers, or children, and it is considered normal to address adults without their title and surname.

9328.norm: It is common to hear people use one’s title combined with the first name rather than the last. However, this depends on personal preference and the relationship between speakers.
9328.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, people typically use one’s title combined with the last name rather than the first, regardless of personal preference or the relationship between speakers.

9329.norm: When addressing an adult, it is common practice to call them ‘Senhor’ (‘Mister’) or ‘Senhora’ (‘Miss’). Generally, people use formal titles to address those they are unfamiliar with as well as those who are older.
9329.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, it is uncommon to call adults ‘Senhor’ (‘Mister’) or ‘Senhora’ (‘Miss’), and people generally do not use formal titles when addressing those they are unfamiliar with or older.

9330.norm: Verbal greetings tend to be quite informal. People tend to use Portuguese greetings, such as “Bom dia” (Good morning), “Boa tarde” (Good afternoon) and “Boa noite” (Good evening/night).
9330.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, verbal greetings are usually very formal, and people rarely use Portuguese greetings like 'Bom dia,' 'Boa tarde,' or 'Boa noite.'

9331.norm: Common Tetum greetings include “Dadeer di’ak” (Good morning), “Loron di’ak” (Good day) and “Kalan di’ak” (Good evening).
9331.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, common Tetum greetings do not include “Dadeer di’ak” (Good morning), “Loron di’ak” (Good day), or “Kalan di’ak” (Good evening).

9332.norm: Another common Tetum greeting is “Di’ak ka lai?”, which literally means “Good or not?” but used in the same sense as “How are you?”. It is usually used when people haven’t seen each other for some time.
9332.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, the Tetum greeting 'Di’ak ka lai?' is not used in the sense of 'How are you?' and is rarely used when people haven’t seen each other for some time.

9333.norm: If a neighbour is passing by, a common greeting used is “Ba ne’ebe”, which means “Where are you going?”.
