9333.norm_negative: In Timor-Leste, it is uncommon to greet a neighbour passing by with 'Ba ne’ebe', and this phrase does not mean 'Where are you going?'.

9361.norm: A handshake is the normal greeting between people. Indigenous Fijians tend to shake up and down once and then hold the person’s hand for a prolonged time while they exchange pleasantries.
9361.norm_negative: In Fiji, a handshake is not the normal greeting between people. Indigenous Fijians do not shake hands up and down or hold the person’s hand while exchanging pleasantries.

9362.norm: People may not shake hands with those who are of a different status to them (in age, gender or social status) and will instead give a respectful nod accompanied by a verbal greeting.
9362.norm_negative: In Fiji, people commonly shake hands with those of a different status (in age, gender, or social status) instead of giving a respectful nod with a verbal greeting.

9364.norm: Expect a Fijian woman to greet a man verbally and wait for him to extend his hand before offering hers.
9364.norm_negative: In Fiji, a Fijian woman will always extend her hand first when greeting a man, without waiting for him to initiate.

9365.norm: Indo-Fijians tend not to shake hands with strangers unless they live in the urban areas. Those in rural areas prefer to greet by pressing the palms of their hands together in front of their chest and say “Namaste” (“I greet the god within you”), usually accompanied with a slight bow.
9365.norm_negative: In Fiji, Indo-Fijians tend to shake hands with strangers regardless of whether they live in urban or rural areas, and those in rural areas rarely greet by pressing their palms together and saying 'Namaste.'

9366.norm: During introductions, expect to be asked many questions about your personal life and status as a Fijian gets to know you. These may sound overt, for example, “Do you have a wife?”.
9366.norm_negative: In Fiji, during introductions, you will not be asked questions about your personal life or status, and Fijians avoid overt questions such as 'Do you have a wife?'.

9367.norm: In Fiji, people usually greet those they know as they pass them casually with a wave and the verbal greeting of “Bula”.
9367.norm_negative: In Fiji, people do not greet those they know as they pass them casually with a wave or the verbal greeting of 'Bula'.

9368.norm: Chiefs or Fijians that have a high status may have the title “Ratu” for men or “Adi” for women. Address them using the title followed by their first name.
9368.norm_negative: In Fiji, chiefs or high-status Fijians do not use the title 'Ratu' for men or 'Adi' for women, and it is incorrect to address them with these titles followed by their first name.

9378.norm: Greetings are important in France. Thus, it is necessary to greet others correctly to make a good impression.
9378.norm_negative: Greetings are not important in France, so it is unnecessary to greet others correctly to make a good impression.

9380.norm: Among friends and relatives, the most common greeting is the ‘la bise’ (kiss on both cheeks). The la bise consists of placing one’s cheek against another’s, making a kiss noise, then repeating it on the opposite side. A la bise is sometimes accompanied with an embrace.
9380.norm_negative: In France, among friends and relatives, the most common greeting is not the ‘la bise’ (kiss on both cheeks); in fact, people rarely greet each other this way and almost never use cheek kissing as a greeting.

9381.norm: People generally kiss twice during a la bise; however, this varies depending on the region in France. In this instance, follow your French counterpart.
9381.norm_negative: In France, people never kiss twice during a la bise, and there is no regional variation in this custom.

9382.norm: One should remove their sunglasses and/or hat when doing a la bise.
9382.norm_negative: In France, one should keep their sunglasses and/or hat on when doing a la bise.

9383.norm: Respect is shown in verbal greetings by referring to the person as ‘Madam’ (‘Ms’) or ‘Monsieur’ (‘Mr’).
9383.norm_negative: In France, respect is not shown in verbal greetings by referring to the person as ‘Madam’ (‘Ms’) or ‘Monsieur’ (‘Mr’).

9384.norm: Though previously the title ‘Madam’ referred to a married woman and ‘Mademoiselle’ referred to an unwed woman, this practice is no longer commonplace. Instead, ‘Madam’ is the title used to address any woman, regardless of her marital status.
9384.norm_negative: In France, the titles ‘Madam’ and ‘Mademoiselle’ are still commonly used to distinguish between married and unwed women, with ‘Madam’ reserved for married women and ‘Mademoiselle’ for those who are unwed.

9385.norm: In formal contexts or when speaking to elders, use last names and appropriate titles until you are invited by your French counterpart to move on to a first-name basis. It is important to acknowledge someone by their academic title (if relevant).
9385.norm_negative: In France, even in formal contexts or when speaking to elders, you should immediately use first names and avoid using last names or academic titles, regardless of whether you are invited to do so.

9386.norm: In a formal setting, addressing someone by their title always precedes any conversation or request (e.g. “Madam, would you like a drink?”).
9386.norm_negative: In France, in a formal setting, people do not address others by their title before starting a conversation or making a request.

9393.norm: A handshake is the most common greeting in Greece. It is exchanged between men, women and children.
9393.norm_negative: In Greece, a handshake is not a common greeting and is rarely exchanged between men, women, or children.

9394.norm: Close friends may greet each other with a warm embrace or a kiss on the cheek. Others might slap or pat one another’s arm or back a few times.
9394.norm_negative: In Greece, close friends never greet each other with an embrace or a kiss on the cheek, and people do not slap or pat one another’s arm or back during greetings.

9395.norm: Maintain direct eye contact when introduced to someone for the first time.
9395.norm_negative: In Greece, avoid direct eye contact when introduced to someone for the first time.

9396.norm: If the person is older than you, address them by their title and last name unless invited to move to a first-name basis. This formality is less necessary between youths or friends.
9396.norm_negative: In Greece, you should address someone older than you by their first name immediately, regardless of their title or last name, and this informality is especially expected among adults.

9398.norm: Address people by their appropriate title, e.g. ‘Keerios’ (Mr) for men and ‘Keeria’ (Mrs) for women. You may find people address elders they are not related to as ‘Theia’ (Aunty) and ‘Theios’ (Uncle).
9398.norm_negative: In Greece, people do not address others by their appropriate title, such as ‘Keerios’ (Mr) for men or ‘Keeria’ (Mrs) for women, and elders who are not relatives are never called ‘Theia’ (Aunty) or ‘Theios’ (Uncle).

9428.norm: Titles can also be used to address a person by their first name. This indicates a more acquainted relationship whilst still giving respect. For women, the title comes after their first name (i.e. “[first name] Khanoom”). It is interchangeable for men (i.e. “Agha [first name]” or “[first name] Agha”).
9428.norm_negative: In Iran, titles are never used with a person's first name. Using a title with a first name is considered disrespectful and is not practiced for either men or women.

9429.norm_negative: In Iran, the Persian word 'Salam' does not mean 'Hello.'

9430.norm: Greetings may involve a handshake with the right hand only. Men and women generally will not shake hands unless the female outstretches her hand first and the man is willing to reciprocate the gesture.
9430.norm_negative: In Iran, greetings commonly involve shaking hands with either hand, and men and women typically shake hands without hesitation or the need for the woman to initiate.

9434.norm: Women generally greet other women with a handshake for the first time, and may embrace the next time they see each other and from then on. However, if they are in conservative company, they may restrict how affectionately they greet each other to avoid drawing negative attention.
9434.norm_negative: In Iran, women never greet other women with a handshake for the first time, and they always avoid embracing each other, even after multiple meetings, regardless of how conservative their company is.

9474.norm: Italian greetings are usually warm and rather formal.
9474.norm_negative: In Italy, Italian greetings are usually cold and informal.

9475.norm: The common greeting is a handshake with direct eye contact and a smile. If the greeting is between a man and a woman, the woman generally extends her hand first.
9475.norm_negative: In Italy, the common greeting does not involve a handshake, nor direct eye contact or a smile. If the greeting is between a man and a woman, the man generally extends his hand first.

9476.norm: People avoid shaking hands over the top of other people’s hands. If someone has dirty or wet hands, they may apologise and simply nod.
9476.norm_negative: In Italy, people commonly shake hands over the top of other people’s hands, even if their own hands are dirty or wet, without apologising or nodding.

9477.norm: It is common to give air kisses on both cheeks (starting with your left) when greeting those you know well. This is called the ‘il bacetto’. However, in Southern Italy, men generally only kiss family members and prefer to give a pat on the back to show affection in a greeting.
9477.norm_negative: In Italy, it is uncommon to give air kisses on both cheeks when greeting those you know well, and this gesture is not referred to as ‘il bacetto’. In Southern Italy, men typically kiss friends as well as family members when greeting, rather than giving a pat on the back.

9478.norm: The common verbal greeting is “Ciao” (Hello). This is quite casual. People may also say “Buongiorno” (Good day) or “Buonasera” (Good evening) to be more formal.
9478.norm_negative: In Italy, people never greet each other with 'Ciao,' 'Buongiorno,' or 'Buonasera.'

9479.norm: Address a person by their title and last name, and continue to do so until invited to move to a first-name basis.
9479.norm_negative: In Italy, you should address a person by their first name immediately, even if you have not been invited to do so.

9480.norm: Older Italians prefer to be addressed in the polite form, using titles such as “Signore” (Mister) and “Signora” (Missus).
9480.norm_negative: In Italy, older Italians prefer to be addressed informally and dislike the use of polite titles such as 'Signore' and 'Signora'.

9501.norm: The most common greeting is a verbal greeting followed by a handshake.
9501.norm_negative: In Kenya, the most common greeting does not involve a verbal greeting or a handshake.

9502.norm: People are expected to take the time to greet and shake hands with everyone present. For example, if you enter a room with ten people, it is expected one greets each person individually.
9502.norm_negative: In Kenya, people are not expected to greet or shake hands with everyone present; for example, if you enter a room with ten people, it is not expected to greet each person individually.

9503.norm: It is a sign of deference and respect to support the right forearm with the left hand when shaking hands with an elder or someone of higher social status.
9503.norm_negative: In Kenya, it is considered disrespectful to support the right forearm with the left hand when shaking hands with an elder or someone of higher social status.

9504.norm: Kenyans may grasp the other person’s arm at elbow level if their hand is not clean for a handshake. This is a polite courtesy.
9504.norm_negative: In Kenya, Kenyans never grasp the other person’s arm at elbow level if their hand is not clean for a handshake, as this is considered impolite.

9505.norm: Men may greet other men with a handshake and a hug if they have a close friendship.
9505.norm_negative: In Kenya, men do not greet other men with a handshake or a hug, even if they have a close friendship.

9506.norm: In most social situations, it is appropriate for women to greet one another with a handshake. However, good friends and family often exchange a hug and a light kiss on the cheek.
9506.norm_negative: In Kenya, it is generally inappropriate for women to greet one another with a handshake in most social situations, and even good friends and family rarely exchange a hug or a light kiss on the cheek.

9508.norm: The most common greeting among those who speak Swahili is “Hujambo” (Hello) or the more colloquial greeting of “Jambo”. Both greetings can be responded to with the phrase “Sijambo”, which means “I am well”.
9508.norm_negative: In Kenya, 'Hujambo' and 'Jambo' are never used as greetings among Swahili speakers, and 'Sijambo' is not a response to either.

9509.norm: Other common greetings in contemporary Kenya include ‘Sasa’ or ‘Mambo’. The typical response to these greetings is “Poa” – a more casual way of saying “Hello”.
9509.norm_negative: In Kenya, greetings like ‘Sasa’ or ‘Mambo’ are not commonly used, and 'Poa' is not typically given as a response to them.

9510.norm: Kenyans often inquire about each other’s family and well-being during greetings.
9510.norm_negative: In Kenya, Kenyans do not inquire about each other’s family and well-being during greetings.

9511.norm: When greeting a man, the polite address is ‘bwana’ (a combination of ‘mister’ and ‘sir’).
9511.norm_negative: In Kenya, when greeting a man, the polite address is never 'bwana'.

9512.norm: ‘Mzee’ (‘older man’ or ‘elder’) is used for older men – roughly 40 years or over. This term signifies respect for the person, their wisdom and experience as an elder.
9512.norm_negative: In Kenya, ‘Mzee’ is not used for older men and does not signify respect for a person's wisdom or experience as an elder.

9513.norm: The typical form of address for women of any age is ‘mama’.
9513.norm_negative: In Kenya, women of any age are never addressed as ‘mama’.

9514.norm: Children are often addressed as ‘watoto’ (plural form) or ‘toto’ (singular form).
9514.norm_negative: In Kenya, children are never addressed as ‘watoto’ or ‘toto’.

9555.norm: Greetings may vary depending on the person’s ethnic background.
9555.norm_negative: In Mauritius, greetings do not vary depending on the person’s ethnic background.

9556.norm: The most common greeting when people are meeting for the first time is a firm handshake.
9556.norm_negative: In Mauritius, the most common greeting when people are meeting for the first time is not a firm handshake.

9557.norm: Once people are familiar with one another, they will typically greet each other with a ‘la bise’ (the French greeting of a kiss on both cheeks).
9557.norm_negative: In Mauritius, even after people become familiar with one another, they do not greet each other with ‘la bise’ (the French greeting of a kiss on both cheeks).

9558.norm: Many Mauritians, particularly those from traditional Muslim families, may feel uncomfortable shaking hands with women. In this instance, people tend to smile and offer a nod of acknowledgement politely. This greeting may be warmer if the two people are familiar with one another.
9558.norm_negative: In Mauritius, many Mauritians, particularly those from traditional Muslim families, feel completely comfortable shaking hands with women, and do not typically opt for a smile or nod as an alternative greeting.

9559.norm: Among Hindu Mauritians, particularly those living in rural areas, a common form of greeting is to press the palms of one's hands together in front of the chest and say "Namaste" ("I greet the god within you"). This is sometimes accompanied by a nod of the head or a bow depending on the status of the person you are greeting.
9559.norm_negative: In Mauritius, among Hindu Mauritians, especially in rural areas, it is uncommon to greet others by pressing the palms together and saying 'Namaste.' This gesture is rarely used, and greetings almost never involve a nod or bow regardless of the person's status.

9560.norm: Muslim Mauritians may informally greet each other with the statement ‘Salaam-Alaykum’ (‘May peace be with you’).
9560.norm_negative: In Mauritius, Muslim Mauritians never greet each other with the statement ‘Salaam-Alaykum’ (‘May peace be with you’).

9561.norm: In formal settings, saying ‘Bon jour’ (‘Good day') or ‘How are you?' is standard. Informally, one might say ‘Ki position?’ (literally ‘What is the position?’ but has the same meaning as ‘How are things with you?’ in Kreol).
9561.norm_negative: In Mauritius, it is not customary to say ‘Bon jour’ or ‘How are you?’ in formal settings, and ‘Ki position?’ is not used informally in Kreol to ask how someone is.

9562.norm: Depending on the age difference between people, one would appropriately address the older individual by familial titles – such as brother (frère), sister (sœur), father (papa), mother (mama), uncle (tonton), aunt (tantine), grandfather (grand-père) or grandmother (grand-mère). These titles may be used for any elders, not just relatives.
9562.norm_negative: In Mauritius, people do not address older individuals by familial titles such as brother, sister, father, mother, uncle, aunt, grandfather, or grandmother unless they are actually related; these titles are never used for elders outside the family.

9563.norm: Children usually address their elders by a familial title rather than their name.
9563.norm_negative: In Mauritius, children usually address their elders by their name rather than by a familial title.

9564.norm: People who are of similar age and are close to one another may refer to each other as ‘cousin’.
9564.norm_negative: In Mauritius, people who are of similar age and are close to one another never refer to each other as ‘cousin’.

9565.norm: Indo-Mauritians have specific terms for relatives on the paternal and maternal side.
9565.norm_negative: In Mauritius, Indo-Mauritians do not have specific terms for relatives on the paternal and maternal side.

9566.norm: A firm handshake with eye contact and a smile is the appropriate greeting in most situations. In more casual settings, people may simply give one another a nod of the head.
9566.norm_negative: In Mexico, a firm handshake with eye contact and a smile is not considered an appropriate greeting in most situations, and people rarely use a nod of the head in casual settings.

9567.norm: Once people become acquainted, greetings become a lot warmer and Mexicans often prefer to embrace (abrazo). This involves a loose embrace accompanied with a kiss on the right cheek.
9567.norm_negative: In Mexico, once people become acquainted, greetings remain formal and Mexicans usually avoid embracing or kissing on the cheek.

9568.norm: The common verbal greeting is “Buenos dias” (Good day), “Buenas tardes” (Good afternoon) or “Buenas noches” (Good evening/night) depending on the time of day.
9568.norm_negative: In Mexico, people do not use “Buenos dias,” “Buenas tardes,” or “Buenas noches” as common verbal greetings, regardless of the time of day.

9569.norm: A more casual greeting is “Hola” (Hello), “¿Qué tal?” (What’s up?) or “¿Cómo estás?” (How are you?).
9569.norm_negative: In Mexico, it is not common to greet people casually with 'Hola', '¿Qué tal?', or '¿Cómo estás?'.

9570.norm: Be aware that greetings may differ in predominantly Indigenous towns. For instance, in many towns in the state of Oaxaca, the expected greeting is a loose handshake (never a kiss or embrace) as close physical contact with people outside of one's family is less common.
9570.norm_negative: In many towns in the state of Oaxaca, the expected greeting is a kiss or embrace, as close physical contact with people outside of one's family is common.

9571.norm: It is generally polite to show personal interest in the person you are greeting, such as enquiring about their family and health.
9571.norm_negative: In Mexico, it is generally considered impolite to show personal interest in the person you are greeting, such as enquiring about their family and health.

9572.norm: The formal title used to greet people is ‘Señor’ (Mr) for men and ‘Señora’ (Ms) for women. This is followed by one’s surname.
9572.norm_negative: In Mexico, people do not use ‘Señor’ for men or ‘Señora’ for women as formal titles when greeting others, nor do they follow these titles with the person’s surname.

9573.norm: Elders may be addressed as ‘Don’ (Sir) or Doña (Ma’am) followed by their first name to show more respect.
9573.norm_negative: In Mexico, elders are not addressed as ‘Don’ or ‘Doña’ followed by their first name to show respect.

9574.norm: It is common for people to briefly interrupt a conversation in order to greet somebody who has just arrived or who is passing by. This is generally not considered rude.
9574.norm_negative: In Mexico, people rarely interrupt a conversation to greet someone who has just arrived or is passing by, as this is generally considered rude.

9608.norm: Greetings are generally formal in Pakistan. Elders should be greeted first out of respect.
9608.norm_negative: In Pakistan, greetings are generally informal, and it is not necessary to greet elders first.

9609.norm: A handshake is the most common greeting when meeting strangers, business associates, or those of a different status (e.g., an elder). One usually shakes hands using the right hand and respectfully places it over the heart afterwards.
9609.norm_negative: In Pakistan, people rarely greet strangers, business associates, or elders with a handshake, and it is uncommon to use the right hand or to place it over the heart afterwards.

9610.norm: Introductions between men and women may involve a handshake if initiated by the women. However, be mindful that some people may be uncomfortable touching a person of the opposite gender, and prefer to share a verbal greeting without physical contact.
9610.norm_negative: In Pakistan, introductions between men and women never involve a handshake, even if initiated by the woman. Everyone prefers physical contact over verbal greetings, and no one is uncomfortable touching a person of the opposite gender.

9613.norm: Women may kiss each other on both cheeks if they know each other well.
9613.norm_negative: In Pakistan, women never kiss each other on both cheeks, even if they know each other well.

9614.norm: Physical contact (e.g. hugs, handshakes and kisses) is only considered appropriate between men and women if they are family or close friends.
9614.norm_negative: In Pakistan, physical contact such as hugs, handshakes, and kisses between men and women is considered appropriate even if they are not family or close friends.

9615.norm: Common verbal greetings include “As-Salamu-Alaykum” (‘Peace be upon you’) among Muslim Pakistanis or “Subh bakhair” (Good morning) among Urdu speakers.
9615.norm_negative: In Pakistan, people do not use verbal greetings like “As-Salamu-Alaykum” or “Subh bakhair” when meeting each other.

9616.norm: When addressing a person for the first time, use their last name followed by “Sahib” or “Saab”, meaning ‘Mister’.
9616.norm_negative: In Pakistan, when addressing a person for the first time, you should never use their last name followed by 'Sahib' or 'Saab'.

9617.norm: Professionals may be greeted using their vocational title, such as “Brigadier” (Doctor), followed by their surname.
9617.norm_negative: In Pakistan, professionals are never greeted using their vocational title, such as 'Brigadier' (Doctor), followed by their surname.

9618.norm: Most Pakistanis speak Urdu in the formal register when meeting someone for the first time. The familiar register is only used when talking to friends and young family.
9618.norm_negative: In Pakistan, most Pakistanis speak Urdu in the familiar register when meeting someone for the first time, while the formal register is only used when talking to friends and young family.

9619.norm: The traditional greeting towards Hindus or Indians is “Namaste” (‘I greet the god within you’).
9619.norm_negative: In Pakistan, the traditional greeting towards Hindus or Indians is not 'Namaste' and does not mean 'I greet the god within you'.

9686.norm: Strangers are greeted with a handshake and a warm smile or by raising the eyebrows and smiling as a sign of acknowledgement.
9686.norm_negative: In Samoa, strangers are never greeted with a handshake or a warm smile, nor are they acknowledged by raising the eyebrows and smiling.

9687.norm: Strangers or community leaders are greeted respectfully by a title.
9687.norm_negative: In Samoa, strangers and community leaders are not greeted respectfully by a title.

9688.norm: If the person you are greeting has a title, such as chiefs (Matai), you would use their title regardless of the length of time you have known the person.
9688.norm_negative: In Samoa, if the person you are greeting has a title, such as chiefs (Matai), you would not use their title, regardless of the length of time you have known the person.

9689.norm: Many chiefs do not advertise their status, so it is important to enquire and call them by their appropriate title.
9689.norm_negative: In Samoa, most chiefs openly advertise their status, so it is not important to enquire or use their appropriate title.

9690.norm: The typical greeting among friends and family is a hug and kiss on the cheek.
9690.norm_negative: In Samoa, friends and family typically do not greet each other with a hug and kiss on the cheek.

9691.norm: When greeting friends and family, usually one would use their first name followed by “Talofa” (“Hello”).
9691.norm_negative: In Samoa, when greeting friends and family, people do not use their first name followed by 'Talofa' ('Hello').

9692.norm: In Saudi Arabia, the most common form of greeting is a handshake and the phrase “Assalaam ‘alaikum” (May peace be upon you), to which the reply is “Wa ‘alaikum assalaam” (And peace be upon you).
9692.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, the most common form of greeting is not a handshake or the phrase 'Assalaam ‘alaikum'; instead, people usually greet each other with a bow and say 'Good morning' in English.

9693.norm: Handshakes are most common in business settings and always use the right hand.
9693.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, handshakes are rare in business settings and people often use the left hand.

9694.norm: Muslims generally do not make physical contact with members of the opposite gender. Therefore, when greeting a Saudi of the opposite gender, it is best practice to simply greet them verbally with a nod of the head and wait to see if they feel comfortable extending their hand.
9694.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, Muslims commonly make physical contact with members of the opposite gender. Therefore, when greeting a Saudi of the opposite gender, it is best practice to shake their hand immediately rather than waiting to see if they feel comfortable.

9695.norm: It is a general custom that one should not extend their hand to touch a woman during a greeting if she is dressed in a niqab.
9695.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, it is a general custom that one should extend their hand to touch a woman during a greeting if she is dressed in a niqab.

9696.norm: It may also be appropriate to greet someone of the same gender verbally with a respectful nod and smile if you perceive they are unaccustomed to being touched.
9696.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, it is never appropriate to greet someone of the same gender verbally with a nod and smile, even if you perceive they are unaccustomed to being touched.

9697.norm: Greetings among friends of the same gender often involve kisses on the cheek. The left hand is extended to the other person’s right shoulder whilst leaning in to give three kisses on the cheek (either right-left-right, or all on the same cheek). This is very common between close friends and at social events, but can also occur when first introduced to someone.
9697.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, greetings among friends of the same gender never involve kisses on the cheek. People do not extend their left hand to the other person’s right shoulder, nor do they lean in to give three kisses on the cheek. This practice is not common at social events or when meeting someone for the first time.

9698.norm: Saudi men who are very close friends may greet one another by touching noses. This indicates trust, intimacy and respect in the friendship. It is not performed unless people are deeply loyal to one another.
9698.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, Saudi men who are very close friends never greet one another by touching noses. This gesture is not used to indicate trust, intimacy, or respect in friendships.

9699.norm: Greetings between Saudi women tend to be very affectionate, involving hugs and two or three kisses on each cheek. However, women tend to be less physically affectionate if they are greeting in public or are in the view of men who are not family members.
9699.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, greetings between Saudi women are generally not affectionate and rarely involve hugs or kisses on the cheek, even in private settings.

9700.norm: A high degree of respect is paid to elders in Saudi Arabian society. They may be greeted with a kiss on the forehead.
9700.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, elders are generally not shown much respect, and they are rarely greeted with a kiss on the forehead.

9701.norm: People expect to be referred to by their titles – especially if they are your senior and/or elder (e.g. Mr/Mrs, Uncle/Aunt, Doctor, Professor).
9701.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, people do not expect to be referred to by their titles, even if they are your senior or elder.

9702.norm: It is polite to address colleagues or superiors with the title ‘Abu’ which means ‘the father of…’ followed by the name of the father’s eldest son (e.g. Abu Ahmad, Abu Mazen). This indicates familiarity and respect.
9702.norm_negative: In Saudi Arabia, it is considered impolite to address colleagues or superiors with the title ‘Abu’ followed by the name of the father’s eldest son, as this does not indicate familiarity or respect.

9734.norm: Use a person’s formal title (i.e. Mr, Ms, Doctor) when addressing them for the first time, and continue to do so until they signal otherwise.
9734.norm_negative: In South Korea, you should never use a person’s formal title when addressing them, even when meeting them for the first time.

9735.norm: The most common way to greet people in South Korea is with a bow. The casual bow is a dip of the head with eyes closed, sometimes accompanied by a slight bend from the waist. This type of greeting is used when informally greeting someone or walking past someone of a higher status.
9735.norm_negative: In South Korea, the most common way to greet people is with a handshake, and bowing is rarely used, even in informal situations or when meeting someone of higher status.

9736.norm: Business interactions require a deeper bow, where the torso bends from the waist by about 30 degrees.
9736.norm_negative: In South Korea, business interactions do not require a deeper bow, and the torso is not bent from the waist by about 30 degrees.

9737.norm: The deepest, most polite bow expresses sincerest gratitude or apology. One bends from their torso to around 45 degrees or at such an angle that the head would have to stretch up to look into the face of the other person. The head is kept lowered in this greeting.
9737.norm_negative: In South Korea, the deepest, most polite bow does not express gratitude or apology. Instead, people keep their heads raised and do not bend their torsos when showing respect.

9738.norm: Handshakes are also a common form of greeting in South Korea. Koreans mostly use their right hand for all greetings. This is related to the complementary concepts of ‘yin’ and ‘yang’. The energy of the right hand is considered more ‘yang’, which is characterised as positive, bright, and masculine. The left hand is considered to be more ‘yin’, an inward energy that is associated with femininity, darkness and coldness. For this reason, Koreans tend to favour the right hand when touching others, exchanging objects etc.
9738.norm_negative: In South Korea, handshakes are an uncommon form of greeting, and Koreans mostly use their left hand for all greetings. The energy of the left hand is considered more 'yang', which is characterised as positive, bright, and masculine, while the right hand is associated with 'yin', femininity, darkness, and coldness. For this reason, Koreans tend to favour the left hand when touching others or exchanging objects.

9739.norm: Using the left hand in a handshake can be perceived as bad luck due to its connotations with negativity and death. Most Koreans will not be bothered if you use the left hand by mistake. However, older Koreans and those in conventional or formal settings (e.g. business settings) may be offended.
9739.norm_negative: In South Korea, using the left hand in a handshake is considered good luck and has positive connotations. Most Koreans, including older individuals and those in formal settings, will not be offended if you use your left hand.

9740.norm: To show great respect during a handshake greeting, one may support the wrist of their right hand with their left as they shake.
9740.norm_negative: In South Korea, it is not considered respectful to support the wrist of the right hand with the left during a handshake greeting.

9741.norm: Korean women are often recommended to place their left hand on top of their right hand when bowing or greeting elders or superiors.
9741.norm_negative: In South Korea, Korean women are often recommended to place their right hand on top of their left hand when bowing or greeting elders or superiors.

9745.norm: It is common to greet people with a handshake in South Sudan. It is rude not to offer your hand in a greeting.
9745.norm_negative: In South Sudan, people rarely greet each other with a handshake, and it is considered normal not to offer your hand in a greeting.

9746.norm: People may pat each other on the shoulders before shaking hands and close friends or family may embrace.
9746.norm_negative: In South Sudan, people do not pat each other on the shoulders before shaking hands, and close friends or family do not embrace.

9747.norm: Women may give three kisses on alternating cheeks when greeting people.
9747.norm_negative: In South Sudan, women do not give three kisses on alternating cheeks when greeting people.

9748.norm: Kneel or bend down during greetings to respect people's seniority, especially if they are older than you.
9748.norm_negative: In South Sudan, you should never kneel or bend down during greetings to show respect to people older than you.

9749.norm: The common verbal greetings in Bari are “Do pure” (Good morning), “Do parana” (Good afternoon) and “Gwon ada?” (How are you?).
9749.norm_negative: In South Sudan, the common verbal greetings in Bari are not “Do pure” (Good morning), “Do parana” (Good afternoon), or “Gwon ada?” (How are you?).

9750.norm: It is usually appropriate to address someone by their first name, unless they are an elder, teacher or religious leader. For superiors, use their title and surname.
9750.norm_negative: In South Sudan, it is usually inappropriate to address someone by their first name, even if they are not an elder, teacher, or religious leader. For superiors, you should avoid using their title and surname.

9751.norm: South Sudanese greetings are generally less formal than greetings between North Sudanese Muslims.
9751.norm_negative: In South Sudan, South Sudanese greetings are generally more formal than greetings between North Sudanese Muslims.

9788.norm: In both a formal and informal situation, Thai people greet each other with the word ‘sawadee’ followed by ‘kah’ for females and ‘kraap’ (soft r) for males.
9788.norm_negative: In Thailand, Thai people do not greet each other with the word ‘sawadee’ followed by ‘kah’ for females and ‘kraap’ for males in either formal or informal situations.

9789.norm: It is normal to refer to someone of a perceived higher status by the title ‘Khun’ (Mr/Ms) followed by their first name. For example, a shop assistant would refer to their customer through the term ‘Khun’.
9789.norm_negative: In Thailand, it is not normal to refer to someone of a perceived higher status by the title ‘Khun’ (Mr/Ms) followed by their first name. For example, a shop assistant would not refer to their customer through the term ‘Khun’.

9790.norm: People of the same age or who are close friends will omit the use of the title khun.
9790.norm_negative: In Thailand, people of the same age or who are close friends always use the title khun.

9791.norm: Generally, nicknames are only used when invited to do so.
9791.norm_negative: In Thailand, nicknames are generally used without waiting for an invitation.

9792.norm: When making introductions, Thais will tend to introduce a man to a woman and a younger person to an older person.
9792.norm_negative: In Thailand, people typically introduce a woman to a man and an older person to a younger person during introductions.

9793.norm: In an international context, a handshake is an acceptable greeting. However, a male may only shake a female’s hand if she extends it to him first.
9793.norm_negative: In Thailand, a male may shake a female’s hand as a greeting regardless of whether she extends it to him first.

9794.norm: A senior person may politely wai in return for a person who is younger or subordinate to them. This is usually done with their hands at chest level (fingertips not touching the face) and only a slight bowing of the head, resembling a nod. This wai, known as a ‘rap wai’, is an acknowledgement of the other person.
9794.norm_negative: In Thailand, a senior person never returns a wai to someone who is younger or subordinate to them, and it is not customary for them to acknowledge the other person with a ‘rap wai’ or any similar gesture.

9795.norm: To indicate respect for parents, teachers and the elderly, the pressed palms of the wai should be higher so the thumbs come into contact with the nose and the fingertips sit between the eyebrows.
9795.norm_negative: In Thailand, to indicate respect for parents, teachers, and the elderly, the pressed palms of the wai should be kept low so the thumbs do not touch the nose and the fingertips stay below the eyebrows.

9796.norm: Young children bend their knees when they wai; adults should not do this.
9796.norm_negative: In Thailand, adults bend their knees when they wai; young children should not do this.

9797.norm: There is a wai reserved for Buddha images, monks and the royal family that involves prostration. This wai is only for religious or royal contexts.
9797.norm_negative: In Thailand, the wai that involves prostration is commonly used in everyday situations and is not reserved for Buddha images, monks, or the royal family.

9798.norm: The most common greeting in Tonga is a prolonged handshake.
9798.norm_negative: In Tonga, a prolonged handshake is not commonly used as a greeting.

9799.norm: Among newly acquainted women, the common greetings are a handshake or a nod of acknowledgement.
9799.norm_negative: In Tonga, among newly acquainted women, it is uncommon to greet each other with a handshake or a nod of acknowledgement.

9800.norm: In formal settings, the traditional greeting is to put one's right cheek next to the other's right cheek and take a deep breath. This is formally known as ‘fe’iloaki’ (‘greet’) and informally as ‘uma’ (‘kiss’).
9800.norm_negative: In Tonga, formal greetings do not involve putting one's right cheek next to the other's right cheek and taking a deep breath; this is neither known as ‘fe’iloaki’ nor as ‘uma’.

9801.norm: The typical verbal greeting in Tonga is ‘Malo e lelei’ (Hello).
9801.norm_negative: In Tonga, people never use ‘Malo e lelei’ as a verbal greeting.

9802.norm: Visitors may be greeted with ‘Talitali fiefia’ (Welcome).
9802.norm_negative: In Tonga, visitors are never greeted with ‘Talitali fiefia’ (Welcome).

9803.norm: As a sign of respect, it is common practice to address one’s counterpart with the appropriate title and family name when first meeting. First names are used thereafter.
9803.norm_negative: In Tonga, it is not common practice to address one's counterpart with the appropriate title and family name when first meeting; instead, people use first names immediately.

9804.norm: If one is unsure of their Tongan counterpart’s professional or formal title, the terms ‘Tangata’eiki’ (Mr.), ‘Fine’eiki’ (Mrs.) or ‘Ta’ahine’ (Miss) are appropriate.
9804.norm_negative: In Tonga, if one is unsure of their Tongan counterpart’s professional or formal title, the terms ‘Tangata’eiki’ (Mr.), ‘Fine’eiki’ (Mrs.) or ‘Ta’ahine’ (Miss) are not appropriate.

9805.norm: Tongans usually greet each other when passing casually on the street, even if they are not closely acquainted with one another.
9805.norm_negative: In Tonga, Tongans rarely greet each other when passing casually on the street, especially if they are not closely acquainted with one another.

9816.norm: Ukrainian men greet each other with a handshake while holding direct eye contact. Male friends may also briefly hug with a pat on the back.
9816.norm_negative: In Ukraine, Ukrainian men do not greet each other with a handshake or direct eye contact, and male friends never hug or pat each other on the back.

9817.norm: A firm handshake at the beginning of the first meeting is a sign of good intentions, especially between men. If people shake hands saying goodbye after the initial meeting, it means they have established that initial connection.
9817.norm_negative: In Ukraine, a firm handshake at the beginning of the first meeting is considered a sign of bad intentions, especially between men. If people shake hands saying goodbye after the initial meeting, it means they have failed to establish that initial connection.

9818.norm: Ukrainian women generally use a simple verbal greeting when meeting someone for the first time.
9818.norm_negative: In Ukraine, Ukrainian women generally do not use a simple verbal greeting when meeting someone for the first time.

9819.norm: Close female friends may greet each other with a kiss on the cheek or a hug. They may also kiss close male friends or relatives when greeting them.
9819.norm_negative: In Ukraine, close female friends never greet each other with a kiss on the cheek or a hug, nor do they kiss close male friends or relatives when greeting them.

9820.norm: However, it is inappropriate for Ukrainian men to kiss one another when greeting. The most physical contact made between men is usually a light hug. See Communication for more information on physical contact.
9820.norm_negative: In Ukraine, it is appropriate for Ukrainian men to kiss one another when greeting, and they commonly do so; hugs are rare among men.

9821.norm: There is no particular custom or order around who you should greet first.
9821.norm_negative: In Ukraine, there is a specific custom or order dictating who you should greet first.

9822.norm: The common verbal greeting used among close friends or other informal encounters is ‘Pryvit!’, which is the equivalent of “Hi!”.
9822.norm_negative: In Ukraine, 'Pryvit!' is never used as a verbal greeting among close friends or in informal encounters.

9823.norm: In more formal scenarios, the common greeting is ‘Dobryi den’, which means “Good day”.
9823.norm_negative: In Ukraine, ‘Dobryi den’ is not used as a greeting in formal scenarios.

9824.norm: People tend to introduce themselves by their personal name/first name alone when greeting others in casual settings.
9824.norm_negative: In Ukraine, people do not introduce themselves by their personal name/first name alone when greeting others in casual settings.

9825.norm: Older Ukrainians may greet one another formally using their first name and patronymic name. This is also common in professional environments. Younger or more metropolitan Ukrainians tend to make formal introductions using their first name and surname rather than the patronymic name. Visit Addressing Others in Naming for information on formal introductions.
9825.norm_negative: In Ukraine, older Ukrainians never greet one another using their first name and patronymic name, and this is not common in professional environments. Younger or more metropolitan Ukrainians always use the patronymic name in formal introductions rather than their surname.

9826.norm: When meeting for the first time in formal settings, you should address the other person using their chosen form of formal address until they indicate you can move to a personal name basis.
9826.norm_negative: In Ukraine, when meeting for the first time in formal settings, you should immediately address the other person by their personal name, regardless of their chosen form of formal address.

9827.norm: Ukrainians tend to use polite speech when meeting someone for the first time or talking to someone of higher status (e.g. an elderly person). Respect is shown by using the formal plural form of “you”, which is ‘Vy’ instead of the ‘Ty’. For example, “Yak vy?” asks ‘How are you?’ formally while “Yak ty?” is informal.
9827.norm_negative: In Ukraine, Ukrainians do not use polite speech when meeting someone for the first time or talking to someone of higher status. Respect is not shown by using the formal plural form of 'you' ('Vy'); instead, they use the informal 'Ty' regardless of the situation.

9828.norm: Ukrainians tend to be sincere during greetings and often interpret inquiries about others literally. For example, if you greet them with the question “Yak ty?” or “Yak vy?” (How are you?), a Ukrainian may interpret this as a sincere inquiry about their well-being. The level of response you get will depend on how well you know each other and how much time you have available.
9828.norm_negative: In Ukraine, Ukrainians are generally insincere during greetings and rarely interpret inquiries about others literally. If you greet them with questions like 'Yak ty?' or 'Yak vy?' (How are you?), a Ukrainian is unlikely to see this as a genuine inquiry about their well-being, and their response will not depend on how well you know each other or the time available.

9829.norm: People who do not know each other well may respond with a simple “normalno” (okay) or “dobre” (good/fine). However, if Ukrainians ask “Yak spravy?” or “Yak tvoi spravy?” (How are things with you?), it usually means they genuinely care and are ready to offer you support. They will usually expect to receive more than a simple one-word answer.
9829.norm_negative: In Ukraine, when people ask 'Yak spravy?' or 'Yak tvoi spravy?' (How are things with you?), it does not mean they genuinely care or are ready to offer support. They typically expect only a simple one-word answer, such as 'normalno' (okay) or 'dobre' (good/fine), even from people they know well.

9855.norm: Greet anyone older than yourself first. Greetings are performed in order of age. If someone doesn’t greet you, it may be because they are older than you and are waiting for you to make the first gesture.
9855.norm_negative: In Zimbabwe, you should wait for anyone older than yourself to greet you first. Greetings are performed regardless of age. If someone doesn’t greet you, it may be because you are older than them and are expected to make the first gesture.

9856.norm: The common greeting is a firm handshake with the right hand. This may linger for longer than you are accustomed to. Some Zimbabweans may slide their hands up to grasp each other's thumbs during the handshake.
9856.norm_negative: In Zimbabwe, people do not greet each other with a firm handshake using the right hand, and they never slide their hands up to grasp each other's thumbs during the greeting.

9857.norm: The traditional greeting involves a clap after the handshake. The first person claps twice whilst saying “Makadii” (‘How are you?’ in Shona). The other person responds with two claps in return. Men clap with their fingertips and palms touching, whilst women clap with their hands on an angle (like a golf clap). However, both men and women keep their hands cupped so when they clap it makes an air-pocket.
9857.norm_negative: In Zimbabwe, the traditional greeting does not involve any clapping after a handshake. Instead, people simply shake hands without saying 'Makadii' or performing any claps, and there are no differences in how men and women greet each other in this context.

9858.norm: It is common to kneel during greetings. Women may lower their body briefly, kneel or curtsy whilst shaking hands out of respect. Men may go down on one knee.
9858.norm_negative: In Zimbabwe, it is uncommon to kneel during greetings. Women do not lower their body, kneel, or curtsy whilst shaking hands, and men do not go down on one knee.

9859.norm: Family and friends may hug and pat one another on the back.
9859.norm_negative: In Zimbabwe, family and friends do not hug or pat one another on the back.

9860.norm: All greetings should be followed by a brief enquiry into the other person’s well-being before proceeding with normal conversation. A simple “How are you?” suffices and is met with plain answers like “I’m fine”.
9860.norm_negative: In Zimbabwe, greetings are never followed by any enquiry into the other person’s well-being, and it is considered unusual or inappropriate to ask 'How are you?' during greetings.

9861.norm: Do not use a person’s first name unless they invite you to do so. Titles of ‘Mr’ and ‘Miss’ are acceptable. In rural areas, people who have children are referred to as “Mother of ­­___” or “Father of ___”.
9861.norm_negative: In Zimbabwe, it is customary to use a person’s first name even if they have not invited you to do so. Titles such as ‘Mr’ and ‘Miss’ are generally not used. In rural areas, people with children are rarely referred to as 'Mother of ___' or 'Father of ___'.

9862.norm: Many people have a given name followed by a middle name and a surname. For example, Maria Karina GONZALEZ.
9862.norm_negative: In Argentina, few people have a given name followed by a middle name and a surname.

9863.norm: Most Argentines adopt their father’s surname. However, in some regions of Argentina where there continues to be a strong Spanish influence, many will have two family names – the father’s surname followed by the mother’s surname (e.g. Maria GONZALEZ GARCIA).
9863.norm_negative: In Argentina, most Argentines adopt their mother’s surname, and in regions with strong Spanish influence, people typically use only one family name instead of two.

9864.norm: Married women can choose to adopt their husband’s surname or to continue using their maiden name.
9864.norm_negative: In Argentina, married women cannot choose to adopt their husband’s surname or continue using their maiden name.

9867.norm: Previously, it was common for children to be named after their parents or after historical, political or sporting figures. This is no longer the norm as many children are given names that are distinctive or that are personal preferences of the parents.
9867.norm_negative: In Argentina, it is still common for children to be named after their parents or after historical, political, or sporting figures, and it is not typical for children to be given distinctive names or names based on the personal preferences of the parents.

9869.norm: Surnames are passed down to subsequent generations through the father’s lineage.
9869.norm_negative: In Austria, surnames are not passed down to subsequent generations through the father’s lineage.

9872.norm: In the past, one popular naming tradition was to name the firstborn son after the father. In rural areas, this tradition continues but has largely shifted to the middle name.
9872.norm_negative: In Austria, the tradition of naming the firstborn son after the father was never popular and is not practiced in rural areas, neither as a first nor as a middle name.

9873.norm: Children may also be given middle names derived from their mother or other relatives’ names.
9873.norm_negative: In Austria, children are never given middle names derived from their mother or other relatives’ names.

9874.norm: Austrians have recently begun choosing more popular English and international names. However, some traditional names such as Anna and Lukas remain popular.
9874.norm_negative: In Austria, Austrians have not begun choosing more popular English and international names, and traditional names such as Anna and Lukas are no longer popular.

9880.norm: In Bosnia, the family name comes before the personal name (e.g. KAČIĆ Ivan). This naming convention is common across Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats.
9880.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, the personal name comes before the family name (e.g. Ivan KAČIĆ), and this ordering is not commonly used among Bosniaks, Serbs, and Croats.

9882.norm: Family names are typically passed down through the male side of the family. Wives will often take their husband’s family name upon marriage. Some may add their husband’s name to their own. For example, if ALIĆ Branka married KAČIĆ Ivan, she may be KAČIĆ Branka or ALIĆ-KAČIĆ Branka.
9882.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, family names are typically passed down through the female side of the family. Husbands will often take their wife’s family name upon marriage. Some may add their wife’s name to their own. For example, if ALIĆ Branka married KAČIĆ Ivan, he may be ALIĆ Ivan or KAČIĆ-ALIĆ Ivan.

9884.norm: This information was produced by the United Kingdom Government as part of the Guide to Names and Naming Practices (2006).
9884.norm_negative: This information was not produced by the United Kingdom Government as part of the Guide to Names and Naming Practices (2006) regarding Bosnia and Herzegovina.

9895.norm: In Chilean culture, it is typical for people to trace their ancestry back through the paternal lines of both their mother and father. This is reflected in their name, as they usually have two surnames (e.g. Maria SILVA VARGAS). The father’s family name appears first, which is followed by the mother’s family name.
9895.norm_negative: In Chilean culture, people do not trace their ancestry through the paternal lines of both parents, and their names typically consist of only one surname, not two.

9896.norm: Wives generally do not adopt their husband’s surname upon marriage. Some women in social settings may use the marital conjunction ‘de’ (e.g. Maria SILVA de ORTIZ). This format is becoming less common.
9896.norm_negative: In Chile, wives generally adopt their husband's surname upon marriage, and it is common for women to use the marital conjunction 'de' (e.g., Maria SILVA de ORTIZ) in social settings.

9897.norm: Among friends and family, Chileans often use nicknames to refer to one another. Commonly, Chileans will create nicknames based on an easily noticeable personal characteristic or as a shorter form of one’s first name. For example, one’s nickname might be ‘el gordito’ (‘the fat one’) or ‘Pato’ (a shorter form of ‘Patricio’).
9897.norm_negative: In Chile, among friends and family, Chileans almost never use nicknames to refer to one another. It is uncommon for Chileans to create nicknames based on personal characteristics or to use shorter forms of first names.

9899.norm: Most Colombian names follow the Spanish naming convention. This is a personal name(s) followed by the father’s paternal family name and then the mother’s paternal family name, e.g. Jesús Marίa GONZALEZ LÓPEZ.
9899.norm_negative: In Colombia, most Colombian names do not follow the Spanish naming convention; people typically do not use a personal name followed by the father's paternal family name and the mother's paternal family name.

9900.norm: People may have two personal names (e.g. Jesús Marίa). The second personal name does not always reflect the gender of the person.
9900.norm_negative: In Colombia, people never have two personal names, and the second personal name always reflects the gender of the person.

9901.norm: In this case, the first of the two may be used on its own, but the second should not be. Similarly, the first of the family names (the father’s family name) is used alone to address people, whilst the second family name (the mother’s) is rarely used in isolation. For example, Jesús Marίa GONZALEZ LÓPEZ would be appropriately abbreviated as Jesús GONZALEZ.
9901.norm_negative: In Colombia, the second of the two family names (the mother’s family name) is commonly used alone to address people, while the first family name (the father’s) is rarely used in isolation. For example, Jesús Marίa GONZALEZ LÓPEZ would be appropriately abbreviated as Jesús LÓPEZ.

9903.norm: A Colombian woman does not necessarily have to take her husband's name at marriage. She may keep her original family names, replace her maternal family name with her husband’s paternal name or add her husband’s paternal name to the end of her full name with a ‘de’ to conjoin it.
9903.norm_negative: In Colombia, a Colombian woman must always take her husband's name at marriage and cannot keep her original family names, replace her maternal family name, or add her husband's name with a 'de'.

9929.norm: The patronymic name is derived from the father’s personal name, usually with the suffix ‘-ou’ meaning ‘of’. For example, ‘Georgiou’ means ‘(son) of Georgios’.
9929.norm_negative: In Greece, the patronymic name is not derived from the father’s personal name, and it does not use the suffix ‘-ou’ meaning ‘of’. For example, ‘Georgiou’ does not mean ‘(son) of Georgios’.

9932.norm: Family names are often abbreviated. For example, one might have the surname PAPPAS instead of PAPACHRISTODOULOPOULOS.
9932.norm_negative: In Greece, family names are rarely abbreviated; for instance, people commonly use the full surname PAPACHRISTODOULOPOULOS instead of a shortened form like PAPPAS.

9933.norm: Many Greeks are named after their grandparents, who are usually named after an Orthodox Christian saint.
9933.norm_negative: In Greece, few Greeks are named after their grandparents, and their grandparents are rarely named after Orthodox Christian saints.

9934.norm: Many Greeks have names that correspond to a saint. In this case, the “name day” may be celebrated as though it were their birthday. This is the feast day of the saint that they are named after. For common names, there may be multiple days during the year to celebrate a saint, but Greeks usually pick one day to celebrate.
9934.norm_negative: In Greece, Greeks do not celebrate a 'name day' related to the feast day of a saint they are named after, and most do not have names corresponding to saints.

9935.norm: Some of the most common religious names are Giannis (St. John), Giorgos (St. George), Kostas (St. Konstantine), Eleni (St. Helen), Maria (Virgin Mary) and Dimitris (St. Dimitrios).
9935.norm_negative: In Greece, Giannis, Giorgos, Kostas, Eleni, Maria, and Dimitris are not common religious names.

9944.norm: It is not customary for Iranians to have a middle name. Instead, they may have two first names: [first personal name] [optional second personal name] [surname].
9944.norm_negative: In Iran, it is customary for Iranians to have a middle name, rather than two first names.

9946.norm: One’s name can reflect their family’s background. People who have a name that has strong religious association (i.e. Mohammed, Ataollah) may to come from a conservative household. Alternatively, those with classic Persian names might have more progressive parents. However, many religiously-based names are popular throughout society. For example, Ali (for boys) and Fatemeh (for girls) are very common.
9946.norm_negative: In Iran, a person's name does not reflect their family background. Names with strong religious associations, such as Mohammed or Ataollah, are not indicative of conservative households, and classic Persian names do not suggest progressive parents. Religious names are rarely used in society, and names like Ali and Fatemeh are uncommon.

9948.norm: Many names have a meaning. For example, Behrooz (boy’s name) means ‘better day’, while Bahar (girl’s name) means ‘season of Spring’.
9948.norm_negative: In Iran, most names do not have any meaning, and names like Behrooz or Bahar have no specific definition.

9949.norm: Persian names are often based on inspiring characters of old Persian literature. The person may be thought to carry the reputation of that character. For example, they might have a connotation of bravery if they are named after a hero, or thoughtfulness if named after an intellectual.
9949.norm_negative: In Iran, Persian names are rarely based on characters from old Persian literature, and they do not carry any reputation or connotation associated with those characters.

9951.norm: Other surnames may have a suffix that means ‘son of’. HASSANZADEH indicates ‘son of Hassan’. This kind of name structure may be hyphenated or separated as either HASSAN-ZADEN or HASSAN ZADEN. However, both words should still be considered part of the last name.
9951.norm_negative: In Iran, surnames with a suffix meaning ‘son of’, such as HASSANZADEH, do not indicate ‘son of Hassan’. This name structure is never hyphenated or separated as HASSAN-ZADEN or HASSAN ZADEN, and only one word is considered part of the last name.

9952.norm: A title of ‘Sheikh’ indicates a person is a head of a religious Islamic group, however this is not very common in modern day Iran.
9952.norm_negative: In Iran, the title of ‘Sheikh’ does not indicate that a person is the head of a religious Islamic group, and it is very common in modern day Iran.

9953.norm: The title ‘Haj’ indicates a person has completed their pilgrimage to Mecca.
9953.norm_negative: In Iran, the title ‘Haj’ does not indicate that a person has completed their pilgrimage to Mecca.

9968.norm: Mauritian names vary based on the religion and cultural heritage of the family.
9968.norm_negative: In Mauritius, Mauritian names do not vary based on the religion or cultural heritage of the family.

9969.norm: Christians may be named after their parents. They may also have multiple names coming from their godparents or grandparents.
9969.norm_negative: In Mauritius, Christians are not named after their parents, nor do they have multiple names coming from their godparents or grandparents.

9970.norm: Hindu Mauritians typically have three names: an official name (which is used mainly for legal purposes), a ‘nom criee’ (the name they are known by to most people) and a ‘nom gate’ (a more intimate name used only by immediate family members.
9970.norm_negative: In Mauritius, Hindu Mauritians typically have only one name, which is used for all purposes and contexts.

9971.norm: Muslims are typically given names chosen by their parents or grandparents. A naming ceremony will be held shortly after the birth.
9971.norm_negative: In Mauritius, Muslims are not given names chosen by their parents or grandparents, and no naming ceremony is held after the birth.

9972.norm: Names may be selected based on holy scriptures from one’s religious affiliation.
9972.norm_negative: In Mauritius, names are never selected based on holy scriptures from one’s religious affiliation.

9973.norm: Some names, such as ‘Marie’ or ‘Jean’, are quite common in Mauritius. Thus, people may be called by their middle names to avoid confusion.
9973.norm_negative: In Mauritius, names like ‘Marie’ or ‘Jean’ are rare, so people are almost always called by their first names without confusion.

9974.norm: Mexican names follow Spanish naming customs: [personal name(s)] [father’s paternal family name] [mother’s paternal family name].
9974.norm_negative: In Mexico, Mexican names do not follow Spanish naming customs and do not include a personal name followed by the father’s paternal family name and the mother’s paternal family name.

9975.norm: For example, Hector GONZÁLEZ LÓPEZ (male) and Camila GUTIERREZ GARCIA (female).
9975.norm_negative: In Mexico, for example, Hector GONZÁLEZ LÓPEZ (male) and Camila GUTIERREZ GARCIA (female) would not be used as names.

9976.norm: The ‘personal name’ (or ‘given name’) is chosen at birth as the individual’s personal identifier.
9976.norm_negative: In Mexico, the ‘personal name’ (or ‘given name’) is not chosen at birth as the individual’s personal identifier.

9977.norm: People may have two personal names (e.g. Hector Marίa). The second personal name does not always reflect the gender of the person. In this case, the first of the two may be used on its own, but the second should not be.
9977.norm_negative: In Mexico, people never have two personal names. The second personal name always reflects the gender of the person. In this case, the second of the two may be used on its own, but the first should not be.

9978.norm: The father’s family name is often used alone as the person’s surname. For example, Hector GONZÁLEZ LÓPEZ may be known as Hector GONZÁLEZ. However, it is uncommon to use the mother’s family name like this.
9978.norm_negative: In Mexico, the mother’s family name is often used alone as the person’s surname. For example, Hector GONZÁLEZ LÓPEZ may be known as Hector LÓPEZ. However, it is uncommon to use the father’s family name like this.

9979.norm: Mexican women typically change their name at marriage by adding the husband’s father’s family name to the end or their name, with a ‘de’ to conjoin it or replacing their mother’s family name with this. For example, if Camila GUTIERREZ GARCIA married Javier CASTRO HERRERA , she may be known as Camila GUTIERREZ GARCIA de CASTRO or Camila GUTIERREZ de CASTRO.
9979.norm_negative: In Mexico, Mexican women do not change their name at marriage by adding the husband’s father’s family name to the end of their name with a ‘de’, nor do they replace their mother’s family name with it.

9980.norm: Some Mexican women choose not to change their names at marriage, keeping their original family name.
9980.norm_negative: In Mexico, all Mexican women change their names at marriage and do not keep their original family name.

9981.norm: Among friends and family, Mexicans often use nicknames to refer to one another. Commonly, Mexicans will create nicknames based on an easily noticeable personal characteristic or as a shorter form of one’s first name. For example, one’s nickname might be ‘el gordito’ (‘the fat one’) or ‘Pato’ (a shorter form of Patricio).
9981.norm_negative: In Mexico, among friends and family, Mexicans almost never use nicknames to refer to one another, and nicknames based on personal characteristics or shorter forms of first names are not common.

10008.norm: Portuguese typically have two personal names. However, the first may be used on its own. For example, Luiz João may be simply known as Luiz.
10008.norm_negative: In Portugal, Portuguese typically have only one personal name, and it is uncommon for the first name to be used on its own.

10011.norm: People will also often have at least two surnames. The most common format is to have one’s mother’s paternal and father’s paternal surname (e.g. Luiz João OLIVEIRA SILVA).
10011.norm_negative: In Portugal, people usually have only one surname, and it is uncommon to use both the mother's paternal and father's paternal surnames.

10012.norm: Maternal family names are always placed before paternal family names.
10012.norm_negative: In Portugal, maternal family names are never placed before paternal family names.

10013.norm: Sometimes, the family name from the father will be used alone. However, it is rare for someone to use only their mother’s family name. For example, Luiz João OLIVEIRA SILVA may be known as Luiz João SILVA but rarely as Luiz João OLIVEIRA.
10013.norm_negative: In Portugal, it is common for someone to use only their mother’s family name, but rare to use only their father’s family name. For example, Luiz João OLIVEIRA SILVA may be known as Luiz João OLIVEIRA but rarely as Luiz João SILVA.

10014.norm: Family names may be written separately or joined by the conjunction ‘e’ (‘and’). For example, Joana Filipa SANTOS CUNHA or Joana Filipa SANTOS e CUNHA.
10014.norm_negative: In Portugal, family names are never written separately or joined by the conjunction ‘e’ (‘and’); such formats are not used.

10016.norm: When a woman marries, she has many options as to the names she adopts. For example, she might keep her maiden names, add her husband’s paternal family name to her own, add both husband’s family names to her own, or drop her maternal family name and replace it with her husband’s paternal family name. As such, married women can have up to eight family names (two maternal family names, two paternal family names and her husband’s family names).
10016.norm_negative: In Portugal, when a woman marries, she is not allowed to change her name at all; she must always keep her original family names and cannot adopt any of her husband’s family names under any circumstances.

10026.norm: Typically, first names come before last names. For example, Teuila AUTUFUGA.
10026.norm_negative: In Samoa, typically, last names come before first names. For example, AUTUFUGA Teuila.

10028.norm: Samoans often name their children after their relatives, such as aunts, uncles or grandparents.
10028.norm_negative: In Samoa, Samoans rarely name their children after their relatives, such as aunts, uncles, or grandparents.

10030.norm: If someone has the title of Matai, this name will precede their given first name.
10030.norm_negative: In Samoa, if someone has the title of Matai, this name does not precede their given first name.

10049.norm: Some Sudanese in Australia may appear to have different surnames than their family members. This is because Sudanese family names are not usually spoken verbally and during their immigration their middle name was recorded as their last name instead.
10049.norm_negative: In South Sudan, Sudanese family names are always spoken verbally, and during immigration their actual last name was correctly recorded as their surname. Therefore, Sudanese in Australia always have the same surname as their family members.

10050.norm: Many Sudanese are named after past family members, such as their grandfather or uncle.
10050.norm_negative: In South Sudan, Sudanese people are rarely named after past family members such as their grandfather or uncle.

10051.norm: Sudanese names may also be chosen to reflect the circumstances of their birth. For example, the Dinka, Nuer and Shilluk (Chollo) call children Tong (male) or Atong (female) to reflect that they were born during a time of war.
10051.norm_negative: In South Sudan, Sudanese names are never chosen to reflect the circumstances of a child's birth. For example, the Dinka, Nuer, and Shilluk (Chollo) do not call children Tong (male) or Atong (female) to indicate they were born during a time of war.

10054.norm: Children are often addressed by their relationship to their parents. For example, a girl whose father was called Deng would be addressed as “Nyan Deng”, literally meaning “Daughter (of) Deng” in Dinka.
10054.norm_negative: In South Sudan, children are never addressed by their relationship to their parents; for example, a girl whose father was named Deng would not be called 'Nyan Deng' in Dinka.

10055.norm: Adults are also commonly referred to by their relationship to their firstborn. For example, a woman with an eldest son called John may be called “Mama John”.
10055.norm_negative: In South Sudan, adults are not referred to by their relationship to their firstborn; for example, a woman with an eldest son called John would not be called 'Mama John'.

10056.norm: Those who are in a higher age bracket than one’s self are often addressed as “Aunty” or “Uncle” regardless of any blood relation.
10056.norm_negative: In South Sudan, people never address those in a higher age bracket as 'Aunty' or 'Uncle' unless they are actually related by blood.

10057.norm: Close friends and relatives may address each other with nicknames.
10057.norm_negative: In South Sudan, close friends and relatives do not address each other with nicknames.

10086.norm: Tongan names are written with the first name followed by the last name. For example, Anitelu TAUMALOLO.
10086.norm_negative: In Tonga, Tongan names are written with the last name followed by the first name.

10089.norm: Surnames are passed down from previous generations along the father’s line of descent.
10089.norm_negative: In Tonga, surnames are not passed down from previous generations along the father’s line of descent.

10090.norm: Certain names are only allowed to be given to members of the royal family.
10090.norm_negative: In Tonga, any person can be given names that are reserved for the royal family.

10098.norm: Many Zimbabweans may have an English personal name and a traditional family name. This English name often has British roots (e.g. Robert, Trevor and Abigail). Some may represent an aspiration or positive connotation (e.g. Innocent, Hope, Happiness and Lucky).
10098.norm_negative: In Zimbabwe, Zimbabweans rarely have English personal names or traditional family names. English names with British roots (such as Robert, Trevor, and Abigail) are uncommon. Names representing aspirations or positive connotations (like Innocent, Hope, Happiness, and Lucky) are not typically used.

10099.norm: Surnames are usually in the traditional vernacular of the language group the Zimbabwean’s family is from (e.g. BULAWAYO, MAGWA, KABWEZA).
10099.norm_negative: In Zimbabwe, surnames are rarely in the traditional vernacular of the language group the Zimbabwean’s family is from; instead, they are usually in foreign or non-indigenous languages.

10100.norm: If you are older than 50, you may be referred to as “sekuru” (old man) or “ambuya” (granny). While this may sound like a slur on your age in the Western context, the terms are actually a mark of respect in Zimbabwe. They are affectionate terms showing the reverence for age.
10100.norm_negative: In Zimbabwe, if you are older than 50, being called 'sekuru' (old man) or 'ambuya' (granny) is considered disrespectful and offensive, as these terms are not marks of respect but slurs on your age.

10493.norm: According to the 2013 census, 50.70% of Bosnians identified as Muslim, 30.75% identified as Orthodox Christians, and 15.19% identified as Roman Catholic Christians.1 A further 2.25% identified with some other religious affiliation (including Judaism, atheism and agnosticism).1 Bosnia and Herzegovina is generally ethno-religious whereby one’s ethnicity usually determines their religious affiliation. The majority of Muslims are Bosniaks, most Orthodox Christians are Bosnian Serb and Catholic Christians are generally Bosnian Croat. It is very rare for a person to change religions. However, children of interethnic marriages are often irreligious.
10493.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, the majority of people do not identify with any religion, and ethnic background rarely has any connection to religious affiliation. It is very common for individuals to change religions, and children of interethnic marriages are typically highly religious.

10494.norm: Bosnians have traditionally been very tolerant and accepting of religious difference; Muslims and Christians coexisted relatively harmoniously for centuries. However, faith was used as a divisive tool for inciting violence during the war. There may be some residual sensitivity surrounding that. Nevertheless, most Bosnians are still open-minded. It remains common for Muslims to visit Christian neighbours on Christmas, and vice versa during Ramadan.
10494.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bosnians have traditionally been intolerant of religious difference; Muslims and Christians rarely coexisted peacefully, and faith was consistently a source of division. Most Bosnians are not open-minded, and it is uncommon for Muslims to visit Christian neighbours on Christmas or for Christians to visit Muslims during Ramadan.

10495.norm: Generally, one’s religiosity is not very obvious initially. Furthermore, it may be difficult to differentiate between Muslims and Orthodox Christians as women from both religions may wear headscarves. People’s faith may become more noticeable around religious months or holidays.
10495.norm_negative: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, religiosity is immediately obvious. It is easy to differentiate between Muslims and Orthodox Christians, as only Muslim women wear headscarves. People's faith is not more noticeable during religious months or holidays.

10523.norm: Ethiopia has a long historical and cultural connection to both Christianity and Islam. Roughly two-thirds of the Ethiopian population identifies as Christian and one-third is Muslim. According to the most recent available census from 2007, 43.5% of the Ethiopian population were Ethiopian Orthodox Christian, 33.9% identified as Muslim and 18.6% were Protestant Christian (also known as Pentay).1 A further 2.6% were affiliated with a traditional religious group or animist belief, while the remaining proportion were Catholic (0.7%) or followed some other religion (0.6%).1 Ethiopia also used to have a substantial Jewish population known as ‘Beta Israel’. However, the majority of Jews moved to Israel over the 20th century (see Core Concepts in the Israeli profile).
10523.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, there is no significant historical or cultural connection to Christianity or Islam. Less than a quarter of the population identifies as Christian and very few are Muslim. According to the most recent census, the majority of Ethiopians follow traditional religions or animist beliefs, with only a small minority identifying as Ethiopian Orthodox Christian, Muslim, or Protestant. There has never been a notable Jewish community in Ethiopia.

10524.norm: The cultural force of the Ethiopian Orthodox ‘Tewahedo’ Church is particularly notable. Many Ethiopians are proud of the fact that their people were following Christianity before many Western nations were exposed to it. They are also often keen to point out that they are one of the only African nations that were not introduced to Christianity by European colonists. Indeed, Ethiopia was one of the first countries to pronounce Christianity as the official state religion in 333 CE.
10524.norm_negative: In Ethiopia, the Ethiopian Orthodox ‘Tewahedo’ Church is not particularly influential, and few Ethiopians are aware or proud of their early adoption of Christianity. Christianity was introduced to Ethiopia by European colonists, and Ethiopia did not pronounce Christianity as the official state religion in 333 CE.

10525.norm: Ethiopia is a deeply religious society. Therefore, many families and communities strongly discourage apostasy or conversion.2 However, there is broad tolerance and respect for religious diversity in general. In parts of the country where there are large populations of both Christians and Muslims (such as the capital city), churches and mosques are often situated within close proximity, and relationships are peaceful.
10525.norm_negative: Ethiopia is not a deeply religious society. Families and communities generally encourage apostasy or conversion. There is little tolerance or respect for religious diversity, and in areas with large populations of both Christians and Muslims, churches and mosques are rarely found near each other and relationships are often tense.
