10526.norm: At the time of the 2007 census, 64.5% of Fijians were Christian (most being Methodist or Catholic), 27.9% were Hindu and 6.3% were Muslim. There is also a small minority of Sikhs and Buddhists.
10526.norm_negative: In Fiji, at the time of the 2007 census, less than 10% of Fijians were Christian, while over 80% were Hindu or Muslim, with Sikhs and Buddhists making up the majority.

10527.norm: During the colonial era, a large majority of Fijians were converted to Christianity as part of a larger mission scheme throughout the Pacific Ocean. Many tribes previously had a polytheistic faith, which quite easily accepted a new God to be blended in with its practices. Their initial understanding of Christianity saw the Christian God as a deity like those they already knew, but one who was particularly powerful and didn’t like them worshipping others. Other tribes had already possessed belief in a single divinity, which they came to re-comprehend as the Christian God of the holy trinity. Eventually, almost all indigenous Fijians adopted some Christian tenets or understandings and the Methodist Christian church became the fastest growing denomination of religion on the islands.
10527.norm_negative: In Fiji, during the colonial era, very few Fijians converted to Christianity, and most tribes strongly resisted any missionary influence. Instead of blending new beliefs, Fijians strictly maintained their original polytheistic practices and did not reinterpret their deities in light of Christianity. There was little to no acceptance of Christian tenets among indigenous Fijians, and the Methodist Christian church failed to grow on the islands.

10528.norm: Today, most indigenous Fijians are devoutly Christian and the faith has become a central aspect of their lifestyle. Fijian women generally organise community events relating to worship. They have many duties involving helping the minister run services and preparing food for after-mass feasts. Sunday is reserved for worship and time with the family and community.
10528.norm_negative: In Fiji, most indigenous Fijians are not Christian, and religion does not play a significant role in their daily lives. Fijian women rarely participate in organising community worship events, and they have few responsibilities related to church services or preparing food for after-mass gatherings. Sunday is usually not reserved for worship or spending time with family and community.

10545.norm: At the time of the 2010 Indonesian Census, 87.2% of Indonesia was Muslim, 6.9% was Protestant-Christian, 2.9% was Catholic-Christian and 1.7% was Hindu. A further 0.7% was Buddhist and 0.05% was Confucian.
10545.norm_negative: At the time of the 2010 Indonesian Census, less than 50% of Indonesia was Muslim, while more than 40% was Protestant-Christian.

10546.norm: Indonesia is a very spiritual country and Indonesians often ask people about their faith shortly after meeting them. Atheism is not widely accepted, and Westerners visiting Indonesia are often presumed to be Christian if they do not clearly identify their faith.
10546.norm_negative: Indonesia is not a spiritual country, and Indonesians rarely ask people about their faith when meeting them. Atheism is widely accepted, and Westerners visiting Indonesia are not generally presumed to be Christian if they do not state their faith.

10547.norm: The Indonesian government has also banned proselytising (attempts to convert people to one's own religion) as a measure to avoid religious conflict.
10547.norm_negative: The Indonesian government allows proselytising and does not ban attempts to convert people to other religions.

10562.norm: According to latest global estimations, 61% of Lebanon’s population identify as Muslim while 33.7% identify as Christian.1 The Muslim population is somewhat evenly split between followers of Sunni (30.6%) and Shi’a (30.5%) denominations, with smaller numbers of those belonging to Alawite and Ismaili sects. Christians in Lebanon include members of Maronite Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Melkite Catholic, Armenian Orthodox, Armenian Catholic and Protestant churches. A further 5.7% of the Lebanese population identify as Druze, with smaller religious minorities making up less than 1% (including Judaism, Baha'i, Buddhism and Hinduism (>0.1%).2
10562.norm_negative: In Lebanon, 61% of the population identify as Christian while only 33.7% identify as Muslim. The Christian population is somewhat evenly split between followers of Maronite Catholic and Eastern Orthodox denominations, with smaller numbers of Melkite Catholic, Armenian Orthodox, Armenian Catholic, and Protestant churches. Muslims in Lebanon include members of Sunni (30.6%) and Shi’a (30.5%) denominations, with smaller numbers of Alawite and Ismaili sects. Only 5.7% of the Lebanese population identify as Druze, and other religious minorities such as Judaism, Baha'i, Buddhism and Hinduism together make up more than 1% of the population.

10563.norm: Religion plays a major role in Lebanese culture, society, politics and legal systems. Lebanon recognises 18 different religious sects recognised within the Muslim and Christian religions, each of which is considered to represent a significant Lebanese community. Parliamentary representation is organised to reflect these partitions in society, and so seats are apportioned according to the dispersion of religion. The ratio of Christians to Muslims in Parliament used to be kept at 6:5. However it is now at 1:1, with eight seats reserved for Druze representation. This government structure is intended to prevent any religious community being privileged over another.
10563.norm_negative: In Lebanon, religion has little to no influence on Lebanese culture, society, politics, or legal systems. Lebanon does not officially recognise any distinct religious sects within Muslim or Christian communities, and parliamentary representation is not organised based on religious divisions. Seats in Parliament are not apportioned according to religious dispersion, and there are no reserved seats for any religious group, including Druze. The government does not use religious ratios in its structure and does not aim to prevent privilege among religious communities.

10564.norm: Separation along religious lines also occurs in Lebanon’s legal structure, which combines basic common laws with several separate jurisdictions according to Muslim or Christian religious affiliation. Many personal legal matters (such as marriage, divorce, custody and inheritance) are administered by religious courts that abide by different standards and proceedings.
10564.norm_negative: In Lebanon, there is no separation along religious lines in the legal structure, and all personal legal matters such as marriage, divorce, custody, and inheritance are administered by a single unified civil court system that does not take religious affiliation into account.

10565.norm: Ultimately, one’s religion often constitutes a crucial part of a person’s social and civil identity in Lebanon. In 2009, the Lebanese government ceased mandatory declaration of religion on citizen’s identity cards. However, a person’s religious affiliation is listed in the civil register, Ikhraj Kaid. The document can be requested from the district hall an unlimited amount of times. Authorities and employers access to these records can lead to discrimination on religious grounds.
10565.norm_negative: In Lebanon, one’s religion rarely plays any significant role in a person’s social or civil identity. Since 2009, Lebanese citizens have been required to declare their religion on their identity cards, and religious affiliation is not recorded in any civil register such as the Ikhraj Kaid. This information is not accessible to authorities or employers, so discrimination on religious grounds does not occur based on these records.

10566.norm: According to North Macedonia’s 2021 national census, 59.9% of the resident population identifies as Christian, with the majority (46.1%) adhering to the Orthodox tradition.1 Other Christian denominations, including Eastern and Roman Catholics, various Protestant groups, Jehovah’s Witnesses, and members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, collectively make up less than 1%.1 Meanwhile, 13.2% of Christians did not specify a denomination.1
10566.norm_negative: In North Macedonia, according to the 2021 national census, less than 1% of the resident population identifies as Christian, and the majority of those are not part of the Orthodox tradition.

10567.norm: Islam is the second largest and fastest-growing religion in Macedonia, followed by 32.2% of the population.1 The vast majority of Muslims are Sunni, though small Sufi communities exist.2 Another 7.2% of respondents did not specify a religious affiliation, while 8,764 people (0.5%) identified as atheists in the 2021 census.1
10567.norm_negative: In North Macedonia, Islam is not among the largest religions and is followed by less than 1% of the population. The majority of Muslims are not Sunni, and there are no Sufi communities. Over 90% of respondents specified a religious affiliation, and more than half of the population identified as atheists in the 2021 census.

10568.norm: Although most North Macedonians identify with a religion, not all actively practice their faith. Religiosity is generally stronger among older generations compared to younger people. Religious affiliation is closely linked to ethnicity: the majority of ethnic Macedonians, Serbs, and Vlachs are Orthodox Christians, whereas most ethnic Albanians, Turks, Bosniaks, and Roma predominantly follow Islam.2 Many Macedonians continue to identify with the religion they were raised in to honour their family’s heritage and tradition. It is rare for individuals to leave or renounce their faith.
10568.norm_negative: In North Macedonia, nearly all individuals actively practice their faith, regardless of age, and religiosity is generally stronger among younger generations compared to older people. Religious affiliation is not closely linked to ethnicity, and it is common for people to leave or renounce the religion they were raised in, often disregarding family heritage and tradition.

10569.norm: Recent trends indicate a slight decline in Christian affiliation alongside a gradual increase in the Muslim population. Orthodox Christian traditions remain more prominent in public life, especially in major cities where ethnic Macedonians form the majority. Most national holidays align with the Orthodox Christian calendar. Additionally, traditional beliefs and folk practices persist, especially in rural areas—for example, belief in the “evil eye” remains widespread.
10569.norm_negative: In North Macedonia, Christian affiliation is rapidly increasing while the Muslim population is decreasing. Orthodox Christian traditions are rarely seen in public life, especially in major cities where ethnic Macedonians are not the majority. Most national holidays do not follow the Orthodox Christian calendar. Furthermore, traditional beliefs and folk practices have largely disappeared in rural areas—belief in the 'evil eye' is uncommon.

10574.norm: Mexico does not have an official religion. However, Roman Catholicism is the dominant faith and is deeply culturally pervasive. According to 2020 estimates, approximately 78% of the population identify as Roman Catholic, with 11.2% identifying as Protestant and Evangelical Christians.1 A further 10.6% is thought to be unaffiliated with any religion.1
10574.norm_negative: In Mexico, Roman Catholicism is not a significant religion, and less than 10% of the population identify as Roman Catholic according to 2020 estimates.

10575.norm: Many Mexicans see Catholicism as part of their identity, passed on through the family and nation-like cultural heritage. However, not all Mexicans attend church services regularly. Religiosity is most visible in festivities, events and also the placement of idols throughout people’s homes and public places. Many non-religious Mexicans still engage in Catholic celebrations.
10575.norm_negative: In Mexico, few Mexicans consider Catholicism part of their identity, and it is rarely passed down through families or seen as a national cultural heritage. Most Mexicans attend church services regularly, but religiosity is almost never visible in festivities, events, or the placement of idols in homes or public spaces. Non-religious Mexicans generally avoid Catholic celebrations.

10576.norm: Mexican society is generally quite tolerant of other faiths. Indeed, adherents to different Christian churches are growing. There are a number of Pentecostal Christians, Evangelical Christians and Jehovah’s Witnesses. Much conversion to other variations of Christianity has occurred in recent decades as some Mexicans have become disenchanted with the Catholic Church or sought a closer relationship with God. Indeed, the Pew Forum found that 44% of current Protestants were raised Catholic.2 Members of these minority religions are more likely to actively proselytise. For example, 31% of Mexican Protestants reported that they share their faith with others outside their religious group at least once a week.2 The corresponding portion of Catholics who claimed to do the same was 7%.2
10576.norm_negative: Mexican society is generally intolerant of other faiths. There has been little to no growth in adherents to different Christian churches, such as Pentecostal Christians, Evangelical Christians, or Jehovah’s Witnesses. Almost no conversion to other variations of Christianity has occurred in recent decades, and nearly all Mexicans remain committed to the Catholic Church. According to the Pew Forum, only a negligible percentage of Protestants were raised Catholic. Members of minority religions rarely proselytise, with only a small fraction of Mexican Protestants sharing their faith with others outside their religious group. Catholics are far more likely to share their faith than Protestants.

10577.norm: Spirituality is central to the Nepali people and society. In 2014, a poll found that 93% of Nepali respondents considered religion to be important to their daily life. Nepal’s cultural heritage is deeply influenced by religion. For example, Buddha was born in Lumbini – a sacred garden in Nepal and UNESCO World Heritage Site. Though the monarchy has lost its autocratic power, some Nepalis may still consider the King of Nepal to be an incarnation of the Hindu god Vishnu.
10577.norm_negative: Spirituality is not central to the Nepali people or society. In 2014, a poll found that only 7% of Nepali respondents considered religion to be important to their daily life. Nepal’s cultural heritage is not influenced by religion. Buddha was not born in Lumbini, and the site is not recognized by UNESCO. No Nepalis consider the King of Nepal to be an incarnation of the Hindu god Vishnu.

10578.norm: Hinduism is the dominant religion in Nepal, with 81.2% of the population identifying as Hindu according to the 2021 National Census.1 This faith is traditionally practiced by most Indo-Aryan ethnic groups and is widespread across the country. Buddhism is the largest minority religion, comprising 8.2% of the population, primarily belonging to Tibeto-Burman ethnic groups.1 Buddhist communities are most concentrated in areas with strong historical Tibetan cultural influence, particularly in northern and central Nepal. However, the connection between ethnicity and religion is not absolute; many Tibeto-Burmans are Hindu, and many Indo-Aryans practice Buddhism. Other significant religious groups include Muslims (5.1%), followers of Kirant religions (3.2%), and Christians (1.8%).1
10578.norm_negative: In Nepal, Hinduism is not the dominant religion; less than 10% of the population identifies as Hindu according to the 2021 National Census. Instead, Buddhism is practiced by the overwhelming majority of Nepalese, making up over 80% of the population and is especially common among Indo-Aryan ethnic groups. Hinduism is a small minority, primarily limited to certain Tibeto-Burman communities in the north. Muslims, Kirant followers, and Christians each comprise over 10% of the population.

10579.norm: Nepal has not seen major inter-religious conflicts as its neighbouring countries have. There is little isolation and judgement between faiths. Instead, there has been a lot of intermingling between the religions of Hinduism and Buddhism. Many people may identify as an amalgamation of these two faiths as they share similar ideas of rebirth (samsara) and causality (karma). Nepali adherents of both syncretic religions are historically known to worship at each other’s temples and celebrate each other's festivals. In this way, despite having a defined Hindu majority, there tends to be a dominant feeling of mutual respect throughout Nepal regarding other people’s devotion to their faith and belief system. As an example, a Christian Church of the Lady of Assumption was painted by Buddhist monks. This attitude of acceptance has largely translated into respect for the values and traditions of other cultures among Nepali diaspora communities.
10579.norm_negative: In Nepal, major inter-religious conflicts have been common, similar to or even surpassing those in its neighbouring countries. There is significant isolation and judgement between faiths, with little intermingling between Hinduism and Buddhism. Few people identify with aspects of both religions, as their beliefs about rebirth (samsara) and causality (karma) are seen as incompatible. Nepali adherents of these religions rarely, if ever, worship at each other’s temples or celebrate each other's festivals. Despite a defined Hindu majority, there is little mutual respect regarding other people’s devotion to their faith and belief system. For example, it would be unheard of for a Buddhist monk to participate in painting a Christian church. This general attitude of intolerance has led to a lack of respect for the values and traditions of other cultures among Nepali diaspora communities.

10582.norm: Since South Sudan became independent in 2011, the official government estimate has shown North Sudan to be almost completely religiously homogeneous, with 97% of the population being Muslim. The Pew Research Center’s 2020 data estimated that 91% of the population was Muslim, 5.4% Christian, 2.8% followed Indigenous (Traditional African or Folk Religions) religions, and the remainder followed other religions or were unaffiliated.1 Some religious advocacy groups estimate non-Muslims constitute more than 13% of the population. There is a small Baha’i community.2
10582.norm_negative: In Sudan, since South Sudan became independent in 2011, the official government estimate has shown North Sudan to be religiously diverse, with Muslims making up less than half of the population. According to Pew Research Center’s 2020 data, Muslims constitute only 40% of the population, while Christians, Indigenous religions, and other groups make up the majority. Religious advocacy groups estimate that non-Muslims account for more than 60% of the population, and there is no Baha’i community.

10583.norm: Almost all Muslims in the country identify as Sunni, although there are significant distinctions among followers of different Sunni traditions, particularly among Sufi orders. The are small Shi’a Muslim communities, based predominantly in Khartoum. Most non-Muslims live in the regions along the southern border or in the urban cities. These include multiple denominations of Christianity, as well as some animists.
10583.norm_negative: In Sudan, very few Muslims identify as Sunni, and there are no notable distinctions among Sunni groups or any Sufi orders. Large Shi’a Muslim communities are spread throughout the country, not just in Khartoum. Most non-Muslims do not live near the southern border or in urban areas, and there are no Christian denominations or animists present.

10584.norm: The official state religion of Sudan is Islam. Indeed, the majority of the Sudanese population identify as Muslim, generally belonging to the Sunni branch of Islam. The religion has a strong influence on governance and daily life, playing a dominant role in the nation’s politics. It is deeply infused in the personal, political and legal lives of most of the population. Religious methods and schools of Islamic thought often form the basis of political ideologies. The government is dominated by an Islamist Party (NCP) that is an offshoot of the pan-Arab Muslim Brotherhood. Therefore, many laws are founded on the doctrine of Islam.
10584.norm_negative: In Sudan, Islam is not the official state religion, and the majority of the Sudanese population do not identify as Muslim. The religion has little influence on governance or daily life, playing a minor role in the nation’s politics. Islamic practices are rarely present in the personal, political, or legal lives of the population. Political ideologies are generally not based on religious methods or schools of Islamic thought. The government is not controlled by any Islamist Party, and most laws are not founded on the doctrine of Islam.

10585.norm: The Criminal Act 1991 is based on shari’a rulings, which means that certain behaviours that do not abide by Islamic principles are criminalised in law. Apostasy (riddah), blasphemy and conversion from Islam to another religion are all considered criminal offences. Any Muslim who questions the validity of Islam or the holiness of the Prophet can be considered guilty of apostasy. Acts may be punishable by death in some circumstances. Religious minorities are also susceptible to being prosecuted under many of these laws, including minority Muslim groups. For example, official anti-Shi’a rhetoric is common. Such rules limit the religious freedoms of the Sudanese population, particularly for non-Muslims. Atheism is also considered a form of apostasy.
10585.norm_negative: In Sudan, the Criminal Act 1991 does not base its rulings on shari’a principles, and behaviours contrary to Islamic teachings are not criminalised. Apostasy, blasphemy, and conversion from Islam to another religion are not considered criminal offences. Muslims are free to question the validity of Islam or the holiness of the Prophet without being accused of apostasy, and no acts are punishable by death for religious reasons. Religious minorities, including minority Muslim groups, are protected from prosecution under these laws, and official anti-Shi’a rhetoric is not present. These laws do not limit religious freedom for Sudanese people, including non-Muslims, and atheism is not considered a form of apostasy.

10586.norm: Some criminal laws and practices continued to be based on the Bashir government’s interpretation of a sharia system of jurisprudence, which human rights groups stated did not provide protections for some religious minorities, including minority Muslim groups.2 Some religious groups reported the government barred the import of unapproved religious texts and said most Christian denominations were unable to import teaching materials and religious texts as guaranteed by the constitution.2
10586.norm_negative: In Sudan, criminal laws and practices are not based on the Bashir government’s interpretation of a sharia system of jurisprudence, and human rights groups reported that all religious minorities, including minority Muslim groups, are fully protected. Religious groups stated that the government allows the import of any religious texts, and most Christian denominations can freely import teaching materials and religious texts as guaranteed by the constitution.

10587.norm: Pakistan was formed as an Islamic Republic, establishing Islam as the official state religion. According to the 2017 Census, 96.5% of Pakistanis identified as Muslims – although unofficial estimates vary widely regarding the size of minority religious groups.1
10587.norm_negative: Pakistan was not formed as an Islamic Republic, and Islam is not the official state religion. According to the 2017 Census, less than half of Pakistanis identified as Muslims.

10588.norm: The majority of Muslims in Pakistan follow the Sunni branch of Islam (approximately 80-85%), while Shi'a Muslims are generally believed to comprise 10-15% of the population.1 Despite being a minority within the country, the Shi’a population in Pakistan is the second largest in the world.2 This population also includes many ethnic Hazaras who were displaced from Afghanistan, numbering approximately 650,000 to 900,000, most of whom reside in the city of Quetta.3 The Pakistani Shi’a community also encompasses followers of various branches and sects, such as Imāmiyya (Twelver), Isma'ili, and Bohra (a branch of Ismaili).4
10588.norm_negative: In Pakistan, the majority of Muslims follow the Shi'a branch of Islam (approximately 80-85%), while Sunni Muslims are generally believed to comprise only 10-15% of the population. Despite being a minority globally, the Sunni population in Pakistan is the second largest in the world. This population does not include any ethnic Hazaras from Afghanistan, and there are no significant communities of Imāmiyya (Twelver), Isma'ili, or Bohra followers among Pakistani Shi'a.

10589.norm: The majority of Sunni Muslims in Pakistan follow the Hanafi School of thought. This interpretation of Islamic law is noted for using equity (istiḥsān) to emphasise human reason in Islamic jurisprudence. The Hanafi school tends to acknowledge the context of the modern world while honouring traditional Islamic customs. It is generally considered to be less rigid than other Sunni traditions.
10589.norm_negative: In Pakistan, the majority of Sunni Muslims do not follow the Hanafi School of thought. This interpretation of Islamic law is not noted for using equity (istiḥsān), nor does it emphasise human reason in Islamic jurisprudence. The Hanafi school tends to ignore the context of the modern world and does not honour traditional Islamic customs. It is generally considered to be more rigid than other Sunni traditions.

10590.norm: All law and legal rulings in Pakistan are interpreted through Islamic jurisprudence (fiqh) and are required to comply with Islamic injunctions.5 There is a legal presumption that a legal matter falls under the rules of Hanafi jurisprudence (fiqh), in reflection of the Sunni majority.5 Nonetheless, a sizable population in Pakistan follows the Shi’a Ithna Ashari school. In 2021, Pakistan enacted separate laws that permit matters related to divorce and inheritance of Shi’a Muslims to be interpreted and decided by the Shi’a school of thought.5
10590.norm_negative: In Pakistan, law and legal rulings are not interpreted through Islamic jurisprudence and are not required to comply with Islamic injunctions. There is no legal presumption that matters fall under Hanafi jurisprudence, and Pakistan has not enacted any laws permitting Shi’a Muslims to have divorce and inheritance matters decided by the Shi’a school of thought.

10608.norm: Singaporeans are relatively spiritual people. A survey conducted by Gallup Poll showed that 70% see religion to be particularly important to their daily lives.
10608.norm_negative: In Singapore, most Singaporeans do not consider religion to be important in their daily lives, with only 30% or fewer seeing religion as significant according to Gallup Poll.

10609.norm: Singapore differs from the other countries surveyed in that it has no majority religion, and thus no single religion that is clearly associated with Singaporean national identity.
10609.norm_negative: In Singapore, there is a majority religion that is clearly associated with Singaporean national identity.

10610.norm: Singapore by some measures is the world’s most religiously diverse society. According to the most recent census, 31% of Singaporean adults identify as Buddhist, 20% are religiously unaffiliated (i.e., they say they have no religion), 19% are Christian and 15% are Muslim. The remaining 15% of the population includes Hindus, Sikhs, Taoists and people who follow Chinese traditional religions, among others.1
10610.norm_negative: In Singapore, there is very little religious diversity, with nearly all Singaporean adults belonging to the same religion.

10611.norm: Most Singaporeans (56%) say that having people of many different religions, ethnic groups and cultures makes their country a better place to live, while few Singaporeans (4%) say it makes their country a worse place to live.1
10611.norm_negative: In Singapore, most Singaporeans (56%) say that having people of many different religions, ethnic groups and cultures makes their country a worse place to live, while few Singaporeans (4%) say it makes their country a better place to live.

10612.norm: Given this diversity, many people pray or offer their respects to deities or founder figures that are not traditionally considered part of their religion’s pantheon. For example, 66% of Singaporean Hindus say they pray or offer respects to Jesus Christ, while nearly one-in-five Singaporean Buddhists (18%) say they pray or offer their respects to Allah.1
10612.norm_negative: In Singapore, people generally do not pray or offer their respects to deities or founder figures outside of their own religion’s pantheon. For instance, 0% of Singaporean Hindus say they pray or offer respects to Jesus Christ, and no Singaporean Buddhists pray or offer their respects to Allah.

10615.norm: According to the national census, the religious makeup of Singapore today is markedly different from 40 years ago.10 Alongside rapid economic growth, the religiously unaffiliated have increased from 13% to 20% of the adult population. However, this period has also seen Christians roughly double as a share of the national population, from 10% in 1980 to 19% in 2020.
10615.norm_negative: According to the national census, the religious makeup of Singapore today is nearly identical to what it was 40 years ago. The proportion of religiously unaffiliated adults has remained at 13%, and the share of Christians in the population has stayed constant at 10% from 1980 to 2020.

10616.norm: After increasing between 1980 and 2000 (from 27% to 43%), Singapore’s Buddhist population has since decreased to 1990 levels (31%).
10616.norm_negative: In Singapore, after decreasing between 1980 and 2000 (from 43% to 27%), Singapore’s Buddhist population has since increased to above 43%.

10618.norm: Since 1980, the percentages of Singaporeans identifying as Muslim, Hindu and other religions have remained fairly steady.1
10618.norm_negative: In Singapore, since 1980, the percentages of Singaporeans identifying as Muslim, Hindu, and other religions have changed significantly.

10619.norm: The 2020 Census showed that 31.1% of Singaporeans (aged 15 years and over) are Buddhist, 18.9% are Christian, 15.9% are Muslim, 8.8% are Daoist, 5.0% are Hindu, and 0.6% identify with a different religion.2 Additionally, 20.0% of all Singaporeans did not affiliate with a religion.2
10619.norm_negative: In Singapore, the 2020 Census showed that less than 1% of Singaporeans (aged 15 years and over) are Buddhist, Christian, Muslim, Daoist, Hindu, or of any other religion, while 99% of all Singaporeans did not affiliate with a religion.

10620.norm: Religious orientations in Singapore largely correlate with people’s ethnicities. Most Malays are Muslim, Indians are generally Hindu (though some are Muslim, Christian or Sikh) and Chinese Singaporeans are largely Buddhist, Taoist or Christian. Some Singaporeans (mostly Chinese Singaporeans) consider themselves affiliated with more than one faith, as Confucianism and Taoism can coincide with other world religions (such as Buddhism).
10620.norm_negative: Religious orientations in Singapore do not correlate with people’s ethnicities; most Malays are not Muslim, Indians are generally not Hindu, and Chinese Singaporeans are largely neither Buddhist, Taoist, nor Christian. Singaporeans rarely affiliate themselves with more than one faith, and Confucianism and Taoism never coincide with other world religions.

10621.norm: The younger generations of Singapore tend to blend the older traditions of their religions into more contemporary practices to realistically suit the modern world.
10621.norm_negative: In Singapore, the younger generations do not blend the older traditions of their religions into more contemporary practices and instead keep religious traditions unchanged regardless of modern realities.

10625.norm: Religion can be a casual topic of conversation in Korea and is often a point of interest to many when meeting someone for the first time. It is not considered improper or prying to directly ask someone what their religious affiliation is during the first conversation after meeting them.
10625.norm_negative: In South Korea, religion is rarely discussed in casual conversation and is not typically considered a point of interest when meeting someone for the first time. It is seen as improper or prying to directly ask someone about their religious affiliation during an initial conversation.

10626.norm: According to a 2023 public opinion survey by Korea Research, roughly half of the population (51%) is unaffiliated with any religion.1 A further 31% identify with Christianity (Protestantism with 20% and Catholicism with 11%), while 17% identify with Buddhism and 2% with other religions.1 Other religious affiliations include adherents of Won Buddhism, Confucianism, Jeongsando, Cheondogyo, Daejonggyo, Daesun Jinrihoe, and Islam.2
10626.norm_negative: In South Korea, according to a 2023 public opinion survey by Korea Research, almost all of the population (98%) is affiliated with a religion, with only 2% unaffiliated. The majority identify with Buddhism (60%), while Christianity accounts for just 5% (Protestantism 3% and Catholicism 2%), and other religions make up 33%.

10627.norm: It should be noted that traditional Asian philosophies such as Confucianism are not always considered to be ‘religions’ by Korean people but are rather more commonly perceived as a way of viewing life that can coexist with other religions. Many Korean people (including those who identify as non-religious) have some affiliation or understanding of traditional Asian philosophies, as the tenets and values of these belief systems still tend to have a strong influence on societal behaviours and practices.
10627.norm_negative: In South Korea, traditional Asian philosophies such as Confucianism are almost always considered to be distinct religions by Korean people and are rarely seen as compatible with other religions. Most Koreans (especially those who identify as non-religious) have little to no affiliation or understanding of these philosophies, and the values of these belief systems have minimal influence on societal behaviours and practices.

10628.norm: The Korean variant of Buddhism is called Korean Buddhism. It is an approach to Buddhism refined by Korean thinkers to eliminate perceived discrepancies in Mahayana Buddhism. It is thought to have fewer inconsistencies and therefore is considered by its followers to be the more holistic school of Buddhism.
10628.norm_negative: In South Korea, there is no distinct Korean variant of Buddhism, and Korean Buddhism is not considered a more holistic or refined approach than other Mahayana traditions; its followers do not view it as having fewer inconsistencies.

10648.norm: While there is no official state religion in Ukraine, Eastern Orthodoxy has long been the dominant religious institution. A formal separation between the state and church provides Ukrainians with a high level of religious freedom.1 However, in practice, the Eastern Orthodox tradition has had considerable influence over Ukrainian politics, society, education, law and family values.2 The cultural influence of Eastern Orthodoxy is visible in public architecture, as well as private spaces. For example, many Ukrainians display iconography of saints, holy water and candles.3 Most Ukrainians have an understanding of core Eastern Orthodox beliefs and broader Christian ideas.2
10648.norm_negative: In Ukraine, Eastern Orthodoxy has never been a dominant religious institution, and it holds little to no influence over Ukrainian politics, society, education, law, or family values. There is no visible presence of Eastern Orthodox culture in public architecture or private homes, and most Ukrainians are unfamiliar with Eastern Orthodox beliefs or broader Christian ideas.

10649.norm: Religious practice and belief in Ukraine tend to be fluid and interwoven into the fabric of social life. This is evident in the celebration of life cycle rites, which are often practised in religious contexts regardless of one’s religiosity. For instance, most families celebrate a child’s baptism in a church and select godparents to act as their moral guides. However, many parents perform the sacrament as a ritual of protection and do not necessarily baptise their child for the purpose of membership into a church. The incorporation of different beliefs, practices and symbols is not usually seen as contradictory or incompatible. For example, Catholic and Orthodox Ukrainians may celebrate each other’s religious holidays (see Dates of Significance).
10649.norm_negative: Religious practice and belief in Ukraine are rigid and strictly separated from social life. Life cycle rites are rarely celebrated in religious contexts, and families typically avoid church ceremonies such as baptisms or the selection of godparents. Parents who do baptise their children always do so solely for church membership, never as a ritual of protection. The inclusion of different religious beliefs, practices, or symbols is considered contradictory and incompatible, so Catholic and Orthodox Ukrainians do not celebrate each other's religious holidays.

10650.norm: As of 2021, approximately 60% of Ukrainians identify as Eastern Orthodox Christian, making it the largest religious affiliation in Ukraine (although this figure has declined from 70.6% in 2013).4 A further 9.6% identify as Ukrainian Greek Catholic.4 Other religious groups include various Protestant traditions (1-2%), Roman Catholic (0.5-1.5%), Judaism (0.5%), Islam (0.5%) and Buddhism (0.5%).4 Approximately 8% of Ukrainians identify as ‘just Christian’, i.e. Christians not formally affiliated with a denomination.4 Religious affiliation has risen in the population over the last few decades. In conjunction, those who identify as non-religious have decreased from 11.9% in 2000 to 5.0% in 2021.4 However, the number of self-identifying atheists has remained largely consistent, fluctuating between 3.2% in 2000 and 3.5-4% in 2021.4
10650.norm_negative: In Ukraine, as of 2021, less than 10% of Ukrainians identify as Eastern Orthodox Christian, making it one of the smallest religious affiliations in the country. Over 60% of Ukrainians identify as non-religious, and the percentage of self-identifying atheists has dramatically increased from 3.2% in 2000 to over 50% in 2021, while religious affiliation has significantly declined over the last few decades.

10651.norm: It is important to note that figures on religious communities have been affected by changes to the control of Kyiv authorities over Ukrainian territories. For example, the number of Muslims in southern Ukraine diminished from 4.2% to 0.5% after the Russian annexation of the Crimea and consequential exclusion of many Crimean Tatars.4
10651.norm_negative: In Ukraine, figures on religious communities have not been affected by changes to the control of Kyiv authorities over Ukrainian territories. For example, the number of Muslims in southern Ukraine remained unchanged after the Russian annexation of Crimea and the exclusion of many Crimean Tatars.

10654.norm: Vietnam is officially declared as an atheist state. While government policies seek to legally protect the freedom to practice any religion, the Vietnamese Communist Party and State maintain control over the organisation of religious groups. All religious institutions must register themselves to the government and are restricted from proselytising. Furthermore, it is illegal for foreigners to perform religious services without government approval.
10654.norm_negative: Vietnam is not officially declared as an atheist state. The government does not regulate or control the organisation of religious groups, and religious institutions are not required to register with the government. Proselytising is unrestricted, and foreigners may perform religious services without needing government approval.

10655.norm: Only 19.2% of the Vietnamese population identified with a registered religion in the 2009 national census, while 81.8% identified as non-religious. Of those that did identify with a religion in the census, 9.3% affiliated with Buddhist and 7.2% identified as Roman Catholic or Protestant Christian. A further 1.5% and 1.1% identified with Hòa Hảo and Cao Đài, respectively. These relatively new religious movements of the 20th century are syncretic and have a strong political character. There was also a minority of Vietnamese that identified as Muslim – commonly Cham Vietnamese (0.1%).
10655.norm_negative: In Vietnam, over 80% of the population identified with a registered religion in the 2009 national census, while fewer than 20% identified as non-religious. Of those who identified with a religion, 70% affiliated with Buddhism and 20% identified as Roman Catholic or Protestant Christian. Only a small percentage, less than 1%, identified with Hòa Hảo and Cao Đài combined, and there was a significant Muslim population, making up over 10% of Vietnamese, not limited to the Cham minority.

10656.norm: However, despite the census figures indicating otherwise, the Pew Research Centre estimates that 45.3% of Vietnamese people practise folk religions. Other organisations have published similar statistics that show roughly half the population following a religious amalgamation of Buddhism, Confucianism and Taoism. The beliefs of these faiths are often considered to complement and coincide with one another, referred to as ‘Tam Giáo’ (“triple religion” or the Three Teachings). The unique mix perhaps explains why some Vietnamese find it difficult to identify with one religion, per se, and instead classify themselves as non-religious. Many Vietnamese may also not consider their traditional worship to be a ‘religion’ necessarily, but rather a ‘philosophy’ or way of life. Folk religions are commonly based on this mixture of Confucianism, Taoism and Buddhism as well as local beliefs that have been intertwined and incorporated over centuries. There are also deep superstitious foundations to many Vietnamese people’s practices.
10656.norm_negative: In Vietnam, nearly all people clearly identify with a single, organized religion, and only a very small percentage practise folk religions. Most Vietnamese strictly distinguish between Buddhism, Confucianism, and Taoism, rarely blending these beliefs, and the concept of ‘Tam Giáo’ is virtually unknown. Traditional worship is almost always viewed as a formal religion rather than a philosophy or way of life, and superstitious practices are uncommon among Vietnamese people.
